Joint replacement demand is soft: Stryker's hip sales fell 1.0% and knees rose 1.1%, and Stryker cut its outlook, while Tenet's hospital surgeries fell 1.1%.
CMS proposed a 2.4% outpatient payment update for 2027 and a further phase-out of the inpatient-only list; the final rule is due later this year.
Abbott, Intuitive Surgical, Boston Scientific, Medtronic, Stryker, Edwards Lifesciences

Revenue splits into capital equipment, single-use or implanted products, and service. At Intuitive Surgical in Q3 2026, instruments and accessories were 59.0% of $3,048.7M revenue, systems 25.2% and service 15.8%. Orthopaedic and cardiac makers mostly sell implants and disposables, and Abbott adds diabetes sensors in its devices total of $5,826M for the quarter.

Customers are hospitals, surgery centres and, for wearables, patients through insurers. Government payers shape demand: CMS proposes a 2.4% 2027 outpatient payment update. Fortune Business Insights puts hospitals and ambulatory surgery centres at 48.97% of its device market in 2026.

Principal costs are manufacturing, sales forces, clinical trials and R&D, plus tariffs and litigation. Intuitive guides non-GAAP gross margin of 68.7% to 69.3% for 2026 including a tariff cost of 0.9% of revenue, and non-GAAP operating expense growth of 11% to 13%. Abbott took about $670M of specified charges for infant formula claims in Q3.

Pricing power rests on clinical evidence, surgeon training and switching costs. Edwards earned an adjusted gross margin of 78.7% and an adjusted operating margin of 30.3% in Q3, and Intuitive a non-GAAP gross margin of 69.9%. We think weaker pricing power shows in Stryker's reported gross margin of 65.2% in more commoditised implants.

Major assets are plants, intangible assets and goodwill from acquisitions, plus cash. At 30 Sep 2026 Intuitive had $6.80B of cash and investments, Edwards about $3.1B of cash and about $600M of debt, and Stryker $3.3B of cash against $14.2B of long-term debt. Impairments of $293M at Stryker and $220.2M at Edwards followed past deals.

The industry is moderately capital-intensive: it needs plants and clinical trials but little heavy industry. Damodaran's January 2026 table for US Healthcare Products shows net capex of 4.53% of sales and capex at 79.54% of depreciation. Intuitive also funds leasing of systems, with lease revenue of about $300M in Q3.

One research firm, Fortune Business Insights, values the global medical device market at $572.31B in 2025 and $604.99B in 2026, growing 6.90% a year to 2034. Definitions vary widely by publisher and this includes diagnostics, so we treat it as an order of magnitude, not an exact market for this sub-industry.

Main segments are cardiovascular, orthopaedics, surgery and robotics, diabetes care, neuromodulation and monitoring. In Abbott's Q3, electrophysiology grew 15.5%, rhythm management 10.0%, diabetes care 6.7% and vascular 5.7%. At Boston Scientific, Cardiovascular was $3.406B and MedSurg $1.733B.

Makers sit between component suppliers and hospitals. Intuitive cites manufacturing in Mexico and Germany and component imports from China. The buyers are hospitals, surgery centres and patients, and reimbursement decides what they can pay: Tenet reported 18% lower exchange admissions in Q3.

The industry has shifted from simple implants to platforms: robots, catheter-based valves and sensors worn on the body. Dealmaking is active: PwC counted $36.5B of medtech acquisitions in the first half of 2026, including Boston Scientific's $14.5B Penumbra deal and Danaher's $9.9B Masimo deal.

North America is the largest region, holding 38.1% of the market in 2025 according to Fortune Business Insights. Boston Scientific's Q3 growth was 0.5% in the US and 6.1% in EMEA on an operational basis.

A few diversified giants and many specialists. This brief covers Abbott, Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Stryker, Edwards and Intuitive; Fortune Business Insights also names Johnson & Johnson, GE HealthCare, Philips, Siemens Healthineers, BD and Fresenius. The 49 holdings of IHI show how many US-listed names there are.

Leadership is by niche rather than overall share. Intuitive has an installed base of 12,094 da Vinci systems, Edwards holds a TAVR franchise of $1,241.6M a quarter, and Boston Scientific and Abbott compete in ablation and heart implants. We did not find published market shares for these niches.

The industry is consolidated at the top and fragmented below. Large firms keep buying: Medtronic bought CathWorks for $585M, Stryker bought Amplitude Vascular for $435M upfront, and Boston Scientific agreed to buy Penumbra for $14.5B.

Barriers to entry are high for implants and robots. CDRH authorised 151 novel devices in fiscal 2026, so approval is possible, but clinical evidence, surgeon training and hospital contracts take years. Intuitive's release lists domestic competitors in China as a risk.

Scale matters through sales forces and trial funding. Stryker's adjusted operating margin was 26.2%, Edwards' 30.3% and Intuitive's roughly 41.6% on our calculation from its non-GAAP figures. These margins do not look like a commodity business.
Products are differentiated by clinical data, not price. Edwards' TMTT line grew 44.3% as a new category, while hips at Stryker fell 1.0% in a more mature segment.

Hospitals hold bargaining power through group purchasing and Medicare rates, but surgeons choose products and prefer familiar systems, which lowers customer power in robots and implants. Suppliers have moderate power: Intuitive warns that suppliers may pass on tariff costs.

Revenue growth follows procedure volumes, new products and pricing. Intuitive's revenue rose 22% while procedures grew about 14%; our read is that system placements, up to 546 from 427, and a richer mix explain the gap. Edwards guided TAVR growth of 9.0% to 9.5%.

Operating margins depend on gross margin, operating leverage and one-off charges. Stryker's adjusted operating margin rose 60 basis points to 26.2% while reported margin was 15.9% after a $293M impairment. Damodaran's January 2026 data show a 15.34% operating margin for the broad Healthcare Products group.

Key cost variables are materials, labour, tariffs, freight and currency. Intuitive guides to a tariff cost of 0.9% of revenue in 2026. Edwards names currency and hedging as its main margin headwind. Boston Scientific recorded an $83M benefit from recovering IEEPA tariffs over nine months.

Interest rates matter through hospital capital budgets, deal financing and equity multiples. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026, with two members wanting an increase. Edwards has about $600M of debt and Stryker $14.2B, so balance sheets differ greatly.

Inflation, unemployment and GDP act mainly through insurance coverage and elective surgery. Tenet said exchange admissions fell 18% and its hospital surgeries fell 1.1%. The Fed says activity is expanding at a strong pace and inflation remains elevated. Commodity exposure is small compared with labour and components.

The industry is a mix. Cardiac and diabetes lines are secular growers, as Abbott's electrophysiology rose 15.5%. Orthopaedics and other elective lines are more cyclical, with Stryker's hip sales down 1.0%. Devices tied to life-threatening disease, such as valves, behave more defensively.

Growth is solid but uneven. Q3 2026 revenue growth was 22% at Intuitive, 10.5% at Edwards, 7.7% at Stryker and 1.5% at Boston Scientific. Adjusted EPS rose 10.3% at Stryker and 19% at Edwards, but Boston Scientific's adjusted EPS slipped to $0.73 from $0.75.

Margins are high versus most industries. Damodaran's January 2026 table for 204 US Healthcare Products companies shows a gross margin of 54.00%, an operating margin of 15.34% and a net margin of 9.61%. Leaders run above that: Edwards had a 78.7% adjusted gross margin and Intuitive 69.9%.

Damodaran's January 2026 return on equity for Healthcare Products is 11.26% unadjusted and 9.37% adjusted for R&D. We did not obtain a sourced ROIC for this sub-industry. Goodwill from deals likely holds reported returns below the underlying business, which is our judgment.

Leverage ranges from light to heavy. Edwards has about $3.1B of cash and about $600M of debt. Stryker has $14.2B of long-term debt. Boston Scientific's Q3 interest expense was $100M against $87M a year earlier, and its $14.5B Penumbra deal adds to financing needs.

Free cash flow is generally strong but we found few reported figures. Intuitive's cash and investments fell $1.83B in Q3 mainly from buybacks and capital spending, including $2.94B of repurchases. Stryker bought back $1.0B of stock in Q3 and its board added $3.0B in October. Edwards and Boston Scientific did not report free cash flow in the releases we read.

Capital spending is modest. Damodaran's table shows net capex of 4.53% of sales for US Healthcare Products and capex at 79.54% of depreciation, suggesting plants are being maintained rather than rapidly expanded. R&D and acquisitions matter more than plant spending.

Multiples are high. Damodaran's January 2026 data show EV/EBITDA of 19.78 for firms with positive EBITDA and a forward P/E of 42.33 for US Healthcare Products. These cover all 204 firms, many smaller and loss-making, so they are not directly comparable with the large-cap leaders.

Regulation and legislation: Commerce's Section 232 probe of medical device imports remains open, CMS proposes a 2.4% outpatient update and removal of 638 more procedures from the inpatient-only list, and CDRH has lost about 22% of its staff, including 30% of reviewers. FDA user-fee talks (MDUFA VI) are headed to Congress by January 2027.

Technology and AI: Boston Scientific announced a collaboration with Heartflow on AI-powered CT planning for heart procedures, and robotics keeps raising the bar, with Intuitive's da Vinci 5 placements at 315 of 546 systems in Q3. The risk is that software and AI reduce hardware differentiation, in our view.

Demographics are a tailwind: older populations need more heart, joint and diabetes care. Intuitive's procedure growth of about 14% and Abbott's CGM growth of 7.7% comparable fit that. We do not have a cited figure for ageing's contribution specifically.

Changing behaviour includes the move of joint surgery to surgery centres and deferral of elective care. Tenet's USPI joint replacements rose 12.8% while its hospital surgeries fell 1.1%, and Stryker's hips and knees were flat to down. Coverage losses on ACA exchanges add pressure.

New competitors and business models: large firms are buying rivals in hot niches, with intravascular lithotripsy a crowded example, and Boston Scientific and Abbott have entered it. Medtronic's Hugo challenges Intuitive in robotics, though we found no Hugo sales figure in the sources we read.

Geopolitics and supply chains: Intuitive makes products in Mexico and Germany and imports components from China, and warns that additional tariffs could have a material impact. Intuitive also names domestic competitors in China as a risk. Boston Scientific's August cyber incident shows operational fragility.

Substitutes include drugs and non-device therapies. We found no sourced figure for substitution this quarter, but we think the biggest watch item is whether new obesity and diabetes medicines change demand for some cardiac and orthopaedic procedures. That is our judgment, not a cited fact.
Cardiac ablation and structural heart are growing fast, with Medtronic's ablation line up 88% and Abbott's electrophysiology up 15.5%.
Robotic surgery keeps expanding as installed base rises 12% to 12,094 systems and procedures grow about 14%.
Ageing populations and new categories such as mitral and tricuspid repair, up 44.3% at Edwards, widen the market.
Consolidation lets leaders buy growth in faster niches, as $36.5B of first-half deals show.
Tariffs could widen beyond the current level, with Section 232 still open and Intuitive guiding to a 0.9% revenue cost.
Elective procedures remain weak as exchange coverage falls, hitting orthopaedics and hospital volumes.
Competition from domestic makers in China and possible price pressure could weigh on international growth.
FDA staffing losses and payment rule changes could slow approvals or adoption.

We think the next three to five years favour companies in cardiac rhythm, structural heart and robotics, where procedure growth is double-digit and the evidence moat is deep. Orthopaedics and other elective lines look more exposed to coverage, site-of-care shifts and price pressure. Margins should hold at the leaders, though tariffs, which Intuitive puts at 0.9% of 2026 revenue, take a bite out of gross margin. Execution risk is concentrated in large deals and in single events such as Boston Scientific's incident, which pushed its Q4 guidance below zero growth. Policy risk is real but still unresolved.

Medical devices sit in a cycle driven less by the economy than by hospital volumes and insurance coverage. FactSet's 6 Nov 2026 report shows the S&P 500 blended Q3 earnings growth at 31.4%, while the Health Care sector as a whole is growing 9.3% and its revenue 6.3%. That sector includes drug makers, insurers and services, so it describes the group only loosely.

Interest rates are a secondary input. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10 to 2 vote, with both dissenters preferring an increase, and said activity is expanding at a strong pace while inflation remains elevated. Higher rates raise financing costs for hospitals and deal-making firms, though large device makers carry modest debt: Edwards had about $600M and Stryker $14.2B of long-term debt.

Coverage and labour matter more. Tenet said exchange admissions and revenues fell 18% in Q3 and its hospital surgeries fell 1.1%. Currency also moves reported results: Edwards' sales rose 10.5% reported and 11.2% in constant currency. Our read is that the cycle is supportive for emergency and cardiac care and less so for elective orthopaedics.

Demand rests on ageing populations, chronic disease and technology that makes less invasive treatment possible. Fortune Business Insights estimates the global device market at $572.31B in 2025 and $604.99B in 2026, growing 6.90% a year to 2034, with North America at 38.1%. Publishers differ, and this estimate covers diagnostics and other products beyond this sub-industry.

Company data show demand is strongest in procedure-led categories. Intuitive's da Vinci procedures grew about 14% in Q3 and its installed base reached 12,094 systems, up 12%. Abbott's electrophysiology grew 15.5% and rhythm management 10.0%. Edwards expects 2026 TAVR growth of 9.0% to 9.5% and mitral and tricuspid sales of $780M to $790M.

Elasticity is higher in elective care. Stryker's knee sales rose 1.1% and hips fell 1.0% in Q3, and the company cut its 2026 organic growth guidance to 6.5% to 7.0%. Tenet's ambulatory surgeries fell 1.5% while its joint replacements at surgery centres rose 12.8%. We read this as a shift of venue and a patient-affordability squeeze, not an end of demand. Long-term prospects remain good because of demographics.

Porter's five forces point to an attractive but uneven industry. Threat of new entrants is low in implants and robots because approval, clinical evidence and surgeon training are slow; CDRH authorised 151 novel devices in fiscal 2026, so entry happens but not quickly. Substitutes, including drugs and alternative treatments, are a watch item.

Buyer power rests with hospitals and Medicare, whose rates set budgets: CMS proposes a 2.4% update for 2027. Supplier power is moderate, and Intuitive warns that suppliers may pass on tariff and inflation costs. Rivalry is intense in contested categories such as intravascular lithotripsy and PFA, where Boston Scientific, Abbott and Medtronic compete.

Concentration is high at the top. Medtronic, Stryker, Abbott, Boston Scientific and Edwards each sell billions of dollars a quarter; Boston Scientific reported $5.138B in Q3 and Abbott's devices $5,826M. We did not find sourced market shares. Moats come from installed bases, evidence and switching costs: Intuitive's 12,094 systems and Edwards' 78.7% adjusted gross margin are examples. Pricing power is strong in new categories and weaker in hips and knees.

Regulation is the dominant outside force. The FDA's CDRH authorised 151 novel devices in fiscal 2026 but has lost about 22% of its staff over 18 months, including 30% of reviewers, and says it remains on track for nearly all review goals. A new user-fee agreement (MDUFA VI) for fiscal 2028 to 2032 is headed to Congress, targeted for January 2027.

Reimbursement policy is proposed to tighten. CMS released the 2027 hospital outpatient rule on 2 Jul 2026, proposing a 2.4% payment update, removal of 638 more procedures from the inpatient-only list over a three-year phase-out, and site-neutral payments for some imaging; comments closed on 31 Aug 2026. Moving procedures outpatient favours surgery centres.

Trade policy is a live political risk. Commerce opened its Section 232 investigation of medical devices on 2 Sep 2025; the 270-day report period appears to have passed near the end of May 2026, but as of 28 Oct 2026 no report or proclamation had been published. Intuitive includes a tariff cost of 0.9% of revenue in its guidance and warns more tariffs could have a material impact.

Technology cuts both ways: AI-guided planning, robotics and cyber exposure. Boston Scientific disclosed a cybersecurity incident on 26 Aug 2026 and later guided Q4 sales lower. Intuitive names domestic competition in China as a risk factor.

Margins are structurally high. Q3 2026 non-GAAP gross margin was 69.9% at Intuitive, adjusted gross margin 78.7% at Edwards and adjusted 65.4% at Stryker. Adjusted operating margins were 30.3% at Edwards and 26.2% at Stryker; on our calculation from the releases, about 41.6% at Intuitive and 26.5% at Boston Scientific.

Operating leverage is visible at the leaders: Intuitive's non-GAAP operating margin rose from about 39.0% to about 41.6% as revenue rose 22%, and Edwards' adjusted operating margin widened from 27.5% to 30.3%. It cuts the other way when volume stalls, as Boston Scientific's adjusted EPS slipped to $0.73 from $0.75 on 1.5% growth.

Damodaran's January 2026 US Healthcare Products data show a 54.00% gross margin, 15.34% operating margin and 11.26% return on equity. The gap between this and the leaders is explained by many smaller, loss-making firms in his group. Capital intensity is low to moderate, at net capex of 4.53% of sales.

Free cash flow is strong but under-reported in the releases we read. Intuitive spent $2.94B on buybacks in Q3, Stryker $1.0B and Edwards about $700M year to date. We did not obtain sourced ROIC figures; reported returns are likely depressed by acquisition goodwill, which is our judgment.

Revisions are mixed. Edwards raised its 2026 sales growth guidance to about 11.5% from 10% to 11% and its adjusted EPS range to $2.97 to $3.05. Intuitive narrowed procedure growth to 14% to 15% and expects results near the midpoint. Medtronic raised fiscal 2027 organic growth guidance to 7.25% to 7.75% and adjusted EPS to $5.94 to $6.00 on 1 Sep 2026.

Others cut. Boston Scientific now expects about 3.75% organic growth in 2026, with Q4 sales down 1% to 3% and adjusted EPS of $3.16 to $3.18 for the year. Stryker lowered organic growth guidance to 6.5% to 7.0% and adjusted EPS to $14.80 to $14.90. Abbott guided about 6.0% comparable sales growth and tightened adjusted EPS to $5.50 to $5.55.

Sector context: FactSet shows the Health Care sector's Q3 blended earnings growth at 9.3% and revenue growth at 6.3%, against 31.4% earnings growth for the S&P 500. These are sector figures that include drugs and insurers. We found no consensus EPS growth for this sub-industry and do not estimate one.

Where we differ: we would not read Medtronic's 13.7% growth as a run rate, since the extra week in a 53-week year added about $570M, and Medtronic's next update on 24 Nov 2026 will show the cleaner base. We also see Boston Scientific's weakness as largely event-driven, but the Q4 guide shows the effect runs beyond one quarter.

The best sub-industry gauge we found is the iShares U.S. Medical Devices ETF, which is 99.84% Health Care Equipment and traded on a P/E of 33.58 on 12 Nov 2026. We could not obtain a forward multiple for the group, nor its own ten-year average. For context, FactSet shows the S&P 500 at 17.7 times forward earnings, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1.

On Damodaran's January 2026 data, US Healthcare Products traded at EV/EBITDA of 19.78 for firms with positive EBITDA and a forward P/E of 42.33. These cover 204 firms and many are small or unprofitable, so they overstate what large profitable names trade on. We read the group as priced at a premium to the market, which is a judgment from these two sources, not a ranking of any stock.

Growth implied by a premium multiple is high-single-digit to low-double-digit revenue and expanding margins. The leaders are delivering that in some lines, such as Intuitive's 22% revenue growth and Edwards' guidance of about 11.5%, but not all: Boston Scientific's 1.5% growth and Stryker's cut show how a premium can compress. We did not obtain free cash flow yields for the group and do not compute them.

The IHI ETF had net assets of $4.03B and 49 holdings on 12 Nov 2026, and its NAV return year to date was -7.20%, with a NAV of $57.46 inside a 52-week range of $47.53 to $64.50. By the sector-wide measure, devices have lagged the broader market, which FactSet shows is still at healthy earnings growth. We found no fund-flow figure for the ETF.

Company buybacks are a clear source of demand. Intuitive repurchased 7.8M shares for $2.94B in Q3, Stryker $1.0B with a further $3.0B authorisation added in October, and Edwards about $700M year to date with about $1.3B left. Boston Scientific's weighted diluted share count fell to 1,452.0M from 1,495.5M a year earlier.

Momentum is weak and dispersed: the ETF's one-day move on 12 Nov 2026 was -1.24%. Earnings reactions in the quarter appear to have been sharp for single names, though we did not open price data to confirm. We obtained no short interest, institutional positioning or breadth data for the group and make no claim about them.

Large biotech reported a strong third quarter. Amgen grew revenue 8% and raised its 2026 outlook, Gilead's product sales rose 13%, Vertex raised its revenue guidance and Regeneron's revenue rose 36%. Moderna posted a $162M profit after deep cost cuts. The Health Care sector's blended Q3 earnings growth is 9.3% against 31.4% for the S&P 500. Biotech shares have rallied, with the iShares biotech ETF up 26.64% this year and XBI up 28.00% to 31 Oct. Drug tariffs and Medicare price setting remain the main policy risks.

Biotechnology companies discover and sell medicines made from living systems or built on biology: antibodies, proteins, vaccines, gene and cell therapies and small molecules guided by genetics. Customers are patients, reached through insurers, Medicare and hospitals, with wholesalers and specialty pharmacies in between. A few large firms such as Amgen, Gilead, Vertex and Regeneron earn billions in profit. Hundreds of small firms have no sales and live on trial results and outside funding. GICS puts big diversified drug makers and generics in Pharmaceuticals, and lab tools and contract research in Life Sciences Tools and Services.

Monoclonal antibodies: Lab-made immune proteins that block a specific target. They treat cancer, inflammation, eye disease and high cholesterol, and are usually given by injection or infusion. e.g. Regeneron Dupixent (with Sanofi) and Eylea HD, Amgen Repatha and Tezspire

Antivirals and HIV medicines: Daily pills and long-acting injections that keep a virus under control for life. Patients stay on treatment for years, so revenue is steady. e.g. Gilead Biktarvy, Descovy and Yeztugo
Rare and genetic disease drugs: Treatments for small patient groups with a known genetic cause, sold at high prices per patient. e.g. Vertex cystic fibrosis medicines and Casgevy

mRNA medicines and vaccines: Medicines that deliver genetic instructions so the body makes its own protein. First proven in COVID-19 vaccines, now tested in flu, cancer and rare disease. e.g. Moderna Spikevax and mRESVIA, intismeran melanoma vaccine
Oncology biologics and antibody drug conjugates: Antibodies that engage immune cells or carry a toxic payload straight to tumour cells. e.g. Amgen Imdelltra, Gilead Trodelvy, Regeneron Libtayo
Biosimilars: Near copies of biologic drugs whose patents have ended. They are cheaper and take sales from the original product. e.g. Amgen biosimilar portfolio, rivals to Prolia and Eylea
Trial and approval results: A positive Phase 3 or an FDA approval can lift a company's value in a day, and a failure can remove it. Small, single-asset firms swing most.
Drug pricing policy: Medicare negotiation, MFN deals and insurer rebates set net price per patient. Lower net prices cut revenue without losing a single patient.
Patent expiry and biosimilars: When protection ends, sales of the original fall as cheaper versions arrive, so firms must replace lost revenue with new drugs or acquisitions.
Interest rates and funding: Unprofitable firms rely on equity and debt markets. Lower rates and stronger share prices make financing cheaper and open the market to new listings.
Mergers and acquisitions: Large drug makers buy biotechs to fill pipelines. Takeover premiums lift targets, and the buyers' earnings carry deal charges.
Launch uptake: Sales of a new drug build over months. Faster uptake lifts revenue and operating leverage, because selling costs do not rise in step.
Trade policy and manufacturing location: Tariffs on imported medicines depend on where a product is made and whether a firm has agreements. They raise costs or force new US plants.
Pipeline: The set of drug candidates a company is developing. Value rests largely on the chance each candidate reaches the market.

Phase 1, 2, 3 trials: Three stages of human testing. Phase 1 checks safety, Phase 2 checks early effectiveness, Phase 3 proves benefit in large groups before approval. Most candidates fail along the way.
PDUFA date: The deadline by which the FDA aims to decide on an application. Share prices of small firms can move sharply around it.
BLA / NDA: Biologics License Application for biologic drugs and New Drug Application for chemical ones: the formal requests to the FDA for permission to sell.
Patent cliff (loss of exclusivity): The point when a patent or market exclusivity ends and cheaper copies arrive. Sales of the original often fall fast.
Biosimilar: A highly similar, lower-priced version of an off-patent biologic. It erodes sales of the original, as Prolia's decline shows.
Collaboration revenue: Income from a partner that sells or co-develops a drug. Regeneron books a share of Dupixent through Sanofi this way.
Milestone and royalty: Payments a licensee makes when a trial or approval goal is hit, and a percentage of future sales.
Non-GAAP earnings: Earnings adjusted for items management calls one-off, such as acquired research costs. They can differ a great deal from reported earnings.
Acquired IPR&D: The cost of buying unfinished research in a deal. It is often expensed at once, so acquirers can report a large loss that quarter.
Orphan drug: A medicine for a rare disease. It gets extra market exclusivity and tax credits, and now has a wider carve-out from Medicare price negotiation.
Most favoured nation (MFN) pricing: A US policy aim of tying US prices to the lowest paid in comparable rich countries. Firms that agree can obtain tariff relief.
Cash runway: How long a loss-making company can fund itself with the cash it holds. A short runway forces a share sale or a deal.
Cell and gene therapy: Treatments that modify a patient's cells or genes, often one-time and very costly to make and deliver.
Vertex's FDA decision date for povetacicept in IgA nephropathy is 30 Nov 2026, the next test of its pipeline beyond cystic fibrosis.
Regeneron expects an FDA decision on cemdisiran for generalized myasthenia gravis next month, and plans a Phase 3 MASH study to start in Q4 2026.

Section 232 tariffs on patented drugs began on 31 Jul and 29 Sep 2026, with a 100% default rate and 0% for firms with pricing and onshoring deals, so smaller biotechs without deals face the most uncertainty.
Medicare's third negotiation round (prices effective 2028) is the first to include Part B drugs and covers Gilead's Biktarvy among 15 products.
Amgen's MariTide obesity drug is still in Phase 3, and the FDA has asked Amgen to withdraw Tavneos, which Amgen is contesting.
Amgen, Gilead Sciences, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, Regeneron, Moderna, Biogen

Revenue comes mostly from product sales of patented medicines, plus collaboration, royalty and milestone income. Amgen's Q3 2026 total revenue was $10.4B, of which product sales were $9.9B and other revenues $482M. Regeneron's Q3 revenue of $5.1B includes $2.7B of collaboration revenue from Sanofi, up 68%.

Customers are patients served through insurers, Medicare, hospitals and specialty pharmacies, so payers hold real influence. Amgen noted that Enbrel grew despite lower net pricing tied to Medicare Part D price setting. Vertex's Q3 revenue was $2.17B in the US and $1.27B outside it.

Principal costs are R&D, selling and manufacturing. At Amgen in Q3, non-GAAP R&D was 21.3% of product sales, SG&A 17.0% and cost of sales 19.3%. Regeneron's GAAP R&D was $1.795B, up 22%, and it guides to $6.05B to $6.15B of non-GAAP R&D for 2026.

Pricing power comes from patents, clinical benefit and the lack of close substitutes. Gilead's non-GAAP operating margin was 50.2% and Amgen's 47.3% of product sales. It erodes when biosimilars arrive: Amgen's Prolia sales fell 45% to $632M.

Major assets are intellectual property, cash and acquired research. Regeneron held about $18.9B of cash and marketable securities, Vertex $9.8B after paying about $9.0B net for Crinetics, and Amgen $13.2B of cash against $54.0B of debt. Moderna has about $3.0B of convertible notes.

The business is asset-light for most small firms and moderately capital-intensive for large ones that make their own biologics. Amgen guides to about $2.6B of capital spending in 2026 and Regeneron to $1.05B to $1.10B. Damodaran's data show net capex of -3.57% of sales for 496 US biotech firms.

Market size depends on the definition. Fortune Business Insights values the global biotechnology market, a broad measure that includes tools, research services and non-drug uses, at $1,376.1B in 2025 and $1,491.5B in 2026, with a 14.3% annual growth forecast to 2034. We treat it as an order of magnitude, since the GICS group is narrower.

Main segments are antibodies and other biologics, HIV and infectious disease, rare and genetic disease, oncology, vaccines and gene or cell therapy. Within Amgen's Q3 sales, Repatha was $1,085M, Evenity $751M, Tezspire $538M and Enbrel $611M. Gilead's HIV franchise was $6.2B of $8.3B.

Biotechs sit between research institutions, contract manufacturers and trial sites upstream, and payers, hospitals and pharmacies downstream. Large firms also license assets from smaller ones: Regeneron's expanded Sanofi deal brought $1.0B upfront and up to $7.0B of milestones.

The industry has moved from simple biologics to genetic medicines, obesity drugs and cell therapy, with deal-making central. IQVIA counts $130B of biopharma M&A value in the first half of 2026 across 42 transactions of $250M or more, nearly matching all of 2025. The FDA's list shows 48 novel drug approvals for 2026 as of 9 Nov.

North America dominates: Fortune puts it at 43.34% of the global biotech market in 2025. Amgen's US product sales were $7.26B of $9.88B in Q3, about 73% on our arithmetic. Vertex's Q3 revenue was $2.17B in the US and $1.27B abroad.
There are hundreds of listed companies. Damodaran's January 2026 dataset counts 496 US biotechnology firms, and IBB holds 243 stocks while XBI holds 165. Only a handful earn large profits.

Leaders by size include Amgen with $10.4B of Q3 revenue, Gilead with $8.3B of product sales, Regeneron with $5.1B, Vertex with $3.44B and Moderna with $1.3B. We did not find a published market share, because each competes in different disease areas.

The industry is fragmented at the bottom and concentrated by disease. Vertex's CF medicines and Gilead's HIV drugs hold leading positions in their niches. Consolidation continues: Gilead's year-to-date acquisition outflows were $11.3B, and AbbVie/Apogee ($10.9B) and GSK/Nuvalent ($10.6B) were among first-half deals above $10B.

Barriers to entry are high: years of trials, FDA approval, patents and manufacturing know-how. Amgen's Phase 3 programmes and Vertex's priority-review filing show the scale of work needed. New firms still enter, and XBI's modified equal weighting spreads exposure over many small names.

Economies of scale help in manufacturing, sales and trial funding. Amgen's non-GAAP SG&A fell 1% while revenue grew 8%, but Vertex's Q3 SG&A nearly doubled to $844M with the Crinetics deal, so scale gains can be offset by deals.
Products are differentiated by clinical data and patents until copies arrive. After that they commoditise quickly: Amgen's biosimilars grew to $258M from $151M a year ago while Prolia dropped 45%.

Payers and regulators hold bargaining power over price, while suppliers such as contract manufacturers hold little. Medicare's third negotiation round covers 15 drugs and is the first to include Part B products. Prescribers and patients have limited choice for a first-in-class drug, which shields pricing.

Revenue growth follows new launches, volume gains and pricing. Amgen's Q3 product sales grew 8% driven mainly by volume, and Vertex's Casgevy sales were $99M, nearly six times the $17M in Q3 2025. Gilead's Yeztugo reached $305M from $39M.

Operating margins depend on gross margin, R&D intensity and one-off deal charges. Amgen's non-GAAP operating margin of 47.3% and Gilead's 50.2% compare with Damodaran's 8.97% unadjusted pre-tax operating margin for the 496-firm group, which is dragged down by unprofitable firms.

Key cost variables are clinical trial costs, headcount, manufacturing and acquired research. Gilead recorded $12.4B of acquired IPR&D charges, which turned its guided non-GAAP 2026 EPS negative at $(1.20) to $(0.85). Regeneron lifted its 2026 R&D guidance.

Interest rates matter through financing and valuation. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10 to 2 vote, with both dissenters preferring a rise. Vertex borrowed a $4.5B term loan, and Moderna raised about $2.6B net through convertible notes. Rate-sensitive biotech valuations are our judgment, not a cited figure.

Inflation, unemployment and GDP matter little to demand because drugs are paid by insurance, but they do shape payer budgets and policy. The Fed describes inflation as elevated and growth as strong. Commodity prices have a small effect compared with R&D and patent timing.

The group is secular growth with defensive demand, but earnings are event-driven. Gilead's HIV sales rose 18% while Moderna's 2026 revenue growth guidance is a wide 15% to 25%, showing how much depends on a few products and seasons.

Large caps are growing, with wide dispersion. Q3 growth was 8% at Amgen, 13% at Gilead, 12% at Vertex, 36% at Regeneron and 29% at Moderna. FactSet shows Health Care sector earnings growth of 9.3% and revenue growth of 6.3%.

Margins are high at the leaders but low across the whole group. Damodaran's January 2026 table for 496 US biotech firms shows a 60.78% gross margin, 8.97% unadjusted pre-tax operating margin and a net margin of -5.00%. Amgen's non-GAAP cost of sales was 19.3% of product sales in Q3.

Returns are weak for the group because many firms are loss-making. Damodaran's January 2026 return on equity for biotech was -5.67% unadjusted and -2.21% adjusted for R&D, against 24.04% and 11.38% for pharmaceuticals. We did not find a sourced ROIC.

Leverage differs sharply. Amgen has $54.0B of debt, Vertex a new $4.5B term loan, Moderna about $3.0B of convertible notes, while Regeneron held about $18.9B of cash and securities. We did not source leverage for the small firms in the group.

Free cash flow is strong at large firms. Amgen's was $3.7B in Q3, down from $4.2B. Gilead produced $5.0B of operating cash flow in Q3 and $11.2B year to date. Large firms return cash: Gilead paid $1.0B of dividends in Q3.

Capital spending is light. Damodaran shows capex at 32.55% of depreciation and net capex of -3.57% of sales for US biotech, versus 80.48% and 1.12% for pharmaceuticals. Research spending and acquisitions are the real investments.

Multiples are mixed. Damodaran's January 2026 data show EV/EBITDA of 15.78 for the biotech firms with positive EBITDA and 51.49 across all firms, with a forward P/E of 63.76. These cover 496 firms, so are inflated by small earners and not typical of the large caps.

Regulation is the biggest risk. Section 232 tariffs set a 100% default rate on patented drugs with 0% for firms with MFN and onshoring agreements, and generics and biosimilars are exempt for now. Medicare negotiation reaches Part B drugs and 15 products for 2028.

Technology and AI offer faster discovery, but the risk is that new medicines in obesity, gene editing and cell therapy make older products obsolete. We did not find a sourced figure on AI's effect on biotech costs; Moderna's R&D fell 27% in Q3, mainly from lower clinical development costs.

Ageing populations raise demand for treatments in cancer, eye disease and inflammation. Regeneron's Eylea HD grew 62% to $699M in the US, which fits that trend. We have no sourced figure isolating the effect of demographics.

Patient and payer behaviour is shifting toward lower-cost biosimilars. Amgen's biosimilar sales grew to $258M while Prolia fell 45%. Medicare's rules exempt a drug from selection once a biosimilar launches.

New competitors include large drug makers buying into the same disease areas. IQVIA lists Gilead/Arcellx, Lilly/Centessa and Merck/Terns among first-half deals of $5B to $10B. We do not have a sourced figure on competition from Chinese-originated assets for 2026.

Geopolitics and supply chains: tariffs apply by country, at 15% for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland and 10% for the UK in the proclamation. Orphan-only drugs, cell and gene therapies and antibody drug conjugates have conditional exemptions.

Substitutes include other drug classes and non-drug care. Obesity medicines are a possible substitute for cardiovascular and diabetes drugs, and Amgen's MariTide is still in Phase 3. Whether obesity therapy lowers demand for other drugs is our open question, not a cited fact.
Strong launches and label expansions are lifting growth, such as Amgen's Repatha up 37% and Tezspire up 43%.
Large drug makers have patent expiries to replace and are buying pipelines, as $130B of first-half 2026 M&A shows.
New categories such as cancer vaccines may widen the market, with Moderna's intismeran cutting the risk of recurrence or death by 42% in a melanoma Phase 3.
Firms with pricing and onshoring deals can face 0% tariffs through 20 Jan 2029, which supports earnings visibility.
Medicare negotiation and US pricing policy could lower net prices, with 15 more drugs in the 2028 round.
Biosimilars and patent expiries remove sales quickly, as Prolia's 45% decline shows.
Tariff terms could change for firms without deals, and Commerce is due to report on whether generics should be covered.
Acquisition charges and heavy deal spending can depress reported earnings, as at Gilead and Vertex.

We think the next three to five years favour established firms with several growing products and large cash flows, such as Amgen, Gilead and Regeneron, which are growing revenue 8% to 36% with non-GAAP operating margins of 47% to 50% at Amgen and Gilead. Valuations differ: the equal-weighted XBI trades at 18.15 times FY1 earnings while IBB, weighted to large caps, trades at 29.33. Pricing policy is the main source of uncertainty, since Medicare negotiation is widening and tariffs depend on company deals. For small firms the outcome rests on trial results and access to funding. Dealmaking should stay active while patent expiries loom, but acquirers carry integration and charge risk.

Biotech earnings follow clinical and pricing events more than the business cycle, but funding conditions and policy still matter. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10 to 2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a quarter-point rise, and said inflation remains elevated while activity is strong. Higher rates raise the cost of capital for the many unprofitable firms in the group.

FactSet's 6 Nov 2026 report shows the S&P 500's blended Q3 earnings growth at 31.4%, while the Health Care sector is at 9.3%, up from 5.2% a week earlier after beats from Pfizer, Moderna, CVS and Amgen. That sector includes pharmaceuticals, insurers and services, so it describes biotech only loosely.

Large firms are using debt and convertibles to fund deals and cash needs. Vertex took a $4.5B term loan alongside its Crinetics purchase, and Moderna raised about $2.6B net from convertible notes. Our read is that the cycle is supportive for large profitable firms and for equity funding, as the sector's rally suggests, but biotech is more exposed to policy than to GDP.

Demand comes from ageing populations, chronic disease and new therapies. Fortune Business Insights values the broad global biotechnology market at $1,376.1B in 2025 and $1,491.5B in 2026, growing 14.3% a year to 2034, with North America at 43.34% in 2025. The estimate includes tools and services, so it overstates the narrower drug-maker group.

Company results show demand is strongest where new products have launched. Amgen's Repatha rose 37% to $1,085M and Tezspire 43% to $538M. Gilead's HIV sales rose 18% to $6.2B, with Descovy up 49% and Yeztugo reaching $305M. Regeneron's Libtayo grew 51% to $550M and Eylea HD 62% to $699M in the US.

Demand for medicines is inelastic in the short term because insurers pay, but products lose volume once copies arrive: Prolia fell 45%. Vaccines are more seasonal and policy-dependent. Moderna's 2026 revenue growth guidance of 15% to 25% reflects that uncertainty. The FDA's list of 48 novel approvals in 2026 as of 9 Nov shows a steady supply of new products.

Porter's five forces point to an attractive industry for winners and a hard one for most firms. The threat of new entrants is low for approved products because of trials, patents and FDA review, but high for ideas, with 496 US biotech firms in Damodaran's data. Rivalry is intense within each disease area, and the threat of substitutes comes from biosimilars and other drug classes.

Buyer power sits with payers and the government. Medicare's third negotiation round selects 15 drugs, including Gilead's Biktarvy, and applies to Part B drugs for the first time. Supplier power is moderate. Biosimilar entry exempts a drug from selection, which is why Prolia and Eylea were not on the list.

Concentration is high in each niche. Gilead's HIV franchise is $6.2B a quarter, Vertex expects $13.15B to $13.25B of 2026 revenue and Regeneron booked $2.7B of collaboration revenue from Sanofi in Q3. We did not find market share data. Moats rest on patents and evidence, and last only as long as exclusivity: Amgen's Enbrel grew 5% despite lower net pricing.

Policy is the dominant outside force. The Section 232 proclamation of 2 Apr 2026 sets a 100% default tariff on patented drugs and ingredients. Rates are 15% for the EU, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, 10% for the UK, 20% for firms with approved onshoring plans, and 0% to 20 Jan 2029 for firms with both MFN pricing and onshoring agreements. Duties began on 31 Jul for 17 named large firms and on 29 Sep 2026 for all others.

Exemptions are conditional. Orphan-only drugs, cell and gene therapies, antibody drug conjugates and plasma-derived products are at 0% subject to conditions, and generics and biosimilars are exempt for now, with Commerce due to report on them within a year. Smaller firms without agreements carry the most uncertainty, in our view.

Medicare negotiation widens. The 2028 list was published on 27 Jan 2026 and holds 15 drugs, ten under Part D and five under Part B, with an expanded orphan exclusion that delays some oncology drugs. Amgen has already pointed to Part D price setting reducing Enbrel's net price.

FDA activity continues: 48 novel approvals were listed for 2026 as of 9 Nov. Vertex's povetacicept has a decision date of 30 Nov 2026, while the FDA has asked Amgen to withdraw Tavneos, which Amgen contests.

Economics are lopsided. Amgen's non-GAAP operating margin was 47.3% of product sales, and Gilead's 50.2%. Damodaran's January 2026 table for 496 US biotech firms shows a 60.78% gross margin, but a net margin of -5.00% and an 8.97% unadjusted pre-tax operating margin. The gap is the cost of the many companies with no product.

Operating leverage is visible: Amgen's non-GAAP SG&A fell 1% while R&D rose 11% and sales grew 8%. It can reverse with deal costs: Vertex's operating income fell to $713M from $1.19B as SG&A rose to $844M from $445M. Moderna cut R&D 27% to $583M and made a $162M profit on $1,313M of revenue.

Returns on capital are low across the group, with return on equity of -5.67% (-2.21% R&D-adjusted) against 24.04% for pharmaceuticals. Capital intensity is light: capex is 32.55% of depreciation and net capex -3.57% of sales. We did not obtain a sourced ROIC for the group.
Free cash flow is strong at the leaders. Amgen's was $3.7B in Q3, Gilead's operating cash flow $5.0B and Regeneron held $18.9B of cash and securities after $2.3B of buybacks in nine months.

Guidance moved up. Amgen raised 2026 revenue guidance to $38.9B to $39.7B and non-GAAP EPS to $22.90 to $23.70. Gilead raised 2026 product sales to $31.0B to $31.3B from $30.1B to $30.4B. Vertex lifted revenue guidance to $13.15B to $13.25B. Moderna raised 2026 revenue growth to 15% to 25% from up to 10%.

Beats were large. FactSet shows Amgen's non-GAAP EPS of $6.45 against $5.79 expected and Moderna's $0.38 against a loss of $1.10 expected, and the Health Care sector reported the largest aggregate positive earnings surprise of any sector at 13.7%.

Deal accounting distorts reported earnings. Gilead's guided non-GAAP EPS for 2026 is $(1.20) to $(0.85) after $12.4B of acquired research charges, with non-GAAP operating income of $2.0B to $2.4B. We did not find consensus EPS growth for the biotech group alone and do not estimate one.

Where we differ: Moderna's profit looks like a combination of one-off cost cuts and a seasonal vaccine quarter, with a nine-month net loss of $1,963M. We would not read a single quarter as a new run rate. Regeneron's Q4 should also include the $1.0B Sanofi upfront payment.

Valuation depends heavily on the index. IBB, weighted toward large caps, traded on a P/E of 29.33 and a price-to-book of 6.23 on 12 Nov 2026, while XBI, which is modified equal weighted, showed a P/E of 18.15 on FY1 earnings. FactSet puts the S&P 500's forward P/E at 17.7, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1. The measures are not on the same basis, so the comparison is rough.

Damodaran's January 2026 data show US biotech at a forward P/E of 63.76, EV/EBITDA of 15.78 for firms with positive EBITDA and 51.49 across all firms. The group's PEG ratio is 0.84, against 1.40 for pharmaceuticals. Many of these 496 firms have little or negative earnings, so the multiples are distorted.

We read the large caps as priced for continued double-digit growth in new products, and the small-cap names as priced for pipeline success rather than earnings. We did not obtain free cash flow yields for the group, but Amgen's quarterly FCF of $3.7B shows the cash base behind the large names.

Momentum is strong. IBB's NAV return was 26.64% year to date as of 12 Nov 2026, with net assets of $10.97B, 243 holdings, a NAV of $212.49 and a 52-week range of $160.42 to $221.08. XBI returned 28.00% year to date and 38.84% over one year to 31 Oct 2026, with net assets of $10.42B.

XBI is modified equal weighted, so its top holding, Moderna, is only 2.55% and Amgen, Regeneron and Gilead each carry about 1.7% to 1.8%. Its gains therefore reflect the broad small and mid-cap group as well as the large caps.

Buybacks and dividends are a source of demand. Regeneron repurchased $2.3B in nine months and declared a $0.94 dividend. Gilead paid $1.0B of dividends and $370M of buybacks in Q3. Amgen raised its dividend 6% to $2.52 a share and guides to up to $3.0B of buybacks in 2026. We did not obtain short interest or fund-flow data and make no claim about them.

Managed care is recovering from a two-year margin squeeze, but unevenly. UnitedHealth cut its medical care ratio to 88.4% from 89.9% and guides to at least $20.50 of adjusted EPS; Elevance raised its outlook to at least $29.00; CVS lifted Aetna's benefit margin. Humana is still growing Medicare Advantage fast but at a 93.7% insurance benefit ratio. The pressure points are Medicaid and the ACA exchanges: Centene's Marketplace membership fell to 3.4 million from 5.8 million. Employer family premiums reached $28,303. The provider ETF IHF is up 26.81% this year on a 27.08 P/E.

These companies are health insurers and managed-care organisations. They collect premiums from employers, individuals and governments (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, ACA exchange plans), pay doctors and hospitals for members' care, and keep the difference after administrative costs. Most also own pharmacy benefit managers, clinics or data businesses. GICS places hospital operators, labs and drug distributors in other Health Care sub-industries. Insurers earn thin margins on very large revenue, so a one-point shift in the share of premium spent on care moves profit sharply.

Employer and commercial insurance: Plans bought by employers for workers, either fully insured (the insurer bears claims risk) or self-funded (the employer bears it and pays a fee). e.g. UnitedHealthcare, Elevance Anthem, Cigna Healthcare, Aetna

Medicare Advantage: Private plans that replace traditional Medicare for people aged 65 and over. The government pays a fixed monthly amount per member, adjusted for how sick the member is. e.g. Humana, UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Elevance
Medicaid managed care: State-contracted plans covering low-income people for a fixed monthly payment per member. e.g. Centene, Molina, Elevance, UnitedHealthcare Community & State
ACA individual (exchange) plans: Plans sold to individuals on the government marketplaces, mostly subsidised by federal tax credits. e.g. Centene Ambetter, Molina Marketplace, Oscar

Pharmacy benefit management: Negotiates drug prices with manufacturers, runs formularies and processes prescriptions for health plans and employers. e.g. Optum Rx, Express Scripts (Cigna Evernorth), CVS Caremark, CarelonRx

Care delivery and services: Owned clinics, home health, analytics and technology that insurers use to manage cost and earn fees from third parties. e.g. Optum Health, CenterWell (Humana), Carelon Services
Medical cost trend versus pricing: If claims per member grow faster than premiums were priced for, the loss ratio rises and earnings fall. Insurers reprice yearly, so errors show up for 12 months.
Government rates: Medicare Advantage payment rates and state Medicaid rates set revenue per member. A rate below cost trend squeezes margins in that book.
Membership mix: Gaining or shedding members changes revenue and risk. New members, especially in Medicare Advantage, often cost more at first.
Risk pool health: On ACA exchanges, if healthier people leave when subsidies shrink, the remaining pool is sicker and costs per member rise.
Reserve estimates: Insurers estimate unpaid claims. Favourable revisions boost earnings, and unfavourable ones can trigger sharp guidance cuts.
Policy and regulation: Changes to Medicare payment, Medicaid eligibility, ACA subsidies, PBM rules and coding audits can reset the profit pool for a whole line.
Services and pharmacy profits: PBM and care-delivery arms add earnings that do not depend directly on claims cost, though they carry their own regulatory risk.

Medical loss ratio (MLR) or medical care ratio: Claims paid for care divided by premium revenue. It is the main profit gauge: each 1 point is about 1% of premium. Companies label it differently: medical care ratio, benefit expense ratio, health benefits ratio or medical benefit ratio.
Capitation: A fixed monthly payment per member from a government or employer, regardless of how much care the member uses.
Medical cost trend: The yearly growth in cost per member from price and usage. Insurers must price premiums ahead of it.
Risk adjustment: A formula that pays more for sicker members. It rewards accurate diagnosis coding and attracts regulatory scrutiny.
Star ratings: CMS quality scores for Medicare Advantage plans. Four stars or more earns quality bonus payments.
Fully insured vs self-funded (ASO): In fully insured plans the insurer takes claims risk. In administrative-services-only plans the employer does, and the insurer earns a fee.
Pharmacy benefit manager (PBM): An intermediary that negotiates drug prices and manages formularies. Several insurers own one.
Prior authorization: A requirement that insurers approve certain care before it is delivered. It restrains cost but draws regulatory and political criticism.
Days claims payable: Claims liabilities divided by daily claims cost. A sharp fall can signal under-reserving.
Prior-period reserve development: Later revisions to estimates of last period's unpaid claims. Favourable development lifts current profit.
Vertical integration: Owning providers, pharmacies and data businesses alongside the plan, so more of each health dollar stays inside the group.
Redetermination: A state's check that a person still qualifies for Medicaid. More frequent checks cut membership.
Medicaid work requirements and six-month redeterminations start on 1 Jan 2027, and Centene expects them to reduce its Medicaid membership.
Humana's Q4 insurance benefit ratio is guided to just above 95.5%, so the seasonal Q4 cost step-up and 2027 Medicare Advantage pricing are the next test.
UnitedHealth's long-running Justice Department case over Medicare risk-adjustment coding is unresolved, and Elevance has accrued $935M for possible exposure on historical risk adjustment data.
Cigna exits individual ACA coverage on 1 Jan 2027 and Centene's Marketplace book has shrunk by more than 40%, so exchange risk pools are the main swing factor for 2027 pricing.
Commercial cost trend remains the key unknown: Molina says medical cost trend appears to be plateauing but is still elevated.
UnitedHealth Group, Elevance Health, Cigna, CVS Health (Aetna), Centene, Humana, Molina Healthcare

Revenue is mainly premiums, plus fees from self-funded employers and income from services businesses. UnitedHealth's Q3 2026 revenue was $112.7B, of which UnitedHealthcare contributed $86.3B and Optum $66.9B before eliminations. Cigna's Evernorth services arm had $63.8B of adjusted revenue against $11.7B at Cigna Healthcare.

Customers are employers, individuals, the federal government (Medicare Advantage, Part D) and states (Medicaid). UnitedHealthcare's Q3 revenue split was $20.2B employer and individual, $42.4B Medicare and Retirement, and $23.7B Community and State. Medicare and Medicaid are therefore bigger than the commercial book.

The principal cost is medical claims, followed by administration. UnitedHealth spent 88.4% of premium on care in Q3 with an operating cost ratio of 12.8%. Elevance's benefit expense ratio was 90.6% and its operating expense ratio 11.4%. Insurers have little control over what hospitals and doctors charge.

Pricing power is limited. Medicare Advantage rates are set by CMS, Medicaid rates by states, and exchange rates need regulatory approval. Employer contracts reprice yearly. Scale in provider contracting helps, and our read is that vertical integration into pharmacy and care delivery is the main way to earn above the pure insurance spread.

The big assets are investment portfolios, goodwill and cash held for regulatory capital; liabilities are claims payable and debt. UnitedHealth carried $74.3B of debt and $104.1B of equity at 30 Sep 2026, and Elevance $30.8B of debt. Days claims payable of 47.0 at UnitedHealth shows the size of the unpaid-claims liability.

The business is asset-light compared with hospitals or industrials. UnitedHealth's capital expenditure was $2,421M over nine months. Capital is held mainly as reserves and investments, and dividends and buybacks are limited by regulators' minimum capital rules.

We did not find a sourced global market size for managed care. In the US, KFF reports 35.2M Medicare Advantage members in 2026, 55% of eligible beneficiaries, and employer family premiums averaging $28,303 a year. Revenue for the group's leaders runs to hundreds of billions of dollars, as UnitedHealth's quarterly $112.7B shows.

Main segments are employer and commercial, Medicare Advantage and Part D, Medicaid and ACA exchange plans, plus pharmacy benefit and care services. Centene's Q3 membership included 11.9M in Medicaid, 8.9M in Medicare prescription drug plans and 3.4M in the Marketplace.

Insurers sit between payers (employers, governments, individuals) and providers (hospitals, doctors, pharmacies). They also own parts of the chain: Optum Health has 92M consumers served and Optum Rx 393M adjusted scripts in Q3. Hospitals' pricing and drug costs are the inputs that matter most.

The industry shifted from selling employer plans to government programmes, then to owning services. Medicare Advantage now covers 55% of eligible beneficiaries. Growth has slowed and margins have been squeezed since 2024 by higher utilisation.

The industry is almost wholly US-based, so geography is state by state. Medicaid is run by states, and ACA exchange pricing and enrolment varied widely across states in 2026. Cigna's customer relationships fell 6% in 2026 partly from a government behavioural contract ending, showing even service lines are mostly domestic.

Seven large public groups dominate: UnitedHealth, Elevance, Cigna, CVS (Aetna), Centene, Humana and Molina, plus Blue Cross plans and Kaiser outside the listed set. Smaller listed names and regional plans hold niches. This brief covers the seven.

In Medicare Advantage, KFF puts UnitedHealth at 26% of enrolment (down from 29%) and Humana at 20% (up from 17%) in 2026. By membership, UnitedHealthcare has 48.3M medical members, Elevance 44.9M, CVS 26.1M, Molina 4.9M. We found no overall US market-share figure.

The industry is concentrated at national scale and fragmented by state and product. Medicare Advantage is concentrated: UnitedHealth and Humana together hold 46%. Medicaid and exchange markets have more local competitors, and rivals bid for state contracts.

Barriers to entry are substantial: regulatory licences, minimum capital, provider networks, data and Star rating track records. Our read is that network contracts and enrolment scale take years to build, but new entrants appear in small exchange and Medicare niches.

Economies of scale are real in provider contracting, data, pharmacy purchasing and claims processing. Elevance's operating expense ratio of 11.4% and UnitedHealth's 12.8% suggest smaller firms such as Molina must run lean to compete.

Insurance is largely a commodity at the plan level: customers compare price and network. Differentiation comes from Star ratings (69% of Aetna's members are in 4-star-plus plans for 2027), brokers, care programmes and integrated pharmacy and clinics.

Bargaining power is shared. Employers and governments are strong buyers because rates are set or negotiated; hospitals and drug makers are strong suppliers where they dominate a region or a drug. Insurers hold power over small physician groups and in markets with scale.

Revenue growth follows membership, rate increases and mix. Elevance's revenue rose 0.7% in Q3 while Medicare Advantage membership fell 15.5% and Medicaid revenue rose 5.7%. Humana's individual Medicare Advantage membership rose 23% in nine months.

Operating margins depend mainly on the medical loss ratio. UnitedHealthcare's Q3 operating margin was 3.3% against 2.1% a year earlier as its ratio improved. Elevance's Health Benefits margin was 1.0% against 1.4%. Small ratio changes drive large profit swings.
Key cost variables are hospital prices, utilisation, specialty drugs and behavioural health. Molina says trend appears to be plateauing but is elevated.

Interest rates matter through investment income, which supports earnings, and through debt service. We did not find a sourced figure for investment income. Debt is large: UnitedHealth's debt-to-capital was 41.7% and Humana's 40.9%. Higher rates raise financing cost.

Unemployment matters because employer coverage follows jobs, and it matters most for commercial membership. UnitedHealth said employer membership fell 165,000 in Q3 on employer attrition. Inflation drives hospital and labour prices; commodity exposure is minor.

The industry is defensive in demand but cyclical in profit. Care is needed in a downturn, but margins swing with the pricing cycle: UnitedHealth's medical care ratio moved from 89.9% to 88.4% within a year. Medicare ageing is a secular tailwind, and policy changes add event risk.

Revenue growth is low single digits at the big groups. UnitedHealth's Q3 revenue fell to $112.7B from $113.2B, Elevance's operating revenue rose 0.7%, Cigna's 6% and CVS's 5.4%. Earnings have recovered faster than revenue as margins repair.

Margins are thin. Damodaran's January 2026 table for US Healthcare Support Services (104 firms, the nearest category we found, not a pure insurer group) shows a gross margin of 12.08%, an operating margin of 3.21% and net margin of 1.25%. UnitedHealthcare's Q3 operating margin was 3.3%.

Return on equity for Damodaran's Healthcare Support Services group was 9.89% in January 2026. The page gives no ROIC. Leaders such as UnitedHealth earn more, but we did not obtain a sourced ROIC for the sub-industry and do not estimate one.

Leverage is meaningful. UnitedHealth's debt-to-capital was 41.7% with a target of about 40% by year-end. Humana's was 40.9%. Elevance had $30.8B of debt and Molina $3.8B of long-term debt. Debt is used mainly for acquisitions.

Free cash flow is strong but not smooth. UnitedHealth's operating cash flow was $5.1B in Q3 and $25.1B over nine months, Elevance's $7.5B over nine months, and CVS's $15.3B. Cash flow benefits from timing of Medicare payments and claims, so we would not treat it as a run rate.
Capital spending is light. UnitedHealth spent $2,421M over nine months. Cash goes to buybacks: UnitedHealth repurchased $5,031M, Elevance $1,688M and Cigna about $500M by 4 Nov.

Multiples are modest relative to the market. Damodaran's January 2026 EV/EBITDA for Healthcare Support Services was 11.17 for firms with positive EBITDA. The iShares healthcare providers ETF trades on a P/E of 27.08, a fund-level figure for a broader providers group.

Regulation is the largest risk. CMS finalised a 2027 Medicare Advantage increase of nearly 5% per enrollee but will exclude unlinked chart-review diagnoses, which it expects to cut average payments by 1.5%. Medicaid work requirements begin on 1 Jan 2027, and UnitedHealth faces a Justice Department risk-adjustment case.

Technology and AI cut both ways. Insurers use data and automation to manage claims and prior authorization, while providers' AI-driven coding may raise billed intensity. We did not obtain a sourced figure for AI's effect, and our read is that it is a cost and scrutiny risk on both sides.

Demographics are a tailwind for Medicare, since 35.2M people are already in Medicare Advantage, but a headwind to margins because older and sicker members cost more. Our read is that new members, who often cost more at first, raise Humana's near-term ratio, though we did not find a sourced figure.

Consumer behaviour is shifting under affordability pressure. Worker contributions to family coverage rose 9% to $7,471 and 44% of large firms raised workers' share of premiums. On exchanges, effectuated enrolment fell 12% to 19.2M. Cost-conscious members drop coverage or trade down.
New competitors and models include provider-owned plans, employer-direct contracting, and PBM models that remove rebates. We did not find a sourced figure for new-entrant share.

Geopolitics and supply chains matter little for premiums, but drug prices and tariffs on pharmaceuticals can raise claims costs. We did not find a sourced figure for this and treat it as a minor factor, which is our judgment.

Substitutes include self-funding by employers, direct primary care, public options and traditional Medicare. Traditional Medicare is the main alternative: 45% of eligible beneficiaries remain there, by our subtraction from KFF's 55% Medicare Advantage share.
Margins are repairing as insurers reprice and prune unprofitable books: UnitedHealth's medical care ratio fell 1.5 points and Aetna's 1.5 points in a year.
Medicare Advantage still draws members, at 55% of eligible beneficiaries, and 2027 payments rise nearly 5% per enrollee.
Star-rating gains and integrated pharmacy and care services can add earnings not tied to claims cost, as Humana targets a 3% pre-tax margin in 2028.
Smaller exchange risk pools are being repriced, and Centene's commercial health benefits ratio improved to 89.0% from 89.9%.
Medical cost trend is high and commercial premiums are already $28,303 for a family, leaving little room for price rises.
Medicaid work requirements and tighter redeterminations from January 2027 will reduce membership.
Risk-adjustment audits and coding rules may cut Medicare Advantage payments, with Elevance already accruing $935M and UnitedHealth in litigation.
ACA exchange pools remain fragile after enhanced subsidies expired and enrolment fell 12%.

We think the next three to five years favour disciplined insurers with scale, good Star ratings and services arms, and challenge those that are concentrated in one government programme. The 2026 recovery came from repricing, benefit cuts and exits, shown by UnitedHealth's lower ratio and shrinking Medicare Advantage book. That playbook is mostly used up, so growth now depends on membership and on policy. Medicaid reductions from 2027 and exchange instability could offset gains in Medicare Advantage. Rate setting remains political, which keeps earnings visibility lower than the defensive label suggests. Humana's 2028 margin target will be a test of whether repair lasts.

Managed care is defensive in demand but exposed to a pricing cycle and to policy. FactSet's 13 Nov 2026 report shows blended S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth of 31.9% and Health Care revenue growth of 6.3%, with Health Care showing the largest positive earnings surprise of any sector at 13.7%, led by Centene, Elevance and Humana beating estimates. That sector includes drug makers, so it describes managed care only loosely.

The cycle for insurers is the medical cost cycle. Employer premiums rose 5% to $28,303 for family coverage in 2026, while workers' share rose 9%. Labour-market softness shows up as lost employer members: UnitedHealth said employer and individual membership contracted by 165,000 in Q3 on employer attrition.

Interest rates and fiscal policy matter mainly through government programmes and investment income. We did not obtain a sourced path for rates or inflation and do not claim one. Fiscal policy is the larger lever: expiry of enhanced ACA tax credits cut effectuated marketplace enrolment 12% to 19.2M, and Medicaid work requirements start 1 Jan 2027. Our read is that policy, not the economy, is setting the cycle.

Demand rests on ageing, chronic disease and government programmes. In 2026, 35.2M of 64.2M eligible Medicare beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage, 55%. Special needs plans make up 23% of Medicare Advantage enrolment. Humana added about 1,208,000 individual Medicare Advantage members in nine months, a 23% rise.

Commercial demand is stable in volume but expensive. Family premiums reached $28,303, up 28% in five years against 27% for wages, and 44% of large firms raised workers' share of premiums. Our read is that employer demand for coverage is inelastic, but affordability pressure shifts members to higher deductibles.

Elastic demand sits in subsidised segments. Marketplace effectuated enrolment fell 12% to 19.2M and total individual-market enrolment fell 18% to 20.5M by June 2026 after enhanced tax credits expired. Insurers proposed a median 15% increase for 2027. Medicaid membership is policy-driven, with CBO projecting 5.2M adults losing coverage by 2034 under the House version of the work-requirement law. Long-term, ageing supports Medicare growth, while Medicaid and exchange volumes depend on legislation.

Porter's five forces give a mixed picture. Rivalry is intense in price-sensitive employer and exchange markets but more rational in Medicare Advantage, where UnitedHealth and Humana hold 46% of enrolment. Threat of new entrants is low because of licences, capital and network needs. Threat of substitutes is moderate: traditional Medicare and self-funding remain alternatives.

Buyer power is high. Governments set Medicare Advantage and Medicaid rates, and CMS's 2027 notice raised payments by nearly 5% per enrollee about double the initial proposal, as KFF reports. Supplier power sits with hospitals and drug makers. Insurers answer by integrating: Optum had 92M consumers served and 393M adjusted scripts at Optum Rx, and Cigna's Evernorth had $63.8B of adjusted revenue in Q3.

Concentration is high at the top. UnitedHealthcare has 48.3M medical members, Elevance 44.9M, CVS 26.1M, Cigna 18.5M medical customers, and Molina 4.9M. Pricing power is weak; moats come from scale in contracting, Star ratings and data. Share is moving: UnitedHealth's Medicare Advantage share fell to 26% from 29%, while Humana's rose to 20% from 17%.

Regulation and politics dominate. CMS finalised 2027 Medicare Advantage rates on 6 Apr 2026, raising average per-enrollee payments by nearly 5%, about $26B, but will exclude diagnoses from chart reviews not tied to a provider encounter, expected to reduce average payments by 1.5%. MedPAC estimates MA payments are 14%, or $76B, higher than for similar traditional Medicare beneficiaries, which keeps the programme a political target.

Medicaid and the ACA are changing under the 2025 reconciliation law. States must apply work requirements of 80 hours a month from 1 Jan 2027, with checks every six months. Enhanced ACA tax credits have expired, and effectuated enrolment fell to 19.2M. Cigna leaves the individual market on 1 Jan 2027.

Legal risk is material. UnitedHealth discloses a Justice Department False Claims Act suit over risk-adjustment submissions, risk-adjustment data validation audits by CMS and the Inspector General, and an IRS proposal to increase taxable income for 2017 to 2020. Elevance accrued $935M in nine months for potential exposure on historical risk-adjustment data after a CMS notice dated 27 Feb 2026.
Technology and pharmacy policy matter too. We did not obtain sourced detail on federal PBM legislation.

The economics are high revenue, thin margin and strong cash conversion. UnitedHealthcare's Q3 operating margin was 3.3% (2.1% a year ago), Optum's 5.6%, Elevance's adjusted operating margin 2.7%, and Cigna Healthcare's pre-tax margin 10.2% against Evernorth's 2.9%. Damodaran's January 2026 Healthcare Support Services group shows a 3.21% operating margin, so single-digit margins are normal.

Operating leverage runs through the loss ratio. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio fell 1.5 points to 88.4%, lifting earnings from operations to $6.6B from $4.3B on slightly lower revenue. CVS's ratio improved 1.5 points and Health Care Benefits adjusted operating income rose to $912M from $314M. The reverse happens fast: Humana's Q3 insurance benefit ratio was 93.7% and it guides just above 95.5% for Q4.

Return on equity for Damodaran's Healthcare Support Services group was 9.89%. We have no sourced ROIC. Free cash flow is strong: UnitedHealth's nine-month operating cash flow was $25.1B against $2.4B of capital spending. Capital intensity is low, and cash goes to buybacks, with UnitedHealth's at $5.0B over nine months.

Revisions are upward. UnitedHealth guides to at least $20.50 of adjusted EPS, from $14.22 for nine months last year to $18.30 this year. Elevance raised to at least $29.00, CVS to at least $8.20 from $7.90 to $8.10, Cigna to at least $30.60, Humana to at least $9.50 from $9.00 and Centene's floor to above $5.20. Molina reaffirmed at least $5.25.

Q3 beats were large. FactSet shows Centene earned $0.58 against $0.10 expected, Elevance $6.99 against $4.71 and Humana a loss of $0.70 against a $1.00 loss. FactSet also notes Elevance's figure included a $1.85 non-operating benefit, so its beat is flattered. Molina's adjusted EPS was only $0.89 on a 92.9% medical care ratio, showing the Medicaid squeeze.

Forward markers are mixed. Elevance targets at least 12% adjusted EPS growth in 2027 from a base of at least $26.75, a lower base than 2026. Cigna expects at least 10% growth from a base of about $30. Humana sees 2027 progress toward a 3% pre-tax margin in 2028. Centene expects Medicaid membership losses from January 2027.

Where we differ: much of 2026's recovery came from repricing and shrinkage, so earnings growth in 2027 must come from medical cost control, not another cut to membership. We found no consensus EPS growth for managed care, so we make no claim on it.

The cleanest sub-industry gauge we found is the iShares U.S. Healthcare Providers ETF (IHF), on a P/E of 27.08 at 12 Nov 2026. IHF holds 61 stocks and covers providers more broadly, so it is a proxy for insurers, not an exact match. We did not obtain a forward multiple or a ten-year average for managed care.

For market context, FactSet shows the S&P 500 at 18.3 times forward earnings against a 5-year average of 19.8 and a 10-year average of 19.1. Damodaran's January 2026 data show Healthcare Support Services at an EV/EBITDA of 11.17 for firms with positive EBITDA. That group is broad and, we think, only partly insurers.

Our read is that after the sharp 2026 rebound the group is no longer cheap against its own recent trough, and prices already reflect margin repair. Implied growth depends on loss ratios holding near 2026 levels while membership stabilises. We did not compute free cash flow yields, and give no view on any single stock.

Momentum is strong. IHF returned 26.81% year to date to 12 Nov 2026, with a NAV of $60.40 at the top of a 52-week range of $41.02 to $60.91. Its net assets were $1.58B on 13 Nov 2026. The ETF is a broader providers fund, so part of the move may reflect non-insurers.

Buybacks are visible. UnitedHealth repurchased $5,031M of stock over nine months and its board authorised up to 50 million more shares in November 2026. Elevance bought $1,688M over nine months and has about $5.0B authorised. Cigna repurchased about $500M through 4 Nov.

We did not obtain short interest, fund-flow or breadth data and make no claim about them. Results show dispersion: Humana raised its outlook while Molina only reaffirmed. FactSet shows Health Care with the largest positive earnings surprise of any sector.

Life sciences tools makers just reported a firm third quarter. Thermo Fisher grew organic revenue 6% and raised its 2026 outlook, Danaher's core sales rose 5.5% excluding respiratory testing, IQVIA booked $3.2B of new research work at a 1.2x book-to-bill, and Waters, Mettler-Toledo and Revvity beat their own guidance. Pharma and biotech customers are the strength; US academic and government demand was flat at Thermo. Tariff refunds flattered margins at several firms. Damodaran's January 2026 data put healthcare products at a 42.3 forward P/E.

These companies sell the instruments, chemicals, plastics and services that scientists use to discover and make drugs: lab analyzers, DNA sequencers, cell-culture media, filters and bioreactors, and outsourced clinical trials. Customers are drug and biotech companies, universities, hospitals, labs and industrial firms. Revenue comes from one-off instrument sales plus repeating consumables and service. GICS also puts contract research firms and drug-packaging components here. Drug makers sit in Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology, and medical diagnostics products sit in Health Care Equipment.

Analytical instruments: Machines that identify and measure substances, such as mass spectrometers, chromatographs and microscopes, used in drug discovery, quality control and food and environmental testing. e.g. Agilent LC and GC, Waters LC-MS, Thermo Fisher Orbitrap, Danaher SCIEX

Bioprocessing: Equipment and single-use consumables used to grow cells and purify biologic drugs at scale, including bioreactors, filters, resins and media. e.g. Danaher (Cytiva, Pall), Thermo Fisher, Merck KGaA
Genomic sequencing: Machines and reagents that read DNA, sold with a repeating supply of consumables for each run. e.g. Illumina NovaSeq X
Lab consumables and reagents: Pipette tips, plates, chemicals and antibodies that labs use up and reorder constantly. e.g. Thermo Fisher Fisher Scientific brands, Revvity, Danaher Abcam
Contract research and development services: Outsourced clinical trials, lab work and data services sold to drug companies, paid as work is done. e.g. IQVIA, Thermo Fisher PPD
Precision weighing and inspection: Lab balances, pipettes and industrial scales used in labs and factories. e.g. Mettler-Toledo
Drug containment and delivery components: Rubber stoppers, plungers and syringe parts that must touch injectable drugs and are qualified into each drug's approval. e.g. West Pharmaceutical Services
Pharma and biotech R&D budgets: Drug developers are the largest buyers. When they spend more on discovery and trials, orders for instruments, reagents and trial services rise with a short lag.
Biologic drug production: More biologic drugs and larger volumes mean more bioreactors, filters and media. Customers also run down or build stock, which makes orders swing.
Public research funding: Grant budgets and indirect-cost rules decide how much universities can spend on instruments and supplies. Cuts or freezes show up as flat or falling academic sales.
China and other regions: Stimulus, local-brand preference and trade policy change regional demand and prices. A recovery in China lifts growth fast for the instrument makers with large sales there.
Tariffs and supply chains: Companies make and import goods across several countries. Duties raise costs, and refunds of them are a one-off boost to margins.
Mix and operating leverage: Consumables and services carry higher margins than instruments. Revenue growth on a largely fixed cost base widens margins.
Acquisitions: The group is built by deals. They add growth and debt, and integration and purchase accounting weigh on reported earnings.
Organic growth: Sales growth excluding acquisitions, divestitures and currency. It is the cleanest read of underlying demand.
Core growth: Danaher's term for organic growth. It strips out currency, acquisitions and divestitures.
