Prescription volume and drug mix: Revenue rises with volume and with the share of expensive specialty and GLP-1 drugs, which inflate sales faster than profit because margins are a small percentage of high prices.
Generic sourcing performance: Profit depends on buying generics well. Deflation outpacing sourcing gains cuts gross profit; good performance lifts segment profit.
Drug pricing policy: List price cuts, most-favored-nation deals and Medicare price negotiation change revenue per unit and fee structures, with uncertain profit effects.
Customer contracts: Large pharmacy and health system contracts renew every few years. Renewal terms and any loss shift volume and margin.
Medical procedure volumes and costs: Medical-surgical products follow hospital and clinic activity, and freight, petroleum-based materials and tariffs move costs.
Capital deployment: Distributors generate cash and use it for buybacks and acquisitions, so deal prices and share repurchases lift or dilute per-share earnings.
Wholesale acquisition cost (WAC): A manufacturer's list price to wholesalers. Distributors' fees are often a percentage of it, so list price cuts reduce reported revenue.
Generic sourcing venture: A joint buying arrangement that purchases generics from manufacturers at scale. It is the main profit source in pharmaceutical distribution.
Generic deflation: The steady fall in generic drug prices over time. It squeezes distributor margins unless offset by sourcing gains.
Brand inflation: Manufacturer price increases on branded drugs. Historically they helped distributors' profit, but recent list price cuts reverse the effect on revenue.
Biosimilar: A lower-cost, near-copy of a biologic drug. Distributors earn useful fees on them, so adoption matters to profit.
340B program: A federal drug discount scheme for qualifying safety-net providers. Wholesalers process 340B orders, so rule changes can disrupt contract pharmacy flows.
Group purchasing organization (GPO): A buying group that negotiates prices for hospitals or practices. It strengthens customers' bargaining power.
Specialty drug: A high-cost drug, often injected or infused, needing special handling. Distribution revenue is large and margins are percentage-based.
Buy and bill: A model in which a physician practice buys a drug, administers it and then bills the payer. Distributors finance and supply the inventory.
Customer concentration: Reliance on a few large buyers, such as national pharmacy chains. A lost or repriced contract moves revenue and profit sharply.
Working capital: Receivables plus inventory less payables. For distributors it swings operating cash flow from quarter to quarter.
Opioid settlement: Payments by the three big wholesalers to states and others over many years to resolve opioid distribution lawsuits.
McKesson plans a phased separation of its Medical-Surgical unit (to be called Wellverse) from January 2027, with Apollo funds holding about 13%, which will reshape the group's earnings mix.
Medical-surgical earnings are under pressure: McKesson's segment operating profit fell 10% and Cardinal's Global Medical Products and Distribution profit fell 28% in their latest quarters.
Generics and biosimilars are exempt from the 0% to 100% Section 232 drug tariffs for now, but the administration may revisit that within a year of April 2026.
The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge runs from 1 Jul 2026 to Dec 2027 at $245 net per month to Medicare, so GLP-1 volume depends on policy and payer behavior.
Customer concentration is high: CVS Health was 24% of McKesson's fiscal 2026 revenue, and renewal terms are a key swing factor.
McKesson, Cencora, Cardinal Health, Henry Schein

Revenue comes mostly from selling drugs and supplies at a small markup. McKesson's North American Pharmaceutical segment brought in $91.4B of its $111B quarterly revenue, with Oncology and Multispecialty at $15B and Prescription Technology Solutions at $1.5B. Cencora's U.S. Healthcare Solutions was $298.1B of $337.4B in fiscal 2026.

Customers are pharmacy chains, health systems, physician practices and dental offices. CVS Health was 24% of McKesson's fiscal 2026 revenue and its ten largest customers 73%. Drug Channels projects five companies (CVS Health, Cigna, Walgreens, Walmart and UnitedHealth Group) will account for more than 40% of US drug distribution revenue in 2026.

The main cost is the product itself, so gross margin is tiny: McKesson's was 3.61% in fiscal 2026. Remaining costs are warehousing, freight, labor and technology. On our arithmetic, Cencora's adjusted operating income of $4.81B on $337.4B of revenue is about 1.4%.

Pricing power is weak against large customers and manufacturers, who set list prices. Profit comes from scale, generics sourcing and fees. Cardinal credited brand and specialty products and positive generics program performance for its 17% pharmaceutical segment profit rise.

Main assets are inventory, receivables and goodwill from acquisitions; liabilities are payables and debt. McKesson's total debt was $9.2B at 30 Sep 2026, up from $6.5B in March, with a stockholders' deficit of $3.95B. Cencora's long-term debt was $11.06B against $4.88B of cash.

The business is asset-light relative to revenue but capital-intensive in working capital. Cencora guides to capital spending of about $1.0B on adjusted free cash flow of about $3.5B for fiscal 2027. Cardinal spent $157M on capex in one quarter.

We did not find a single sourced global market size. For the US, Drug Channels Institute projects drug distribution revenue for the Big Three at $933B in 2026, with growth slowing from double digits through 2025 to mid-single digits. By our sum of reported fiscal results, McKesson, Cencora and Cardinal alone are hundreds of billions each.

Segments are pharmaceutical distribution, specialty and oncology, medical-surgical products, dental and office-based supplies, and technology services. McKesson's trailing revenue was $345.6B in North American Pharmaceutical, $54.9B in oncology and multispecialty and $11.8B in medical-surgical. Henry Schein's U.S. dental total was $933M in Q3.

Distributors sit between manufacturers and dispensers, and increasingly between payers and care. They buy from drug makers and sell to pharmacies, hospitals and practices; Drug Channels says the largest wholesalers have spent over $20B on stakes in physician management organizations.

The industry evolved from regional wholesalers to three national giants, then into specialty, oncology networks and technology. McKesson will invest about $1.4B for roughly 49% of Option Care Health and has closed Precision Medicine Group for about $2.25B. Cencora financed the OneOncology deal with $3.0B of notes and $1.5B of term loans.

The big drug wholesalers are overwhelmingly US-centred. Foreign operations were about 4% of McKesson's fiscal 2026 revenue, while Cencora's International Healthcare Solutions was $30.7B of $337.4B. Henry Schein's international distribution was $901M of $3.47B of Q3 sales.

In US pharmaceutical wholesale there are three dominant public competitors: McKesson, Cencora and Cardinal Health. In dental and office-based supplies Henry Schein competes with other distributors; we did not obtain share data for that niche.

Market leaders by reported scale are Cencora with $337.4B of fiscal 2026 revenue, McKesson (about $111B in one quarter) and Cardinal ($67.5B in one quarter). We did not find a sourced percentage share for each, so we do not give one.

The industry is consolidated at the top. Drug Channels projects the Big Three's drug distribution revenue at $933B in 2026, and we found no sourced figure for how much of the US market the rest of the field holds.

Barriers to entry are high: national warehouse and logistics networks, licenses, access to manufacturer supply, capital for inventory and customer contracts. Our read is that these barriers explain why the Big Three have lasted while retail pharmacy has shrunk; Drug Channels notes two remaining national drugstore chains have closed more than 3,000 locations since 2018.

Economies of scale are central: fixed distribution networks spread across huge volume, and generic purchasing is done jointly. McKesson's 3.61% gross margin shows that profit rests on volume and cost discipline.

Distribution is mostly commoditized: a pharmacy gets the same drug from any wholesaler. Differentiation comes from service, specialty networks, technology and financing, which is why all three have moved into oncology and data.

Customers hold more bargaining power than suppliers in generics and with large chains; CVS Health alone was 24% of McKesson's revenue. Manufacturers hold power on branded drugs and have cut list prices on more than 30 brands, changing wholesalers' fee base.

Revenue growth follows drug volume, mix and list prices. McKesson's revenue rose 8% in the quarter even though January 2026 list price cuts trimmed North American Pharmaceutical growth by about 4 points. GLP-1 revenue of $16B, up 26%, was a major driver.

Operating margins depend on generics sourcing, brand and specialty mix, service fees and cost control. McKesson's North American Pharmaceutical operating profit rose 22% on 6% revenue growth, partly because list price cuts had no meaningful profit effect.

Key cost variables are product cost, freight and fuel, labor and warehouse capacity. Cardinal flagged that Iran-related cost increases and supply disruptions could affect results, though the release did not quantify the impact.

Interest rates matter through financing of inventory and acquisitions. Cencora guides to net interest expense of $490M-$510M in fiscal 2027. We did not obtain a sourced rate sensitivity for the group.

Inflation matters through drug prices and costs, but wholesalers earn on percentage fees, so inflation passes through. GDP and unemployment have only a modest effect because prescription demand is largely non-discretionary. Commodities matter mainly through petroleum-based supplies.

The business is defensive with secular growth. Medical-surgical results are more cyclical: McKesson's segment profit fell 10% and Cardinal's fell 28% while pharmaceutical segments grew. Ageing and specialty drug growth are the structural tailwinds.

Revenue growth is mid-to-high single digits. McKesson's was 8%, Cencora's 5.0% for fiscal 2026 and Cardinal's 5%. Earnings grew faster: McKesson adjusted EPS rose 18%, Cencora's 12.3% and Cardinal's non-GAAP EPS 28%.

Margins are razor thin. Damodaran's January 2026 table for US Healthcare Support Services (104 firms, the nearest category and not a pure distributor group) shows a 12.08% gross margin, 3.21% operating margin and 1.25% net margin. McKesson's actual gross margin was 3.61%.

Damodaran's ROE for Healthcare Support Services was 9.89% in January 2026. That page gives no ROIC, and we did not find a sourced ROIC for the distributors. McKesson's negative equity makes its own ROE not meaningful.

Leverage is moderate and rising with acquisitions. McKesson's debt was $9.2B; Cencora's long-term debt rose to $11.06B from $7.54B; Cardinal's was about $8.8B against $5.26B of cash. Henry Schein's was $3.52B.

Free cash flow is solid but lumpy. McKesson guides to $4.5B-$4.9B for fiscal 2027, Cencora about $3.5B versus $3.8B in fiscal 2026, and Cardinal had adjusted free cash flow of $1.58B in one quarter. Working-capital swings make single quarters unreliable.

Capital expenditure is modest relative to sales: Cencora guides to about $1.0B on $337B of revenue. Cash goes to buybacks, with McKesson planning about $5B in fiscal 2027 and Cardinal completing $500M in its fiscal Q1.

Damodaran's January 2026 EV/EBITDA for Healthcare Support Services was 11.17 for firms with positive EBITDA. On our arithmetic McKesson's 4 Nov price of $1,065.70 is about 23 times the $46.00 midpoint of its fiscal 2027 EPS guidance.

Regulatory risk is large: most-favored-nation pricing, Medicare negotiation from 2028 for some Part B drugs, 340B changes and tariff policy. The 340B program reached $100B of net drug sales, and McKesson says it cannot predict changes but does not expect a material impact now.

Technology and AI offer efficiency in warehousing and ordering but also risk. McKesson disclosed a cybersecurity incident on 25 Aug 2026 that led to putative class actions. We did not find a sourced figure for AI's effect on margins.

Demographics are a tailwind through ageing and chronic disease, though we found no sourced demographic figure for this brief. Expanded GLP-1 coverage adds volume: the Medicare Bridge could cover about 3.8 million eligible enrollees at a $50 copay.

Consumer behavior is shifting toward direct-to-patient and cash-pay channels. The Medicare Bridge prices Wegovy, Zepbound and Foundayo at $245 net per month. Our read is that direct channels could bypass some wholesale margin, but we have no sourced share figure.

New competitors and models include manufacturers selling direct and physician networks owned by wholesalers. Drug Channels notes wholesalers' MSO investments exceed $20B, a defensive move to protect channel roles. Retail pharmacy closures also shrink the customer base.

Geopolitical and supply-chain risk centers on tariffs and imports. Proclamation 11020 applies up to 100% tariffs on patented drugs but exempts generics and biosimilars for now, with a possible re-evaluation within one year. Henry Schein booked a $0.19 per share net benefit from tariff refunds in Q3.

Substitutes include manufacturers shipping direct, hospital-owned distribution and online pharmacies. We did not find a sourced figure for how much volume has moved, so we make no estimate. Litigation is a legacy risk: McKesson carried about a $5.2B opioid liability at 30 Sep 2026.
Specialty, oncology and biosimilar growth, as McKesson's Oncology and Multispecialty revenue rose 24% to $15B.
GLP-1 volume expansion, helped by the Medicare Bridge running to December 2027.
Technology and services businesses that add higher-margin earnings, such as Prescription Technology Solutions with $307M of operating profit.
Capital return from steady cash flow, with McKesson planning about $5B of buybacks and Cencora raising its dividend 10%.
Drug pricing policy and tariffs could change fee bases or generics supply costs.
Customer concentration, with CVS Health at 24% of McKesson revenue, makes contract renewals pivotal.
Medical-surgical weakness and the separation of McKesson's unit add execution risk.
Rising debt after acquisitions, as McKesson's rose to $9.2B and Cencora's long-term debt to $11.06B.

We think the next three to five years favour the large distributors that keep pushing into specialty, oncology and technology while holding costs. Revenue growth is slowing toward mid-single digits at the Big Three, so earnings growth increasingly depends on mix, sourcing and buybacks. McKesson and Cencora guide to high-single to high-teens EPS growth. Policy is the main uncertainty: pricing reform, 340B and tariffs could alter fee structures, and customers hold most of the bargaining power. Medical-surgical is the weakest piece, which may explain McKesson's decision to separate it. We make no estimate beyond those company targets.

Health care distribution is defensive: prescription demand does not move much with the economy, so the cycle matters less than drug mix and policy. FactSet's 13 Nov 2026 report shows blended S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth of 31.9% and Health Care revenue growth of 6.3%, with Health Care showing the largest positive earnings surprise of any sector at 13.7%. That sector includes drug makers and insurers, so it describes distributors only loosely.

Distributors' own revenue is growing faster than that: McKesson 8%, Cardinal 5% and Cencora 5.0% for fiscal 2026. Drug Channels expects growth to slow to mid-single digits in 2026 after double-digit growth through 2025.

Interest rates and currency matter mainly at the margin. Cencora guides to $490M-$510M of net interest expense and a roughly 20% tax rate for fiscal 2027. Foreign operations were only about 4% of McKesson's fiscal 2026 revenue. We did not obtain a sourced rate or inflation path and do not claim one. Fiscal and trade policy matter more: Proclamation 11020 tariffs on patented drugs began on 31 Jul and 29 Sep 2026, while generics are exempt for now.

Demand rests on prescription volume, an ageing population, specialty drugs and new categories such as GLP-1s. McKesson's GLP-1 distribution revenue reached $16B in its latest quarter, up 26% year on year and 8% sequentially, though management says payer dynamics can cause quarterly swings.

Policy is widening GLP-1 access. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge started on 1 Jul 2026 and runs 18 months to December 2027, with a $245 net monthly price to Medicare and a $50 copay; KFF found about 3.8 million Part D enrollees met all criteria using 2023 claims data. Projected federal cost ranges from $1.3B to $3.3B if 10% to 25% of eligible enrollees take part.

We did not obtain a sourced estimate of the overall addressable market. Drug Channels projects Big Three drug distribution revenue at $933B in 2026. Specialty and oncology are growing faster than the base: McKesson's Oncology and Multispecialty revenue rose 24% to $15B. Medical-surgical demand is weaker, with McKesson's segment revenue up 5% but operating profit down 10%. Over the long term, our read is that ageing and specialty therapies support volume, while price policy, not demand, is the main uncertainty.

Porter's five forces point to a stable but low-margin industry. Rivalry among the Big Three is intense on price but disciplined. Threat of new entrants is low because of national logistics, licensing, capital and manufacturer relationships. Supplier power sits with drug makers, who have cut list prices on more than 30 brands, while buyer power is high.

Customer concentration is the clearest bargaining-power issue. CVS Health was 24% of McKesson's fiscal 2026 revenue and the ten largest customers 73%. Drug Channels projects five companies to account for more than 40% of US drug distribution revenue in 2026. McKesson's CVS renewal runs through June 2032.

The threat of substitutes is modest: manufacturers could sell direct, but wholesalers respond by owning physician networks, with more than $20B invested in management organizations. We did not find sourced market shares for the Big Three. Scale shows in size: Cencora's fiscal 2026 revenue was $337.4B, McKesson's quarterly revenue $111B and Cardinal's $67.5B. Moats come from logistics scale, specialty relationships and technology, not pricing power; McKesson's gross margin was 3.61%.

Regulation is the central factor. Drug Channels highlights Medicare price negotiation for some Part B drugs from 2028, most-favored-nation policies, 340B program growth to $100B of net sales, and manufacturers changing 340B terms for external pharmacies (more than 40 have done so). McKesson says 340B changes are hard to predict but it does not expect a material impact now.

Trade policy is a live variable. Proclamation 11020 of 2 Apr 2026 sets a 100% baseline tariff on certain patented drugs and ingredients from 31 Jul 2026 for large companies and 29 Sep for others, with 15% for Japan, the EU, Korea and Switzerland, and lower rates for firms with onshoring or pricing agreements. Generics and biosimilars face 0% but may be revisited within a year. Cardinal's release cites tariff cost and Iran-related disruption as risks without quantifying them.

Legal and security risks remain. McKesson carried about a $5.2B opioid liability at 30 Sep 2026 and disclosed a cybersecurity incident on 25 Aug 2026 with putative class actions. On technology, we did not find a sourced estimate of automation or AI effects on distributors' costs, and make no claim. Social factors, including GLP-1 access under the Medicare Bridge, affect volume.

The economics are enormous revenue, tiny margin and good cash conversion. McKesson's fiscal 2026 gross margin was 3.61%. On our arithmetic, McKesson's Q2 adjusted operating profit of $1.9B on $111B of revenue is about 1.7%, Cencora's fiscal 2026 adjusted operating income of $4.81B on $337.4B is about 1.4%, and Cardinal's Q1 non-GAAP operating earnings of $1,001M on $67.5B is about 1.5%. Henry Schein, with more product margin and services, earned about 5.6% on our calculation.

Operating leverage appears when mix improves. McKesson's North American Pharmaceutical operating profit rose 22% on 6% revenue growth, and Cardinal's pharmaceutical segment profit rose 17% on 6% revenue growth. The reverse shows in medical-surgical: McKesson's operating profit fell 10% on 5% revenue growth and Cardinal's fell 28% on flat revenue.

Damodaran's January 2026 category for Healthcare Support Services shows operating margin of 3.21% and ROE of 9.89%; it is a broader group than distributors. We did not find a sourced ROIC. Free cash flow is strong relative to capex: McKesson guides to $4.5B-$4.9B for fiscal 2027, and Cencora's fiscal 2026 free cash flow was $3.88B after $909.5M of capex.

Guidance is moving up. McKesson raised fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS to $45.60-$46.40 from $44.20-$45.00, or 17% to 19% growth, with revenue growth of 6% to 10%. Cardinal raised to $12.80-$13.00 from $12.40-$12.60 and lifted pharmaceutical segment profit growth to 10%-12%. Henry Schein raised to $5.50-$5.56, including a net tariff refund benefit. Cencora guided to $19.40-$19.75, 8% to 10% growth.

Results beat expectations. McKesson's adjusted EPS of $11.68 compared with a $10.75 consensus, per 24/7 Wall St. We did not obtain consensus for Cencora or Cardinal beyond company results. FactSet shows S&P 500 CY2027 expected earnings growth of 16.2%, but we found no sourced consensus EPS growth for distributors as a group.

Quality of earnings deserves care. Cardinal's baseline excludes an IEEPA tariff refund benefit and it reports growth of 17% to 19% on that basis versus 14% to 15% on reported fiscal 2026. Henry Schein's EPS growth was 19.1% excluding tariff refunds versus 13.0% as reported. Where our view differs: Precision Medicine Group adds only $0.10-$0.20 to fiscal 2027 EPS. Buybacks cut McKesson's share count 6%.

We found no sourced forward P/E or ten-year average for the distributors as a group, and no distributor ETF page, so we limit the claim. Our own arithmetic: McKesson closed around $1,065.70 on 4 Nov 2026, a new 52-week high, against the $45.60-$46.40 EPS guidance range, which is about 23 times the $46.00 midpoint. We did not obtain current prices for Cencora, Cardinal or Henry Schein.

For context, FactSet shows the S&P 500 at 18.3 times forward earnings, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and its 10-year average of 19.1. Damodaran's January 2026 EV/EBITDA for Healthcare Support Services was 11.17 for firms with positive EBITDA, though that group is broader than distributors. The iShares U.S. Healthcare Providers ETF trades on a P/E of 27.08 as of 12 Nov 2026, but it is a providers fund and we could not confirm that it holds the distributors.

Our read is that McKesson's multiple sits above the market's forward multiple, which looks like a premium for specialty growth and buybacks, though we did not compute free cash flow yield. FactSet shows analysts' bottom-up price targets implying 8.3% upside for the Health Care sector, among the smallest of the eleven sectors. We give no view on any single stock.

Momentum at McKesson is strong: it made a new 52-week high of $1,069.02 on 4 Nov 2026, after a prior peak on 20 Oct, with a market capitalisation cited at about $124B. We did not obtain price momentum for Cencora, Cardinal or Henry Schein.

Buybacks are the clearest capital flow. McKesson plans about $5B of repurchases in fiscal 2027, with about $3.4B completed in the first half. Cencora repurchased $1.0B in fiscal 2026 and raised its dividend 10% to $0.66. Cardinal completed a $500M accelerated repurchase. Henry Schein bought back $450M year to date.

The only fund data we opened was the iShares U.S. Healthcare Providers ETF (IHF), up 26.81% year to date to 12 Nov 2026 with net assets of $1.58B. It is a providers fund, and we could not verify its holdings, so we do not treat it as a distributor measure. We did not obtain short interest, fund flows or breadth for the group and make no claim about them. FactSet shows 60% of Health Care sector ratings are Buy.

Health care supplies is a slow-growth, discretionary-exposed corner of medtech where profits are holding up better than sales. Align grew Q3 revenue 1.9% and guides 2026 to $4.11-$4.13B; Dentsply Sirona's sales fell 7.6% and half its adjusted EBITDA gain was a one-off; Cooper trimmed FY2026 guidance. Hospital-facing ICU Medical reaffirmed guidance. Tariff refunds flattered several quarters. We found no sourced forward multiple for the sub-industry; the nearest ETF trades near 19.7x FY1 earnings against 18.3x for the S&P 500.

Health care supplies companies make the consumable and semi-durable products used in every patient encounter: contact lenses, clear orthodontic aligners, dental products, IV sets and infusion consumables, wound-care and surgical supplies. Customers are eye-care practitioners, dentists and orthodontists, hospitals and distributors, and revenue repeats because each patient or procedure needs fresh product. GICS puts larger capital equipment such as scanners, implants and monitors in Health Care Equipment, hospitals in Facilities, and distributors in Health Care Distributors. Some of the companies here also sell equipment alongside consumables.

Contact lenses: Soft lenses worn daily, biweekly or monthly to correct vision, plus specialty lenses for myopia control. Sold through eye-care practitioners, optical chains and online. e.g. CooperVision Biofinity, MyDay and MiSight; Alcon, Johnson & Johnson Vision and Bausch + Lomb compete
Clear aligners: Custom plastic trays that move teeth in steps, prescribed by dentists and orthodontists and made in volume from digital scans. e.g. Align Technology Invisalign

Dental consumables: Restorative materials, preventive products and instruments used chairside every day, often paired with imaging and CAD/CAM equipment. e.g. Dentsply Sirona Essential Dental Solutions; Solventum Dental Solutions
Infusion consumables: IV sets, connectors and related disposables that run on installed pumps, so each pump creates a stream of repeat purchases. e.g. ICU Medical Consumables and Infusion Systems

Wound care and surgical supplies: Dressings, negative-pressure therapy, drapes and infection-prevention products used in hospitals and the home. e.g. Solventum Advanced Wound Care and Infection Prevention and Surgical Solutions
Fertility and women's health supplies: Media, lab tools and devices used in IVF clinics and OB/GYN offices. e.g. CooperSurgical

Procedure and visit volumes: Consumables are used per patient visit or treatment, so revenue follows dental visits, eye exams and hospital activity. Weak consumer demand shows up first in elective items such as aligners.
Pricing and mix: Premium products such as daily lenses and new aligner features raise revenue per unit; promotions, lower-priced offerings and customer consolidation lower it.

Capital equipment cycle: Dentists and hospitals buy scanners, imaging systems and pumps when borrowing is cheap and confidence is high. When they delay purchases, equipment revenue falls and later consumable pull-through slows.

Tariffs and input costs: Plastics, resins and components cross borders before reaching patients. Duties raise cost of goods and compress gross margin unless prices rise, and refunds create one-off gains.
Portfolio changes: Spin-offs, sales and restructuring change reported growth and margins. Separation costs depress GAAP earnings while adjusted figures hide them.
Regulation and clinical evidence: Clearances, reimbursement and safety recalls decide which products can be sold and for how much, so a single approval or quality issue can move a revenue line.
Consumable (razor-and-blade) model: A company sells a platform once and earns repeat revenue from the disposables it needs. It makes revenue steadier than equipment sales.
Case starts: New aligner treatments begun in a period. Align's volume and revenue track this number more closely than any other.
Average selling price (ASP): Revenue per case or unit. It falls when companies add cheaper products or promotions, even when volume rises.
Daily disposable: A contact lens thrown away each day. It is the fastest-growing lens type and carries higher revenue per wearer.
Organic growth: Sales growth excluding currency, acquisitions and divestitures. Analysts use it to see underlying demand.
DSO: Dental service organization, a corporate group that runs many dental practices. Its purchasing power can press prices.
Installed base: The count of pumps, scanners or other equipment already in customers' hands. A larger base supports consumable revenue.
510(k): The US FDA route that clears a device by showing it is substantially equivalent to one already sold.
Group purchasing organization (GPO): A buying group that negotiates supply contracts for many hospitals. It concentrates demand and limits suppliers' pricing.
Adjusted EPS: Earnings per share excluding items such as restructuring and amortisation. Companies in this group use it heavily, so the gap to GAAP matters.
Free cash flow (FCF): Operating cash flow minus capital spending. It shows how much a company can fund buybacks, debt paydown and deals.
Tariff refund: Money returned after duties were ruled unlawful. It lifts reported results once but is not repeatable income.

Dental and clear aligner demand is soft: Align's CFO described a softer environment for discretionary health care spending and capital equipment, and Dentsply's Connected Technology and Orthodontic and Implant segments fell 11% and 17% in Q3.

Tariff policy is unsettled: the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs on 20 Feb 2026 but Section 232 and other authorities remain possible, while refunds already boosted Dentsply, Solventum and ICU Medical results.
Cooper's board kept CooperSurgical after a strategic review that included a proposed sale and raised its buyback authorization to $3B, so execution in both segments now carries the story.
Solventum is still separating from 3M and is reviewing strategic alternatives for its Health Information Systems business, which could change its earnings mix.
The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 with two dissents in favor of a hike, which keeps financing costs for elective procedures and dental equipment high.
Align Technology, Cooper Companies, Dentsply Sirona, ICU Medical, Solventum

Revenue comes mainly from repeat consumables: Cooper's CooperVision contact lenses (Biofinity is its highest-grossing product) and CooperSurgical fertility and women's health products, Align's aligner cases, and ICU Medical's consumables and infusion systems. Some firms add equipment, such as Align's scanners (Systems and Services $715M-$725M guided for 2026).

Customers are eye-care practitioners, optical chains and mass merchandisers for lenses; dentists, orthodontists and DSOs for dental; and hospitals, clinics and distributors for infusion and surgical supplies. Cooper reported no single customer at 10% or more of revenue in fiscal 2025.

Principal costs are materials, manufacturing labor, sales and R&D. Align has about 20,290 employees, about 91% outside the US, with large sites in Mexico, Costa Rica and China. Cooper manufactures in Belgium, Costa Rica, Hungary, Puerto Rico, the UK and the US. Damodaran's Healthcare Products group has a 54.00% gross margin.

Pricing power rests on brand with clinicians, clinical evidence, regulatory clearance and switching costs: a dentist trained on a digital workflow or a hospital with installed pumps rarely switches. It weakens against DSOs and group buyers, and Align says promotions and rivals could reduce ASPs. We think premium lens and aligner brands hold more pricing power than commodity hospital disposables.

Major assets are plants, intellectual property, goodwill from acquisitions and inventory; liabilities are mostly debt, and Damodaran's healthcare products group carries debt of 2.74x EBITDA and book debt to capital of 35.70%. Dentsply's long-term debt was $1,985M and Solventum's about $4.6B net of cash at 30 Sep 2026 on our arithmetic.

Mostly asset-moderate rather than asset-light. Damodaran shows net capital spending of 4.53% of sales and capex at 79.54% of depreciation for Healthcare Products; Align guides 2026 capex of $125M-$150M on about $4.1B of revenue. The heavy investment is in R&D and acquired intangibles, not in buildings.

No sub-industry-wide market size is published that we could open. One sub-segment, contact lenses, is estimated at $13.2B in 2026 and growing 5.0% a year to 2035 by Roots Analysis. US dental spending was $189B in 2024, up 3.6% on an inflation-adjusted basis, with consumer dental spending up 4% in the year to January 2026.

Main segments are vision care (lenses), orthodontics and dental consumables, infusion and hospital consumables, wound care and surgical supplies, and fertility and women's health. Roots sizes soft lenses at about 75% of contact lens sales and daily disposables at about 40%. Solventum alone reports five segments, including wound care ($528M in Q3) and dental ($317M).

These companies sit between component and resin suppliers upstream and clinicians, hospitals and distributors downstream. Align sells directly and through distributors in more than 100 countries, and Cooper in over 130, using its own sales force, distributors, practitioners and optical chains. Patients and insurers or payers ultimately fund the purchase.

The industry has moved from conventional to disposable lenses, from wire braces to digital clear aligners, and from stand-alone products to digital workflows tied to scanners and software. Align estimates it holds about 10% of the roughly 22 million annual orthodontic case starts, and over 22 million people have been treated with Invisalign. Corporate carve-outs such as Solventum from 3M reshape the group.

Concentration follows the end markets: North America holds about 40% of contact lens sales. Production is global and often near low-cost hubs: Align's aligner plants are in Mexico, China and Poland, Cooper's in Europe, Costa Rica and the US, and employees at Align work in 48 countries.

Each product niche has a handful of significant competitors rather than one crowded field. In contact lenses Cooper's 10-K names Johnson & Johnson Vision Care, Alcon and Bausch + Lomb; Roots lists those plus Menicon, SEED, HOYA and others. In aligners Align faces wire braces, other aligner makers, direct-to-consumer firms and doctors who 3D-print their own.

Leaders by niche: CooperVision, J&J Vision, Alcon and Bausch + Lomb in lenses; Align in aligners; Dentsply Sirona and Solventum in dental; ICU Medical in infusion consumables. We did not find a reliable, sourced market share table for lenses; Align puts its own share of annual orthodontic case starts at about 10%.

Concentrated at the top in lenses, more fragmented in dental and hospital disposables. We read the sector as a set of oligopolies in specific products inside a diverse group, not one consolidated industry, because each competitor named in filings differs by niche.

Barriers to entry include FDA clearance, ISO 13485 quality systems, clinician training and distribution reach. Align's Invisalign was FDA-cleared in 1998 and about 130,015 doctors were active users at end-2025. Entry is easier in commodity disposables and in 3D-printed aligners made at the practice.

Scale matters in manufacturing and R&D: Align's 11 fabrication and treatment-planning sites and regional plants spread fixed costs across 690,635 cases in a single quarter. Rivals with larger budgets and sales forces are a stated risk in Cooper's filing.

Mixed. Aligners and daily lenses are differentiated by materials, fit and software, while many hospital consumables behave as commodities competing on price and supply. Align's ASP guided down about 1% in Q4 2026 shows how promotions and mix can erode price even for a differentiated product.

Customers hold growing power: DSOs and large group practices, and in hospital supplies group buyers and distributors, which Align names as a dependency. Suppliers have power where inputs are sole-sourced: Align says some components and materials come from sole-source suppliers.

Revenue growth is driven by procedure and visit volumes, new products and share gains, geographic expansion and price or mix. Align guides 2026 Clear Aligner volume up about 5% to 6% with ASP slightly down, and Solventum organic growth toward the high end of 2.5% to 3.0%.

Operating margin depends on gross margin (mix and manufacturing), operating leverage on fixed sales and R&D cost, and restructuring. Align's non-GAAP operating margin was 24.4% in Q3 with 26% guided for Q4; Solventum's adjusted operating margin was 19.9%; Dentsply's adjusted EBITDA margin was 17.3% including a $39M one-off.

Key cost variables are resins and plastics, labor, freight, tariffs and currency. Align says tariffs on Mexico-made aligners shipped to the US could pressure margin, and Solventum's gross margin guide includes a 1.2-point benefit from a tariff refund. Consumer or practice demand is not a cost but changes absorption.

Rates matter through the customer, not the company. Align's filing says elective orthodontic spending can fall with higher interest rates or a weaker outlook, and dental practices may delay equipment purchases. The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 with two members preferring a hike.

Inflation lifts input costs and squeezes patient budgets: HPI reports 17% of adults aged 19 to 64 skipped needed dental care because of cost versus 7.4% for medical care. GDP and unemployment affect discretionary care first. The Fed said inflation remains elevated and the unemployment rate has changed little. Commodity exposure is mainly petrochemical resins, which we did not find sourced figures for.

A blend. Hospital and lens consumables are close to defensive because patients need them regardless; aligners, dental equipment and elective procedures are cyclical; and secular drivers include myopia, aging and digital dentistry. Align's own filing says malocclusion affects 60% to 75% of people and only about 22 million of 600 million who could benefit elect treatment each year.

Growth is modest. Align's Q3 revenue rose 1.9%, Cooper's 0.6%, ICU Medical's about 4% and Dentsply's fell 7.6%, while Solventum's nine-month organic growth was 2.9%. Damodaran lists a forward P/E of 42.33 for Healthcare Products, implying the market expects faster growth than recent prints show.

Damodaran's January 2026 data for 204 US Healthcare Products firms show a 54.00% gross margin, 17.40% operating margin and 9.61% net margin. Solventum's adjusted gross margin was 57.1% and Align's non-GAAP gross margin 70.4% in Q3 2026.

Damodaran puts ROE for Healthcare Products at 11.26% unadjusted and 9.37% adjusted for R&D. We did not find a sourced ROIC for the sub-industry; acquisitive models such as Dentsply and Cooper carry large goodwill, which depresses return on capital in our view.

Leverage varies. Damodaran shows debt of 2.74x EBITDA and book debt to capital of 35.70%. ICU Medical's net leverage was 2.04x on $858.0M of net debt; Dentsply's net debt was about $2.0B against $195M of cash; Solventum's about $4.6B (our arithmetic from reported debt and cash).

Free cash flow is solid but lumpy. ICU Medical generated $83.4M in Q3 including tariff refunds; Dentsply's Q3 free cash flow was zero; Solventum's nine-month free cash flow was negative $32M against a $200M-$300M full-year guide. Align holds $1,144.9M of cash and plans about $500M of buybacks in 2026.

Capital spending is moderate: net capex is 4.53% of sales and 79.54% of depreciation in Damodaran's group, and Align guides $125M-$150M for 2026. Dentsply's Q3 capex was $32M. R&D is the larger commitment, at $1.03B net across the Damodaran group.

On Damodaran's January 2026 data, EV/EBITDA is 19.78 (positive-EBITDA firms) and 23.42 across all firms, EV/EBIT 29.99, and trailing P/E 55.87. The SPDR Health Care Equipment ETF trades at 19.65x FY1 earnings on 13 Nov 2026. Damodaran's category is broader than this sub-industry.

Tariff and trade law is the live regulatory risk. The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on 20 Feb 2026 that IEEPA does not authorize broad tariffs, but the administration may use other authorities and no refund process was set by the ruling. Align cites a Section 232 investigation into medical devices. FDA clearance, EU MDR and privacy law also apply.

AI and digital workflows are mostly an opportunity for incumbents (treatment planning, scanning), but they lower the cost for new entrants, and cybersecurity threats including AI-enabled attacks are a flagged risk at Align. 3D printing lets practices make their own aligners.

Aging populations raise demand for infusion, wound care and restorative dental products, and children's myopia increases lens demand; we think this is a slow tailwind. Usage gaps persist: in 2022 18% of Medicaid adults saw a dentist versus 57% with private insurance.

Consumers are price-sensitive on elective care and increasingly buy through DSOs, online and direct-to-consumer channels. Align's CFO cited a softer environment for discretionary health spending. Align's filing says patients may choose lower-cost treatments in weaker economies.

New competitors and models include direct-to-consumer aligner companies, in-office 3D-printed aligners, and regional rivals. In lenses, Cooper's filing names smaller firms with limited lines alongside the three majors. Corporate separations create new focused rivals, such as Solventum from 3M.

Geopolitical and supply-chain exposure is large: Align cites operations in Israel (iTero) and manufacturing in Mexico, and sole-source components. AdvaMed says device supply chains are hard to change because components must meet FDA and international requirements, and switching suppliers can take years.

Substitutes include spectacles, refractive surgery and monthly lenses against daily disposables; Cooper names eyeglass makers and ophthalmic surgery as lesser competitors. In orthodontics wires and brackets remain the main alternative to aligners. For infusion, hospital protocol changes could reduce consumable use, which we do not see sourced.
Undertreated demand: only about 22 million of roughly 600 million people who could benefit from straightening elect treatment each year, and Align holds about 10% of annual orthodontist case starts.
Contact lens growth of about 5.0% a year to 2035, with specialty and myopia lenses growing faster, supports CooperVision's mix.
Cost and portfolio actions: Solventum has exited about 90% of 3M transition services and Cooper raised its buyback authorization to $3B.
Dental spending is growing, up 4% in the year to January 2026, giving a steady base for consumables.
Tariffs and trade policy remain unresolved after the IEEPA ruling, with Section 232 outstanding.
Discretionary dental and orthodontic demand could stay weak while interest rates stay near 3.75%-4.00%.
ASP erosion and competition from direct-to-consumer and in-office aligners.
Execution risk in restructurings: Dentsply's Q3 net sales fell 7.6% and free cash flow was zero.

Over three to five years we think demand for the products in this group (lenses, aligners, dental and hospital consumables) is structurally supported by aging, myopia and under-penetrated orthodontics, but recent results show that growth is low single digit and that margins rely partly on cost cuts and one-off tariff refunds. The winners are likely to be companies with differentiated, clinician-embedded products and clean balance sheets, such as those with leverage near 2x EBITDA. The losers are likely to be firms in commodity or restructuring-heavy niches, where Dentsply's 2026 sales guide of about $3.5B shows how volumes can shrink. Policy is the swing factor: tariffs and refunds can move margins by a point or more, as Solventum's 1.2-point gross margin benefit shows.

We think the sub-industry sits in a late-cycle, rate-constrained phase for discretionary spending but not for core hospital use. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by 10 to 2, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferring a quarter-point increase, and it said inflation remains elevated while job gains have kept pace with the workforce. That backdrop matters for elective care and for equipment purchases that practices finance.

Align's filing says consumer spending on elective orthodontics can fall with inflation, interest rates or a weaker outlook, and practices may delay equipment purchases. Align's CFO described a softer environment for discretionary health care spending and capital equipment investment in Q3 2026, and Align's imaging revenue fell 7.6%. Dentsply's Connected Technology Solutions fell 11% to $230M, which is consistent with weak equipment demand.

Currency is a second cyclical factor: Align's filing notes a large share of revenue and expenses in foreign currencies. Against that, dental spending data are less weak than the equipment data: consumer dental spending was up 4% as of January 2026 versus a year earlier. We read the pattern as consumers still visiting but deferring big-ticket treatment and practices deferring capital purchases.

Structural demand is anchored by aging, myopia and under-penetrated orthodontics rather than by any single large market. Roots Analysis puts the contact lens market at $13.2B in 2026, up from $12.7B in 2025 and growing 5.0% a year to $20.5B by 2035; soft lenses are about 75% of sales and daily disposables about 40%. That is a third-party estimate and figures differ by publisher.

In orthodontics, Align says malocclusion affects 60% to 75% of the global population, about 600 million people could benefit from straightening, but only about 22 million elect treatment each year, and Align holds about 10% of those starts. US dental spending reached $189B in 2024, up 3.6% inflation-adjusted.

Demand is partly elastic. Align's volume grew 6.6% in Q3 while revenue grew 4.2% for clear aligners as ASP slipped, and it guides 2026 volume growth of 5% to 6% with ASP down slightly. Cost barriers are real: 17% of adults aged 19 to 64 skipped dental care because of cost. Hospital consumables behave more defensively: ICU Medical's Consumables revenue was $298.4M, up $13.3M.

Using Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense in lenses, where Cooper's 10-K names Johnson & Johnson Vision Care, Alcon and Bausch + Lomb as the main rivals. Threat of new entrants is moderate: FDA clearance, ISO 13485 quality systems and clinician adoption protect incumbents, but Align lists direct-to-consumer firms and doctors who 3D-print aligners as competitors.

Buyer power is rising: Align names reliance on DSOs and large group practices as a risk, while Cooper has no customer at 10% or more of revenue, which limits buyer leverage in lenses. Supplier power is meaningful for sole-source components. The threat of substitutes comes from wires and brackets in orthodontics and from eyeglasses and surgery in vision correction.

Moats come from brands, clinical workflows and scale. Align counts about 130,015 active Invisalign-trained doctors and over 22 million treated patients. Pricing power is real but eroding where cheaper options exist: Align guides Q4 ASP down about 1%. We did not find sourced market-share tables for lenses or dental consumables.

Politically the biggest factor is trade. The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on 20 Feb 2026 in Learning Resources v. Trump that IEEPA does not authorize broad tariffs, leaving refunds to lower courts and the administration and signalling that other trade laws may be used; AdvaMed noted that device supply chains cannot be changed quickly and costs are hard to pass through. Align's filing notes a Section 232 investigation into medical devices.

Refunds already show up in results: Dentsply's 2026 guide excludes a $0.17 one-time benefit from tariff refunds, Solventum's Q3 free cash flow was helped by an IEEPA refund, and ICU Medical excluded $19M of refunds from its FY2026 outlook. We treat these as non-recurring.

Regulation covers FDA 510(k), PMA and de novo pathways, EU MDR and IVDR, UK MHRA, China NMPA and Japan PMDA for Cooper, plus anti-kickback and privacy laws. Align flags PFAS and chemical restrictions. Technologically, digital scanning, 3D printing and AI-assisted planning favor scaled incumbents but lower entry costs. Social factors include aging and rising myopia in children, which supports lens makers.

Margins are high at the product-brand end and lower in broad supplies. Damodaran's January 2026 table for 204 Healthcare Products firms shows gross margin 54.00%, operating margin 17.40% and net margin 9.61%. Align's Q3 non-GAAP gross margin was 70.4% and non-GAAP operating margin 24.4%, versus Solventum's adjusted gross margin of 57.1% and adjusted operating margin of 19.9%.

Operating leverage is visible in weak quarters: Dentsply's net sales fell 7.6% and adjusted EBITDA margin slipped to 17.3% from 18.4%, and that included a $39M non-recurring benefit, so underlying margin was lower. ICU Medical's adjusted EBITDA grew to $113.9M from $105.9M on a 4.4% revenue rise.

Returns are modest. Damodaran's ROE is 11.26% (9.37% R&D-adjusted); we found no sourced ROIC for the sub-industry. Capital intensity is moderate: net capex is 4.53% of sales. Free cash flow is uneven: Dentsply produced none in Q3, ICU $83.4M, and Solventum is negative for nine months against a $200M-$300M guide. Debt is manageable at 2.74x EBITDA for the Damodaran group.

Guidance is mixed to softer. Align guides 2026 revenue to about $4.11B-$4.13B with non-GAAP operating margin about 23.7%, and Q4 revenue of $1.00B-$1.02B. Cooper cut FY2026 revenue guidance to $4.229B-$4.252B from $4.285B-$4.321B and adjusted EPS to $4.51-$4.55 from $4.58-$4.66. Dentsply guides sales of about $3.5B and adjusted EPS of $1.20-$1.30 excluding a $0.17 refund.

Brighter spots: Solventum raised adjusted EPS guidance to $7.20-$7.30 from $7.10-$7.20 with organic growth toward the high end of 2.5%-3.0%. ICU Medical reaffirmed adjusted EPS of $8.60-$9.00 and expects the high end.

Across the S&P 500, FactSet shows Q3 2026 blended earnings growth of 31.9%, and the Health Care sector reported the largest aggregate positive earnings surprise at +13.7%, with revenue growth of 6.3%. That is sector-wide and driven by managed care and pharma, not supplies. A sourced consensus EPS growth figure for this sub-industry was not available to us.

Our view: consensus probably still assumes recovery in dental equipment and aligner pricing in 2027; Align's ASP decline and Dentsply's restructuring suggest that risks lean to the downside, while tariff refunds flatter 2026 comparisons.

A sub-industry forward P/E was not publicly available. The closest listed proxy is the State Street SPDR S&P Health Care Equipment ETF, which shows a P/E of 19.65 on FY1 earnings as of 13 Nov 2026. FactSet puts the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.3, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1. On that basis the equipment group trades at a premium of about 1.3 turns to the index, though the ETF covers more than supplies.

Damodaran's January 2026 data for Healthcare Products show EV/EBITDA of 19.78 for positive-EBITDA firms, EV/EBIT of 29.99, forward P/E of 42.33, current P/E of 55.87 and a PEG ratio of 2.74. Those multiples are high against the broad market, but the category contains growth-heavy names and the data predate recent moves.

Cooper's shares fell about 14% overnight to $54.55 after it cut guidance and kept CooperSurgical, which suggests the market was already pricing weak growth for contact lenses. Align repurchased 627.3 thousand shares at an average of $164.73 in Q3. FactSet's bottom-up analyst targets imply 8.3% upside for Health Care versus 22.2% for the index.

Relative performance has been unremarkable. The SPDR S&P Health Care Equipment ETF returned 3.49% year to date and 14.30% over one year to 31 Oct 2026 on a NAV basis, against 3.76% and 14.67% for its benchmark. That compares with an S&P 500 whose forward earnings estimate has risen 3.3% since 30 Sep while its price fell 0.8%.

The ETF held $156.59M of assets on 13 Nov 2026 across 73 holdings, with the largest weight at only 2.21% (Enovis), so it behaves like an equal-weighted basket of mid-sized names. We could not find sourced flow or short-interest data for the sub-industry, so we make no claim on positioning there.

Company-level signals: buybacks are the main capital-return tool. Align plans up to $300M in Q4 and about $500M in 2026, with $630.0M remaining on its authorization, and Cooper raised its authorization to $3B from $2B.

Health care technology is growing fast where it sells software that saves providers or drug makers money, and shrinking where it sells to consumers. Veeva raised fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $3.682-$3.687B after 18% growth; Waystar grew 21% with a 43% EBITDA margin; Tempus lifted 2026 revenue guidance to $1.60B. Doximity grew only 4% and Teladoc's BetterHelp fell 13%. Hospital EHR buying fell 40% in 2025. We found no sourced forward multiple for the sub-industry; Damodaran's group EV/EBITDA is 21.3x.

Health care technology companies sell software and data services to hospitals, doctors, insurers and drug makers, and increasingly directly to patients. They mostly earn subscription fees, usage fees on transactions, or advertising and data revenue. GICS places electronic health records, revenue-cycle software, life-sciences cloud software, telehealth and health data analytics here. Hospital operators sit in Health Care Facilities, insurers in Managed Health Care, and medical devices in Equipment and Supplies, even when they are connected.

Electronic health records and clinical software: The system of record for a patient's chart, orders and results, sold to hospitals and clinics on long contracts. Switching is costly and slow. e.g. Epic (private), Oracle Health, MEDITECH, TruBridge

Revenue-cycle and payments software: Tools that check insurance eligibility, submit claims, handle denials and collect patient payments. Vendors are paid by subscription and by volume. e.g. Waystar, R1 RCM
Life-sciences cloud software: Software for drug makers covering sales and marketing, clinical trials, regulatory filings, quality and safety. e.g. Veeva Vault CRM, Vault Clinical, Vault Safety
Telehealth and virtual care: Video visits, remote monitoring and online therapy, paid by employers, insurers or consumers. e.g. Teladoc Integrated Care and BetterHelp
Physician networks and clinical AI: Professional platforms and AI tools for clinicians, usually monetised through pharma marketing and subscriptions. e.g. Doximity, Doximity Ask
Health data and precision medicine: Companies that combine lab testing with large clinical datasets and license the data to drug developers. e.g. Tempus AI diagnostics and data licensing
Provider IT budgets: Hospitals decide when to replace systems. When margins are tight or policy is uncertain they delay big projects, which slows new-contract revenue for EHR and workflow vendors.
Drug-maker commercial and R&D spend: Life-sciences software follows pharma budgets and product launches. Cuts or reorganisations slow new modules, while migrations to new products add revenue.

Insurer and government payment rules: Reimbursement, prior authorisation and telehealth rules decide whether a service is paid, and therefore whether the software or virtual-care product is worth buying.
AI adoption: AI features can raise prices and engagement, but they also cost compute and can let new entrants compete, so margins and market share can both move.
Switching costs and installed base: Records and workflows are hard to move, so incumbents keep customers for years. Revenue growth then depends on cross-selling modules into the base.
Consumer demand and marketing cost: Direct-to-consumer services depend on advertising and willingness to pay. A shift to insurance can cut price but widen the market.
EHR (electronic health record): The digital patient chart. It is the core hospital IT system and the platform other software connects to.
Revenue cycle management (RCM): The process of getting paid by insurers and patients, from registration to claim to collection. Software here lowers hospitals' denials and labor cost.
SaaS: Software as a service: customers pay a recurring subscription instead of buying a licence. It gives predictable revenue.
Net revenue retention (NRR): Revenue this year from last year's customers as a percentage of what they paid last year. Above 100% means existing clients are spending more.
Interoperability: The ability of different health IT systems to exchange data. Rules in this area decide how open the big EHR vendors must be.
FHIR: A standard way for health systems to share data through application programming interfaces (APIs). Regulators are building their requirements on it.
Information blocking: A US rule that penalises vendors and providers who unreasonably restrict access to health data.
Bookings and backlog: Contracts signed but not yet live. Revenue arrives only after implementation, so a gap between bookings and revenue is common.
Payer and provider: The payer is the insurer or government that pays; the provider is the hospital or doctor. Vendors sell to both.
Telehealth flexibilities: Temporary Medicare rules that let patients be paid for virtual care at home. Their expiry dates drive sentiment in virtual care.
Cash-pay vs insurance-covered: Whether the patient pays out of pocket or the insurer pays. Moving from cash-pay to insurance changes customer acquisition cost and price.
Convertible notes: Debt that can be exchanged for shares. Several digital-health companies used them, and maturities force refinancing decisions.
Waystar's longer implementation cycles for large clients cut the top of its 2026 revenue range, and it will give 2027 guidance next quarter.
Teladoc's roughly $998M of convertible notes are classed as current liabilities against $850M of cash, so refinancing is a live issue.
Doximity's growth slowed to 4% and its EBITDA margin fell about nine points as it invests in AI; the company's fiscal year ends in March.
Medicare telehealth flexibilities run to 31 Dec 2027, so the next cliff is a year away.
HTI-5 cut 14 of 60 EHR certification criteria and dropped AI model-card requirements, but deferred information-blocking changes.
Veeva Systems, Doximity, Waystar, Tempus AI, Teladoc Health

Revenue comes from three places: recurring subscriptions to software (Veeva's subscription revenue was $766.8M of $928.0M in its July 2026 quarter), volume-based fees on transactions (Waystar's volume-based revenue was $142.9M and subscription $180.7M in Q3 2026), and consumer or advertising revenue, as at Teladoc's BetterHelp and Doximity's pharma marketing.

Customers are hospitals, physician groups and health systems (EHR and revenue-cycle tools), drug makers (Veeva, Tempus data licensing), employers and insurers (Teladoc's Integrated Care, which counted a guided 99.5M-100.5M US members) and, for some products, patients directly. Veeva served more than 1,500 customers in the July 2026 quarter.

The main costs are engineers and implementation staff, cloud hosting and, for service-heavy models, clinicians and labs. Tempus's gross margin was 64.8% on GAAP, against a software-style 71.7% for Damodaran's broad software group and 48.3% for health care information and technology. Consumer products add marketing, which Teladoc reports inside BetterHelp's thin 2.2% EBITDA margin.

Pricing power comes from switching costs and regulatory or workflow lock-in. Veeva and the large EHR vendors can raise prices at renewal because the system holds validated records or regulated content. Where products are easily substituted or sold to consumers, as with BetterHelp's cash-pay revenue, which fell 25% in Q3 2026, pricing power is weak.

Main assets are capitalised software, customer contracts, goodwill from acquisitions, and cash. Main liabilities are deferred revenue and debt. Waystar had $1,470.6M of gross debt and 2.2x net leverage; Teladoc held $849.9M of cash against $997.6M of convertible notes classed as current.

The business is asset-light: Damodaran's data show net capital spending equal to 0.92% of sales for 115 health care information and technology firms. The exceptions are lab-based models such as Tempus, which also invests in sequencing and data assets, and acquisitive firms that carry large goodwill.

No single sourced market size covers the GICS group, because definitions differ. One research firm forecasts the US healthcare IT software market at $203.0B in 2026, growing 13.8% a year to 2035; that is a forecast from a paid-report seller, so treat it as indicative. For listed companies, Veeva's fiscal 2026 revenue was $3.2B, up 16.3%.

Main segments are electronic health records and clinical systems, revenue-cycle and payments, life-sciences software, telehealth and virtual care, and health data and analytics. The Towards Healthcare listing names functions such as patient record management, clinical decision support, claims processing and telemedicine.

In the value chain, these companies sit between the clinical and financial parties. They buy cloud computing and data, and sell to hospitals, insurers and drug makers; some also sell to patients. Waystar's revenue split is $243.4M from providers and $82.2M from patients in Q3 2026, while Veeva sells to large pharma and emerging biotechs.

The industry moved from on-premise hospital systems to cloud subscriptions, then to analytics and now AI. Federal incentives pushed hospitals to digitise records. The new phase is regulatory: HTI-5 cut 14 of 60 certification criteria in October 2026 and dropped AI model-card requirements. New hospital EHR decisions are slowing, with 164 hospitals deciding in 2025 versus 272 in 2024.

Sales and production are concentrated in the United States, because its fragmented, insurance-driven system creates the billing and compliance work these tools address. Epic, Oracle Health and MEDITECH hold the bulk of US acute-care hospital EHRs, and the KLAS-based share data cited here describe the US market; we found no sourced revenue split by country for these firms.

The sub-industry has dozens of listed companies and many private ones. Damodaran's January 2026 dataset counts 115 US firms in healthcare information and technology. The market is a set of niches, each with only a handful of significant vendors.

Leaders vary by niche. In acute-care EHRs, KLAS fiscal 2024 data cited by Towards Healthcare show Epic with 42.3% of hospitals and 54.9% of beds, Oracle Health 22.9% and 22.1%, and MEDITECH 14.8% and 12.7%. In life-sciences CRM, Veeva has more than 180 customers live on Vault CRM, including five of the top 20 biopharmas. Revenue-cycle has Waystar and R1 RCM.

Core niches are consolidated, with a few vendors holding most share, while the wider industry is fragmented with many start-ups. Rock Health counted 164 digital-health M&A deals in 2026 through Q3, showing steady consolidation among smaller firms.

Barriers to entry are high in regulated systems of record: integration into hospital workflow, certification and the trust of clinicians. They are low in consumer apps and point solutions, where venture capital funds many entrants; US digital-health start-ups raised $11.1B across 358 deals in 2026 to date.

Economies of scale matter in data and distribution. Doximity's network includes more than 85% of US physicians, and Tempus's data business grew 33% on its large clinical dataset. Larger vendors spread development cost over more customers and can fund AI features.
Products are differentiated in systems of record, where switching is costly, and closer to commoditised in telehealth visits and consumer therapy, where BetterHelp's paying users fell 12% in Q3 2026.

Bargaining power lies mainly with customers for new contracts, since hospital budgets are tight and purchases have slowed 40%. After go-live, power shifts to the vendor because of switching costs. Suppliers (cloud and AI model providers) have moderate power; we found no sourced data on their share of vendor costs.

Revenue growth is driven by provider and drug-maker IT budgets, transaction volumes, new modules sold into an installed base, and new AI products. Veeva's growth of 18% is partly Vault CRM migrations; Waystar's subscription revenue rose 34%; Tempus's data revenue rose 33%.

Operating margins depend on scale and mix: Damodaran gives 17.1% pre-tax operating margin before stock compensation for health care information and technology versus 40.8% for system and application software. Individual firms differ widely: Doximity's adjusted EBITDA margin was 50.9% and Waystar's was 42.8%.

The key costs are engineering and sales staff, cloud and AI compute, implementation labor, and, for lab-based models, reagents and clinical staff. Doximity's margin fell from 59.8% to 50.9% as it invested in AI, showing how heavy AI spend can compress margins.

Interest-rate sensitivity is moderate and works through valuations and balance sheets. Damodaran shows book debt to capital of 38.3% but market debt to capital of just 13.4%, so most companies are lightly levered; Waystar's net leverage was 2.2x and Teladoc has near-term convertible maturities.

Inflation affects wages and cloud costs; GDP and unemployment matter less because health spending is steady, though employer-funded telehealth can follow employment. Commodity prices barely matter. The main macro channel is hospital margins and the willingness to commit to large projects.

The group is mostly secular growth with a defensive demand base, but not uniformly. Software and data businesses grow through the cycle, hospital system replacement is cyclical (purchases fell 40% in 2025), and consumer virtual care is shrinking.
Growth varies by sub-model. Veeva grew revenue 16.3% in fiscal 2026 and 18% in the July 2026 quarter; Waystar grew 21%; Tempus 23%; Doximity 4%; and Teladoc fell 3%.

Damodaran's January 2026 dataset gives a gross margin of 48.3%, net margin of 7.5% and EBITDA margin of 20.5% for 115 health care information and technology firms. Leading software firms are far higher: Veeva's non-GAAP operating income was $415.9M on $928.0M of revenue, about 45%.

Return on equity for the group is low: 6.40% unadjusted and 5.46% adjusted for R&D in Damodaran's data. The page we opened did not list ROIC for this group, so we cannot quote one. Veeva's fiscal 2026 net income of $908.9M on $3.2B of revenue is the profitable end of the range.

Debt is modest on market value but not trivial on book value: 38.3% book debt to capital, 13.4% market debt to capital and debt to EBITDA of 3.61. Waystar had 2.2x adjusted net leverage; Teladoc's $997.6M of convertible notes is current.

Free cash flow is generally strong for mature subscription companies: Doximity generated $91.3M of free cash flow in the September 2026 quarter, Waystar $114.8M of unlevered free cash flow in Q3, and Teladoc guides to $135M-$165M for 2026.

Capital spending is low. Damodaran shows capital expenditure of 0.92% of sales and 54.4% of depreciation, consistent with asset-light software. Lab-based and acquisitive firms spend more or carry goodwill.

Valuation is above the market average on the sector multiple. Damodaran's EV/EBITDA is 21.3x for positive-EBITDA firms and 25.9x for all firms, while FactSet put the S&P 500's forward P/E at 18.3x on 13 Nov 2026. We found no sourced forward P/E for this sub-industry.

Regulation can cut both ways. HTI-5 eased burdens, removing 14 of 60 certification criteria and AI model-card requirements, but deferred information-blocking changes that could widen data access for rivals. Medicare telehealth flexibilities run to 31 Dec 2027, and payer rules affect Waystar and Teladoc.

AI is both opportunity and threat. Veeva calls AI the next big chapter, Doximity sold its AI suite to more than 190 health systems, and Tempus's data unit grew 33%. Yet general-purpose AI could reduce demand for point software, and spending on AI compresses margins, as at Doximity.

Demographics support demand: an older population raises utilisation and the billing work that Waystar automates. The effect is long-term and indirect, and we found no sourced demographic figure; the more immediate swing factor is provider budgets.

Changing consumer behavior is visible in BetterHelp: cash-pay revenue fell 25% to $174.5M in Q3 2026 while insurance-covered revenue rose to $32.1M from $3.7M. Consumers are moving to insured, lower-priced care, and employers are weighing virtual-care benefits.

New competitors and business models include well-funded start-ups: US digital health raised $3.7B in Q3 2026 alone, and Veeva's Vault CRM push shows incumbents can be challenged in established categories. Oracle Health's share loss to Epic shows incumbents can be displaced.

Geopolitical and supply-chain risk is lower than in hardware sectors, because these firms sell software and services mostly in the US. We found no sourced figures on tariff or trade exposure for the group. Cybersecurity and data privacy are also exposures; we found no sourced loss figures.

Substitutes are in-house build, large general software platforms, and consumer apps. Hospital customers can delay or avoid a vendor when budgets are tight, and telehealth can be replaced by in-person care if reimbursement lapses.
Insurance coverage can widen the market for virtual mental health, as BetterHelp's insurance revenue reached $32.1M in Q3 2026.
AI products can raise engagement and price: more than 190 health systems bought Doximity's AI suite and Veeva reports momentum in AI.
Revenue-cycle automation has a large installed base to sell into, with 1,488 Waystar clients each generating over $100,000 of annual revenue.
Data licensing and diagnostics, as at Tempus, scale with drug developers' demand for clinical datasets.
Hospital IT budgets are cautious: EHR decisions affected 40% fewer hospitals in 2025 than in 2024.
Slower growth at some leaders, such as Doximity's 4%, and margin pressure from AI investment.
Policy cliffs, including the end-2027 expiry of Medicare telehealth flexibilities.
Refinancing and balance-sheet pressure at consumer-heavy names, such as Teladoc's current convertible notes.

Over three to five years we think the group keeps splitting into two. Companies that sit inside regulated workflows and own data, such as Veeva, Waystar and Tempus, should keep compounding at double-digit rates, because switching costs are high and AI gives them new modules to sell. Consumer-facing and advertising-led models face more risk: BetterHelp is shrinking and Doximity has slowed. Hospital budgets and policy decide the pace; the lighter-touch HTI-5 rules and extended telehealth rules help, but weak hospital purchasing shows demand is not guaranteed. Valuations already assume growth, with group EV/EBITDA of 21.3x.

Health care technology is less tied to the economic cycle than most technology, because its customers spend on health regardless of GDP. The cycle reaches it through hospital and drug-maker budgets. FactSet's 13 Nov 2026 report shows a strong market backdrop, with S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth of 31.9% and a forward P/E of 18.3, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1. The Health Care sector reported the largest positive earnings surprise at 13.7%, although that is driven by insurers and drug makers rather than software.

Within the sub-industry, the signal is mixed. Hospitals are being cautious: KLAS counted 164 hospitals making EHR decisions in 2025, down from 272 in 2024, and attributed the pause to policy uncertainty and competing spending priorities. Fiscal policy matters directly. Congress extended Medicare telehealth flexibilities to 31 Dec 2027 through H.R. 7148, signed 3 Feb 2026, which removes the near-term cliff for virtual care. We found no sourced interest-rate or currency sensitivity for the group; its balance sheets are mostly light, with market debt to capital of 13.4%.

Structural demand rests on the digitisation of a large, paperwork-heavy industry. One research publisher forecasts the US healthcare IT software market at $203.0B in 2026, growing 13.8% a year to 2035, though that figure comes from a market-research seller and definitions are broad. Company results are consistent with double-digit growth in the strongest niches: Veeva's revenue rose 18% to $928.0M, Waystar's 21% and Tempus's 23%.

Demand is not uniform. Software that cuts costs or speeds drug development sells well; products that depend on consumer payments or large hospital projects do not. BetterHelp revenue fell 13%, Doximity grew 4% and hospital EHR purchasing dropped 40% in 2025. We think this is a split between essential workflow software and discretionary products, rather than a decline in demand for health IT. Demographics, such as an ageing population, support utilisation, but we found no sourced figure tying them to revenue. Venture funding shows continued interest: $3.7B across 114 deals in Q3 2026.

Porter's five forces vary by niche. Threat of new entrants is low in systems of record, where Epic held 42.3% of hospitals and 54.9% of beds in KLAS's fiscal 2024 data, ahead of Oracle Health and MEDITECH, and high in consumer apps, where US start-ups raised $11.1B across 358 deals in 2026 to date. Buyer power is strong at the point of purchase, as shown by the 40% fall in hospital EHR decisions, but weakens after implementation because of switching costs.

Supplier power is moderate: cloud and AI infrastructure are inputs, but we found no sourced cost share. The threat of substitutes is highest for telehealth and point solutions. Rivalry is intense where Oracle Health's share is under pressure from Epic. Moats come from data and network effects: Doximity's network includes more than 85% of US physicians, and Veeva has more than 180 customers live on Vault CRM. Pricing power follows the moat; revenue retention is a useful test, and Waystar reported 108% net revenue retention.

Policy is currently light-touch. HHS's HTI-5 final rule, reported on 27 Oct 2026, cut 14 of 60 certification criteria, revised seven, removed AI model-card requirements and annual real-world testing plans, and was estimated by regulators to save $1.5B in compliance costs. It deferred information-blocking changes, including proposals to cover autonomous AI systems, so rules for data access remain unsettled. Regulators and vendors will watch whether lighter oversight speeds AI deployment or invites later correction.

Telehealth law is the other major political variable. H.R. 7148, signed 3 Feb 2026, extended Medicare telehealth flexibilities to 31 Dec 2027. Technological change is led by AI: Doximity says more than 190 health systems bought its AI suite and calls its Ask tool HIPAA-compliant generative AI, Veeva says AI opens its next chapter, and Tempus relies on AI-driven data and diagnostics. Emerging risks include cybersecurity and privacy; we found no sourced figures on breaches or fines.

Margins show the spread between models. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 115 health care information and technology firms give a 48.3% gross margin, 20.5% EBITDA margin, 17.1% pre-tax operating margin before stock compensation, and 7.5% net margin. Strong subscription companies exceed that: Veeva's non-GAAP operating income was $415.9M on $928.0M of revenue, Waystar's adjusted EBITDA margin was 42.8%, and Doximity's was 50.9%. Teladoc's BetterHelp earned only 2.2%.

Returns are modest at the group level: Damodaran shows ROE of 6.40% (5.46% R&D-adjusted). Capital intensity is low, with capital spending at 0.92% of sales, so operating leverage is high when revenue grows faster than costs. Free cash flow is solid: Doximity $91.3M, Waystar unlevered $114.8M and Teladoc guided at $135M-$165M for 2026. Tempus is the exception that is only turning profitable, with adjusted EBITDA of $25.6M. We could not source a group ROIC.

Company guidance is mostly rising. Veeva raised fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $3,682M-$3,687M and non-GAAP EPS to about $9.21. Tempus lifted 2026 revenue to $1.60B-$1.605B. Doximity guided fiscal 2027 revenue to $678M-$683M and adjusted EBITDA to $317M-$325M. Teladoc guided 2026 revenue to $2,395M-$2,441M and adjusted EBITDA to $277M-$303M. Waystar raised EBITDA guidance to $543M-$549M but narrowed revenue to $1.277B-$1.287B.

We found no public consensus EPS or revision data for the sub-industry itself. At the sector level, FactSet says Health Care's Q3 2026 revenue growth was revised up to 6.3% from 4.0% since 30 Sep. Our read is that expectations are highest where AI is a visible growth driver and lowest for Teladoc, where revenue is guided down. A point of difference from a simple growth narrative: Waystar's implementation lag and Doximity's margin step-down suggest that AI-driven demand converts to revenue and profit more slowly than headline demand implies.

We found no sourced forward P/E or history for the GICS sub-industry. The nearest sourced yardstick is Damodaran's January 2026 EV/EBITDA for health care information and technology: 21.3x for positive-EBITDA firms and 25.9x for all firms, and 35.0x on EV/EBIT for positive-EBITDA firms. For the market, FactSet put the S&P 500's forward P/E at 18.3 on 13 Nov 2026, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1.

On that comparison the group looks priced for growth: an EV/EBITDA above 20x implies sustained double-digit expansion, which fits Veeva, Waystar and Tempus but not Doximity's 4% or Teladoc's decline. We could not source a group free-cash-flow yield; company free cash flow is positive for Doximity and Teladoc's 2026 guidance, but we do not quote yields without price data. Valuation dispersion across the group is likely wide, which makes the average a weak guide.

We found limited sourced positioning data. The Global X HealthTech ETF (HEAL), one of the few pure-play vehicles, had assets of $37.64M across 42 holdings as of 12 Nov 2026, so the group has little dedicated passive money behind it. Its largest weights were Veeva at 6.19%, IQVIA 6.03%, Oscar Health 5.69%, Pro Medicus 4.93% and Tempus 4.85%, with Waystar at 3.80%. The fund also holds device and insurer names, so it is not a clean read of the GICS group.

For sector context, FactSet shows analysts' bottom-up target for the Health Care sector implies the smallest upside among S&P 500 sectors at 8.3%, and that 60% of its ratings are Buy; this describes the whole sector, not health care technology. Venture flows are stronger than public flows: $3.7B across 114 digital-health rounds in Q3 2026, yet no new IPOs since HeartFlow in August 2025. We found no sourced short-interest or price momentum data for the group.

Broadline retail is now a story of scale players growing and investing heavily. Amazon's Q3 2026 sales rose 12% to $201.9B with a record 13.9% operating margin, but trailing free cash flow turned negative at -$42.4B on AI capex. Alibaba's June-quarter customer management revenue fell 7% as it spends on quick commerce. MercadoLibre grew revenue 45% but operating income fell 6.6%. eBay accelerated; Coupang posted an operating loss after a fulfillment-center fire. US e-commerce was 17.1% of retail in Q2 2026. We found no sourced forward multiple for the sub-industry itself.
