Starbucks' fiscal fourth-quarter comparable sales rose 7.2%, while McDonald's U.S. comparable sales fell 0.2% in the third quarter, Taco Bell's fell 4% after a lettuce-linked outbreak and Chipotle's restaurant-level margin slipped to 23.3% from 24.5%. Darden's same-restaurant sales rose 3.1%. Menu prices keep climbing: food away from home was up 3.5% in the year to September. We found no sourced forward P/E for the sub-industry; Damodaran puts US restaurants at 17.5x EV/EBITDA.

Restaurant companies sell prepared food and drinks to consumers, either from restaurants they own or through franchisees who pay them fees. Customers are households eating out or ordering delivery. Companies make money from food and beverage sales, from rent and royalties on franchised stores, and from licensing. GICS puts restaurant chains, fast food and coffee shops here. Hotels and casinos sit in neighbouring sub-industries, and food distributors such as Sysco are Consumer Staples, not Restaurants. Delivery marketplaces and grocers are classified elsewhere.

Quick-service (fast food): Counter-service chains selling burgers, chicken, tacos and pizza at low prices, with drive-thru and delivery. Volume and speed matter more than check size. e.g. McDonald's, Taco Bell, KFC, Domino's
Fast casual: Counter-service with fresher ingredients and a higher price per meal, often with strong digital ordering. e.g. Chipotle
Coffee and beverage shops: Cafes selling coffee, tea and snacks with high drink share and frequent repeat visits, mostly in the morning. e.g. Starbucks
Casual dining: Sit-down restaurants with table service and alcohol, serving families and groups at a higher check. e.g. Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, Darden brands

Franchising and licensing: The brand owner lets independent operators or partners run restaurants and collects royalties, rent and fees, keeping little capital on the balance sheet. e.g. McDonald's franchise model, Yum's KFC and Taco Bell, Starbucks' licensed stores

Digital, loyalty and delivery: Apps, loyalty programs and delivery channels that bring in orders and customer data, often at the cost of third-party commissions. e.g. McDonald's loyalty program, Chipotle digital orders
Traffic versus price: Comparable sales equal visits times check. Price increases lift check but, if shoppers push back, visits fall, which shows up as flat or negative traffic.
Food and commodity costs: Beef, chicken, coffee, cooking oil and packaging prices move the cost of goods; chains pass some on through menu prices with a lag.
Labor costs and wage rules: Labor is the largest controllable cost. Minimum-wage increases and tight labor markets raise it, squeezing restaurant-level margin unless prices rise.
Consumer confidence and income: Eating out is discretionary at the margin, so weaker incomes shift diners from casual dining to fast food or home cooking.
Value wars: When rivals discount, others follow to protect traffic, which trims margins across the group.
Unit growth and franchising mix: New restaurants add revenue; franchising adds royalty income with little capital, lifting margin and returns.
Food safety and brand events: An outbreak can cut traffic quickly at one brand, as seen with recalls and illness reports, with recovery taking weeks to months.
Digital and delivery: Apps and loyalty add visits and data; third-party delivery adds sales but at a commission cost.
Comparable sales (same-store sales): Sales at restaurants open at least a year. It strips out openings and closures and is the main health gauge, split into traffic and average check.
Traffic (transactions): The number of customer visits. Rising traffic is healthier than growth from price alone, since price increases can drive visits away.
Average check: Revenue per transaction. It rises with menu prices and larger orders.
Franchised vs company-operated: Franchised restaurants are owned by operators who pay royalties and rent. Company-operated ones are owned by the chain, which books full sales and costs.
Royalty: A fee, usually a percentage of franchisee sales, paid to the brand. It is high-margin because the brand bears few of the restaurant's costs.
Restaurant-level margin: Sales less food, labor, occupancy and other restaurant costs, before corporate overhead. It shows how profitable the units themselves are.
Unit growth: The net increase in restaurants. It drives revenue growth for chains with room to expand.
Systemwide sales: Sales at all restaurants, franchised and company-owned. The brand earns only part of this, but it measures the size of the system.
Value menu: Low-priced offers that draw price-sensitive customers. Chains use them to win traffic, at some cost to margin.
Digital mix: The share of sales ordered through apps and websites. Higher mix can lift order size and loyalty but adds delivery and tech costs.
Chipotlane: Chipotle's drive-through lane for pre-ordered digital orders, used to speed service and add convenience.
Refranchising: Selling company-owned restaurants to franchisees to cut capital needs and raise the share of fee income.
McDonald's U.S. comparable sales were negative in Q3, and its entry-level value offer is being tested in about 1,900 U.S. restaurants ahead of a targeted national launch in early 2027.

Taco Bell's recovery from the July outbreak is the test for Yum: the brand is 38% of divisional operating profit, and management said recovered consumers spend 5% more and visit 6% more often than those lost.
Chipotle's margin is being squeezed by beef, freight and labor, with labor at 25.7% of revenue against 25.2% a year earlier.
Starbucks guides fiscal 2027 North America comparable sales of about 4.0% and a 13.5% to 14.0% non-GAAP operating margin, which tests whether its turnaround continues beyond a 7.2% comp.
Restaurant labor rules matter: California's $20 fast food wage is under a council that, per a February 2026 analysis, had not met since February 2025.
McDonald's, Starbucks, Chipotle, Yum! Brands, Darden Restaurants, Restaurant Brands International, Domino's Pizza

Revenue comes from food and beverage sales at company-operated restaurants, and from rent, royalties and fees at franchised ones. McDonald's Q3 2026 revenue was $7,157M: $4,487M franchised, $2,480M company-operated. Starbucks was 32% company-operated and 68% licensed at fiscal year end.

Customers are mainly households choosing where to eat, plus franchisees for franchisors. Starbucks' fiscal 2026 transactions rose 3.2% and ticket 3.0% across 41,607 coffeehouses. Loyalty members matter: McDonald's recorded over $11B of Q3 sales to loyalty members. Franchisees are a second customer, paying rent and royalties.

The main costs are food, labor, occupancy and marketing. At Chipotle in Q3 2026 food, beverage and packaging was 29.5% of revenue and labor 25.7%. Beef and freight were cited for margin pressure. Franchised chains carry far less of these because operators bear them.

Pricing power comes from brand, convenience and perceived value. Starbucks' fiscal Q4 ticket rose 5.2% with transactions up 1.8%, showing room to raise prices on a strong brand. McDonald's U.S. comparable sales fell 0.2% as negative guest counts were largely offset by check growth, which suggests diners are pushing back on price.

Major assets are real estate, kitchen equipment, brand names and, for franchisors, the franchise agreements. Liabilities include debt and leases. Starbucks ended fiscal 2026 with cash of $3,679.9M and total debt of about $13.3B, our derived sum. McDonald's collected rents of $10.44B in 2025 on franchised properties, per a third-party analysis.

The sub-industry mixes asset-light and capital-intensive models. McDonald's guides to about $3.7B of 2026 capex. Starbucks spent $1,263.6M in fiscal 2026 against operating cash flow of $4,988.4M. Chipotle owns almost all its 4,267 restaurants and opened 84 in Q3. Franchisors are much lighter than operators.

The National Restaurant Association projects about $1.55T of US restaurant and foodservice sales in 2026, with real growth of 1.3%, and 15.8M employees. Census data for food services and drinking places show $92.9B for October 2026 (seasonally adjusted, advance estimate). We did not find a sourced global market size.

Main segments are quick service, fast casual, coffee, casual dining and fine dining. Darden reports LongHorn, Olive Garden and Fine Dining separately. Yum runs Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger. Starbucks is the largest coffee chain, with 41,607 coffeehouses.

Restaurants sit between food and packaging suppliers and consumers. Suppliers include farmers, meat and produce processors and distributors, and customers range from individuals to delivery apps. Beef, freight and labor were pressure points at Chipotle. A food safety failure upstream can hit sales quickly: Taco Bell's July outbreak was traced to iceberg lettuce.

The industry has moved toward franchising, digital ordering and loyalty. Starbucks converted about 7,991 China coffeehouses to licensed operations in fiscal Q3 2026, and Yum divested Pizza Hut in two deals this year. Digital was 38.8% of Chipotle's food and beverage revenue, up from 36.7%.

Sales are concentrated in the US but the leaders are global. McDonald's had 46,554 restaurants at 30 Sep 2026, of which China held 8,395. Starbucks' U.S. had 16,781 of 41,607 coffeehouses, or 40%. KFC opened 878 restaurants in 66 countries in Q3.

The group has hundreds of listed and private chains; our sources cover McDonald's, Starbucks, Chipotle, Yum and Darden. Damodaran's January 2026 US restaurant/dining dataset holds 64 listed firms. We did not find a sourced count of all restaurant operators.

McDonald's is the largest by units, with 46,554 restaurants, and systemwide sales above $38B in Q3 2026 alone. Starbucks has 41,607 coffeehouses, Yum's KFC opened 878 restaurants in a quarter and Chipotle has 4,267 company-owned units. We found no sourced market-share table, so we give none.

The industry is fragmented overall, with a few consolidated global brands. Yum sold Pizza Hut to Yum China and LongRange Capital while keeping KFC and Taco Bell. Franchising lets leaders scale: McDonald's targets 50,000 restaurants by end of 2028.

Barriers to entry are low for a single restaurant but high for a national chain. Brand, real estate, supply contracts and franchisee relationships take years to build. A brand event shows the fragility: Taco Bell's first quarterly comparable decline since Q2 2020 followed a July outbreak.

Economies of scale are meaningful in purchasing, marketing and technology. McDonald's operating margin was 50.2% in Q3 2026, our calculation from reported figures, because franchise fees carry little cost. Chipotle's restaurant-level margin of 23.3% shows the margin of a company-operated model.

Food is mostly differentiated by brand, menu and convenience rather than commodity-like, but price competition is intense. McDonald's is testing an entry-level value offer in about 1,900 U.S. restaurants and targets a national launch in early 2027. Starbucks' ticket growth of 5.2% shows a premium brand can sustain pricing.

Customers hold much of the bargaining power because switching costs are near zero. Suppliers matter at the margin, and Chipotle cited higher beef and freight costs. Franchisors hold power over franchisees through contracts: McDonald's franchised revenue of $4,487M in Q3 2026 came from rents and royalties.

Revenue growth comes from comparable sales (traffic plus price) and new units. Chipotle's Q3 comparable sales were up 2.1%, with 0.8% from transactions and 1.3% from check, and it plans 350 to 370 openings in 2026. Starbucks plans about 1,200 net new coffeehouses in fiscal 2027.

Operating margins depend on traffic, price, food and labor costs, and franchise mix. Chipotle's operating margin fell to 13.7% from 15.9% as labor and food costs rose. Starbucks' non-GAAP operating margin was 14.0% in fiscal Q4, up 460 basis points. Damodaran's January 2026 restaurant data show a 15.79% pre-tax operating margin.

Key cost variables are beef and other proteins, coffee, freight, labor and rent. Chipotle named beef, freight and protein usage. Minimum-wage rules push labor: California's fast food council set a $20 hourly minimum, per a February 2026 analysis, although it had not met since February 2025.

Interest-rate sensitivity is moderate. Damodaran's data show debt at 21.4% of capital for US restaurant firms and a 5.07% cost of debt. Franchisees and new-unit growth depend on borrowing costs. We did not find a sourced rate sensitivity estimate for the sub-industry.

Restaurants respond to consumer income, jobs and food inflation. BLS showed food away from home up 3.5% in the year to September 2026, against 1.8% for food at home, and all items up 3.7%. NRA said 60% of operators saw decreased traffic in 2025, and a cooling job market is tightening budgets of low- and middle-income diners.

We read the group as mostly cyclical with defensive pockets. Quick-service chains gain when consumers trade down, but McDonald's U.S. comparable sales were negative in Q3. Secular growth comes from unit expansion and digital: Starbucks' FY2026 net new coffeehouses were 617. Real industry growth was forecast at only 1.3%.

Growth is modest at the industry level and varies by brand. NRA forecasts about $1.55T of sales, real growth 1.3%. McDonald's Q3 revenue rose 1% and diluted EPS rose 10% to $3.51. Chipotle revenue rose 9.6% but EPS fell to $0.27 from $0.29. Starbucks' FY2026 revenue grew 2.0%.

Damodaran's January 2026 data for 64 US restaurant/dining firms show a 32.24% gross margin, a 19.47% EBITDA margin and a 15.79% pre-tax operating margin. Chipotle's restaurant-level margin was 23.3%, and McDonald's franchise-heavy operating margin was 50.2% by our calculation.

Damodaran's net margin for the group was 9.37%. We did not find a sourced ROIC or reliable ROE for the group; Damodaran's ROE table showed a figure we judged unrepresentative, so we do not quote it. Franchisors earn high returns on capital because they hold few restaurants, in our view.

Debt is meaningful, especially at franchisors. Damodaran's data show debt at 21.4% of total capital and a 7.16% cost of capital. Starbucks had about $13.3B of total debt (our sum) and $3,679.9M of cash at fiscal year end, and repaid $2,815.9M of long-term debt in the year.

Free cash flow is generally solid. Starbucks' fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was $4,988.4M against capex of $1,263.6M, about $3.7B of free cash flow by our sum. Chipotle generated $1,922.1M of operating cash in nine months and repurchased $1,464.9M of stock.

Capital needs differ by model. McDonald's guides to about $3.7B of 2026 capex; Starbucks' fiscal 2026 capex fell to $1,263.6M from $2,305.5M. Chipotle opens 350 to 370 restaurants a year, mostly with a Chipotlane. Franchisors need less capital per unit.

Damodaran's January 2026 data show 17.49x EV/EBITDA for restaurant firms with positive EBITDA (21.40x for all firms) and 30.15x EV/EBIT. At sector level, FactSet's forward P/E for Consumer Discretionary was 25.1 on 13 Nov 2026. Those are group or sector measures, not single-company multiples.

Labor rules are the main regulatory risk. California's $20 fast food minimum is overseen by a council that, per a February 2026 analysis, had not met with all nine members since early 2025, so future increases are uncertain. NRA also cites evolving immigration policies as a cost pressure. Food safety rules and menu-labeling laws also apply, though we did not find sourced updates.

AI and technology affect ordering, kitchens and pricing. We found no sourced figures on AI adoption in restaurants. Digital already matters: 38.8% of Chipotle's food and beverage revenue and over $11B of McDonald's Q3 sales to loyalty members. In our view, AI is more likely to change operations and marketing than replace restaurants.

Demographics matter through population growth, age mix and household size. We found no sourced figures here. NRA notes cooling hiring is tightening budgets of low- and middle-income households, a key customer group. Our view is that younger diners' preferences for value and convenience drive the biggest effect.

Consumer behavior is shifting toward value and, in some cases, premium experiences. McDonald's is testing an entry-level value offer while Starbucks' comparable sales rose 7.2%. NRA said 60% of operators reported decreased traffic in 2025. Price sensitivity remains high as food away from home rose 3.5%.

New competitors include convenience stores, grocers' prepared food, ghost kitchens and delivery-led brands. We did not find sourced share data. Within the group, challengers can scale fast, but incumbents have more capital: McDonald's targets 50,000 restaurants by end of 2028 and Chipotle plans up to 370 openings in 2026.

Geopolitics and supply chains matter through commodity prices, freight and international exposure. Chipotle cited beef and freight. McDonald's had 8,395 restaurants in China, while its Developmental Licensed markets grew comparable sales 4.2%. A single ingredient can disrupt: Taco Bell's outbreak was traced to iceberg lettuce.

Substitutes are home cooking, grocery prepared meals and meal kits. Food at home inflation was 1.8% against 3.5% for food away from home in the year to September 2026, which widens the price gap and makes cooking at home more attractive. Restaurants answer with value offers and loyalty programs.
Unit growth and franchising can keep lifting revenue with little capital: McDonald's targets 50,000 restaurants by end of 2028 and Starbucks plans about 1,200 net new coffeehouses in fiscal 2027.
Value offers and loyalty can restore traffic: McDonald's is testing entry-level value in about 1,900 U.S. restaurants with a national launch targeted for early 2027.
Digital ordering is growing, at 38.8% of Chipotle's food and beverage revenue versus 36.7% a year earlier.
Turnarounds can rebuild margin: Starbucks' non-GAAP operating margin rose 460 basis points to 14.0% in fiscal Q4.
Weak low-income consumers and falling traffic: NRA reported 60% of operators saw decreased traffic in 2025.
Food and labor inflation: food away from home rose 3.5% in the year to September 2026 and Chipotle's margin fell on beef, freight and labor.
Wage mandates, such as California's $20 fast food minimum, can raise costs.
Food safety events can hit a brand quickly, as Taco Bell's first quarterly comparable decline since Q2 2020 showed.

Over three to five years we think restaurants grow modestly in the aggregate, with real industry growth forecast at only 1.3% in 2026, so winners will be chains that add units, hold traffic with value and keep margin. Franchisors with global unit targets, such as McDonald's, should keep steady fee growth. Operators face a harder margin test: Chipotle's restaurant-level margin fell to 23.3%, while Starbucks is rebuilding profit after restructuring. Our view is that traffic, not price, will decide which chains earn their valuations, since menu price increases are already running ahead of food at home.

Restaurants are consumer discretionary at the margin, so they follow household income, jobs and prices. The National Restaurant Association forecasts about $1.55T of 2026 sales but only 1.3% real growth, and notes that a cooling job market is tightening budgets for low- and middle-income households. Monthly Census data still show growth: food services and drinking places were $92.9B in October 2026 (seasonally adjusted advance estimate), up from $90.1B in June, about 3.1% in four months by our calculation.

Inflation matters both ways. BLS showed food away from home up 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026 against 1.8% for food at home, with all items up 3.7%. October food away from home rose 0.5% on the month, though BLS could not publish 12-month changes for October because it did not collect October 2025 data during a lapse in appropriations. We did not find a sourced interest-rate path or currency view for the group. Our read is that menu prices are outrunning grocery prices, which supports value-seeking and puts traffic, not check, at the center of the cycle.

Structural demand rests on eating-out habits, convenience and unit growth. NRA projects $1.55T in 2026 sales and 15.8M employees, with real growth of 1.3%. That is slow growth for a large base, so chains grow mostly by adding units, franchising and digital. McDonald's had 46,554 restaurants at 30 Sep 2026 and aims for 50,000 by end of 2028. Starbucks plans about 1,200 net new coffeehouses in fiscal 2027.

Demand is cyclical and elastic at the low end. McDonald's U.S. comparable sales were down 0.2% in Q3 2026 as negative guest counts were largely offset by check growth, while Starbucks posted a 7.2% comp with transactions up 1.8%. In casual dining, Darden's LongHorn grew same-restaurant sales 6.2% against 1.1% at Olive Garden. Demographics matter modestly; we did not find a sourced demographic dataset, so we treat age and household size as slow variables. Long-term, our view is that international and licensed markets grow faster: McDonald's Developmental Licensed comparable sales were up 4.2%.

Using Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense and price-led, with McDonald's testing an entry-level value offer in about 1,900 U.S. restaurants. Threat of new entrants is high for single restaurants but low for national chains, which need brand, sites and supply contracts. Buyer power is high, as diners switch easily; NRA says 60% of operators saw decreased traffic in 2025. Supplier power is moderate: Chipotle cited beef and freight costs. Substitutes include home cooking and grocery prepared food, with food at home inflation of 1.8% versus 3.5% for food away from home.

Concentration is high at the top and low overall. McDonald's has 46,554 restaurants, Starbucks 41,607 coffeehouses and Yum's KFC alone opened 878 restaurants in Q3. We found no sourced market-share table. Moats are brand, scale, real estate and franchise networks. Pricing power is uneven: Starbucks' ticket rose 5.2% while Taco Bell's same-store sales fell 4% after a food safety event.

Regulation centers on labor. California's fast food council set a $20 hourly minimum for most fast food workers, and a February 2026 analysis said the council had not met with all nine members present as of December 2025, so further increases are uncertain. NRA lists food and labor costs and evolving immigration policies among operators' pressures. We did not find sourced details on tariff effects or on federal tip and overtime rules, so we do not quantify them.

Technology is mainly digital ordering, loyalty and kitchen automation. Digital was 38.8% of Chipotle's food and beverage revenue, and McDonald's recorded over $11B of Q3 sales to loyalty members. Social factors include health trends and food safety: Taco Bell's July outbreak, traced to iceberg lettuce, cut its comparable sales by 4%. Environmental and supply factors show up in commodity costs such as beef. Our view is that labor policy and food safety are the two most likely sources of sudden shocks, while AI is a slower efficiency story we cannot size from sources.

Margins depend on the model. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 64 US restaurant/dining firms show a 32.24% gross margin, 19.47% EBITDA margin, 15.79% pre-tax operating margin and 9.37% net margin. Chipotle's restaurant-level margin was 23.3% and its operating margin 13.7%, while McDonald's Q3 operating income of $3,595M on revenue of $7,157M gives a 50.2% margin by our calculation. Starbucks' fiscal 2026 non-GAAP operating margin was 11.9%, up 200 basis points.

Operating leverage is high: a few points of traffic move margins. Chipotle's labor cost rose to 25.7% of revenue from 25.2%. Capital intensity differs: McDonald's guides to about $3.7B of 2026 capex and Starbucks' capex fell to $1,263.6M from $2,305.5M. Starbucks generated about $3.7B of free cash flow in fiscal 2026 by our sum. Damodaran's data show debt at 21.4% of capital. We did not find a reliable industry ROE or ROIC.

Sub-industry consensus was not publicly available in the sources we opened. At sector level, FactSet reported Consumer Discretionary's Q3 2026 net profit margin at 10.0% against 10.2% a year earlier, and revenue 0.2% above estimates. Company results diverged: McDonald's EPS rose 10% to $3.51, Chipotle's fell to $0.27 from $0.29, and Starbucks' non-GAAP EPS rose 53.8% to $0.80.

Guidance is cautious to constructive. Starbucks guides fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS of $3.15 to $3.25 and North America comparable sales of about 4.0%. Darden reaffirmed fiscal 2027 EPS of $11.10 to $11.35. Chipotle kept low-single-digit comparable growth. McDonald's release gave no full-year guidance. Our read: consensus likely hinges on traffic recovery at McDonald's and Taco Bell, and margin risk sits with operators such as Chipotle.

We found no forward P/E or FCF yield specific to Restaurants. At the sector level, FactSet put Consumer Discretionary's forward 12-month P/E at 25.1 on 13 Nov 2026, the highest of the 11 sectors, versus 18.3 for the S&P 500, whose 5-year average is 19.8 and 10-year 19.1. That sector figure is dominated by non-restaurant companies.

Damodaran's January 2026 data for 64 US restaurant/dining firms show 17.49x EV/EBITDA for firms with positive EBITDA, 21.40x for all firms, and 30.15x EV/EBIT. The cost of capital is 7.16% with a beta of 0.92. We did not find a sourced multiple history for the group, so we cannot say whether it trades above its own average. In our view, a roughly 17.5x EV/EBITDA looks like a premium to a defensive, mature business with 1.3% real industry growth, and implies that investors pay for franchise fee streams and unit growth. Starbucks' fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS guide of $3.15 to $3.25 would let a reader compute a company-level multiple.

We did not find a restaurant-only ETF page we could open. The Invesco Leisure and Entertainment ETF (PEJ) is a partial proxy: it held 33 stocks and $385.22M in assets, with Starbucks at 5.11% and Sysco at 4.69% among its top ten, with holdings dated 13 Nov 2026 and price data to 17 Nov 2026. It is a broader leisure fund, not a restaurant fund. We found no sourced short-interest, flow or breadth data for the group.

Momentum signals come from company reports. Starbucks' stock-specific story is a rebound, with non-GAAP EPS up 53.8%. Taco Bell's first quarterly comparable decline since Q2 2020 and McDonald's negative U.S. comparable sales weigh on the large franchisors. Chipotle repurchased $110.0M of stock in Q3 at an average $34.05 and has $1.6B of authorization left; Darden bought back $222.3M. We read buybacks as management confidence, not as positioning data.

Lodging and cruise are both running at record volumes, but the two halves are in different places. Marriott's third-quarter RevPAR rose 6.5% and Hilton's 5.8%, and both raised 2026 guidance. Booking Holdings' room nights grew 7%. Carnival's constant-currency net yields rose 2.4% with record deposits, Royal Caribbean raised its outlook, while Norwegian's yields fell 6.5% and its net leverage is 5.5x. Airbnb's nights grew 16%, helped by a payment feature. The sector trades at 25.1x forward earnings against 18.3x for the S&P 500. Global arrivals are nearly flat.

This sub-industry groups companies that sell stays and sea voyages. Hotel brands such as Marriott and Hilton mostly collect fees from owners who hold the buildings; cruise lines own their ships and sell all-inclusive trips; online travel agencies such as Booking and Airbnb take a commission for connecting travellers with rooms. Restaurants, casinos and leisure facilities sit in neighbouring sub-industries, and airlines and cars are in Industrials and Consumer Discretionary autos.

Hotel franchising and management: A brand owner licenses its name and booking system to hotel owners, or runs the hotel for them. It is paid a percentage of revenue and sometimes of profit, so it carries little building cost. e.g. Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, Wyndham

Owned hotels and resorts: The company owns or leases the property and keeps the full room revenue, but also carries the costs and the debt. e.g. Some Hyatt and Hilton Grand Vacations properties, Playa Hotels
Ocean cruises: Ships sell a fixed-price trip that bundles cabin, meals and entertainment, then add onboard spending such as drinks, spa and excursions. e.g. Carnival, Royal Caribbean, Norwegian

Online travel agencies: Websites and apps list hotels and rentals and take a commission when a booking is made. They are asset-light and compete on traffic and choice. e.g. Booking.com, Expedia, Trip.com
Home-sharing platforms: Marketplaces where individuals rent out spare rooms or homes, with the platform charging both host and guest a fee. e.g. Airbnb

Timeshare and vacation ownership: Customers buy the right to use a resort for a set period each year, usually financed by loans, with annual maintenance fees. e.g. Marriott Vacations Worldwide, Hilton Grand Vacations
Travel demand and consumer confidence: Leisure travel is discretionary, so job security, wealth and confidence shift room nights and cruise bookings. It shows up first in occupancy and booking pace.
Supply growth: New hotel rooms and new ships add capacity. When supply grows faster than demand, rates fall and RevPAR or net yield weakens.
Pricing and mix: Higher rates for the same room or cabin go almost straight to profit. Premium and luxury tiers and onboard spend lift revenue per guest.
Fuel and labour costs: Cruise lines burn large amounts of fuel, and hotels depend on staff. Costs that rise faster than prices squeeze margins.
Interest rates and financing: Owners need credit to build hotels, and cruise lines carry heavy debt. Higher rates slow new development and raise interest expense.
Currency and international flows: Strong or weak home currencies change who travels and what reported revenue is worth, so reported and constant-currency growth can differ.
Geopolitics and disruption: Wars, health scares and weather divert travellers and force route changes, hitting a region's bookings quickly.
RevPAR: Revenue per available room: room revenue divided by all rooms available, whether sold or not. It equals occupancy times average daily rate and is the main hotel yardstick.
ADR: Average daily rate: the average price paid for a sold room night. It shows pricing power.
Occupancy: Share of available rooms that are sold. Hotels have high fixed costs, so occupancy swings move profits a lot.
Franchised versus managed: A franchisor licenses the brand and takes a fee. A manager also runs the hotel and takes a base fee plus an incentive fee tied to profit. Neither owns the building.
Net unit growth: New rooms opened minus rooms leaving the system, as a percent of the base. Brand owners watch it because fees scale with rooms.
Pipeline: Hotels signed or under construction but not yet open. It shows future fee growth, though some projects are delayed or cancelled.
Net yield: Cruise revenue less direct costs such as commissions and onboard costs, per passenger cruise day. It is the cruise equivalent of price.
Capacity days (ALBD): Lower berths multiplied by days in service. It measures how many passenger nights a fleet can sell.
Booked position: Share of future sailings already sold and at what price. Cruise lines sell months ahead, so it gives early read on demand.
Customer deposits: Cash cruise passengers pay ahead of sailing, recorded as a liability. It funds operations and signals future demand.
Gross bookings: The total value of travel booked on an online platform. The platform's revenue is only its commission on this.
Take rate: Platform revenue as a share of gross bookings. A rising rate means more fees per booking.
Asset-light: A model where the company licenses brands or runs a platform instead of owning buildings or ships, which reduces capital needs and lifts returns.
Marriott raised its 2026 RevPAR outlook to 4.5% to 5%, which now sets a higher bar for the fourth quarter.
Booking guides fourth-quarter room nights to just +1% to +3%, against 7% in the third quarter.
Fuel is a swing factor for cruise: Carnival does not hedge and carries a $150 million fuel headwind in its 2026 guide, and share prices moved 4% to 5% on a one-day oil drop on 2 Nov.
Norwegian's yields are falling while its leverage is 5.5x and it plans 16 more ships through 2037.
UN Tourism cut its 2026 world arrivals forecast to 1% to 2% growth from 3% to 4% because of the Middle East conflict, oil and inflation.
Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide, Booking Holdings, Airbnb, Carnival, Royal Caribbean, Norwegian Cruise Line, Expedia

Hotel brands earn franchise and management fees, plus incentive fees tied to profit. Marriott's third-quarter franchise and base management fees were $1,341M and incentive fees $181M. Cruise lines earn ticket revenue plus onboard spending; online platforms earn commissions on bookings; Airbnb's third-quarter revenue was $4.9B on $27.7B of gross booking value.

Customers differ by model. Hotel brands sell to owners and developers, who pay fees, and ultimately to business, group and leisure guests. Marriott reports US and Canada RevPAR up 7.4% and international up 4.4%. Cruise lines sell directly or through travel agents to families and older travellers; 31% of cruisers are first-timers.

For asset-light hotel brands the main costs are sales, technology and reimbursed owner costs. For cruise lines they are fuel, crew, ship depreciation and interest. Carnival put a $150 million fuel headwind into its 2026 outlook, and Royal Caribbean guided 2026 depreciation of $1,870M to $1,890M and net interest near $1.0B.

Pricing power comes from brand, loyalty programs, location and scarce supply. Royal Caribbean says 2027 bookings are pacing ahead of history at higher rates, and Carnival says 2027 booked pricing is at record levels. Online platforms rely on traffic and inventory, and face pressure from regulators on fee display.

Major assets differ sharply. Booking Holdings held $15.8B of cash against $20.1B of debt at 30 September 2026. Royal Caribbean has about $22.4B of debt, and Norwegian $15.1B, mostly against ships. Cruise lines also carry customer deposits as a liability; Carnival's reached a record $7.6B.

The sub-industry splits. Hotel brands and platforms are asset-light, and Damodaran's US hotel and gaming group shows a 24.5% EBITDA margin. Cruise lines are capital-intensive: Royal Caribbean guides about $4.6B of 2026 capital expenditure, of which $1.5B is outside new ships.

Cruise is easiest to size. CLIA counts 37.2 million passengers in 2025, a record, with a 2026 forecast of about 325 ships among members and 690,000 lower berths. For hotels, Marriott alone has nearly 1,834,000 rooms in more than 10,200 properties, and Hilton's pipeline is 543,100 rooms. We did not find a single sourced global market-size figure for the whole sub-industry.

Main segments are hotel brands, owners and operators, ocean cruise, online travel and home-sharing, and timeshare. Booking's 345M room nights and Airbnb's 155M nights and seats show how large the platforms are. Marriott's pipeline of 634,000 rooms shows the brand side is still growing.

Hotel brands sit between owners, who supply buildings and capital, and guests and corporate buyers. Platforms sit between hotels and travellers. Cruise lines are more integrated: they buy ships from yards, sell through agents and direct channels, and own the onboard experience. Norwegian expects 16 more ships through 2037, about 43,000 berths.

The industry has moved toward asset-light brands and larger cruise fleets. Hilton reports 6.0% net unit growth and Marriott 4.6%. Cruise recovered to a record in 2025 and CLIA expects further growth. Booking's gross bookings reached $54.5B in the third quarter, up 10%.

Demand is global. Of 37.2M cruisers in 2025, the US supplied 20.6M and China grew fastest, up 15.8%. The Caribbean, Bahamas and Bermuda hold about 43% of deployments, the Mediterranean about 15%. Marriott's third-quarter RevPAR grew 7.4% in the US and Canada and 4.4% internationally.

Competition is concentrated at the top. Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG and Wyndham dominate hotel brands, and three groups (Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian) lead Western cruising. Online travel has Booking, Expedia and Airbnb, plus Trip.com in Asia. We count roughly a dozen significant listed competitors across all three models.

Marriott is the largest hotel brand owner in our sources, with nearly 1,834,000 rooms; Hilton has a pipeline of 543,100 rooms. We did not find sourced market-share percentages for hotels or for cruise lines, so we do not quote any.

Hotels are fragmented below the big brands, since most hotels are independent or small chains, while the brand layer and the cruise layer are consolidated. Damodaran counts 63 US hotel and gaming companies in its sample, but that includes casinos.

Barriers differ. Hotel brands need loyalty members, reservation systems and owner trust. Cruise lines need ships costing billions: Royal Caribbean plans about $4.6B of 2026 capital spending. Platforms need traffic and supply, and regulators now require all-in pricing.

Scale matters in marketing, loyalty, procurement and fleet costs. A bigger brand spreads technology costs across more rooms, and a larger cruise fleet buys fuel and food more cheaply. Booking's adjusted EBITDA of $4.6B on $9.8B adjusted revenue is about a 47% margin, by our calculation.

Hotel rooms and cruise cabins are differentiated by brand, location and quality, but a basic room is close to a commodity. Brands add loyalty programs and different tiers to avoid pure price competition. Cruise lines differentiate by ship class and itinerary; Norwegian's yields fell 6.5% in the third quarter while Carnival's rose 2.4%.

Owners hold bargaining power over brands because they can switch flags, and big online platforms hold power over small hotels through traffic. Guests have power through price transparency. Cruise lines depend on a few shipyards, so suppliers have power, and Norwegian's delayed Seven Seas Prestige delivery shows that risk.

Revenue growth comes from occupancy, rate, new rooms and new ships. Marriott's third-quarter growth reflected higher ADR and occupancy, while Royal Caribbean's capacity rose 8% in the quarter. For platforms it comes from room nights and take rate.

Operating margins depend on occupancy, because costs are mostly fixed, and on mix. Marriott's adjusted EBITDA rose 12% on 6.5% RevPAR growth, which shows operating leverage. Royal Caribbean's third-quarter adjusted EBITDA margin was 45.4%.

Key cost variables are fuel, labour, food, insurance and, for owners, interest. Norwegian's fuel price per metric ton, net of hedges, rose to $819 from $744. Carnival does not hedge fuel, and Royal Caribbean hedged 58% of its fourth-quarter consumption.

Rates matter because owners finance hotels with debt and cruise lines carry heavy borrowings. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026, with two members preferring an increase. Higher rates also slow new hotel construction, which can help existing owners.

Inflation raises costs but also lets hotels reprice nightly, which helps them. Unemployment and GDP drive business and leisure travel. Oil prices matter most for cruise and for airfares: UN Tourism blamed the Middle East conflict, high oil prices and inflation for the cut to its 2026 forecast.

The sub-industry is cyclical. UN Tourism says world arrivals grew just 0.4% in the first half of 2026 and expects 1% to 2% for the year. Yet long-term demand is secular: arrivals and cruise passengers have reached records, and 2027 cruise bookings are at record pricing.

Growth is strong but uneven. Marriott's third-quarter adjusted EPS was $3.02 against $2.47 a year earlier, and Booking's adjusted EPS was $4.66, up 17%. Norwegian's full-year adjusted EPS guide of about $1.70 reflects falling yields.

Damodaran's US hotel and gaming industry shows a 60.9% gross margin, 21.6% operating margin and 24.5% EBITDA margin as of January 2026. That group includes casinos, so we treat it as a rough guide. Royal Caribbean's own third-quarter adjusted EBITDA margin was 45.4%.

Damodaran puts the US hotel and gaming group's return on equity at 45.4% unadjusted. We think heavy buybacks and thin equity at brand companies inflate that figure, so we would not read it as typical. Royal Caribbean says it is already above its ROIC target, but gives no current figure.

Leverage varies. Norwegian's net leverage is 5.5x; Royal Caribbean has about $22.4B of debt and $7.4B of liquidity; Booking has $20.1B of debt against $15.8B of cash. Carnival redeemed $500M of 7% notes in the quarter.

Cash generation is strong for asset-light companies. Booking generated $7.8B of free cash flow in the first nine months of 2026; Airbnb's third-quarter free cash flow was $1.4B. Hilton expects to return about $3.5B to shareholders in 2026, and Marriott returned about $4.0B year to date.

Cruise lines need heavy capital spending, with Royal Caribbean guiding about $4.6B for 2026 and Norwegian planning $3.1B of gross newbuild spending in 2027. Hotel brands spend little, because owners fund buildings.

Damodaran's US hotel and gaming EV/EBITDA was 14.9x for positive-EBITDA firms and 17.7x for all firms in January 2026. The whole Consumer Discretionary sector trades at 25.1x forward earnings, against 18.3x for the S&P 500.

Regulation focuses on price display. The FTC rule on hidden fees, in force since 12 May 2025, covers hotels and short-term lodging. Booking also booked a $900M revenue reduction and $100M loss accrual tied to an FTC matter in the third quarter, which it excludes from adjusted results.

AI and technology could change how people find and book trips, shifting power between platforms and brands. Airbnb and Booking are both investing in newer products, but we did not find sourced evidence of share changes from AI. Brands could also lose direct bookings if AI assistants route traffic to platforms.

Demographics help cruise: 31% of cruisers are first-time and about a third of guests are under 40. Ageing populations in rich countries support leisure travel spending over time, but we did not find sourced figures on demographic effects for hotels.
Consumer behaviour is shifting toward experiences and alternative lodging. Airbnb's nights grew 16%, with about 13% excluding its Reserve Now, Pay Later effect.

New competitors include short-term rental platforms, lifestyle brands and more cruise ships. Royal Caribbean's capacity grows 4.5% in 2027, 6.0% in 2028 and 6.5% in 2029, and Norwegian plans 16 ships through 2037. More supply could press yields.
Geopolitics is a live risk. UN Tourism reports Middle East arrivals down 22% in the first half of 2026. Norwegian cancelled Seven Seas Voyager sailings through the Suez Canal.

Substitutes include staying with family, camping, land-based all-inclusive resorts and shorter domestic trips. The sources we opened do not quantify substitution, but weak arrivals growth of 0.4% in the first half of 2026 suggests travellers are sensitive to cost.
Pipelines point to further fee growth: Marriott has 634,000 rooms and Hilton 543,100 rooms in development.
Cruise demand looks strong, with Carnival 2027 booked pricing at record levels and Royal Caribbean 2027 bookings up in the high teens.
Asset-light platforms and brands generate strong cash for buybacks, including Airbnb's new $12B authorization.
Fuel relief would help cruise margins if oil prices stay lower.
Weak world arrivals growth and geopolitical disruption could slow demand.
Fee-display rules and legal actions could cut revenue from add-on fees and complicate pricing.
Rising cruise capacity and high leverage could compress yields, as Norwegian is already showing.
Elevated inflation and a Fed that is debating increases could weigh on consumers and owners' financing.

Over the next three to five years we think the asset-light hotel brands and platforms are better placed than the leveraged cruise lines, because their pipelines and cash returns do not depend on new capital spending. Cruise has the stronger visible demand, with record deposits and booking pace at Carnival and Royal Caribbean, but it also has the most new supply coming and the most debt. The main swing factors are consumer health, fuel and the Middle East. We would expect returns to stay high for brands and platforms and to diverge more among the cruise lines, with Norwegian the one to watch.

Travel is in a late-cycle, still-growing phase. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026 with two members preferring a hike, and its statement says inflation remains elevated while job gains have kept pace with the workforce. That is not an easy-money backdrop, yet US hotels are still posting gains: CoStar's week to 31 October showed RevPAR up 9.7% to $101.88, with 20 of the top 25 markets higher.

Globally the picture is softer. UN Tourism estimates 690 million international arrivals in the first half of 2026, up just 0.4%, and has cut its 2026 forecast to 1% to 2% from 3% to 4% because of the Middle East conflict, oil prices and inflation. Marriott's third-quarter RevPAR rose 6.5% worldwide, and it raised its full-year outlook to 4.5% to 5%.

Currency matters because many costs and revenues are in different currencies: Carnival's third-quarter net yields rose 2.4% in constant currency but fell 1.3% in current dollars, as higher fuel prices and currency hit reported results. We think the cycle is more mature than the headline RevPAR numbers suggest, because they are boosted by events such as conferences and the World Series.

Structural demand for travel remains strong. CLIA counts 37.2 million cruise passengers in 2025, a record, and about 90% of cruisers say they intend to sail again; 31% were first-timers and about a third of guests are under 40. Cruise lines are filling ships ahead of time: Carnival says 2027 booked occupancy and pricing are at record levels, with customer deposits of $7.6B, and Royal Caribbean says 2027 bookings are up in the high teens.

In lodging, the pipeline shows where operators expect demand. Marriott has a record 634,000 rooms in its pipeline, and Hilton's is 543,100 rooms, up 5%. Hilton raised its 2026 RevPAR guide to 4.0% to 4.5%. CoStar and Tourism Economics upgraded their 2026 US forecast, with occupancy at 63.1%.

Demand is not very elastic at the top end, but it is cyclical overall. UN Tourism's much weaker first-half arrivals numbers show that leisure travel can slow quickly when fares and prices rise. Online platforms are still taking share: Booking's room nights grew 7% and Airbnb's nights grew 16%, with a 3% lift from a payment feature.

Using Porter's five forces: the threat of new entrants is low for brands and cruise lines because of loyalty programs, scale and the cost of ships, but high for home-sharing and independent hotels. Royal Caribbean plans about $4.6B of capital spending in 2026, and Norwegian expects 16 ships through 2037. Hotel owners hold supplier power over brands, since they can change flag.

Buyer power is highest for online platforms and for price-sensitive travellers, which is why hotel brands push direct booking through loyalty programs. Rivalry is intense in each segment. Norwegian's third-quarter yield fell 6.5% while Carnival's rose 2.4% in constant currency, showing that rivals can diverge sharply. Substitutes are shorter trips, land holidays and rentals, and Airbnb's 155M nights and seats show how big the rental alternative has become.

Concentration is high at the top. Marriott has nearly 1,834,000 rooms; Hilton's net unit growth is 6.0%. We did not find sourced global share percentages. Pricing power is strongest where brands and ships are scarce: Royal Caribbean reports bookings at higher rates. Moats are loyalty programs, scale and, for platforms, traffic, though regulators now require all-in pricing.

Politically, travel is exposed to conflict and trade. UN Tourism reports Middle East arrivals down 22% in the first half of 2026 and attributes weaker growth to the conflict, air disruption, higher oil prices and inflation. Norwegian cancelled Suez Canal sailings for Seven Seas Voyager, and Marriott still guides to RevPAR growth only of 4.5% to 5% for 2026. Carnival's third-quarter results were also hurt by fuel.

Regulation is mostly about pricing transparency. The FTC rule in force since 12 May 2025 requires up-front price disclosure for hotels and short-term lodging. In the third quarter Booking Holdings recorded a $900M reduction to revenue and $100M accrued loss tied to an FTC matter, excluded from its adjusted results.

Technologically, the main change is how travellers search and book. Platforms are building on their lead in traffic, while brands push apps and loyalty to protect direct bookings. We did not find sourced evidence on how AI assistants are changing share. Environmental factors include fuel and emissions rules for ships; Norwegian's third-quarter fuel price rose to $819 per metric ton from $744.

Margins are high at the brand level and lower for owners. Marriott's third-quarter adjusted EBITDA was $1,512M, up 12%, on fee revenue of $1,341M of franchise and base fees plus $181M of incentive fees. Booking's adjusted EBITDA was $4,607M on $9,793M of adjusted revenue, about a 47% margin by our calculation. Airbnb's adjusted EBITDA margin was 52% in the quarter.

Cruise economics are different. Royal Caribbean's third-quarter adjusted EBITDA margin was 45.4% on $5.6B of revenue. Carnival's adjusted EBITDA was $3.0B, in line with last year's record. Norwegian's was $937M on $2.9B of revenue. Damodaran's US hotel and gaming group shows a 21.6% operating margin and a 24.5% EBITDA margin in January 2026 data, but includes casinos.

Operating leverage is high because most costs are fixed. Capital intensity splits the group: Booking produced $7.8B of free cash flow in nine months, while Royal Caribbean guides $4.6B of capital spending. Damodaran's hotel and gaming ROE is 45.4%, which we think is inflated by buybacks and low equity. We did not find a sourced sector-wide ROIC, so we do not quote one.

Earnings are growing but the mix is changing. Marriott raised its 2026 global RevPAR outlook to 4.5% to 5%, and Hilton raised its to 4.0% to 4.5% with adjusted EBITDA of $4.06B to $4.08B. Booking expects full-year adjusted EPS growth in the low to mid-teens, but Q4 room nights of just 1% to 3% and flat adjusted EBITDA.

Cruise guidance has been rising. Royal Caribbean lifted 2026 adjusted EPS to $17.85 to $17.95 and guides Q4 net yields up 4.4% to 4.9% as reported. Carnival said its third-quarter yields were better than guidance and that fuel is a $150M headwind in its 2026 outlook. Norwegian guides full-year adjusted EPS of about $1.70 and its full-year net yield is expected down about 4.4% in constant currency.

We did not find a sourced consensus EPS growth figure for this sub-industry. Our view differs in one respect: we think Q4 and 2027 are the real test, because Booking and Norwegian have guided to weaker fourth-quarter yields or room nights. The S&P 500's own earnings growth for Q3 2026 is a blended 31.9% according to FactSet, which sets a high bar for relative earnings.

We found no sourced forward P/E for this sub-industry alone. At the sector level FactSet puts Consumer Discretionary at 25.1x forward 12-month earnings as of 12 November 2026, the highest of any sector, against 18.3x for the S&P 500 and above its 5-year average of 19.8x and 10-year average of 19.1x for the index. That sector includes Amazon and Tesla-style companies, so it says little about lodging and cruise.

On enterprise value to EBITDA, Damodaran's January 2026 data show 14.9x for US hotel and gaming companies with positive EBITDA and 17.7x for all firms. Because the group includes casinos, we treat it as a loose reference. Asset-light brands and platforms typically earn higher multiples than ship owners because of their lower capital needs, which we think is justified by the cash flow evidence.

Cash yields are a better lens than P/E for this group. Booking produced $7.8B of free cash flow in nine months and has $12.4B left on its buyback authorization; Airbnb has a new $12B buyback. At current prices, Royal Caribbean guides to $17.85 to $17.95 of 2026 EPS, so its share price of $321.77 on 2 November implies about 18x trailing-year guidance, by our calculation.

Cruise stocks have diverged. As of 2 November 2026, Royal Caribbean was up 17% year to date, Carnival up 0.7% and Norwegian down 18%, after a rally of 4% to 5% on a one-day fall in oil prices on hopes of US-Iran talks. That pattern matches fundamentals: Royal Caribbean raised its outlook and Norwegian's net yields are falling.

For hotels and platforms we did not find sourced year-to-date performance, ETF flow or short-interest data, and we do not estimate it. Capital return gives a clue about management confidence: Marriott repurchased 3.5 million shares for $1.3B in the third quarter, Booking bought back $2.1B in the quarter and has $12.4B of authorization left, and Hilton plans about $3.5B of shareholder returns in 2026.

Breadth within the group is mixed because consumers are splitting between leisure strength and slower arrivals globally. Consumer Discretionary has the highest forward P/E of any S&P 500 sector, which suggests positioning is already crowded in the sector at large, though that is our inference from valuation, not a flow figure.

This group is split in two. Jewelry and a few top-end names are growing fast: Richemont's first-half sales rose 17% at constant rates, Hermès' third-quarter sales rose 4.3% and Coach grew 16%. Leather-goods and fashion houses that lean on China are weak: LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods organic sales fell 5% in the third quarter and Gucci's comparable sales fell 6%. US tariff refunds flattered margins this quarter. The sector's forward P/E is 25.1x; we found no sourced multiple for this sub-industry alone.

These companies design, make and sell clothing, handbags, watches, jewelry and other accessories under brand names. Customers range from wealthy luxury shoppers to everyday buyers of jeans and activewear. Profit comes from the brand: a recognised name lets the company charge more than the cost of the materials and labor. GICS also puts the big luxury groups here. Footwear makers such as Nike sit in the neighbouring Footwear sub-industry, and the stores that sell clothing from many brands sit in Apparel Retail.

Leather goods and handbags: Bags, small leather goods and luggage. For luxury houses this is usually the biggest and most profitable line, because craftsmanship and scarcity support high prices. e.g. Louis Vuitton, Hermès Birkin and Kelly, Gucci, Coach

Ready-to-wear clothing: Seasonal clothing collections sold through the brand's own stores, department stores and online. Fashion cycles make demand harder to predict than for bags. e.g. Ralph Lauren Polo, Tommy Hilfiger, Dior, Saint Laurent

Everyday and athletic apparel: Jeans, basics and activewear sold at accessible prices in large volumes, often through wholesale partners as well as the company's own stores. e.g. Levi's, lululemon, PVH's Calvin Klein

Jewelry and watches: Fine jewelry and luxury timepieces, sold at high prices and often seen as stores of value. Gold and gemstones are major input costs. e.g. Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Tiffany, Vacheron Constantin

Eyewear, fragrance and other licensed goods: Add-on categories where the brand name is applied to sunglasses, perfume or home goods, sometimes made by partners under license. e.g. Kering Eyewear, Ralph Lauren licensed fragrance and home

Consumer confidence and wealth: High-end spending follows stock markets and property values for wealthy buyers, while mass apparel follows jobs and incomes. A fall shows up first in traffic and in sales to aspirational customers.
Chinese demand and tourism: Chinese shoppers are a large share of luxury sales, at home and when travelling. A slowdown cuts sales and, because stores have fixed costs, cuts profit by more.
Creative direction: A new designer or product line can revive a brand, and a miss can stall it. This shows up in comparable sales over several quarters rather than at once.
Pricing: Brands raise prices to offset costs. Gross margin rises if customers accept the increase and falls if they trade down or stop buying.
Tariffs and sourcing costs: Duties on imports, freight and material costs raise the cost of goods sold. Companies pass part on through prices, and the rest hits gross margin.
Currency: A stronger home currency reduces reported sales and profit for companies selling abroad, even when local demand is unchanged.
Channel mix: Shifting sales to own stores and websites raises gross margin but adds rent and labor, so operating margin depends on how well sales cover those fixed costs.
Organic growth: Sales growth excluding currency swings, acquisitions and disposals. Global luxury groups report in euros but sell in dollars, yuan and yen, so this is the cleaner read.
Constant currency: Growth recalculated as if exchange rates had not changed. A strong euro can shrink reported sales while demand is fine.
Comparable sales: Sales from stores open at least a year, plus online. It strips out the effect of opening or closing stores.
DTC (direct-to-consumer): Sales through the brand's own stores and websites rather than through other retailers. It earns a higher margin per item but costs more to run.
Wholesale: Selling to department stores and other retailers, who set the final price. Volumes are steadier but margins per item are lower.
Gross margin: Sales minus the direct cost of making the goods, as a share of sales. A high figure signals pricing power.
Recurring operating margin: Operating profit before one-off items, as a share of sales. It is the headline profitability measure for the European luxury groups.
Aspirational customer: A shopper who stretches to buy an entry-level item, such as a small bag, from a luxury brand. This group is sensitive to prices and the economy.
Sell-through: The share of stock a company sells at full price. Low sell-through forces markdowns and hurts margin.
Tariff: A tax on imported goods. Apparel is made largely in Asia, so duties on imports into the US raise costs unless prices rise.
Brand heat: Informal measure of how much customers want a brand right now. It can rise or fall quickly when a new designer arrives or a product misses.
China is the swing factor: LVMH said slowing Chinese demand hit Fashion & Leather Goods in the third quarter, Hermès' Asia ex-Japan sales were flat, yet Tapestry's Greater China sales rose 43%.
Gucci's turnaround is Kering's stated priority; comparable sales fell 6% in Q3 after a 2% fall in Q2, and Kering plans at least 125 net store closures in 2026.
Tariff refunds boosted Q2 and Q3 margins at lululemon, Levi's and Ralph Lauren, so underlying margins may look weaker once the one-offs fade.
Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% replaced the expired Section 122 surcharge on 24 July 2026, keeping import costs for US-bound apparel in play.
lululemon guides Q3 revenue down 10% to 11% and has interim co-CEOs, so its Americas weakness is the clearest US demand risk in the group.
LVMH, Hermès, Kering, Richemont, Ralph Lauren, Tapestry, lululemon, Levi Strauss

Revenue comes from selling branded goods: bags, clothes, jewelry and accessories. Ralph Lauren sells through its own stores, department stores and online across North America, Europe and Asia. Licensing and wholesale add smaller streams, and Levi's reports direct-to-consumer at 45% of revenue.

Customers are individual consumers, from wealthy collectors to mainstream buyers of jeans and activewear, plus wholesale accounts such as department stores. Bain says the Americas are the strongest region for luxury in 2026 while the Gulf customer base shrank 15% to 25% early in the year. Tourists are a significant slice of luxury demand in Europe and Japan.

The main costs are materials and manufacturing, then store rent, staff and marketing. Raw materials weigh on Richemont's gross margin, notably gold for jewelry. For brands that import into the US, tariffs are a further cost. Luxury houses spend heavily on stores and advertising to protect the brand.

Pricing power comes from brand desirability and scarcity. Hermès' 41% recurring operating margin in the first half of 2026 shows what the strongest brands can earn, and LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods division earned about 35% in 2025. Mass-market names have less pricing power: US apparel's pre-tax operating margin is 9.1%.

The largest assets are brands (often not fully on the balance sheet), inventory and store leases. Hermès held net cash of €12.9 billion at end-June 2026 and Richemont €7.7 billion at end-September. Ralph Lauren reported $1.2 billion of inventory and $1.2 billion of debt against $1.8 billion of cash. Lease obligations are the main liability for store-heavy brands.

The model is mixed. Design, brand management and retail are asset-light, but luxury houses own workshops and flagship stores. Hermès' operating investments were €344 million in the first half against €8.2 billion of sales, and US apparel's capex runs 133% of depreciation. Most mass brands outsource manufacturing.

Bain sizes the personal luxury goods market at €358 billion in 2025, down 2% at current rates but up 1% at constant rates, and forecasts 2% to 4% growth in 2026. McKinsey and BoF expected low single-digit growth for global fashion in 2026. Our read is that the group is a mature market where growth comes from share gains.

The main segments are leather goods and fashion, jewelry and watches, and everyday apparel and activewear. Bain says jewelry is leading, with apparel, eyewear and fragrance holding up, while leather goods and footwear remain under pressure but are improving. Richemont's jewelry houses grew 19% at constant rates against 10% for watchmakers.

Brands sit between suppliers (tanneries, mills, ateliers, gold and diamond sources) and customers who buy through brand stores, department stores and online. Control of distribution is a strategic goal. Direct distribution gives a brand control of price and presentation. Levi's still sells 55% of revenue through other channels.

The industry moved from family houses to global groups that own many brands, such as LVMH and Kering, while Hermès and Richemont stayed more focused. After a post-pandemic boom, luxury growth stalled in 2025, and it has since split by brand and region. A 2025 reset in China is part of that story.

Production is concentrated in Europe for luxury leather goods and in Asia for mass apparel. Hermès is expanding manufacturing sites in France. Sales are spread across the Americas, Europe and Asia: Hermès' Asia excluding Japan is its largest market at €1.65 billion in Q3, and Ralph Lauren's Asia sales were $571 million in Q2 against $886 million in North America.

There are a few dozen significant listed competitors, plus thousands of private labels. The large global groups are LVMH, Kering, Richemont and Hermès in luxury, and Ralph Lauren, Tapestry, PVH, Levi's, VF and lululemon in the US. Damodaran's US apparel set holds 35 firms.

LVMH is the largest by sales: its Fashion & Leather Goods division had €37.8 billion in 2025 and the group €80.8 billion. Hermès had €12.3 billion in nine months, Richemont €12.3 billion in six months and Kering €10.6 billion in nine months. We found no sourced market-share data for the full sub-industry.

The industry is fragmented overall but concentrated at the top of luxury, where a handful of groups account for much of the brand value. Bain notes that performance gaps between brands are narrowing in 2026. Within mass apparel, thousands of brands compete, and consolidation is slower.

Barriers to entry are brand heritage, scarce craft skills, prime store locations and the capital to advertise globally. Hermès' manufacturing expansion shows how scarce artisan capacity is. New labels can enter cheaply, but building a billion-euro brand takes decades, which is why most growth comes from existing houses.

Economies of scale come from sourcing, advertising and real estate. LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods margin of 35% exceeds the 9.1% for US apparel, though that gap reflects brand power more than scale. Large groups can cross-fund a weak brand: Kering is reworking Gucci while jewelry grows 12%.

The industry is differentiated by brand rather than commoditized. Gucci's retail fell 9% while Saint Laurent and Bottega Veneta grew, which shows how differently brands in the same price tier can perform. Basic apparel such as jeans is closer to a commodity and competes on price, fit and promotion.

Customers hold the stronger hand in mass apparel, where retailers and shoppers can switch brands, and brands rely on promotions. In luxury, brands hold the power: Hermès' customers wait for products and its margin stays at 41%. Suppliers have leverage in scarce inputs such as gold, which Richemont says weighs on gross margin.

Revenue growth comes from volume, price increases, new stores and new categories. McKinsey and BoF found nearly three-quarters of fashion executives plan price increases, with 45% of North American companies planning above 5%. Hermès' Q3 growth came from leather goods up 10.8% while ready-to-wear fell 2%.

Operating margin depends on gross margin, which reflects pricing power and input costs, and on store and marketing costs against sales. Hermès held 41%. lululemon's operating margin was 18.8%, which includes about 560 basis points from tariff refunds. High fixed costs make margins swing with sales.

Key cost variables are leather, cotton, gold and other materials, freight, labor, store rent and advertising. Richemont cited elevated raw material costs, and Levi's redeployed part of its tariff refund into promotion and marketing. Tariff costs for US-bound goods are now set by Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5%.

Interest rates act through consumers and balance sheets. Many luxury groups hold net cash (Hermès €12.9 billion, Richemont €7.7 billion), so direct sensitivity is low. The indirect effect is through wealth and confidence. US apparel's interest coverage is 7.9 times. We found no sourced rate-sensitivity estimate for the sub-industry.

Inflation raises input and labor costs but lets brands raise prices, and weak employment and GDP hurt aspirational buyers first. Bain notes that experiences are growing 1.5 times faster than tangible goods in 2026. Currency matters too: Hermès' H1 sales rose 6.1% at constant rates but 1.6% reported.

The group is cyclical at the mass end and a mix at the top. Luxury has secular growth in jewelry and wealth creation, but the market was flat at constant rates in 2025. LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods organic sales fell 5% in 2025 and again 2% over nine months of 2026, while Richemont grew 17%.

Revenue growth is low single digits in the base case, with large differences by brand. Ralph Lauren guides full-year constant-currency growth of 6% to 7%, Tapestry guides $8.5 billion to $8.6 billion of revenue, while lululemon guides a 5% to 7% decline. Bain forecasts 2% to 4% for personal luxury goods in 2026.

Gross margins are high: Damodaran's US apparel set shows a 56.9% gross margin and a 9.1% pre-tax operating margin. Individual brands exceed that: Tapestry reported a 78.6% gross margin, Ralph Lauren 70.5% adjusted and Levi's 66.2% including tariff refunds. Hermès' recurring operating margin was 41%.

Returns on capital are strong because brands need little physical capital. Damodaran shows an unadjusted after-tax ROIC of 19.75% for US apparel. We found no sourced sub-industry ROE figure; Damodaran's page reports ROIC only. LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods earned 35% margins on its sales.

Leverage is moderate for the US set: Damodaran shows debt to EBITDA of 3.47 and interest coverage of 7.9 times, with market debt to capital of about 25%. The best luxury houses hold net cash: Hermès €12.9 billion and Richemont €7.7 billion. LVMH cut net financial debt 26% to €6.9 billion in 2025.

Free cash flow is strong at premium brands. Hermès' adjusted free cash flow rose 18% to €2.18 billion in the first half, and LVMH's operating free cash flow was €11.3 billion in 2025. Ralph Lauren holds $1.8 billion in cash. Tapestry plans $2 billion of capital returns this year.

Capex needs are moderate. US apparel's capex is 133% of depreciation and net capex 2.1% of sales. Hermès' operating investments were €344 million in the first half. Spending goes to stores, workshops and technology, and is small against operating cash flow for the leaders.

Valuations depend on brand quality. Damodaran's US apparel EV/EBITDA is 10.3 times for profitable firms against 19.7 times for the whole US market. In August 2026 Saxo put Hermès at a mid-30s trailing P/E and LVMH near 20 times. The Consumer Discretionary sector's forward P/E is 25.1.

Regulation includes trade policy, product-safety and sustainability rules. The key legislative risk is tariffs: IEEPA refunds lifted recent margins at lululemon, Levi's and Ralph Lauren, while Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% from July 2026 replaced the expired Section 122 surcharge. About 40% of fashion executives flagged tariffs and deglobalisation as a major risk.

AI is mainly an efficiency and discovery tool. McKinsey and BoF's survey ranks scaling AI as the biggest opportunity for fashion, and Bain says roughly half of luxury shoppers use AI in their purchase journey. The risk is that AI-led search shifts attention away from brand-owned channels; we found no sourced measure of this effect.

Demographics matter through wealth and age. Bain notes more than 70% of customers who left luxury intend to return, though not necessarily to the same brands. Younger shoppers are less loyal, and demand from wealthy older buyers is steadier. We found no sourced population-level estimate for the sub-industry.

Consumer behavior is shifting toward experiences, resale and value. Bain says experiences are growing 1.5 times faster than goods and that about half of luxury shoppers check the secondhand market before buying new. lululemon's Americas comparable sales fell 12%, showing how quickly a popular brand can lose momentum.

New competitors include fast-growing newer brands and the in-house brands of retailers. Bain notes that US-native brands grew roughly 10% to 15% in Q1 2026. Within established houses, creative resets matter: LVMH cites renewal at Louis Vuitton, Dior and Loro Piana, while Kering is working on Gucci.

Geopolitics and supply chains are material. Chinese demand weakened for LVMH and Hermès, tourism flows shifted (Bain cited European tourist spending down about 20% in February and a smaller Gulf customer base), and tariffs reshape sourcing. Production for mass apparel remains concentrated in Asia.

Substitutes include secondhand and resale, rental, and spending on experiences rather than goods. Within luxury, jewelry has become a substitute for leather goods as customers favor assets that hold value, with Richemont's jewelry up 19% and Kering's up 12%. Lab-grown stones and cheaper dupes are a further risk we could not size.
Jewelry keeps taking share of luxury spending, with Richemont's Jewellery Maisons up 19% at constant rates and Bain naming jewelry the leader in 2026.
Asia could recover: Tapestry's Greater China sales rose 43%, Ralph Lauren's Asia sales rose 28% and Bain expects modest luxury growth in 2026.
Creative resets at LVMH's and Kering's biggest brands could revive growth in fashion and leather goods.
Lower tariff exposure or refunds, if they persist, support margins for US importers.
Slower Chinese growth and tourism could keep leather-goods demand weak, as in LVMH's Q3.
Tariff changes and unresolved refund questions could raise costs for US-bound apparel.
Aspirational customers could trade down or move to experiences, as lululemon's Americas weakness and Bain's data suggest.
Brand missteps can cost several years of growth, as Gucci shows.

We think the next three to five years favor the strongest brands and punish the middling ones. Pricing power, direct distribution and net cash let Hermès, Richemont and Coach compound growth while the market grows only low single digits. Houses that depend on China or on a single brand, such as Gucci, face a longer repair. Mass apparel faces thinner margins and tariff exposure. Underlying earnings quality matters: one-off tariff refunds flattered recent quarters. We expect dispersion between winners and laggards to stay wide.

The cycle is uneven rather than uniformly weak. Bain puts the personal luxury market at €358 billion in 2025, down 2% at current rates but up 1% at constant rates, and expects 2% to 4% growth in 2026 in its base case, which it gives about a 70% probability. Its downside case is growth of 0% to 2%, and its upside case is 4% to 6%. The US is the strongest region and Europe and the Middle East are drags: Bain cites European tourist spending down about 20% in February and a Gulf customer base 15% to 25% smaller.

Currency is a second force. LVMH's 2025 Fashion & Leather Goods sales fell 8% reported but 5% organic, with the profit decline attributed mainly to currency. Hermès' first-half 2026 sales rose 6.1% at constant rates but only 1.6% reported, with currency cutting more than €360 million. For US firms, the issue is trade policy: the temporary Section 122 surcharge expired on 24 July 2026 and Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% on about 60 economies took effect the same day. We found no sourced policy-rate path for this note, so we do not model it.

Structural demand rests on wealth creation, brand-seeking in emerging markets and a shift of spending toward jewelry and heirloom goods. Bain forecasts personal luxury goods at €365 billion to €373 billion in 2026. McKinsey and BoF expected the wider fashion industry to grow in the low single digits in 2026, with 46% of executives expecting conditions to worsen and 25% expecting improvement. Demand is elastic at the aspirational end and steadier at the top, which is why Hermès still grew 4.3% in Q3 at constant rates while lululemon's comparable sales fell 9%.

Category trends differ. Bain says jewelry leads, apparel, eyewear and fragrance are holding, and leather goods and footwear are under pressure but improving. Richemont's Jewellery Maisons grew 19% at constant rates in its first half, and Kering's jewelry revenue rose 12% in Q3. Bain also says experiences are growing 1.5 times faster than tangible goods and that over 70% of customers who left luxury intend to return. Our read is that long-term demand is intact, but the easy post-pandemic growth is gone and volume growth now depends on winning share.

Porter's five forces point to strong positions for the top brands. Rivalry is intense in mass apparel and between luxury houses for the same customer, but brand differentiation softens it: Gucci's retail fell 9% in Q3 while Saint Laurent and Bottega Veneta grew. The threat of new entrants is low at the top, where heritage and craft are scarce, and higher in activewear and denim. Supplier power is limited except for scarce inputs: Richemont cites elevated raw material costs. Buyer power is high in mass apparel, where Levi's sells 55% of revenue through channels other than its own stores, and low in luxury. The threat of substitutes comes from resale, experiences and jewelry.

Concentration is highest in luxury: LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods had €37.8 billion of sales in 2025, Hermès €12.3 billion in nine months, Richemont €12.3 billion in six months and Kering €10.6 billion in nine months. Moats are visible in margins: 35% at LVMH's fashion division and 41% at Hermès against 9.1% for the US apparel set. We found no sourced market-share table for the whole sub-industry.

Political and trade factors dominate. The temporary 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from 24 February to 24 July 2026, and Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% on about 60 economies replaced it. The same source notes combined rates for the EU and Taiwan are generally capped at 10%. IEEPA tariff refunds then lifted second- and third-quarter results: $134.5 million at lululemon, $84 million (including interest) at Levi's and a gross margin boost at Ralph Lauren. In the McKinsey and BoF survey, about 40% of executives flagged deglobalisation and tariffs as a major risk.

Technology and social factors matter as well. Bain finds about half of luxury shoppers use AI in their purchase journey and half check the secondhand market before buying new. McKinsey and BoF's survey named scaling AI as the biggest opportunity. Economic and social shifts, including a smaller Gulf customer base and weaker Chinese demand, shape sales by region. We found no sourced figures on environmental regulation for this note; sustainability and sourcing rules remain a background factor, not a quantified one.

Margins are high but split. LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods earned a 35% operating margin in 2025, with profit from recurring operations of €13.2 billion on €37.8 billion of sales. Hermès' recurring operating margin was 41% in the first half of 2026 against 41.4% a year earlier. Damodaran's US apparel data show a 56.9% gross margin and a 9.1% operating margin. After-tax ROIC is 19.75%.

Operating leverage is high because stores, staff and advertising are largely fixed. When LVMH's 2025 fashion sales fell 5% organically, profit from recurring operations fell 13%. Capital needs are modest: US apparel capex is 133% of depreciation and net capex 2.1% of sales, and Hermès spent €344 million on operating investments in the first half. Free cash flow is strong: Hermès' adjusted free cash flow was €2.18 billion and LVMH's operating free cash flow €11.3 billion in 2025. Balance sheets are conservative at the top, with Hermès' net cash at €12.9 billion; Damodaran's US set has debt to EBITDA of 3.47. We found no sourced ROE for the group.

Consensus figures for this sub-industry were not publicly available to us, so we describe guidance. FactSet reports that the Consumer Discretionary sector's Q3 net profit margin was 10.0% against 10.2% a year earlier. Ralph Lauren raised full-year guidance to 6% to 7% constant-currency revenue growth and 80 to 100 basis points of operating margin expansion. Tapestry raised revenue guidance to $8.5 billion to $8.6 billion and EPS to $8.25 to $8.35. Levi's raised adjusted EPS guidance to $1.54 to $1.56. lululemon lowered its outlook to a revenue decline of 5% to 7%.

Kering confirmed it expects to improve its recurring operating margin in 2026, and Hermès reaffirmed its medium-term growth ambition. Richemont gave no outlook in the sources we opened. Our view differs from the quarter's headline numbers in one respect: recent margins include tariff refunds that will not repeat, so underlying earnings growth is lower than reported for lululemon, Levi's and Ralph Lauren. We would watch whether China stabilises, since LVMH said it hurt the third quarter while Tapestry reported a 43% gain there.

We found no sourced forward P/E for this sub-industry on its own. FactSet's 13 November data put the S&P 500 at 18.3 times forward earnings against a 10-year average of 19.1, and the Consumer Discretionary sector at 25.1. That sector figure covers the whole sector, not this sub-industry. Damodaran's January 2026 data show US apparel at 10.3 times EV/EBITDA for profitable firms against 19.7 for the whole market.
