Within the group, valuation spreads are wide. A Saxo note of 18 August 2026 put Hermès at roughly mid-30s trailing earnings and LVMH around 20 times. Those are trailing multiples, and Saxo's note is marketing content, so we treat them as indicative. Our read is that Hermès is priced for sustained high-single-digit growth and 40% margins, while the multiple on LVMH and Kering implies investors want proof of recovery. Hermès' Q3 growth of 4.3% missed an expected 5.2%, which shows how little room a premium multiple leaves.

We could not find sourced ETF flow, short-interest or year-to-date relative performance data for this sub-industry, so we cannot quantify positioning. What the opened sources do show is a market sorting winners from losers. Saxo wrote in August 2026 that European luxury shares had come under pressure and that lower prices do not automatically create opportunities. Bain reports that about 60% of luxury players are outperforming their prior-year results and that performance gaps between brands are narrowing.

Operating news will drive momentum into year-end. Richemont's first-half operating profit rose 33%, Coach's revenue rose 16% and Ralph Lauren raised guidance, while LVMH's fashion division fell 5% organically in Q3 and lululemon cut its outlook to a 5% to 7% revenue decline. Breadth is therefore narrow: leadership is concentrated in jewelry and a few high-end or US brands rather than the whole group. Sector-level analyst targets were not available for this group in the FactSet issue we opened.

Apparel retail is splitting in two. Off-price chains are taking share: TJX's comparable sales rose 4% in its October quarter, with Marmaxx up 2%, and Ross guides Q3 comps up 6% to 7% after a 10% gain in Q2. Full-price specialty is mixed: Gap's Q2 comps fell 1% with Old Navy down 4%, while Abercrombie's were flat. Reported profits are inflated by one-off refunds of tariffs struck down in February. Strip those out and TJX's pretax margin fell 0.2 points on freight and fuel, while Gap's adjusted gross margin rose 20 bps. TJX trades at about 25x forward earnings, Ross at 26.6x, Burlington at 20.6x and Gap at under 8x.

Apparel retailers buy clothing, shoes and accessories from brands and factories, or design their own, and sell them to shoppers through stores and websites. They earn the gap between what the goods cost and the shelf price, then try to keep rent, labour and markdowns below that gap. GICS puts the stores here, not the brand owners that make and wholesale clothes (Textiles, Apparel & Luxury Goods), nor department stores and general merchants (Broadline Retail). Off-price chains such as TJX sit here too, selling branded apparel and home goods.

Off-price apparel: Brand-name clothing, shoes and home goods bought opportunistically from brands and other retailers and sold at steep discounts to regular prices. Customers hunt for bargains, so stock turns over fast. e.g. TJ Maxx, Marshalls, Ross Dress for Less, Burlington

Mass-market specialty chains: Retailers selling mostly their own-brand clothing, designed in-house and made by contract factories, at moderate prices through malls, strip centres and online. e.g. Gap, Old Navy, Banana Republic, American Eagle, Abercrombie & Fitch, Hollister

Teen and young-adult fashion: Trend-led chains that change assortments often and rely on social media and mall traffic. Fashion misses show up quickly in markdowns. e.g. Urban Outfitters, American Eagle, Hollister

Intimates and activewear: Focused brands in a single category, selling bras, underwear, loungewear or athletic clothing, often with strong brand loyalty and their own stores. e.g. Victoria's Secret, Athleta (Gap Inc.)

E-commerce and omnichannel: Websites and apps that sell the same goods as the stores, with delivery or store pick-up. Returns and shipping cost more than in-store sales. e.g. tjmaxx.com, oldnavy.com, abercrombie.com

Consumer income and confidence: Clothing is a discretionary purchase, so spending follows jobs, wages and gasoline prices. Squeezed households trade down, which helps off-price chains and hurts full-price mall brands.

Tariffs and trade policy: Most clothing is imported, so duties raise landed cost. Retailers pass some of it into prices, absorb some, and push vendors to share it, which moves gross margin within a few quarters.
Markdowns and inventory control: Buying too much forces discounts. Lean inventories keep prices full and margins up, so inventory growth against sales is a closely watched signal.
Store openings: Off-price chains add stores steadily, which lifts total sales, while very high store density can lower comps through cannibalization.
Freight, fuel and wages: Shipping and fuel costs enter cost of goods; wages and rent sit in operating expenses. Both are hard to pass on in full, so they squeeze margins in inflationary periods.
Fashion and brand heat: Own-brand retailers rise and fall with whether shoppers like this season's product. A hit brand can post double-digit comps; a miss leads to markdowns.
Comparable sales (comps): Sales growth at stores and sites open at least a year. It strips out the effect of opening new stores and is the main health check for a retailer.
Off-price: A model that buys branded goods at a discount from closeouts, cancelled orders and overruns, and passes part of the saving to shoppers, with no promotions.
Opportunistic buying: Buying goods close to when they are needed, as the supply appears, rather than placing orders a year ahead. It lowers the risk of being stuck with unsold fashion.
Markdown: A price cut to clear unsold goods. Rising markdowns signal weak demand or poor buying and hit gross margin directly.
Gross margin: Sales minus the cost of goods (and, at some retailers, buying, freight and occupancy costs), as a share of sales. Higher in own-brand retailers, lower at off-price.
Inventory turnover: How many times a year a retailer sells through its stock. Fast turnover means fresher goods, fewer markdowns and less cash tied up.
Landed cost: What a garment costs by the time it arrives in the US: factory price, freight, insurance and import duties. Tariffs raise it directly.
Packaway: Off-price goods bought at a discount and stored for sale in a later season, which smooths supply.
Cannibalization: New stores taking sales from nearby existing stores of the same chain, which lowers comps even when total sales rise.
Operating leverage: Because rent and payroll are largely fixed, extra sales raise profit faster than sales, and a sales drop cuts it faster too.
IEEPA tariffs: Import duties imposed under an emergency-powers law that the Supreme Court ruled unlawful in February 2026. Importers who paid them can claim refunds.
Sourcing mix: Which countries a retailer's goods come from. Vietnam, Bangladesh and China lead for apparel, so changes in duties on those countries matter.
Ross reports Q3 shortly; it has guided comps up 6% to 7% after a 10% Q2, so the bar is high.
Holiday season: NRF forecasts November-December retail sales up 4.2% to $1.013 trillion, but warns that gas prices, inflation and debt are squeezing budgets unevenly.
Tariff regime: temporary Section 122 duties expired on 24 July and were replaced by Section 301 duties of 10% to 12.5% on 60 economies.
Quality of earnings: Gap, Abercrombie, TJX and Burlington all booked IEEPA refunds, so reported margins overstate the run rate.
Rates and gasoline: the Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% with two dissenters wanting a hike, and gasoline was up 37.4% year on year in October.
TJX Companies, Ross Stores, Burlington Stores, Gap Inc., Abercrombie & Fitch, American Eagle Outfitters, Urban Outfitters, Victoria's Secret

Retailers earn revenue by selling apparel and accessories to the public through stores and websites. TJX's Marmaxx segment alone had net sales of $9.11B in its July 2026 quarter, up 3%. Own-brand chains such as Gap Inc. sell mostly their own brands; Gap's Q2 net sales were $3.65B across four brands.

Customers are overwhelmingly individual consumers, mostly shopping for family apparel. Segments differ by income and age: off-price draws value-seekers across incomes, Old Navy targets families, Abercrombie and Hollister target teens and young adults. Abercrombie & Fitch says its record Q2 sales were its 15th consecutive quarter of growth.

The largest cost is the merchandise itself, followed by occupancy (rent), store labour, freight and marketing. TJX describes a low-cost model with advertising focused on banners rather than products and stores built without heavy fixtures. Freight and fuel cut TJX's adjusted gross margin by 0.5 points in Q3.

Pricing power rests on brand heat and on value. Abercrombie's roughly 71% gross margin (inflated by tariff refunds and defined before depreciation) versus TJX's 32.9% shows, though not like for like, how differently positioned own-brand and off-price models are. TJX prices 20% to 60% below full-price retailers on comparable goods and does not run promotions. Mall brands depend on product appeal and often discount.

The main assets are inventory and store leases. TJX held $9.8B of inventory at 31 Oct 2026, and at 1 Aug 2026 operating lease right-of-use assets of $11.2B against lease liabilities of about $11.4B. Leases are the biggest liability, ahead of long-term debt of $1.9B.

Mostly asset-light compared with industry, but store-heavy. Damodaran puts net capex at 2.1% of sales for apparel and 1.6% for special-line retail, against 4.2% for the whole market. Stores are leased rather than owned, so the real commitment sits in lease liabilities. Gap guides capex of about $650M for fiscal 2026.

One estimate values the US apparel market at about $366B in 2025, growing around 2% a year to 2035. Treat this as a rough guide, since market-research firms define the market differently. Store sales are only part of the total, and online marketplaces are the fastest-growing channel in that estimate at 3.1% a year.

Main segments are off-price, mass-market and teen specialty chains, intimates and activewear brands, and online sellers. Women's apparel is the largest product type, at 48% of the market in one estimate, and mid-market price points hold 40%. Retailers like TJX also sell home goods, which is a separate large profit pool.

Retailers sit between brands or factories and consumers. Suppliers are thousands of manufacturers and brands; TJX alone buys from about 21,000 vendors in more than 100 countries. Own-brand chains commission contract factories mainly in Asia, so US imports of main apparel categories (about $72.7B in 2025) are the key upstream flow.

The industry moved from department stores and malls toward off-price, value and online. TJX has grown to 5,349 stores and targets 7,500 long term, up 500 from its earlier goal. Ross plans 115 new stores in 2026. Meanwhile own-brand mall chains grow slowly: Gap guides 2026 net sales up just 1% to 1.5%.

Sales are concentrated in the US, with large chains also in Canada and Europe. TJX's Q2 sales split into Marmaxx at $9.11B, HomeGoods $2.51B, Canada $1.47B and International $2.09B. Production is concentrated in Asia: Vietnam supplied 26.6% of man-made fibre garment imports and Bangladesh 15.3% of cotton garment imports by value in 2025.

There are hundreds of apparel retailers, but a few dozen significant public chains in the US. The sub-industry includes TJX, Ross, Burlington, Gap Inc., Abercrombie, American Eagle, Urban Outfitters and Victoria's Secret, among others. Many private and international players, plus online-only sellers, also compete.

TJX is the largest, with 5,349 stores and Q3 net sales of $15.95B. Ross follows with about $6.3B of quarterly sales, then Gap Inc. at $3.65B, and Abercrombie at about $1.27B. We found no public market-share table for apparel retail, so ranking here is by sales.

The industry is fragmented overall but concentrated in off-price, where TJX, Ross and Burlington dominate. Apparel retail as a whole competes with department, specialty, off-price, discount, warehouse and outlet stores plus online sellers, as TJX's filing lists. No single retailer sets prices for the whole market.

Entry is easy, scale is hard. Anyone can open a website, but TJX built buying relationships with about 21,000 vendors and a 31 million square foot distribution network over decades. Off-price needs vendors willing to sell surplus goods, and mall brands need product heat that is hard to manufacture. Capital need is modest.

Scale helps in sourcing, distribution, vendor access and technology. TJX's buying organisation of over 1,400 Associates covers more than 100 countries. Scale also helps spread fixed costs, and the largest off-price chains post operating margins near 12.7% to 12.8% while a mid-sized peer like Burlington earns 7.8%.

Mostly differentiated at the brand level but commoditized for basics. Own-brand apparel (Abercrombie, Gap) rests on brand and design, while off-price sells other people's brands and competes on price and selection. Gap's Gap brand comps rose 10% while Old Navy fell 4% in the same quarter, showing how much product relevance matters within one company.

Suppliers are numerous, so buyers have the upper hand with vendors, but customers have the real power: shoppers switch easily and prices are visible online. Large retailers like TJX can demand cost-sharing; Gap booked about $95M of vendor appreciation commitments tied to its tariff refunds, showing that suppliers also share the cost of trade shocks.

Revenue growth comes from comparable sales (traffic, ticket) and new stores. TJX comps were 4% in Q3 with 64 net new stores in the quarter; Ross added transactions to reach 10% comps in Q2. Own-brand chains rely more on brand relevance: Abercrombie's sales grew 5% on flat comps, which means growth came from new space and other sources.

Operating margins depend on gross margin (markdowns, tariffs, freight) minus occupancy and labour. TJX's adjusted pretax margin was 12.5% in Q3; Gap's adjusted operating margin was 7.1% in Q2. Damodaran's pre-tax margin for special-line retail is 7.7% against 12.8% for the whole market.

Key costs are merchandise, freight and fuel, wages and rent, and tariffs. TJX cited higher freight and fuel as the reason adjusted gross margin fell 0.5 points. Gasoline was up 37.4% year on year in October. Refunds of earlier tariffs are now reversing part of that cost in reported numbers.

Direct sensitivity is limited because stores are leased and debt is small relative to profits: Damodaran shows interest coverage of 13.5 for special-line retail. Indirect sensitivity is larger: higher rates dampen housing turnover and consumer credit. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026, with two members voting for a hike.

Apparel is sensitive to jobs, real incomes and prices. Unemployment has changed little and the Fed calls spending resilient, but the last full 12-month CPI reading was 3.7% in September and apparel prices rose 0.1% in October. Commodity prices (cotton, oil for synthetics and freight) matter. NRF says inflation and gas prices will affect income groups differently.

Cyclical at the edges, but defensive within the cycle for off-price: shoppers trade down when budgets tighten. TJX and Ross have grown comps through recent volatility, while mall specialty and teen brands are more cyclical and fashion-dependent. There is no strong secular growth in total apparel spend, about 2% a year in one estimate.

Growth is modest and company-specific. Damodaran's estimate of five-year expected earnings growth is 8.1% for special-line retail versus 14.0% for the whole market. Recent top-line growth ranges from TJX's 6% in Q3 and Abercrombie's 5% in Q2 to Gap's 2% decline.

Gross margins vary by model: Damodaran's January 2026 data shows 35.3% for special-line retail and 56.9% for apparel (brand owners). TJX reports 32.1% adjusted gross margin. Pre-tax operating margins are 7.7% for special-line retail and 9.1% for apparel, versus TJX's 12.5% adjusted pretax margin.

Returns on capital are high at off-price leaders. Damodaran's after-tax lease-adjusted ROIC is 21.7% for special-line retail and 15.8% for apparel. StockAnalysis shows ROIC of 31.5% for TJX and 33.6% for Ross, against 10.2% for Burlington and 10.1% for Gap.

Leverage is moderate once leases are counted. Damodaran puts book debt to capital at 60.2% for special-line retail and 56.3% for apparel, with market debt-to-equity of 20.9% and 33.0%. TJX had about $2.9B of debt at 1 Aug 2026 and $4.6B of cash at 31 Oct 2026. Interest coverage is 13.5 for special-line retail.

Free cash flow is solid at the leaders. FCF yield was 3.9% for TJX, 3.8% for Ross, 2.6% for Burlington and 13.7% for Gap on 18 Nov 2026. Gap's yield is inflated by refunds and a low share price. TJX returned $1.5B to shareholders in Q3 and plans about $3.0B of buybacks this year.

Capital expenditure is low: Damodaran's net capex-to-sales is 1.6% for special-line retail and 2.1% for apparel, versus 4.2% for the whole market. Gap guides about $650M this year. Growth capex goes into new stores, distribution centres and technology, and leases carry the rest of the commitment.

Valuation multiples: Damodaran's forward P/E is 21.5 for special-line retail and 24.9 for apparel against 27.7 for the whole market, in January 2026. In Nov 2026, TJX trades at 25.0x forward, Ross 26.6x, Burlington 20.6x and Gap 7.8x. The XRT ETF is at 14.8x.

Trade policy is the largest regulatory risk. The Supreme Court voided IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, a temporary 10% Section 122 duty followed, and on 24 July Section 301 duties of 10% to 12.5% on 60 economies replaced it. TJX's filing flags tariff and refund timing uncertainty.

AI and technology help with forecasting, pricing and marketing but also let competitors use the same tools; TJX's filing names AI among technologies competitors may integrate faster. We did not find hard numbers on AI's effect on apparel retail earnings, so the effect is hard to quantify here.

Demographics matter little for total spend, since clothing is a staple that follows population and incomes. Younger shoppers drive trend-led chains like Abercrombie and Hollister, and Abercrombie has grown 15 consecutive quarters. Broad population growth is slow, consistent with a roughly 2% annual market growth estimate.

Shoppers are trading down and hunting for value, which helps off-price: Ross comps were up 10% on higher transactions. NRF says consumers will prioritize the holidays but stay mindful of budgets, with gasoline and inflation weighing on lower-income households. Shifts toward online, resale and social-media-led fashion change where spending goes.

New competitors include online marketplaces and value platforms, where online marketplaces are the fastest-growing channel in one estimate, plus off-price entrants. Within off-price, rivals are adding stores quickly: TJX plans 4% annual store growth from fiscal 2028 and Ross plans 115 openings in 2026.

Geopolitics and supply chains matter because supply comes from Asia: Vietnam and Bangladesh are the top sources for fibre and cotton garments. Shipping disruption, port delays and fuel costs hit margins, as TJX's freight and fuel headwind shows. Single-country concentration raises exposure to new duties.

Substitutes include second-hand and resale marketplaces, rental, direct-to-consumer brands and spending on experiences instead of clothing. The XRT ETF lists RealReal, a resale marketplace, among its top holdings, a sign of how mainstream resale has become. Brand-owned stores and wholesale channels also substitute for multi-brand retailers.
Off-price keeps taking share and expanding: TJX lifted its long-term target to 7,500 stores and plans 4% annual store growth from fiscal 2028.
IEEPA refunds provide a one-time cash and profit windfall: Gap booked about $417M net and Abercrombie about $100M in Q2.
Lower tariff costs than in 2025 and easing freight could rebuild gross margins at chains that cut prices or share costs with vendors.
International growth: TJX International comps rose 8% in Q3.
Section 301 duties replaced the temporary tariff on 24 July, which keeps landed-cost assumptions uncertain.
High gasoline prices (up 37.4% year on year in October) could squeeze shoppers and force deeper markdowns at mall chains.
Fashion misses at own-brand chains: Old Navy comps were down 4% and Athleta's down 12% in Q2.
Rate risk if the Fed hikes, with two members already voting for it.

Over three to five years we think the sub-industry keeps its two-speed shape. Off-price chains have a long runway of new stores and a value proposition that suits stretched households, though high multiples already assume steady execution. Mall and teen brands depend on product hits, and their margins depend on tariff policy that remains unsettled. Today's reported profits overstate normal earnings because of refunds, so judging the next two years means looking through them. Our read is that growth in total apparel spend stays near 2% a year, so winners must take share rather than ride the market.

Where we are in the cycle: spending is resilient but uneven. The Fed held the federal funds range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10-2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a quarter-point hike, and described growth as strong and inflation as elevated. That is not the usual easing backdrop for discretionary retail. Higher rates matter less to apparel chains than to housing-linked retailers, because stores are leased and net debt is small, but they weigh on consumer credit.

Prices are the pressure point. apparel prices rose 0.1% in October and gasoline was up 37.4% from a year earlier. The BLS did not publish most year-on-year comparisons for October because it collected no October 2025 data, so the latest 12-month headline is 3.7% for September. NRF still forecasts holiday sales up 4.2% to $1.013 trillion, noting that part of that growth is inflation and that spending differs by income group. Trade policy is the other macro lever: the temporary 10% Section 122 tariff lapsed on 24 July and Section 301 duties of 10% to 12.5% now apply to 60 economies. We think the cycle favours value formats: off-price comps held up in the October quarter while mall-based brands diverged.

Structural demand is steady rather than fast. One market-research estimate puts US apparel at about $366B in 2025, rising at roughly 2% a year to 2035, with women's apparel 48% of the market and online marketplaces the fastest-growing channel at 3.1% a year. We treat the dollar figure as indicative because definitions differ across providers.

Within that slow market, the growth sits in value. TJX increased its long-term store target by 500 to 7,500 and expects store growth to accelerate to 4% a year starting in fiscal 2028; its filing sees potential for 3,000 Marmaxx stores versus 2,603 at the end of fiscal 2026. Ross plans 115 new stores in 2026. Demand for clothing is moderately elastic: households delay purchases when budgets tighten but trade down rather than stop, which benefits off-price. Cyclicality is highest for teen and fashion-led brands. Demographics barely move total volume, so share shifts, not market growth, drive winners and losers.

Porter's five forces point to a competitive but not hopeless industry. Rivalry is intense: TJX's filing lists department, specialty, off-price, discount, warehouse and outlet stores and online sellers as competitors. Threat of new entrants is high for online brands but low for off-price at scale, which needs about 21,000 vendor relationships and a 31 million square foot distribution network. Supplier power is low, since goods are widely sourced from many countries. Buyer power is high because shoppers can compare prices instantly and switch brands. The threat of substitutes comes from resale, rental and other spending.

Concentration is meaningful at the top of off-price. TJX had 5,349 stores and $15.95B of Q3 sales; Ross had $6.3B of Q2 sales; Gap Inc. had $3.65B; Abercrombie $1.27B. We found no published market-share table, so we rank by sales. Moats differ: TJX's is buying scale and vendor trust (it pays promptly and does not ask for markdown allowances); Abercrombie's is brand, reflected in a guided FY2026 operating margin of 14.5% to 15.0% that includes refunds. Pricing power is stronger in brands that are in fashion and weak for undifferentiated mall retailers.

Politics and regulation are dominated by trade. The Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling that IEEPA tariffs were unlawful opened a path to refunds; TJX's filing says timing and administration are unknown. By the August quarter refunds were flowing: Gap recorded about $512M gross, Abercrombie about $100M, and TJX recorded a $0.14 per share benefit in Q2 and $0.05 in Q3. From 24 July Section 301 duties of 10% to 12.5% replaced the temporary Section 122 tariff on 60 economies,.

Economic and social factors are covered above. Technological change cuts both ways: AI tools improve forecasting and marketing, but TJX lists AI among technologies competitors may adopt faster. Environmental and legal exposure comes through vendor compliance, forced-labour rules and supply-chain audits; TJX notes its vendors have not always complied with its code of conduct. Currency matters for international sales, as TJX International's comps of 8% show. We think the biggest emerging risk is policy whiplash: duties that change faster than retailers can re-source.

Retail economics are thin margin, high turnover. Damodaran's January 2026 data gives special-line retail a gross margin of 35.3%, a pre-tax operating margin of 7.7%, a net margin of 5.2% and EBITDA/sales of 9.9%, against 12.8% operating margin for the total market. Apparel (brand owners) shows 56.9% gross margin but 9.1% operating margin. At TJX the adjusted pretax margin was 12.5% in Q3.

Returns are strong because capital intensity is low. Net capex is 1.6% of sales for special-line retail, 2.1% for apparel and 4.2% for the whole market. After-tax lease-adjusted ROIC is 21.7% for special-line retail and 15.8% for apparel against 17.4% for the market. Company screens show ROIC of about 31.5% at TJX and 33.6% at Ross but about 10% at Burlington and Gap. Operating leverage works both ways: Gap's adjusted operating margin was 7.1% in Q2 on a 2% sales decline. Free cash flow yields are 3.9% at TJX, 3.8% at Ross and 2.6% at Burlington. Gap's reported operating margin of 18.5% was inflated by refunds, so we ignore it.

Reported earnings are inflated by refunds, so quality matters. TJX's Q3 diluted EPS was $1.39 (up 9%) but adjusted EPS was $1.34 (up 5%) after a $0.05 refund benefit; adjusted gross margin fell 0.5 points on freight and fuel. TJX guides Q4 comps up 2% to 3% and full-year comps up 4%, with full-year adjusted EPS of $5.17 to $5.20.

Ross raised its outlook to comps of 6% to 7% in Q3 and 4% to 5% in Q4 after a 10% Q2. Abercrombie raised full-year EPS to $13.10 to $13.60 from $10.20 to $11.00, but most of the raise is refunds of about $1.75 per share; its operating margin guide is 14.5% to 15.0%. Gap guides adjusted EPS of $2.35 to $2.45, net sales up 1% to 1.5% and Old Navy comps flat to down 1%.

Our read is that guidance across off-price implies decelerating comps into the fourth quarter (Ross 4% to 5%, TJX 2% to 3%), and that investors will look past refunds to tariff-adjusted margins. We think consensus risk is greater for mall brands that depend on a strong holiday. We did not find consensus estimate tables for the group that we could open, so we do not state where we differ from them.

Valuation is split. On 18 Nov 2026, forward P/E was 25.0x for TJX, 26.6x for Ross, 20.6x for Burlington and 7.8x for Gap. Gap's multiple is flattered by refund-inflated earnings and a 52-week price decline of 16.5%. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT), a basket of many retail formats, trades at 14.8x.

Against history and the market, Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E was 21.5 for special-line retail and 24.9 for apparel against 27.7 for all firms. So TJX and Ross look full relative to the retail group, and justified only if their high returns on capital persist: ROIC is above 30% at both. Their FCF yields of 3.9% and 3.8% are modest. Expected five-year growth is 8.1% for special-line retail against 14.0% for the market, and the PEG ratio is 3.1. Our read is that off-price is priced for execution with little room for a comp miss, while Gap and Burlington carry lower expectations. We did not find 10-year average multiples for these names that we could open, so we do not compare them with their own history.

Momentum favours off-price. Ross shares were up 42.8% over 52 weeks to 18 Nov 2026, while TJX was down 3.4%, Burlington down 9.6% and Gap down 16.5%. The XRT ETF returned 4.75% year to date to 31 Oct 2026 and 10.5% over one year, with net assets of $640M as of 17 Nov.

Short interest tells a story about conviction. Short interest as a share of float was 1.4% for TJX, 2.9% for Ross, 4.7% for Burlington and 11.8% for Gap. The high short interest at Gap reflects doubts about Old Navy and Athleta. XRT's top holdings are spread across formats (Upbound, Academy Sports, RealReal, Kohl's and Victoria's Secret are each about 1.8%), so it is a broad retail proxy rather than an apparel one. We did not find ETF flow data we could open.

Our read is that positioning is crowded in the best-known off-price names and sparse in specialty apparel, which means earnings surprises could move the latter more. Ross reports Q3 shortly with a 6% to 7% comp guide.

Homebuilders are in a margin squeeze rather than a volume collapse. Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.28% on 19 November against 6.26% a year ago, and the NAHB builder index fell to 25, its lowest since April 2012. Net orders were down 6% to 9% at D.R. Horton, Lennar, Pulte and NVR, while home sale gross margin fell to 15.8% at Lennar and 18.3% at NVR. Luxury builder Toll grew signed contracts about 5% in its July quarter. September single-family starts were 859,000 and new-home supply was 8.4 months. We found no sourced consensus estimates.

Homebuilders buy and develop land, build houses and sell them to buyers, usually with a mortgage. Revenue is the number of homes closed times the average price, and profit depends on the gap between that price and the cost of land, labour and materials. GICS puts residential builders and manufactured-home makers here. Building products, home improvement retail and appliances sit in other sub-industries, and rental-housing owners are real estate companies.

Entry-level and first-time homes: Smaller, lower-priced houses built in volume on standardised plans, sold to first-time and budget-conscious buyers who are very sensitive to monthly payments. e.g. D.R. Horton, Lennar

Move-up and active-adult homes: Larger houses and age-restricted communities for existing owners trading up or downsizing, who often bring equity from a prior sale. e.g. PulteGroup (Centex, Pulte, Del Webb brands)
Luxury homes: High-priced, more customised houses for affluent buyers who depend less on mortgage financing. e.g. Toll Brothers

Mortgage and title services: In-house lenders and title companies finance and close buyers' purchases, which captures extra fee income and helps the builder control the sale. e.g. Pulte Mortgage, NVR Mortgage, Lennar Financial Services

Lot development: Some builders develop finished lots themselves or buy them from affiliates and third parties, so they can build without owning years of raw land. e.g. Forestar, which supplies D.R. Horton
Rental homes: Some builders build single-family or multifamily homes to rent or sell to investors, a small side line next to for-sale homes. e.g. D.R. Horton rental operations

Mortgage rates and affordability: Most buyers borrow, so higher rates raise the monthly payment. Builders respond with price cuts and rate buy-downs, which show up as lower gross margin and fewer orders.
Consumer confidence and employment: A house is the largest purchase most people make. Job worries delay it, which shows up as fewer buyers and more cancellations.
Land and construction costs: Land is bought years ahead and moves with prices, and lumber, labour and tariffs affect build cost. If selling prices fall faster than cost, margin is squeezed.
Supply of existing homes: Owners with low-rate mortgages tend to stay put, which limits resale supply and pushes buyers toward new homes. When resale listings rise, builders compete harder on price.
Incentive intensity: Spending on buy-downs and closing costs is a direct cut to price. It rises when sales pace slows.
Land strategy and capital returns: Builders that control land by option need less capital and can return more cash through buybacks, while those that own more land carry more risk in a downturn.
Regulation and permitting: Zoning, building codes, impact fees and slow approvals add cost and delay starts, which limits how fast builders can add supply.
Net new orders: Signed sales contracts in a period after cancellations. It is the earliest read on demand, because homes close months later.
Backlog: Homes under contract that have not yet closed. It sets the next few quarters' revenue.
Closings (deliveries, settlements): Homes handed over to buyers. Revenue is recognised at closing, not at the contract date.
Average selling price (ASP): Home sales revenue divided by homes closed. Mix between cheap and expensive homes moves it as much as price changes do.
Gross margin: Home sale revenue less the cost of the home, including land, construction and capitalised interest, as a percent of revenue. It is the key profitability gauge.
Incentives: Price cuts, mortgage rate buy-downs and closing-cost help given to win a sale. They reduce margin and are higher when affordability is poor.
Cancellation rate: Share of gross orders that buyers cancel before closing. A rise signals buyers failing to qualify for or afford financing.
Spec home: A house started before a buyer signs a contract. Spec building speeds sales but leaves the builder holding completed unsold homes if demand weakens.

Option or controlled lots: Lots the builder has a contract to buy later, paying a deposit instead of owning them. It lowers capital use and risk but can leave impairments if deals are walked away from.
Community count: Number of active selling neighbourhoods. More communities usually means more orders.
Absorption pace: Homes sold per community per month. A builder can cut price or add incentives to hold pace.
Months' supply: Homes for sale divided by the monthly sales rate. Above six months is usually read as an oversupplied market.
Mortgage rates have risen again to 7.28% from 6.26% a year ago, which is the main brake on orders and the reason incentives are rising.
Lennar guides fourth-quarter home sale gross margin to 15.5% to 16.0% and has already cut its 2026 delivery target to 80,000 to 81,000 homes.
Cancellation rates are rising: 23% at D.R. Horton in its September quarter against 20% a year earlier, and 21% at NVR against 19%.
Toll Brothers' fiscal fourth quarter is the next test of whether the luxury buyer keeps defying the slowdown; its latest release reaffirmed about $10.5B of 2026 home sales revenue.
The Federal Reserve held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October with two dissenters preferring a rise, so near-term relief on rates looks limited.
D.R. Horton, Lennar, PulteGroup, NVR, Toll Brothers

Revenue is almost entirely home sales, plus smaller mortgage, title and lot-sale income. PulteGroup's third-quarter home sale revenue was $3.86B on 6,876 closings, and its financial services arm added $46M of pre-tax income. D.R. Horton also earns from Forestar lot sales, with 83% of Forestar's fiscal 2025 lots sold to D.R. Horton.

Customers are individual households, from first-time buyers to affluent move-up buyers, plus some rental investors. The price points differ widely: Lennar's average sales price was $372,000, Pulte's $561,000, NVR's settlements averaged $445,900 and Toll's $996,400.

The largest cost is the house itself: land, labour, materials and capitalised interest, shown as cost of sales. Gross margin ranged from 15.8% at Lennar to 24.8% at Pulte in the latest quarters. Selling, general and administrative costs came to 9.2% of revenue at Lennar and 10.3% at Pulte.

Pricing power depends on location, product and how much buyers rely on financing. In the current market it is weak: 46% of builders cut prices and 68% used incentives in November, per NAHB. Lennar's incentives were about 12.0% of revenue. Luxury builders such as Toll have held up better, with adjusted gross margin of 25.6%.

Main assets are land and homes in inventory, which are financed with debt and cash. D.R. Horton held 28,200 homes in inventory, of which 8,800 were completed and unsold, and 570,600 lots owned or controlled, 130,500 of them owned. Liabilities are mostly notes payable: $6.05B at D.R. Horton and a 12.1% debt-to-capital ratio at Pulte.

The business is capital intensive in land and inventory but light in fixed plant, since subcontractors do most construction. Builders manage this by controlling lots through options: Lennar owns fewer than 2.5% of its roughly 488,000 homesites on its balance sheet. Damodaran's sales to invested capital is 1.42 for US homebuilders.

We did not find a single sourced global market-size figure for homebuilding. In the US, the Census Bureau's new-home sales rate was 676,000 a year in September 2026, and single-family starts ran at 859,000 a year. D.R. Horton alone closed 84,202 homes in fiscal 2026.

Main segments are entry-level, move-up, luxury and age-restricted homes, plus a smaller manufactured-housing and rental segment. D.R. Horton and Lennar lead the entry-level end, with average prices of about $366,000 and $372,000, Pulte is in the middle at $561,000, and Toll is at about $1M.

Builders sit between land developers, subcontractors and materials suppliers on one side, and mortgage lenders and homebuyers on the other. Lot supply is a key link: Forestar supplies D.R. Horton, and Lennar controls most of its homesites by option instead of owning them.

The industry has moved from owning land to controlling it by contract, and from custom building to standardised plans with in-house mortgage and title arms. D.R. Horton describes itself as the largest US homebuilder by homes closed. Spec building has grown too: 17,700 of D.R. Horton's homes in inventory were unsold at 30 September 2026.

Activity concentrates in the South and Sun Belt, where land is cheaper and population is growing. D.R. Horton operates in 126 markets across 36 states. NAHB's regional builder index in November was 27 in the South and 23 in the West, against 34 in the Northeast and 35 in the Midwest.

There are five large listed national builders and hundreds of regional and private ones. D.R. Horton's 10-K says it competes with local, regional and national builders and rental companies, and also with existing homes for sale.

D.R. Horton is the largest by homes closed, with 84,202 closings in fiscal 2026, followed by Lennar with a 2026 delivery target of 80,000 to 81,000 homes. Pulte guides to fewer homes than that at higher prices: it closed 6,876 homes in the quarter. We did not find sourced market-share percentages.

The industry is more fragmented than most, because housing is local and most builders work in a few metro areas. The listed leaders are consolidated by size but still compete locally with many small builders, which is why D.R. Horton lists local and regional competitors.

Barriers to entry include land access, capital, local relationships, labour supply and approvals. Entrenched builders hold lot pipelines: Lennar controls about 488,000 homesites and D.R. Horton 570,600 lots. A newcomer would struggle to match that.

Scale helps with materials purchasing, land deals, in-house finance and brand, but not as much as in manufacturing because every site is local. D.R. Horton competes on price, location, quality and design, and mortgage financing terms. We think its scale and cost position explain how it stayed profitable while margins narrowed.

Homes are partly commoditised at the entry level, where price and monthly payment decide, and more differentiated in luxury, where design and location matter. Toll's adjusted gross margin of 25.6% against Lennar's 15.8% reflects that gap.

Customers have the stronger bargaining position now. With NAHB reporting 46% of builders cutting prices and 68% using incentives, buyers can negotiate. Suppliers of land and labour also have leverage in strong markets, which we think is why land impairments are appearing.

Revenue growth comes from closings and price. D.R. Horton's fiscal 2026 orders rose 2% for the year but fell 7% in the fourth quarter. New-home sales ran at 676,000 a year in September. We think order pace, not price, now sets revenue.
Operating margins depend on price relative to land and build cost, and on incentives. Lennar's gross margin was 15.8% against 17.5% a year earlier,. NVR's fell to 18.3% from 21.0%.

Key cost variables are land, labour, lumber and other materials, and capitalised interest. NVR took impairments of about $24.8M on contract land deposits in the quarter. Pulte took $26M of land impairments.

Rates matter more than anything else. Freddie Mac's 30-year average was 7.28% on 19 November against 6.26% a year earlier. NAHB's builder index of 25 sits with mortgage rates above 7%. We note the Fed's own range is 3.75% to 4.00%, so mortgage rates are pricing in more than the policy rate.

Inflation, jobs, GDP and commodities matter through confidence and cost. The FOMC statement says inflation remains elevated and unemployment has changed little. Builder sentiment suggests buyers are cautious: traffic fell to 16 in the NAHB survey. We did not find sourced commodity price figures.

Homebuilding is strongly cyclical and rate-sensitive. D.R. Horton notes that it generally closes more homes and earns more in its third and fourth fiscal quarters, so seasonality sits on top of the cycle.

Growth has stalled. D.R. Horton's fiscal 2026 revenue was $33.0B and its fiscal 2027 guide is $30B to $32B. Pulte's nine-month diluted EPS was $6.79 against $8.55, and NVR's nine-month net income fell 30%.

Damodaran's US homebuilding data show a 22.70% gross margin, 12.91% operating margin and 9.47% net margin as of January 2026. Reported quarters are mixed against that: D.R. Horton's pre-tax margin was 10.8% in the quarter, and Pulte's was about 15.7% by our calculation.

Damodaran puts US homebuilding return on invested capital at 14.91% and after-tax operating margin at 10.49%. D.R. Horton reports return on equity of 12.2% and homebuilding return on investment of 16.6% for fiscal 2026. We did not find sourced ROE for the rest of the group.
Leverage is low for a capital-heavy business. D.R. Horton's debt to total capital is 20.8%, Lennar's homebuilding figure is 16.6%, Pulte's is 12.1% and Toll's is 24.5%.

Free cash flow is positive and mostly returned. D.R. Horton generated $3.5B of operating cash flow in fiscal 2026 and repurchased 24.0M shares for $3.6B. Pulte bought back $1.0B of shares year to date, and NVR repurchased $1.23B in nine months.

Capital spending on plant is small; the investment is in land and inventory. Pulte's house and land inventory was $14.09B, and Lennar reports an inventory turn of 2.4x. Cash is tied up in lots and unsold homes rather than equipment.

Damodaran's US homebuilding group trades at 8.92x EV/EBITDA on positive-EBITDA firms and 8.43x on all firms, as of January 2026. The iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF showed a price-to-earnings ratio of 14.50 on 18 November 2026, but that fund also holds building products and retailers.

Regulation is mostly local: zoning, building codes and approvals slow supply and raise cost. D.R. Horton lists zoning and entitlement review as part of every land decision. We did not find sourced evidence on a specific national change this quarter.
Technology and AI are unlikely to disrupt the builder model soon, since houses are built on site. We did not find sourced evidence of AI changing homebuilding economics.

Demographics support long-run demand, but we did not find sourced household-formation figures. The practical constraint is affordability: the median new-home price was $400,400 in September 2026, and mortgage rates are above 7%.

Buyer behaviour has shifted to demanding incentives. NAHB says 68% of builders offered them in November, a post-Covid high, and D.R. Horton expects incentives to remain elevated in fiscal 2027. Rising cancellations to 23% at D.R. Horton and 21% at NVR show buyers backing out.

Competition now comes from the resale market and rentals, as well as other builders. D.R. Horton says it competes with existing home sales and rental properties. With supply at 8.4 months, new homes are priced against a market that has plenty of stock.

Supply-chain and geopolitical risk shows up in lumber, materials and labour costs. Our sources did not quantify tariffs or immigration effects, so we do not give a number. D.R. Horton lists skilled labour and raw materials among the things it competes for.

Substitutes are renting, buying an existing home, or moving in with family. Existing homes compete directly with new ones, and D.R. Horton also runs a rental business. If rates stay high we think renting remains a real alternative for entry-level buyers.
Lower mortgage rates would quickly lift affordability, since the 30-year rate has risen from 6.26% to 7.28% in a year.
Low leverage and strong cash flow let builders keep buying back stock: D.R. Horton plans about $3.0B of repurchases in fiscal 2027.
Builders controlling lots by option, as Lennar does, can cut starts quickly and protect returns if demand falls further.
Luxury buyers have held up, with Toll's July-quarter signed contracts up about 5% in units.
Sustained mortgage rates above 7% could keep orders weak and incentives high, as the NAHB index of 25 shows.
Margins are still falling: Lennar guides 15.5% to 16.0% for the fourth quarter and D.R. Horton expects incentives to stay elevated.
Higher cancellations and 8.4 months of new-home supply point to excess inventory if sales do not recover.
The Fed has two members preferring a rate increase, so rates may not fall soon.

Over the next three to five years we think the industry is set for lower-margin growth rather than a collapse. Balance sheets are strong, with debt-to-capital between 12.1% and 24.5% and large buybacks, which means builders can survive a long period of weak demand. But the evidence for rate relief is thin: the Fed held and two members wanted a rise, and mortgage rates are above 7%. Builders that control land cheaply and offer lower-priced homes, such as D.R. Horton and Lennar, face the most pressure on margin, while luxury builders have more pricing room. Our read is that returns will drift toward the Damodaran group norm of about 15% ROIC unless affordability improves.

Homebuilding is in a late-cycle squeeze driven by financing costs, not by a lack of jobs. The Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026 in a 10-2 vote, with two members preferring a quarter-point increase, and said inflation remains elevated while job gains kept pace with the workforce. Mortgage rates have moved the other way from what builders hoped: Freddie Mac's 30-year average was 7.28% on 19 November against 6.26% a year earlier.

The effect is visible in the builders' own results. NAHB's builder index fell to 25 in November, the lowest since April 2012, with prospective buyer traffic at 16 and 46% of builders cutting prices. Census data show September single-family starts at 859,000 a year and single-family permits at 845,000, down 4.0% from August. New-home sales were 676,000 a year, and supply reached 8.4 months.

We think the cycle is closer to a trough in activity than a peak, but the path out depends on rates rather than on the economy. Currency matters little for this domestic group. Fiscal policy was not covered by the sources we opened.

Structural demand rests on the need for housing and on a thin supply of existing homes, but demand is highly elastic to monthly payment. We did not find a sourced figure for the size of the US housing shortage, so we do not quote one. Census data put new-home sales at 676,000 a year in September 2026, with 476,000 new homes for sale.

Orders show how elastic it is. D.R. Horton's fiscal 2026 net orders rose 2% to 84,995 homes, but fourth-quarter orders fell 7%. Lennar's orders fell 9%, Pulte's 6% and NVR's 7%. Toll's July-quarter signed contracts rose about 5% in units to 2,508, which suggests the high end is less sensitive.

Prices have adjusted: the median new-home price was $400,400 in September, 3.9% below a year earlier. Builders also adjusted by offering incentives, such as Lennar's roughly 12.0%. Demographics help over the long run, but affordability decides the near term. Backlogs give some visibility: Pulte's rose 4% to 10,298 homes and NVR's units rose 10%.

By Porter's five forces, rivalry is high but local, and the five large listed builders each hold only a part of the national market. D.R. Horton is the largest by homes closed, with 84,202 closings in fiscal 2026. We did not find sourced share percentages.

The threat of new entrants is moderate: land, capital and approvals are barriers, and big builders control large lot pipelines, such as D.R. Horton's 570,600 lots and Lennar's roughly 488,000 homesites. Buyer power is high now. NAHB says 68% of builders used incentives. Supplier power sits with land owners and subcontractors, though impairments at Pulte and NVR show land risk. Substitutes are resale homes and rentals, which D.R. Horton lists as competitors.

Pricing power is strongest in luxury: Toll's adjusted gross margin was 25.6% and Pulte's was 24.8%, against 15.8% at Lennar. The moats are land position, scale in purchasing, in-house mortgage capture (85% at Pulte). None of these is strong enough to protect margin in a weak market.

Regulation touches homebuilding mainly through land. D.R. Horton's 10-K lists zoning and governmental entitlements as part of its land review, and these slow supply and add cost. We did not find sourced evidence of a specific new federal rule this quarter, so we do not describe one.

Political and economic policy matter through interest rates. The Fed's October decision kept rates at 3.75% to 4.00% with two members wanting a rise, and mortgage rates are 7.28%. Lennar moderated its 2026 delivery target in its latest release. Pulte and NVR took land impairments of $26M and about $24.8M respectively, a sign that deals made at higher prices are being reassessed.

Technology is a smaller factor than in other sectors, because houses are built on site. We did not find sourced evidence of AI or modular construction changing costs. Environmental and social factors, such as energy codes and water limits, are not quantified in the sources we opened.

Margins have fallen from recent highs but remain positive. Damodaran's January 2026 data show a 22.70% gross margin and 12.91% operating margin for 30 US homebuilders, and a 14.91% return on invested capital. Current quarters are below that gross margin at Lennar (15.8%) and NVR (18.3%) and above it at Pulte (24.8%) and Toll (adjusted 25.6%).

D.R. Horton's fiscal 2026 pre-tax margin was 11.8%, with 10.8% in the fourth quarter, and it reported a return on equity of 12.2% and homebuilding return on investment of 16.6%. Lennar's net margin on home sales was 6.6% and SG&A 9.2% of revenue. Pulte's SG&A rose to 10.3% of revenue from 9.4%, showing negative operating leverage as revenue falls.

Capital intensity is in land and inventory, not equipment, and free cash flow is solid. D.R. Horton produced $3.5B of operating cash flow and returned $3.6B through buybacks and $513.3M in dividends. Debt to capital is modest, from 12.1% at Pulte to 24.5% at Toll. Our read is that returns are still healthy but are now compressing, mainly through margin rather than leverage.

Earnings are falling year on year. Pulte's third-quarter net income was $476M against $586M, with EPS of $2.53 against $2.96. NVR's net income fell 27% to $248.6M. Lennar's EPS was $1.19, or $1.23 adjusted, and Toll's July-quarter EPS was $2.97 against $3.73. D.R. Horton earned $2.67 a share in the fourth quarter and $10.11 for fiscal 2026.

Guidance points to more of the same. Lennar guides fourth-quarter orders of 19,500 to 20,500, deliveries of 22,000 to 23,000 and gross margin of 15.5% to 16.0%, and it cut its full-year delivery target to 80,000 to 81,000. D.R. Horton guides fiscal 2027 revenue of $30B to $32B and 79,000 to 84,000 closings, against $33.0B and 84,202 in fiscal 2026. Toll reaffirmed 10,500 to 10,600 deliveries and about $10.5B of home sales revenue for fiscal 2026.

We did not find sourced consensus EPS estimates or revision data for this group, so we cannot say how guidance compares with expectations. Our view is that earnings fall again before they recover, because the order declines of 6% to 9% have not yet worked through closings. For context, FactSet's blended third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth is 31.9%, a high bar next to these declines.

We did not find a sourced forward P/E for the homebuilders alone. The iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF showed a P/E ratio of 14.50 on 18 November 2026, but 63.67% of that fund is homebuilding and the rest building products, retail and chemicals, so it is only a rough guide. FactSet puts the Consumer Discretionary sector at 25.1x forward earnings as of 12 November, against 18.3x for the S&P 500 and its 5-year and 10-year averages of 19.8x and 19.1x. That sector figure is dominated by other businesses and says little about builders.

Damodaran's January 2026 data give an enterprise value to EBITDA of 8.92x for 30 US homebuilders with positive EBITDA, and 8.43x for all firms. That is below the broad market's multiples and fits a business with cyclical earnings and heavy inventory. His data also show a return on invested capital of 14.91%.

Price in the market is easier to judge from capital returns. Pulte repurchased 2.8 million shares at an average of about $124.70 in the quarter, and Lennar bought 3 million at $85.49. Our read is that valuations discount lower earnings already, but we have no sourced price-to-book or forward-earnings figure for individual builders, so we make no firm claim on the cycle history.

The one performance figure we could verify is for the iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF: a year-to-date NAV total return of negative 2.60% as of 18 November 2026, with net assets of about $2.06B and an expense ratio of 0.37%. The fund holds 42 positions, 63.67% in homebuilding, 17.55% in building products and 10.47% in home improvement retail. We did not open data for XHB, so we do not compare them.

We did not find sourced ETF flow, short-interest or institutional positioning data for the group, so we do not estimate them. Company buybacks are the one positioning signal we can see: D.R. Horton repurchased $3.6B in fiscal 2026 and plans about $3.0B in fiscal 2027, Pulte $1.0B year to date and NVR $1.23B in nine months.

Breadth is mixed rather than uniformly weak. Toll's orders grew about 5% in units while the volume builders' fell, and NAHB's regional index is weakest in the West (23) and South (27). Our inference is that the market is already pricing a weak order book and is waiting for evidence on rates.

Automotive retail is splitting in two. Parts retailers are growing on an ageing car fleet: O'Reilly's comparable sales rose 7.2% in the third quarter with a 21.4% operating margin, while Advance Auto Parts' comps fell 1.2%. Dealers face a softer new-car market, with US sales running at a 15.5 million annual pace in October against 16.1 million expected, and AutoNation's net income fell 25%. Used-car sellers are taking share: Carvana's units rose 39% and CarMax's used units 13.8%. Damodaran's US auto retail group trades at 14.8x EV/EBITDA.

This sub-industry covers the businesses that sell vehicles and vehicle supplies to the public: franchised new and used car dealers, online and big-box used-car sellers, auto parts chains and, per GICS, gas station operators. Dealers earn from vehicle sales, financing and insurance products, and the service bay. Parts chains sell to do-it-yourself drivers and professional repair shops. Car makers sit in Automobiles, convenience-store chains with fuel are covered here only where fuel is the core of the business, and tyre makers are in a different industry.

Franchised new-car dealers: Dealers hold a manufacturer's franchise, buy new cars at wholesale and resell them, then earn more from used cars, finance and insurance, and servicing. e.g. AutoNation, Lithia & Driveway, Penske Automotive
Used-car retailers: Sellers that buy used cars from consumers and auctions, recondition them and resell them, often online with home delivery and in-house financing. e.g. CarMax, Carvana

Auto parts retail: Stores and delivery trucks that supply replacement parts, batteries, oil and accessories to drivers who fix their own cars and to professional repair shops. e.g. AutoZone, O'Reilly, Advance Auto Parts
Parts distribution: Wholesalers that stock large ranges of parts and supply independent shops and their own store banners. e.g. Genuine Parts' NAPA
Fuel and convenience retail: Gas station operators earn a small margin per gallon of fuel and use it to bring in customers who buy snacks, drinks and other items inside. e.g. Murphy USA, Casey's
Captive finance arms: Dealers and used-car sellers lend to their own buyers and earn interest, which smooths earnings when vehicle sales slow. e.g. CarMax Auto Finance, AutoNation Finance
Age of the car fleet: Older cars need more repairs, which lifts parts sales and dealer service revenue. It shows up in comparable sales at parts chains.
New-vehicle sales and prices: Volume, price and mix set dealer revenue. Affordability pressure cuts units and gross profit per unit.
Interest rates and credit: Most vehicles are financed, so higher loan rates reduce demand and raise dealers' floorplan costs.
Used-car supply and wholesale prices: Used prices set the margin for used-car sellers. Falling prices help buyers and can squeeze inventory values.
Tariffs and parts costs: Tariffs raise the cost of imported vehicles and parts. Retailers pass some on, which can lift ticket sizes but weigh on volume.
Share shifts between channels: Online sellers, big chains and independent shops compete for the same customers, so share gains show up in unit growth and margins.
SAAR: Seasonally adjusted annual rate of new-vehicle sales, the standard monthly gauge of US car demand.
Comparable store sales: Sales growth at stores open at least a year, which removes the effect of opening new locations.
DIY versus professional: DIY customers fix their own cars; professional customers are repair shops that buy parts in volume, often with delivery. Professional demand is larger and steadier.
F&I: Finance and insurance products sold at the dealership, such as loans and extended warranties. They carry high margins and offset thin vehicle margins.
Fixed operations (after-sales): Service and parts business at a dealership. It brings in repeat revenue and holds up when car sales fall.
Gross profit per unit (GPU): Gross profit earned on each vehicle sold. Dealers watch it with unit volume, since lower prices can lift sales but squeeze profit.
SG&A as a percent of gross profit: Selling, general and administrative cost divided by gross profit. It shows how much of each gross dollar the dealer spends on running the business.
Floorplan: Short-term borrowing that dealers use to hold new and used car inventory. Higher interest rates make it more expensive.
Days' supply: How many days current inventory would last at the current sales rate. High supply pushes prices down; low supply pushes them up.
Wholesale used prices: Prices at auctions where dealers buy used cars, such as the Manheim index. They set the cost base for used-car retailers.
LIFO charge: An accounting cost recorded when parts prices rise. It lowers reported gross margin when inflation or tariffs lift costs.
Fuel margin: The profit per gallon at a gas station, in cents. It swings with wholesale fuel prices and competition.

O'Reilly raised 2026 comp guidance to 5.5% to 6.5%, which with nine-month comps of 7.1% implies a much slower fourth quarter, and its third-quarter results included a $39 million tariff refund benefit.

AutoZone said sales strengthened over the last eight weeks of its fiscal fourth quarter after a difficult start, and expects growth to accelerate in fiscal 2027; its fiscal first quarter ends 21 November and we did not find results yet.
October new-vehicle sales came in at 15.5 million annualised, below Cox's 16.1 million forecast, with rising loan rates cited as a factor.
Dealer margins are slipping: AutoNation's SG&A rose to 70.3% of gross profit and Lithia's net debt to EBITDA rose to 3.07x from 2.63x.
Advance Auto Parts now guides 2026 adjusted EPS of $2.60 to $3.30 and free cash flow of about $150M, with comps improving but its turnaround unproven.
AutoZone, O'Reilly Automotive, Advance Auto Parts, Genuine Parts, AutoNation, Lithia Motors, CarMax, Carvana

Dealers earn from new vehicles, used vehicles, finance and insurance, and parts and service. At AutoNation, parts and service produced $616.6M of the $1,207.6M gross profit in the third quarter of 2026, about 51% by our calculation, so the service bay carries the profit while vehicle margins are thin. Parts chains earn from product sales and, increasingly, from delivery to repair shops.

Customers are consumers and small businesses. O'Reilly describes two groups, professional repair shops and do-it-yourself drivers; in the third quarter its professional business grew double digits and DIY mid-single digits. Dealers sell to retail buyers and, at the margin, fleet customers, while gas stations sell to commuters, with Murphy USA citing the resilience of its customers.

The big costs are inventory, labour and occupancy. Dealers spend about 70 cents of each gross dollar on SG&A: AutoNation's was 70.3% of gross profit and Lithia's 69.3% as reported. Parts chains bear distribution, store and labour costs, and Genuine Parts' North America automotive EBITDA margin fell 40 basis points to 7.6%.

Pricing power is limited on new cars, where manufacturers set sticker prices and buyers compare online, but better in parts and service. O'Reilly's gross margin was 52.4% against 51.9%, helped by a $39 million tariff refund. Dealers lean on finance and insurance: AutoNation earned $2,698 of F&I gross profit per vehicle.

The major assets are inventory, real estate, finance receivables and, for parts chains, stores and distribution centres. Liabilities include floorplan and corporate debt. AutoNation had $4.34B of non-vehicle debt and $2.59B of non-recourse debt at 30 September 2026; O'Reilly's long-term debt was $7.71B.

The group is moderately capital-intensive. O'Reilly guides to $1.3B to $1.4B of 2026 capital spending on about $19B of revenue. Dealers also need heavy working capital for inventory, and captive finance arms such as AutoNation Finance, now about $2.9B, add balance sheet risk, which makes this less asset-light than most retail.

We did not find one authoritative global market-size figure for this sub-industry, so we do not quote one. In the US, roughly 16 million people buy new cars each year, about 1 million fewer than before the pandemic, and used sales are normally about two-thirds of total sales. Cox's 2026 forecast is 16.1 million new units.

The main segments are new-car dealers, used-car retailers, parts retail and distribution, and fuel retail. Revenue scale shows the mix: Lithia reported $9.9B in a quarter, AutoNation $7.0B, CarMax $7.9B in its fiscal second quarter, Carvana $8.04B, O'Reilly $5.12B and Genuine Parts $6.5B.

The value chain runs from car and parts makers, who supply dealers and parts chains, to buyers. Dealers also source used cars from consumers and auctions, so wholesale prices matter: the Manheim index was 206.8 in October 2026, up 2% year on year seasonally adjusted. Parts chains buy from suppliers, and tariffs on steel, aluminium and imports raise their costs.

The industry has moved toward consolidation among dealers and chains, and toward online used sales. Carvana's retail units rose 39% to 217,385 in the third quarter, and CarMax's comparable used units rose 13.0%. Lithia has bought about $1.17B of expected annualised revenue year to date.

Concentration is in the United States, with growth in Mexico and Brazil for parts chains. AutoZone had 8,031 stores at 29 August 2026, of which 6,863 were in the US, 1,001 in Mexico and 167 in Brazil. O'Reilly's 6,758 stores include operations in Mexico and Canada.

There are a few dozen significant listed competitors, but a handful dominate each segment. Damodaran's US group has 34 firms. Parts retail is led by AutoZone, O'Reilly, Advance Auto Parts and Genuine Parts; large dealer groups include AutoNation, Lithia and Penske; used cars are led by CarMax and Carvana.

On store counts, AutoZone has 8,031 stores, O'Reilly 6,758 and Advance Auto Parts 4,325. We did not find sourced market-share percentages for dealers or used-car retailers, so we do not quote any. Scale is visible in the revenue figures instead.

The industry is fragmented at the local level and consolidated at the top. Most US dealerships are still owned by small groups, which is why Lithia keeps acquiring: it added about $1.17B of annualised revenue year to date and four more stores in October. In parts, three national chains hold a large share, but independents and online sellers remain.

Barriers to entry are moderate. Dealers need manufacturer franchises and state licences. Parts chains need dense store and delivery networks, which is why O'Reilly opened 63 net new stores in one quarter. Used-car sellers need inventory sourcing and reconditioning scale, which took Carvana years to build.

Economies of scale are real. Bigger parts chains spread distribution and inventory costs, and O'Reilly's operating margin of 21.4% compares with Advance Auto Parts' adjusted 4.5%. CarMax's SG&A per unit fell $157 to $1,621 as volume grew. Dealers gain from shared finance and technology.

New cars are differentiated by brand but sold at near-identical prices, so dealers compete on service and financing. Parts are partly commodity, but chains differentiate by availability and speed of delivery, and O'Reilly's professional business is growing double digits. Used-car sellers compete on price and convenience.

Manufacturers hold power over franchised dealers through supply and incentives, while customers hold power through online price comparison. Parts suppliers have less power over big chains, which buy at scale. Customers have little power in parts because a needed part is usually bought quickly, but they can switch channels, as Advance Auto's weak DIY sales show.

Revenue growth comes from unit volume, price and mix, store openings and acquisitions. O'Reilly's comps of 7.2% combine traffic and ticket, and AutoZone reported fourth-quarter same-store sales up 2.7%. For dealers, new-car sales running near 16 million a year set the baseline.

Operating margins depend on mix and cost control. Parts chains earn the most, with O'Reilly at 21.4% and AutoZone at roughly 20% by our calculation from its fourth-quarter figures. Damodaran's whole US group averages 6.51%, reflecting the lower-margin dealers. Dealers' SG&A ratio is a key swing: AutoNation's rose to 70.3% from 68.6%.

Key cost variables are vehicle and parts acquisition costs, labour, freight and interest. We did not find a sourced parts-cost figure beyond tariff commentary. For fuel retailers the key cost is wholesale fuel, with Murphy USA's fuel contribution at 37.0 cents a gallon.

Rates matter a lot because most vehicles are financed. New-car loan rates are over 7% and used about 11% per Edmunds, and over a quarter of buyers use 84-month or longer terms. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026, with two members preferring a hike. Floorplan interest also hits dealers.

Inflation lifts prices and tariffs raise costs, but unemployment and GDP drive volume. The Fed says inflation remains elevated while job gains have kept pace with the workforce. New-vehicle prices rose 2.1% to a record $51,109, below inflation. We did not find a sourced figure linking commodity prices to margins.

The group is a mix of cyclical and defensive. New-car dealers are cyclical, while parts chains and service are more defensive because repairs are needed regardless of the cycle, which we think explains why O'Reilly's comps are strong in a soft new-car market. Used cars sit between, with some share-driven growth.

Growth is uneven. O'Reilly's third-quarter sales rose 9% to $5.12B and diluted EPS 14% to $0.97. AutoNation's revenue was flat at $7.0B with GAAP EPS of $4.87 against $5.65. Carvana's revenue rose 42% to $8.04B. AutoZone's fourth-quarter sales rose 5.6% to $6.595B.

Margins vary by model. Damodaran's January 2026 data for US auto retail show a 21.96% gross margin, 6.51% operating margin and 7.24% EBITDA margin. Parts chains are far above that: O'Reilly's gross margin was 52.4% and operating margin 21.4%.

Damodaran puts the US auto retail group's return on equity at 34.38% unadjusted in January 2026, but the table has no ROIC column. We think heavy buybacks and thin equity at the parts chains inflate that figure. We did not find a sourced ROIC for the group.

Leverage is meaningful. Lithia's net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 3.07x against 2.63x a year earlier, AutoNation's covenant leverage was 2.71x, and O'Reilly's adjusted debt to EBITDAR was 2.26x. Advance Auto Parts reports net leverage of 2.2x.

Free cash flow is strongest at the parts chains. O'Reilly generated $1.73B in the first nine months and guides $1.9B to $2.2B for the year. Advance Auto guides about $150M; Genuine Parts guides $550M to $700M. Buybacks are large: O'Reilly spent $3.47B and AutoNation $619.9M year to date.

Capital spending is modest for dealers and higher for parts chains. O'Reilly guides $1.3B to $1.4B and Advance Auto about $300M. AutoNation's finance portfolio grew to about $2.9B, which is capital used in lending rather than in stores.

Damodaran's January 2026 EV/EBITDA for US auto retail was 14.79x for positive-EBITDA firms and 17.56x for all firms. At sector level, FactSet shows Consumer Discretionary at 25.1x forward earnings against 18.3x for the S&P 500, but that sector includes much besides auto retail.

Regulation touches financing, emissions rules and franchise laws. The sources we opened do not detail current rule changes for dealers. Tariffs are the clearest policy risk: they raise costs on steel, aluminium and imports and feed into prices. Genuine Parts lists tariffs as a risk factor without quantifying them.

Technology is changing both channels. Carvana's unit growth of 39% shows the online model working at scale. We did not find sourced evidence on AI's effect on share, and about 6% of new cars sold are electric, which have fewer parts to replace.

Demographics help parts: an ageing fleet needs more repair. We found secondhand reports that the average vehicle age is near 13 years, but we did not open a primary S&P Global Mobility release, so we do not quote it as a hard figure. New-car buyers number about 16 million a year, a million fewer than before the pandemic.

Consumer behaviour is shifting toward longer loans and cheaper alternatives. Edmunds reports over a quarter of buyers use 84-month or longer terms, and AutoNation cited softer vehicle demand. Parts demand held up, but Advance Auto Parts' comps fell 1.2%.

New competitors are online sellers and, in parts, better-run incumbents. Carvana is taking share and CarMax used units rose 13.8%. Advance Auto Parts is in a restructuring with $42M of charges in the quarter, which shows how hard it is for a weaker chain to compete.

Geopolitical and supply-chain risks come through tariffs and component costs. Chip and copper costs have risen on data-center demand. Carvana's margin slipped even as units grew, which we read as a sign of cost and pricing pressure.

Substitutes include ride-hailing, transit, longer vehicle ownership and repairing rather than replacing cars. Longer ownership helps parts and service but hurts new-car dealers. We did not find sourced data on the scale of ride-hailing substitution, so we do not size it.
An ageing car fleet and record after-sales profit support parts and service demand.
Online and used-car sellers are gaining share, with Carvana and CarMax growing units at double-digit rates.
Captive finance and parts-and-service lines add recurring profit that cushions weak vehicle sales.
Large parts chains keep opening stores and generating cash, such as O'Reilly's 63 net new stores in one quarter.
Affordability is stretched, with record new-car prices and loan rates over 7%, which is cutting volume.
Tariffs and parts inflation could lift costs faster than retailers can pass them on.
Dealer leverage is rising while vehicle and F&I margins fall.
Weak chains such as Advance Auto Parts may stay below peer margins for years.

Over the next three to five years we think the sub-industry's profit will keep moving toward service, parts and finance, away from new-car volume. The parts chains look the best positioned because repairs are needed whatever the cycle and O'Reilly shows the model at 21.4% operating margin. Dealers have strong service profit but face affordability limits, rising leverage and falling vehicle margins. Used-car sellers have momentum, but their per-unit margins are thin and sensitive to wholesale prices and interest rates. The main swing factors are loan rates, tariffs and the health of the lower-income buyer. We would expect a wider gap between leaders and laggards, rather than an even sector-wide trend.

Automotive retail sits in a late-cycle, higher-for-longer rate environment. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October 2026, said inflation remains elevated, and had two members who preferred a rise. That matters for a business where most sales are financed: Edmunds puts new-car loan rates above 7% and used about 11%, and more than a quarter of buyers take loans of 84 months or longer.

The effect shows in volumes. Cox says October new-vehicle sales ran at a 15.5 million annual rate, the slowest since January, against an original forecast of 16.1 million, and it cited a rise in loan rates last month. Its full-year forecast is 16.1 million, which would still be a third straight year above 16 million if November and December match last year. Cox also credits wider access to credit for keeping the market firm.

Prices are not falling, though. The average new-vehicle transaction price reached a record $51,109, up 2.1% from a year earlier, which is below general inflation, and tariffs on steel, aluminium and imports are among the causes. We think this squeezes lower-income buyers first and explains why dealers report softer demand while parts retailers, whose customers keep older cars on the road, are growing.

Structural demand rests on the size of the US car fleet and how long people keep their cars. New-vehicle sales are near 16 million a year, about a million below pre-pandemic levels, and used sales are normally about two-thirds of the total. We found secondhand reports that the average vehicle is now about 13 years old, but we did not open a primary source, so we do not rely on that figure.

The ageing of the fleet shows up in aftermarket demand. O'Reilly's comparable sales rose 7.2% in the third quarter and 7.1% over nine months, with professional sales up double digits. AutoNation's parts and service gross profit reached a record $616.6M, with customer-pay up 6%. AutoZone expects sales growth to accelerate in fiscal 2027 in each of its three countries.

Used cars offer growth through share gain. Carvana sold 217,385 retail units, up 39%, and CarMax's comparable used units rose 13.0%. Wholesale values are steady: the Manheim index was 206.8 in October, up 0.5% on the month and 2% year on year, both seasonally adjusted. Demand is elastic to affordability for cars and inelastic for repairs.

Using Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense among dealers, used-car sellers and parts chains, and the gap in performance is wide. O'Reilly's third-quarter comps were +7.2% and Advance Auto Parts' were -1.2%. The threat of new entrants is moderate: franchises, licences and distribution networks are barriers, yet Carvana shows an online entrant can reach $8.04B of quarterly revenue.

Supplier power is high for dealers, because manufacturers allocate vehicles and set prices, and lower for big parts chains that buy at scale. Buyer power is high for new and used cars, where shoppers compare prices online, and lower for urgent repairs. The threat of substitutes comes from ride-hailing and longer vehicle ownership; we did not find sourced data sizing them.

Concentration is high in parts: AutoZone has 8,031 stores, O'Reilly 6,758 and Advance Auto Parts 4,325. Dealers are more fragmented, which is why Lithia keeps buying, adding about $1.17B of annualised revenue this year. We did not find sourced market-share percentages. Moats are density of stores and delivery in parts, and service and finance income in dealers.

Trade policy is the main political factor. Tariffs on steel, aluminium and Canadian imports raise automaker costs, and chip and copper costs have risen on data-center demand. Genuine Parts names tariffs as a risk but does not quantify them. O'Reilly received $39 million of tariff refunds in the third quarter, a one-off gain that lifted results.
Tariff refunds show how fluid the position is, since the same tariffs raise costs and may later be refunded.

Economically, credit availability and interest rates decide demand, and the Fed has kept rates at 3.75% to 4.00%. Technologically, online used-car buying is now mainstream, and about 6% of new cars sold are electric, which changes service mix over time. We did not find sourced evidence on regulation specific to dealer finance, so we do not discuss it.

Margins differ sharply by model. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 34 US auto retailers show a 21.96% gross margin, 6.51% operating margin and 7.24% EBITDA margin. Parts chains earn far more: O'Reilly's operating margin was 21.4% on a 52.4% gross margin, and AutoZone's fourth-quarter EBIT was $1.317B on $6.595B of sales, about 20% by our calculation. Advance Auto Parts, still restructuring, earned an adjusted 4.5%.

Dealers face rising costs against falling gross profit. AutoNation's gross profit fell 2.5% and SG&A rose to 70.3% of it, so operating income fell 16% to $314.6M. Lithia's adjusted SG&A rose to 68.8% of gross profit. Carvana's adjusted EBITDA margin was 10.0%, down from 11.3%.

Operating leverage is real: CarMax's SG&A per unit fell 8.8% as units grew 13.8%, though its retail gross profit per unit fell $111 to $2,105. Damodaran's return on equity for the group is 34.38%, and we think buybacks inflate it; the table has no ROIC. Free cash flow is strongest at O'Reilly, at $1.73B in nine months.

Guidance splits the group. O'Reilly raised 2026 guidance to comps of 5.5% to 6.5%, operating margin of 19.5% to 20.0% and EPS of $3.25 to $3.35.
