Tariffs are the other macro lever: Section 232 duties of 25% on upholstered furniture and 25% on cabinets and vanities are due to step up to 30% and 50% on 1 Jan 2027. We think the cycle favours brand leaders and share-takers over housing-dependent formats.

We could not find a citable estimate of the dollar size of US home furnishings retail; Wayfair's 10-K describes the market only as large. A useful proxy is Williams-Sonoma, whose revenue fell from $8.67B in the year to January 2023 to $7.75B a year later and stood at $7.81B in the year to February 2026. That shows demand is cyclical and has not yet recovered to its post-pandemic peak.

Structural drivers are household formation, the age of the housing stock and the shift online. Williams-Sonoma generated about 66% of its fiscal 2024 revenue through e-commerce, and Wayfair's Q3 US revenue grew 11.4% with active customers up 4.7% to 22.2 million. Demand is elastic: big-ticket items are easy to defer, and Floor & Decor's comps are down 2.4% year to date. Higher-income demand is firmer: Williams-Sonoma raised no guidance but reiterated comps of 4.0% to 6.5% for the year. Demographics matter through first-time buyers, who were 29% of October existing-home sales.

Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense and spans marketplaces, big boxes, furniture chains and specialty brands, as Wayfair's 10-K lists. The threat of new entrants is high online and low at scale, where a catalog of over 40 million items and about 20 thousand suppliers took years to build. Supplier power is low, since no Williams-Sonoma supplier exceeds about 3% of purchases. Buyer power is high because shoppers compare prices instantly and can defer purchases. The threat of substitutes includes resale, rental and discounters selling similar products.

Concentration is modest. Reported quarterly sales were $3.42B at Wayfair, $1.99B at Williams-Sonoma, $1.21B at Floor & Decor, $922M at RH, $368M at Arhaus and $203M at Haverty's. We found no published market-share table, so we rank by sales. Williams-Sonoma is the only S&P 500 member we found in the sub-industry. Moats are brand and design (Williams-Sonoma, RH, Arhaus) and logistics scale (Wayfair); pricing power is strongest in the first group, where Williams-Sonoma's non-GAAP gross margin was 46.2%.

Politics and regulation are dominated by trade. The Supreme Court voided IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and refunds are now flowing: Williams-Sonoma recorded $197.0M of refund income year to date, RH a $55.1M benefit in Q2, Floor & Decor about $56.2M of gross profit over nine months and Haverty's $4.7M. Section 232 duties are separate and remain: 25% on upholstered furniture, rising to 30%, and on kitchen cabinets and vanities, rising to 50%, on 1 Jan 2027 after a one-year delay.

Technology cuts both ways. Williams-Sonoma warns that generative AI may reduce barriers to competition, and Wayfair is using AI in search and service and launched Muse in 2025. Wayfair also notes the end of the de minimis exemption on small Chinese shipments and that it is shifting suppliers outside China. Social and environmental factors include privacy rules (GDPR, CCPA) and sustainability reporting such as California's, which add compliance costs. We think the biggest emerging risk is policy whiplash: duties that change faster than retailers can re-source.

Retail economics here are thin to moderate margin, with wide dispersion. Damodaran's January 2026 data gives Retail (Special Lines) a 35.3% gross margin, 7.7% operating margin and 5.2% net margin, against 12.8% operating margin for the total market. Williams-Sonoma earned an 18.1% operating margin in the year to February 2026 on $7.81B of revenue and 17.4% non-GAAP in Q3, against 2.5% at Wayfair, 5.3% at Floor & Decor and 5.2% at Arhaus on recent trailing figures.

Returns are strong at the leaders and weak elsewhere. After-tax lease-adjusted ROIC is 21.7% for Retail (Special Lines) against 9.6% for the market, and StockAnalysis shows 40.4% at Williams-Sonoma and 43.8% at Wayfair but 4.7% at Floor & Decor and 6.9% at Arhaus. Capital intensity is lowest in special-line retail (net capex 1.6% of sales) and higher in furnishing groups (5.9%). Operating leverage is visible at Arhaus: Q3 revenue rose 6.8% but operating income fell from $16.4M to $10.1M as SG&A grew 14.8%. Williams-Sonoma's trailing free cash flow was $1.06B in the year to February 2026.

Reported earnings are inflated by refunds. Williams-Sonoma's Q3 GAAP EPS was $2.38 but non-GAAP EPS was $2.19 (up 11.7%) after excluding the $29.3M refund; it reiterated fiscal 2026 net revenue growth of 4.7% to 7.2% and non-GAAP operating margin of 17.8% to 18.2%. RH's normalized adjusted EBITDA margin was 13.4% against 19.4% reported, and it guides fiscal 2026 revenue up 5.5% to 7.0%. Haverty's adjusted EPS was $0.25 against $0.39 reported.

Guidance points to uneven demand. Floor & Decor guides fiscal 2026 comps down 3.5% to 2.0% with adjusted EBITDA of $535M to $550M. Arhaus raised revenue guidance to $1.465B to $1.485B but kept net income at $71M to $80M. RH's Q4 guide of 16.1% to 21.2% growth after 5% to 6% in Q3 depends on launches.

Our read is that comps and margins converge toward low-single-digit growth once refunds drop out, with Williams-Sonoma and Wayfair holding share. We did not find consensus estimate tables for the group that we could open, so we do not state where we differ from them.

Valuation is mixed. On 20 Nov 2026 forward P/E was 20.9x for Williams-Sonoma, 25.0x for Wayfair, 24.5x for Floor & Decor, 23.2x for Arhaus, 16.9x for RH and 13.4x for Haverty's. Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E was 21.5 for Retail (Special Lines), 24.0 for Retail (General) and 27.7 for all US firms. The SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF, which holds a basket of housing-linked names, had a forward P/E of 18.1 on 19 Nov 2026.

FCF yields were 5.3% at Williams-Sonoma, 4.6% at Wayfair, 7.0% at Floor & Decor, 5.7% at Arhaus, 12.3% at RH and 8.7% at Haverty's. Williams-Sonoma looks reasonable for 40% ROIC and an 18% margin; Floor & Decor's 24.5x multiple pairs with a 4.7% ROIC, which looks demanding unless comps recover. Expected five-year EPS growth for the retail group is 8.1% with a PEG of 3.1. We did not find ten-year average multiples that we could open, so we do not compare with own history.

Momentum is split. Over 52 weeks to 20 Nov 2026 Arhaus was up 46.4%, Williams-Sonoma up 20.7% and Haverty's up 6.8%, while Wayfair was down 2.7%, Floor & Decor down 17.9% and RH down 26.5%. XHB, a housing-linked ETF holding Homefurnishing Retail at 6.47%, was down 1.01% year to date to 31 Oct and held $1.46B at 19 Nov.

Short interest says where doubt sits. Short interest as a share of float was 5.1% for Williams-Sonoma, 9.1% for Wayfair, 14.3% for Arhaus, 14.9% for Floor & Decor and 31.8% for RH. RH's equity is thin, so its leverage ratios are distorted. We did not find ETF flow data we could open. Our read is that positioning is most crowded in RH on the short side, which makes its Q4 launch ramp a binary event.

Electronics retail is having a better year than expected, but the gains are narrow and partly borrowed. Best Buy's comparable sales rose 4.1% in its July quarter, led by computing, and it raised its full-year guide to comps of 1.9% to 3.0%. Currys reported 7% like-for-like growth in the summer, helped by heatwaves. JB Hi-Fi's Australian comps fell 1.4%. GameStop's sales fell 18.7% as collectibles replaced games. Memory-chip inflation is lifting PC prices and may test demand. Best Buy trades at 13.9x forward earnings.

These retailers sell televisions, computers, phones, appliances, gaming and accessories to households and small businesses through big-box stores and websites. They buy finished goods from a small group of global brands and earn the gap between cost and shelf price, plus fees from services, warranties, advertising and marketplace sales. GICS puts specialist electronics and computer chains here. The brands that make the devices sit in technology hardware, and general merchants such as Amazon or Walmart are in broadline retail or consumer staples distribution.

Computing and mobile: Laptops, desktops, tablets, phones and accessories. This is the largest category at big chains and is tied to replacement cycles and operating-system or chip launches. e.g. Best Buy, Currys, JB Hi-Fi, Yamada, Bic Camera

Consumer electronics: Televisions, soundbars, headphones, cameras and smart-home devices. Prices fall over a product's life, so retailers depend on newer, higher-priced models. e.g. Home theater and audio at Best Buy, Currys and Fnac

Appliances: Large appliances such as fridges and washers, and small ones such as vacuums and coffee makers. Sales follow housing activity and replacement needs, and ranges are broader at Currys, Darty and Yamada. e.g. Darty, Yamada, The Good Guys, Best Buy

Gaming and collectibles: Consoles, games, trading cards and merchandise. Games sell in waves around console launches, while collectibles have become a growth area for specialists. e.g. GameStop, Fnac, Best Buy Entertainment

Services and advertising: Installation, repair, memberships, warranties, financing, mobile contracts, retail advertising paid by vendors, and commissions on third-party marketplace sales. These carry higher margins than product. e.g. Geek Squad, Currys Care, Best Buy Ads and Marketplace
Product cycles and replacement demand: New categories or upgrade waves, such as PC refreshes or AI devices, raise unit sales and prices. Without them, comps drift lower as households delay purchases.
Component and device prices: When chip costs rise, brands lift prices. That can raise revenue per unit but cut volumes, and retailers must decide how much cost to pass on.
Tariffs and trade policy: Most devices are made in Asia, so duties raise landed cost. Margin moves as retailers and vendors share the cost, and refunds can flatter one period.
Consumer confidence, housing and rates: Big-ticket items are bought on credit and when moving home. Higher rates and falling confidence delay purchases of televisions and appliances.
Mix toward services and advertising: Higher-margin income from retail media, marketplace commissions and services can lift gross margin even when product sales are flat.
Competition from online and brands: Online marketplaces and brands selling direct pressure prices and traffic. Stores respond with price matching, service and exclusive ranges.
Comparable sales (comps): Sales growth at stores and sites open at least a year, which strips out the effect of new stores. It is the main health check for a retailer.
Gross profit rate: Gross profit as a share of sales. Electronics retailers run low rates because they resell branded goods, so small changes matter.
Product cycle: The rhythm of new device launches and replacement. A strong cycle, such as a PC refresh, lifts traffic and average prices; a weak one leaves stores waiting.
Vendor concentration: Reliance on a few suppliers. A handful of brands account for most purchases at large chains, which limits a retailer's bargaining power on price and supply.
Vendor funding: Payments from brands for promotions, markdown protection and store displays. It cushions margin but ties retailers to brand priorities.
Omnichannel: Selling through stores and online with shared stock, such as click and collect. Stores help with returns, advice and same-day pickup.
Retail media: Advertising sold to brands on a retailer's site, app and stores. It earns high margin because it needs little extra cost.
Marketplace: A platform where third-party sellers list goods on the retailer's site and the retailer takes a commission. It widens range without holding stock.
Attach rate: The share of device sales that also sell a service, warranty or accessory. Higher attach rates lift profit per customer.
Inventory turnover: How often stock is sold in a year. Electronics lose value fast, so slow turnover brings markdowns.
IEEPA tariff refund: Money returned to importers after the US Supreme Court ruled emergency-law tariffs unauthorized in February 2026. It lifts reported profit but is not repeatable.
Click and collect: An online order picked up at a store. It saves delivery cost and brings customers in, where they may add purchases.
Best Buy's third-quarter report is the next test: it guided comps up 1% to 3% and an adjusted operating margin of 4.1% to 4.2%.
Memory-chip inflation: Counterpoint said memory prices were up 80% to 90% versus the fourth quarter of 2025 as of February, which can raise PC prices and weigh on unit demand.
Holiday trading: JB Hi-Fi said October sales slowed ahead of Black Friday as shoppers focused on value and promotions.
Trade policy: Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% replaced the temporary Section 122 tariff on 24 July, and IEEPA refunds are still flowing through to margins.
Rates and fuel: the Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% with two dissenters wanting a hike, and gasoline was up 37.4% year on year in October.
Best Buy, GameStop, Currys, JB Hi-Fi, Yamada Holdings, Fnac Darty, Bic Camera

Revenue comes mainly from selling third-party devices and appliances, plus a smaller, richer stream from services such as installation, repair, memberships, advertising and marketplace commissions. Best Buy's domestic mix was 47% computing and mobile, 28% consumer electronics, 11% appliances, 7% entertainment and 6% services in fiscal 2026.

Customers are mainly households, with some small businesses. They buy infrequently and compare prices online before buying. GameStop's sales are split into video games, pre-owned goods and collectibles, with collectibles at 45.1% of Q2 sales as the chain leans toward enthusiasts. Currys has also grown its business-to-business sales.

The largest cost is the goods themselves, followed by store labor, rent and delivery. Best Buy's fiscal 2026 gross profit rate was 22.5% and its SG&A was 18.3% of revenue, leaving a GAAP operating margin of 3.3%. Fnac Darty's gross margin was 29.0% in the first half of 2026.

Pricing power is weak on products and stronger on services. Five suppliers (Apple, Samsung, HP, LG and Sony) accounted for about 55% of Best Buy's purchases, and its top 20 for about 80%, and it has no long-term written supply contracts. Retailers gain margin from advertising, marketplace and services, which Best Buy said lifted its domestic gross profit rate.

The main assets are inventory, store leases and cash. Best Buy held $5.23B of inventory, $1.74B of cash and $1.17B of long-term debt at 31 Jan 2026. GameStop is unusual: it held about $4.85B of cash, $206M of marketable securities and an eBay stake it valued at about $4.9B, against $4.17B of long-term debt at 1 Aug 2026.

Asset-light compared with industry, but store-based. Damodaran's net capex to sales was 1.59% for special-line retail against 4.23% for the whole market. Best Buy spent $704M on capital expenditure in fiscal 2026 and expects about $750M in fiscal 2027. Most of the commitment sits in store leases.

The CTA's August 2026 forecast puts US consumer technology retail revenue at $578B in 2026, up 4%. That covers all consumer technology sold, not only specialist chains. Best Buy alone guided to $42.3B to $42.8B of fiscal 2027 revenue, and Fnac Darty to H1 revenue of EUR 4.46B.

The main segments are computing and mobile, consumer electronics, appliances, gaming, and services. At Best Buy, computing and mobile is the largest at 47% of domestic revenue and entertainment the smallest of the product groups at 7%. Gaming has been the weakest recently, with Best Buy's domestic entertainment comps down 6.3% in Q2.

Specialist retailers sit between a few global brands and households. Best Buy's top five suppliers supply about 55% of its purchases, and most merchandise ships directly from manufacturers to its distribution centers. Retailers add value through range, advice, delivery, financing and after-sales service that brands and online sellers often do not provide at scale.

The industry shifted from single-category specialists to omnichannel chains with services and advertising. Best Buy launched a US marketplace and scaled its retail media business, and its domestic online comps rose 5.1% in Q2. In gaming, GameStop has closed stores, sold its French business and moved toward collectibles.

Sales are concentrated in the US (Best Buy, GameStop), the UK and Nordics (Currys), France and Iberia (Fnac Darty), Australia and New Zealand (JB Hi-Fi), and Japan (Yamada, Bic Camera). GameStop's Q2 sales were $608.2M in the US, $120.9M in Australia and $61.1M in Europe. Most devices are made in Asia, so production is far from sales.

There are several dozen significant listed chains worldwide, usually leaders within one country or region. We found no global ranking, so we compare by company reports: Best Buy, Currys, JB Hi-Fi, Yamada, Fnac Darty, Bic Camera and GameStop.

By revenue, Yamada reported about JPY 1.69 trillion in the year to March 2026 and Best Buy $41.7B in fiscal 2026; Currys reported GBP 9.25B for 2025/26. We found no source for market shares in electronics retail, so we do not state them.

Fragmented globally but concentrated nationally. Each market has a few large chains plus online sellers and brands selling direct. Best Buy lists 1,068 stores across its domestic and international segments, and Currys 691 stores across six countries.

Barriers to entry are low online and higher in stores: scale buying, vendor access, delivery networks and after-sales service take years to build. Best Buy says its stores and store-within-store vendor concepts are an important advantage. In practice, brands and marketplaces can sell the same goods online, so the barrier is service, not product.

Economies of scale matter in buying, logistics, advertising and technology. Best Buy's adjusted operating margin was 4.3% in Q2, while Fnac Darty's current operating income was negative in the seasonally weak first half at -EUR 34M. Larger chains also receive more vendor funding for promotions.

Largely commoditized: the same models are sold everywhere and prices are visible online, so retailers compete on price, range, service and exclusives. JB Hi-Fi cited heightened competitive activity and value-focused customers shopping at promotional events.

Suppliers hold the stronger hand on products: a handful of brands account for most of the stock, and Best Buy has no long-term supply contracts securing terms. Customers hold price power because they can compare online. Retailers' leverage comes from reach and advertising, with Best Buy's Q2 gross margin helped by marketplace and ads.

Revenue growth comes from product cycles, price per unit, store and online traffic, and services. Best Buy's Q2 computing and mobile comps rose 6.8% and consumer electronics 5.6%, while entertainment fell 6.3%. In FY2026 as a whole, enterprise comps were only 0.5%.

Operating margin depends on gross margin (mix, vendor funding, tariffs) against labor, rent and delivery. Best Buy's adjusted operating margin rose to 4.3% from 3.9% in Q2 as gross margin rose to 23.9% from 23.2%. Damodaran's pre-tax operating margin for special-line retail is 8.41% against 14.39% for all firms.

Key cost variables are product cost (including memory chips and tariffs), wages, rent and delivery. Counterpoint reported memory prices up 80% to 90% in early 2026 versus the end of 2025, and Context expected further PC price inflation as the year progressed. About $34M of IEEPA refunds helped Best Buy's Q2 domestic gross profit.

Direct sensitivity is modest: Damodaran shows interest coverage of 13.5 for special-line retail against 6.9 for the whole market. Indirect sensitivity is higher, since appliances and televisions are often financed and tied to housing. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026, with two members voting for a hike.

Unemployment and income matter most; the Fed described spending as resilient with the unemployment rate little changed. The last published 12-month CPI was 3.7% for September, and gasoline was up 37.4% in October. Component and commodity costs such as memory chips matter more than raw commodities.

Cyclical with product cycles. Best Buy's comps were -6.8% in fiscal 2024, -2.3% in fiscal 2025 and +0.5% in fiscal 2026 before the 2026 rebound. Services and advertising add some stability, but the core is a discretionary, replacement-driven purchase with sharp swings.

Growth is flat to low single digit over a cycle. Best Buy's revenue went from $43.5B in fiscal 2024 to $41.5B and $41.7B in fiscal 2025 and 2026. Damodaran's expected five-year earnings growth is 8.08% for special-line retail (a group broader than electronics) against 13.95% for the market.

Gross margins are thin for pure electronics retail. Best Buy's was 22.5% in fiscal 2026 and Fnac Darty's 29.0% in the first half of 2026, while Damodaran's special-line retail group (all kinds of specialty stores) shows 35.30%. Best Buy's adjusted operating margin was 4.3% in Q2 FY27.

Returns on capital are high because assets are light and inventory turns fast. Damodaran's lease-adjusted after-tax ROIC is 21.71% for special-line retail against 9.60% for the market. StockAnalysis shows ROIC of 26.0% for Best Buy and 11.2% for GameStop, and ROE of 43.1% for Best Buy.

Leverage is moderate once leases are counted. Damodaran's book debt-to-capital is 60.23% for special-line retail, with debt to EBITDA of 2.88 against 6.52 for the market. Best Buy had $1.17B of long-term debt and $1.74B of cash at 31 Jan 2026. GameStop shows net cash of $727M on StockAnalysis, and about $2.8B of long-term debt after the September 2026 convertible-note exchanges.

Free cash flow is solid at the leaders. StockAnalysis shows a free cash flow yield of 8.61% for Best Buy and 5.12% for GameStop at 20 Nov 2026. Best Buy returned $239M to holders in Q2 and plans about $300M of buybacks in fiscal 2027, plus a $0.96 quarterly dividend.

Capex is low: Damodaran puts net capex at 1.59% of sales for special-line retail against 4.23% for the whole market. Best Buy spent $704M in fiscal 2026 and expects about $750M in fiscal 2027, mostly for stores, distribution and technology.

Multiples are below the market at the sector's leaders. Best Buy trades at 13.9x forward earnings and 8.5x EV/EBITDA, GameStop at 17.7x forward earnings. Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E was 21.52 for special-line retail and 27.66 for all firms.

Trade policy is the biggest regulatory risk. The Supreme Court ruled on 20 Feb 2026 that IEEPA tariffs were unauthorized, and Best Buy's filing warns that new tariff regimes and refund processes create uncertainty. Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% on 60 economies replaced a temporary 10% tariff on 24 July.

AI is both a demand driver and a cost. AI features are lifting interest in new PCs, which Currys describes as increasingly important, but AI data-center demand is also pulling up memory prices that raise device prices. We found no hard numbers on AI's effect on retail earnings.

Demographics matter little for total demand, which follows household formation and replacement cycles. Younger shoppers drive gaming and collectibles: GameStop's collectibles rose to $356.3M from $227.6M in a year. We found no data tying population change to retailer revenue.

Shoppers are value-focused and promotion-led. JB Hi-Fi said customers increasingly shop in promotional events and sales slowed in October. Online and click-and-collect keep growing: Fnac Darty's online sales rose 4.2% in the first half, with click and collect nearly half of them.

New competitors include online marketplaces and brands selling direct. Best Buy's own 10-K lists marketplaces and retail media as new areas of risk and growth for the chain. Consolidation also reshapes the field: EP Group became controlling shareholder of Fnac Darty with 69.3% of the capital by 10 Nov 2026.

Supply chains run through Asia and a small set of chip makers. Memory prices rose 80% to 90% in early 2026 on AI demand, and HP and Dell were testing alternative memory suppliers. Tariff changes also move landed cost. Best Buy's filing flags tariff volatility as a planning risk.

Substitutes include online marketplaces, direct brand stores, refurbished and second-hand devices, and longer device lifetimes. GameStop's pre-owned and refurbished sales were $170.7M, or 21.6% of Q2 sales. Streaming and digital downloads substitute for physical games, and GameStop's video game sales were $263.2M against $494.6M a year earlier.
Higher-margin income from advertising, marketplace and services can lift margins even if product sales are flat, as Best Buy's gross margin rise to 23.9% shows.
A PC and AI-device upgrade cycle supports computing, Best Buy's largest category at 47% of domestic revenue.
Share gains from weaker rivals and consolidation, such as the Fnac Darty takeover and GameStop's store closures.
Strong results at some chains: Bic Camera's half-year operating income rose 25.6% to JPY 18.7B on sales up 6.0%.
Memory-driven price rises could cut unit demand or squeeze margins as retailers absorb costs.
Tariff changes under Section 301 keep landed costs uncertain, and refunds flatter current results.
Value-focused shoppers and heavy promotions could pressure margins into the holidays.
Weak profits at some chains, such as Yamada's fall in operating income to JPY 16.2B in the year to March 2026 from JPY 42.8B, show how fast earnings can slip.

Over three to five years we think the group stays a low-margin, cyclical business whose winners are the chains that add services, advertising and marketplace income to product sales. Best Buy's guide for a 4.4% to 4.5% adjusted margin shows how thin the base is. Product cycles and memory-driven price inflation can help or hurt: higher prices lift revenue per unit but may reduce volume. Tariffs and refunds make reported profit noisy. Chains with weak differentiation, such as those that depend on gaming or on promotions, are most exposed. Our read is that returns on capital stay high as capital needs are low, but growth in sales is limited to the pace of the CTA's forecast of 4% in 2026.

Consumer electronics retail is mid-cycle after a long downturn. Best Buy's enterprise comparable sales fell 6.8% in fiscal 2024 and 2.3% in fiscal 2025, rose 0.5% in fiscal 2026 and then 4.1% in the July 2026 quarter. The Fed held the funds rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 by a 10-2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike, and described activity as expanding at a strong pace and inflation as elevated. That is not an easing backdrop, and big-ticket purchases are rate sensitive.

Prices are the pressure point. The last published 12-month CPI reading was 3.7% for September, the BLS did not publish most October year-on-year figures, and gasoline was up 37.4% from a year earlier. In October, the monthly CPI for televisions rose 3.3%, smartphones 1.4% and computers and peripherals 0.5%, so device inflation is visible. Trade policy is the other lever: a temporary 10% Section 122 tariff lapsed on 24 July and Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% now apply to 60 economies. We think the macro backdrop supports replacement spending but not a broad boom.

Structural demand is steady rather than fast. The CTA forecast US consumer technology retail revenue of $578B in 2026, up 4%, in its August 2026 update. That is for all channels, not only specialist chains. Computing and mobile is the engine: it was 47% of Best Buy's domestic revenue in fiscal 2026, with comps of 5.7%, while consumer electronics and appliances fell 5.4% and 8.9%.

In the July quarter, Best Buy's computing and mobile comps were up 6.8% and consumer electronics 5.6%, but entertainment fell 6.3%. Demand is cyclical because devices are replaced when they wear out or when a new product cycle starts, and elasticity is high on price. Outside the US, JB Hi-Fi's Australian comps fell 1.4% while New Zealand rose 10.7%, and Fnac Darty's H1 revenue grew 0.6% like for like. Memory costs are a new variable: Counterpoint said memory prices were up 80% to 90% in early 2026, which pushes up device prices. Demographics matter little, though younger shoppers drive gaming and collectibles.

Porter's five forces show a hard industry. Rivalry is intense: JB Hi-Fi cites heightened competition and value-focused shoppers. The threat of new entrants is high online but lower for chains with scale in buying, delivery and service. Supplier power is high: five brands (Apple, Samsung, HP, LG and Sony) accounted for about 55% of Best Buy's purchases, and its top 20 for about 80%. Buyer power is high because prices are visible online. The threat of substitutes comes from brand stores, marketplaces and second-hand devices.

Concentration is national rather than global. Best Buy ($41.7B of revenue in fiscal 2026), Yamada (JPY 1.69 trillion) and Currys (GBP 9.25B) lead their home markets. We found no published market-share table. Moats differ: scale and services at Best Buy, where services and advertising earn higher margin; local density and service at Currys and Fnac Darty. Pricing power is weak on products, and retailers rely on vendor funding and services.

Politics and regulation are dominated by trade. The Supreme Court ruled on 20 Feb 2026 that IEEPA tariffs were unauthorized, and Best Buy's filing says refund administration is uncertain. Best Buy booked about $34M of IEEPA refunds in Q2 domestic gross profit, a small share of its $9.78B quarterly revenue. From 24 July, Section 301 duties of 10% or 12.5% on 60 economies replaced the temporary Section 122 tariff, and refunds are generally expected within 60 to 90 days after an importer's claim is accepted.

Technology is both opportunity and threat. AI-capable PCs are an increasingly important part of Currys' computing business, but AI data-center demand is also raising memory prices that feed device costs. Best Buy's filing flags marketplace and retail media as areas of legal uncertainty. Social and environmental rules on repair and recycling also matter, but we did not find a source that quantifies them. Consolidation is also visible: EP Group controls 69.3% of Fnac Darty. We think the biggest emerging risk is policy and cost volatility reaching shelf prices.

Electronics retail has thin margins and high turnover. Best Buy's fiscal 2026 gross profit rate was 22.5%, SG&A 18.3% and GAAP operating margin 3.3%. In Q2 FY27 its adjusted operating margin rose to 4.3% from 3.9%, with a gross rate of 23.9%. Fnac Darty's gross margin was 29.0% for the first half, but its current operating income was -EUR 34M because the second half carries peak trading. Currys' adjusted pre-tax profit was GBP 191M on GBP 9.25B of revenue in 2025/26, about 2% by our calculation.

Returns are strong because capital needs are low. Damodaran's lease-adjusted after-tax ROIC is 21.71% for special-line retail against 9.60% for the market, and net capex is 1.59% of sales against 4.23%. That group is broader than electronics, so we treat it as indicative. StockAnalysis shows ROIC of 26.0% at Best Buy and 11.2% at GameStop. Operating leverage is high: Yamada's operating income fell from JPY 42.8B to JPY 16.2B on higher revenue in the year to March 2026. GameStop is a special case, with an operating margin of 13.87% that rests on collectibles and a large cash pile.

Guidance has moved up. Best Buy raised FY27 comps to +1.9% to +3.0% from -1% to +1%, adjusted operating margin to 4.4% to 4.5% from 4.3% to 4.4%, and adjusted EPS to $6.70 to $6.90 from $6.30 to $6.60. Its Q3 guide of comps up 1% to 3% implies slower growth than Q2's 4.1%. We did not find Q3 FY27 results, which were not out in what we searched.

Elsewhere the picture is mixed. GameStop raised its fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook to above $650M, but net sales fell 18.7%. Currys reported 7% like-for-like growth for the summer and said early trading had been very solid, though it gave no formal forward guidance in the coverage we opened. Fnac Darty confirmed its 2026 outlook. JB Hi-Fi said October sales slowed.

Our read is that the first-half beat leaves holiday expectations high, and that reported margins are flattered by IEEPA refunds at Best Buy. Consensus estimate tables for the group were not publicly available to us, so we cannot say where we differ from them.

Valuation is low for the leader. At the close on 20 Nov 2026, Best Buy traded at 13.9x forward earnings, 16.3x trailing earnings and 8.5x EV/EBITDA, with an FCF yield of 8.61%. GameStop traded at 17.7x forward earnings and 25.2x EV/EBITDA, with an FCF yield of 5.12%. GameStop's enterprise value is distorted by its cash, digital assets and eBay stake.

Against the market, Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E was 21.52 for special-line retail and 27.66 for all firms, with expected five-year growth of 8.08% against 13.95%, and a PEG of 3.08 against 1.90. Best Buy's discount to that group fits a company with flat revenue and low margins, though its ROIC of 26.0% is high. Our read is that the price implies little growth and some risk of margin slippage if memory costs hit volume. We did not find 10-year average multiples we could open, so we do not compare these names with their own history.

Momentum has been positive. Best Buy was up 31.69% and GameStop 30.56% over 52 weeks to 20 Nov 2026. Best Buy's beta is 1.21, a sign of cyclical sensitivity. Those gains came as Best Buy raised guidance and GameStop lifted its adjusted EBITDA outlook, so price momentum follows earnings revisions rather than a change in sector multiples. Best Buy's market capitalization was $20.54B and GameStop's $13.45B at the same close.

Short interest was 7.76% of float at Best Buy and 9.21% at GameStop on StockAnalysis's latest data, which suggests meaningful skepticism, especially about GameStop's shrinking sales. We did not find ETF holdings or flow data for the group, and no sector index data was available to us, so we cannot comment on benchmark weights or flows. Our read is that positioning is mixed: the US leaders have re-rated on the 2026 rebound, while the second half faces tougher comparisons and rising component costs.

Household appliances is a two-speed industry. Housing-linked major-appliance makers are weak: Whirlpool's Q3 net sales fell 8.8% and its ongoing EBIT margin was 2.6%, with North American industry demand down 3.3%. Brands tied to new products, professional tools and small appliances are growing: SharkNinja's sales rose 21.2%, Techtronic's first-half sales rose 5.9% and Stanley Black & Decker's organic sales rose 4%. Tariff refunds flatter several reported profits. Existing-home sales ran at 3.75 million annualized in October with the 30-year mortgage at 7.28%. Whirlpool's market value was $1.63B against SharkNinja's $29.96B on 20 Nov 2026.

These companies make and sell the machines and tools used in and around the home: washers, dryers, refrigerators, dishwashers and ranges (major appliances), plus vacuums, air fryers, blenders and coffee makers (small appliances), and power tools and lawn equipment. Customers are households, mostly buying through big retailers such as Lowe's and Home Depot, builders and increasingly websites. Makers earn the gap between factory cost and wholesale price. GICS puts the cookware, tableware and storage makers in Housewares & Specialties, and homebuilders and cabinet makers elsewhere in Household Durables.

Major appliances: Large machines for laundry, cooling, dishwashing and cooking, bought when homes are built or sold, or when an old unit breaks. Most sales go through big-box retailers and builders. e.g. Whirlpool, KitchenAid, Maytag, Electrolux, Haier and GE Appliances, LG, Samsung, Bosch

Small kitchen and countertop appliances: Air fryers, blenders, coffee and espresso machines and food processors. Items are cheaper and bought more often, so sales depend on product launches and online marketing. e.g. SharkNinja Ninja, KitchenAid mixers, Breville, De'Longhi, Cuisinart
Floor care and robot vacuums: Upright, handheld and robotic vacuums and steam cleaners, sold through retailers and direct online. e.g. Shark, Roomba (iRobot), Dyson, Electrolux

Professional and consumer power tools: Cordless drills, saws and impact drivers sold to tradespeople and homeowners, built around battery platforms that lock customers into one brand's batteries. e.g. Milwaukee and Ryobi (Techtronic), DeWalt and Craftsman (Stanley Black & Decker)

Outdoor and lawn equipment: Mowers, trimmers, blowers and hedge tools, increasingly battery-powered, sold mostly through home-improvement chains and dealers. e.g. Ryobi and Ego outdoor products, DeWalt outdoor lines

Built-in and premium kitchen appliances: Higher-priced ovens, cooktops and refrigeration installed in new or renovated kitchens, usually specified by builders and designers. e.g. BSH Bosch and Miele, Electrolux Professional-style premium lines, Haier's GE Profile and Monogram
Housing activity and home sales: Moves, remodels and new homes trigger appliance and tool purchases. Weak turnover lowers industry unit shipments, which hits makers with fixed factories hardest.

Interest rates and consumer credit: Appliances are often financed and sit alongside mortgages. Higher rates delay purchases that can wait and reduce the share of buyers who upgrade rather than repair.

Tariffs and input costs: Steel, resin, copper and freight make up most of a product's cost. Duties and commodity moves change gross margin within a few quarters, and makers push prices up to recover them.
Product innovation and brand strength: New features such as in-door ice makers, cordless platforms or air fryers let makers raise prices and take share. Weak lines force promotion and lower margins.
Retail channel and online shift: Big-box chains and websites decide shelf space and promotions. Direct-to-consumer sales raise gross margin but need marketing spend.
Cost take-out and footprint: Plant closures, design-to-value redesigns and sourcing programs lower unit costs. Benefits arrive with a lag, while the restructuring charge arrives first.
Major domestic appliances (MDA): Large home machines such as refrigerators, washers, dishwashers and ovens. Whirlpool uses this label for its largest segments.
Small domestic appliances (SDA): Countertop and handheld products such as mixers, air fryers and vacuums. They have higher gross margins and quicker product cycles than major appliances.
Industry shipments (TIV): Total units the industry ships to retailers and builders in a market. It is the cleanest read on underlying demand, separate from one company's share changes.
Replacement versus new-build demand: Most appliance purchases replace broken units, which gives a steady base. New-home and home-sale activity adds a cyclical layer on top.
Price/mix: The change in revenue from selling at higher prices or selling more expensive models. It is the main way makers offset cost inflation.
Volume deleverage: Factories and warehouses cost roughly the same whatever the output, so falling volume spreads fixed cost over fewer units and cuts margin.
Ongoing EBIT: Operating profit before interest and tax with unusual items removed. Companies such as Whirlpool guide to it, so check what was excluded.
Battery platform: A family of cordless tools that share one battery type. Buyers who own the batteries tend to stay with the brand, which supports pricing and repeat sales.

Section 232 duties: US import duties based on national-security reviews, applied here to the steel and aluminium content of appliances and tools. They raise costs for importers and for US factories that use imported metal.

IEEPA tariffs and refunds: Import duties imposed under an emergency-powers law, which the Supreme Court has since ruled unlawful. Companies that paid them are claiming refunds, which appear as one-off profit.
Trade customer concentration: A few retailers buy a large share of a maker's output. Whirlpool's biggest customer, Lowe's, gives the retailer leverage over price and promotions.

Contract manufacturer: A factory that builds products to a brand's design. Asset-light brands such as SharkNinja lean on them, which lowers capital needs but exposes them to supplier and tariff changes.
Housing turnover: October existing-home sales fell to a 3.75 million annual rate and the 30-year mortgage rate was 7.28%, which keeps replacement-and-move demand for major appliances weak.
Whirlpool's price-for-volume trade: a further 7% North American price increase takes effect on 3 Dec 2026, and management expects most cost benefits in 2027.
Quality of earnings: Stanley Black & Decker and SharkNinja both booked one-off tariff refunds in Q3, so reported margins overstate the run rate.
Balance-sheet strain at Whirlpool: long-term debt was $6,838M against $1,103M of cash at 30 Sep 2026, with nine-month free cash flow of -$1,081M.
Tariff policy: Section 232 steel-content duties on appliances were set at 50% from 23 Jun 2025, and Whirlpool says its outlook assumes only currently announced tariffs.
Whirlpool, SharkNinja, Stanley Black & Decker, Techtronic Industries, Electrolux, Haier Smart Home, LG Electronics, iRobot

Revenue comes from selling appliances and tools, mainly to retailers and builders. Whirlpool had about $16B of 2025 net sales and 41,000 employees. SharkNinja's Q3 sales split across cleaning ($617.2M), cooking and beverage ($597.7M), food preparation ($485.5M) and beauty and home environment ($276.1M). Techtronic earns about $5.9B of its $8.3B first-half sales from professional tools.

Customers are big retailers and builders in the first instance and households in the end. Whirlpool says sales to Lowe's were about 15% of 2025 net sales, and that Lowe's was 44% of receivables. Techtronic names The Home Depot as Ryobi's main North American partner. Direct online sales are a growing channel for makers such as SharkNinja.

Main costs are materials, labor, freight and tariffs. Whirlpool cited higher steel, resin and base-metal costs and fuel and logistics costs in Q3, costing 75 basis points of margin for raw materials. Techtronic's research and development was 4.6% of revenue in the first half.

Pricing power depends on brand, product novelty and scale. SharkNinja's gross margin was 50.6% on a trailing basis and Whirlpool's 13.1%, and Whirlpool's retail prices rose 8% to 9% over January 2025 baselines. We think premium and new-category brands hold price better than mature appliance lines, though the figures are from different reporting bases.

Major assets are factories, inventory and receivables. Whirlpool reported long-term debt of $6,838M and cash of $1,103M at 30 Sep 2026. SharkNinja carried $708.8M of debt and $487.8M of cash. Techtronic's working capital was 16.6% of sales.

Mixed. Whirlpool runs a local-for-local factory footprint and says about 80% of the major appliances it sells in the US are made in the US. SharkNinja and Techtronic rely more on contract and own plants in Asia, and Techtronic's capex was only 1.1% of sales. Damodaran's net capex runs 5.9% of sales for Furn/Home Furnishings against 4.2% for the market.

Euromonitor put the 2025 global major-appliance market at 570 million units and $298B, growing 1.4% against 2.7% in 2024. That covers refrigeration, laundry, dishwashers, large cooking and microwaves only; we did not find a comparable sourced total for small appliances, power tools and lawn equipment.

Segments are major appliances, small appliances, floor care and robotics, and power tools and outdoor equipment. A caution on classification: the S&P 500 constituents list places Stanley Black & Decker in Industrial Machinery and Supplies and Components rather than with appliances, so index-based groupings can differ from this sub-industry.

Makers sit between metal, resin and component suppliers and retailers, builders and consumers. Whirlpool's input cost line cites steel, resin and base metals and its retail channel is led by Lowe's at about 15% of sales. SharkNinja and Techtronic depend on Asian manufacturing and distribution through home-improvement chains.

The industry has shifted from US and European incumbents to global Asian groups. Whirlpool lists BSH, Electrolux, Haier, Hisense, LG, Midea and Samsung as major rivals. Electrolux now has a Midea partnership in North America with three joint ventures. iRobot was acquired by its manufacturer Picea after a pre-packaged Chapter 11 in January 2026. Whirlpool cut its Whirlpool India stake below a majority in 2025.

Asia-Pacific is the largest region by size, and Euromonitor says eight of the top ten growth markets are in the Global South. Haier says overseas is more than half its business. Whirlpool says about 80% of the major appliances it sells in the US are made in the US, while Electrolux closed a plant in Rosario, Argentina in Q3; we did not find a sourced country-by-country production split.

Global major-appliance competition is led by roughly nine large groups named by Whirlpool: BSH, Electrolux, Haier, Hisense, LG, Mabe, Midea, Panasonic and Samsung, plus Whirlpool itself. In small appliances it names Breville, De'Longhi, Ninja, Groupe SEB and Cuisinart. In tools, Techtronic and Stanley Black & Decker lead among the companies we looked at.

Market leaders by size of reported results: Whirlpool at about $16B of 2025 sales, Techtronic at $8.3B for the first half, Haier at RMB 221.8B for nine months, Electrolux at SEK 33.9B for Q3, Stanley Black & Decker at $3.7B for Q3, and LG Electronics at 23.82 trillion won of group revenue for Q3, up 8.9% (not split by division in what we opened). We did not find a sourced market-share table, so we rank by sales; Haier says its US industry position is first.

Major appliances are concentrated at the global level but contested by region, while small appliances and tools are more fragmented. Whirlpool describes competition as intense and says many rivals are expanding beyond their existing manufacturing footprints. Haier says China's industry fell about 10% in Q3 and US shipments about 4%, so rivals are fighting over a shrinking pool.

Barriers are moderate to high in major appliances: plants, distribution, service networks and retailer relationships take years to build, and Whirlpool says its local-for-local scale is a cost advantage. Barriers are lower in small appliances, where SharkNinja's cooking sales grew 36.6% in a quarter, but battery ecosystems protect tool brands.

Scale helps with sourcing, logistics and retail leverage. Whirlpool's operating margin was 1.83% on a trailing basis despite its size, so scale alone does not guarantee profit. Electrolux's adjusted EBIT margin was 2.7% in Q3, while Techtronic's EBIT margin was 9.9% in the first half.

Major appliances are close to commodities on price, differentiated by features such as in-door ice makers; small appliances and tools are more differentiated, with Techtronic reporting a record 42.9% gross margin. Competitors also priced up: Whirlpool says its competitors' average pricing rose meaningfully in 2026.

Retail customers hold the most bargaining power, since Lowe's alone was about 15% of Whirlpool's sales and 44% of its receivables. Suppliers of steel and resin have power in spikes: Whirlpool took a 75 basis point raw material hit in Q3. Trade policy shifts power between domestic and import-heavy makers.

Revenue growth follows housing activity, replacement cycles, price and new products. Existing-home sales were 3.75 million annualized in October, down 8.8% on the year. North American industry demand fell 3.3% in Q3, while SharkNinja grew 21.2% on new categories.

Operating margins reflect volume, price, input costs, tariffs and restructuring. Whirlpool's ongoing EBIT margin was 2.6% in Q3 against 4.5% a year earlier, while Techtronic's H1 EBIT margin was 9.9%. Damodaran's pre-tax operating margin in January 2026 was 7.2% for Furn/Home Furnishings and 16.8% for Machinery.

Key cost variables are steel, resin, copper, tariffs, freight and fuel. Gasoline was up 37.4% in the twelve months to October 2026, and Electrolux cited higher raw-material and logistics costs from the Middle East conflict. Whirlpool's net tariff impact cost 225 basis points sequentially in Q3.

Rates matter through mortgages and financed purchases. The 30-year rate was 7.28% on 19 Nov 2026, and the Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00%. Debt matters as well: Whirlpool's long-term debt of $6,838M compares with $1,103M of cash, while Damodaran's market debt-to-capital is 30.5% for Furn/Home Furnishings.

Inflation helps pricing but hurts volume. BLS reported appliance prices up 1.3% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. BLS could not publish most twelve-month comparisons because October 2025 data were not collected. Jobs and income matter through consumer confidence; we did not retrieve unemployment data for this brief.

Mostly cyclical, with defensive replacement demand underneath and secular growth in categories such as cordless tools and countertop appliances. Whirlpool's Latin America sales rose 6.9% in Q3 while North America fell 8.3%, and Techtronic's professional segment grew 9.7% against 2.5% decline in consumer.

Growth is uneven. Damodaran's expected five-year EPS growth is 12.3% for Furn/Home Furnishings, 13.6% for Machinery and 14.0% for the total market in January 2026. Recent company growth ranged from Whirlpool's -8.8% and Haier's nine-month net profit decline of 13.7% to SharkNinja's +21.2%.

Margins vary widely. Damodaran's January 2026 gross margins were 30.3% for Furn/Home Furnishings, 31.8% for Electrical Equipment and 37.5% for Machinery. Company gross margins were 13.1% for Whirlpool, 32.2% for Stanley Black & Decker and 50.6% for SharkNinja on trailing figures. Damodaran has no separate appliance industry, so these are proxies.

Returns are low for the mature appliance makers and high for the growth brands. Damodaran's after-tax lease-adjusted ROIC is 11.9% for Furn/Home Furnishings, 27.2% for Machinery and 9.6% for the market. StockAnalysis shows ROIC of 2.6% for Whirlpool, 5.8% for Stanley Black & Decker and 25.2% for SharkNinja.

Leverage differs. Damodaran's market debt to capital is 30.5% for Furn/Home Furnishings and 12.6% for Machinery, with interest coverage of 3.9 and 7.8. Whirlpool's debt-to-equity is 2.08 and Stanley Black & Decker's 0.58, while SharkNinja's is 0.29.

Free cash flow is lumpy. Whirlpool's nine-month free cash flow was -$1,081M, though it guides about $300M for 2026. Stanley Black & Decker generated $585M in Q3 and guides $1.0B to $1.2B for the year. Techtronic's first-half free cash flow was not in the sections we opened, and SharkNinja's nine-month operating cash flow was $107.4M.

Capex needs are moderate. Damodaran's net capex to sales is 5.9% for Furn/Home Furnishings, 4.1% for Machinery and 4.2% for the market. Techtronic spent US$92M, 1.1% of sales, in the first half, and SharkNinja guides $190M to $210M for 2026.

Multiples: Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E was 20.3 for Furn/Home Furnishings, 24.1 for Machinery and 27.7 for the market. On 20 Nov 2026 forward P/E was 17.3x for Stanley Black & Decker and 29.2x for SharkNinja, while Whirlpool's was not available because of losses.

Trade policy is the biggest regulatory variable. The US set a 50% Section 232 duty on the steel content of washers, dryers, refrigerators, dishwashers and ranges from 23 Jun 2025, and Whirlpool says its outlook reflects only currently announced tariffs. We could not confirm the current rate schedule from a primary notice. Whirlpool's 10-K says energy and environmental rules did not materially affect its capex or competitive position.

AI and technology cut both ways. Euromonitor says AI features are now standard in premium appliances, while Whirlpool's 10-K flags competitive risk from new technologies and new entrants. We found no hard figures on how AI affects earnings. Smart-device data handling also draws attention: iRobot created a separate US subsidiary for consumer data.

Demographics matter through household formation and home moves. First-time buyers were 29% of existing-home sales in October 2026, down from 32% a year earlier. Fewer moves mean fewer purchases of matched appliance sets; we did not find sourced data sizing the long-term demographic effect.

Consumer behavior is shifting toward deferral and value. Whirlpool says industry demand is soft and now expects a North American decline of about 5% for 2026, and Euromonitor links the global slowdown to weak housing, high rates and inflation. Online and direct channels are gaining, shown by SharkNinja's 21.2% growth.

New competitors keep arriving. Whirlpool says rivals are expanding beyond their manufacturing footprints; Midea is now a partner of Electrolux in North America; and Chinese manufacturer Picea now owns iRobot. SharkNinja's beauty and home-environment sales rose 45.8% on new categories.

Geopolitics and supply chains matter. Electrolux cites Middle East conflict costs for raw materials and logistics, plus US tariff costs. Haier booked a RMB 364 million currency loss in Q3. Whirlpool said competitors pre-loaded imported inventory in 2025, which delayed the benefit of tariffs.

Substitutes include repair and second-hand units, which extend replacement cycles, and professional services for tools. We found no sourced data sizing repair or resale in this industry. Lower-priced imports and private labels also substitute for branded products, and Whirlpool notes some customers carry their own brands.
A housing-turnover recovery would lift major-appliance volumes, which are down with industry demand down 3.3% in Whirlpool's North America in Q3.
Cost take-out: Whirlpool expects about $250M of gross savings in 2026 with most benefits in 2027, and Electrolux raised its savings target to about SEK 4.0bn.
Category growth and new products, such as SharkNinja's 36.6% cooking sales growth and Techtronic's cordless conversion of professional trades.
Pricing carry-over: Whirlpool's further 7% North American price increase on 3 Dec 2026 supports 2027 margins if volumes hold.
Prolonged housing weakness: existing-home sales were down 8.8% year on year at a 3.75 million rate with mortgages at 7.28%.
Tariff and metal-cost volatility, since Whirlpool's guidance excludes any future trade-policy change.
Balance-sheet pressure at the weakest names, such as Whirlpool's negative nine-month free cash flow and $6,838M of long-term debt.
Earnings quality: one-off refunds flatter results at Stanley Black & Decker and SharkNinja, and their removal will expose the underlying trend.

Over the next three to five years we think the industry stays two-speed. Brands with new categories, battery platforms or low fixed-cost models, such as SharkNinja and Techtronic, have kept growing through a soft housing market. Major-appliance makers face weak industry shipments and thin margins, but they now have price increases and cost programs set to deliver mostly in 2027, according to Whirlpool. Global Asian groups keep gaining footprint, and partnerships such as Electrolux with Midea show consolidation is under way. The biggest upside lever is lower mortgage rates, which we do not see yet in the latest data. Tariff policy remains the swing factor, and refunds are masking underlying margins today. Our read is that share, price and cost execution matter more than market growth, which Euromonitor put at only 1.4% for major appliances in 2025.

Household appliances is a housing-linked durable goods industry, and the housing cycle is weak. Existing-home sales ran at 3.75 million annualized in October 2026, down 5.5% on the month and 8.8% on the year, and first-time buyers were 29% of sales. The 30-year mortgage rate was 7.28% on 19 Nov 2026 against 6.26% a year earlier. Whirlpool says North American industry demand fell 3.3% in Q3 and it expects about 5% down for 2026. Euromonitor put 2025 global major-appliance growth at 1.4%, down from 2.7%, citing tariff uncertainty, high rates, inflation and weak housing.

Policy is not easing. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026, with two dissenters preferring a quarter-point hike, and said inflation remains elevated. Appliance prices rose 1.3% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, and gasoline was up 37.4% over twelve months, which raises freight and fuel costs. Tariffs are the other lever: a 50% duty on the steel content of washers, dryers, refrigerators, dishwashers and ranges applied from 23 Jun 2025, and Whirlpool booked a 225 basis point sequential tariff drag from incremental Section 232 duties in Q3. Currency adds noise, as Haier's RMB 364 million Q3 FX loss shows. Our read is that volumes are near a floor but not yet turning, so price and cost actions carry results.

Euromonitor sized the 2025 global major-appliance market at 570 million units and $298B, with growth of 1.4% and the fastest-growing markets in Eastern Europe, Africa, South Asia and Latin America. We did not find a sourced total that also covers small appliances, power tools and lawn equipment, so the industry total is larger than that figure but unquantified here. Demand is replacement-led, which gives a floor, but purchases can be deferred, so units fall in downturns: Haier says China's industry fell about 10% in Q3 and US shipments about 4%.

Growth sits in newer categories and professional tools. SharkNinja's cooking and beverage sales rose 36.6% and beauty and home environment 45.8% in Q3. Techtronic's professional segment grew 9.7% in the first half while consumer fell 2.5%, and it cites electrician demand of roughly 81,000 openings a year over the next decade. Latin America rose 6.9% at Whirlpool while North America fell 8.3%. Demographics work through first-time buyers, 29% of October home sales, down from 32% a year earlier. We think long-term growth is low single digit for major appliances and higher for innovative categories.

Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense, with Whirlpool naming BSH, Electrolux, Haier, Hisense, LG, Mabe, Midea, Panasonic and Samsung in major appliances, and Breville, De'Longhi, Ninja, Groupe SEB and Cuisinart in small appliances. Buyer power is high because Lowe's alone was about 15% of Whirlpool's 2025 sales. Supplier power is moderate, with steel, resin and base-metal costs costing Whirlpool 75 basis points in Q3. The threat of new entrants is higher in small appliances than in major appliances, where factories and service networks are barriers. Substitutes include repair and used units; we found no sourced data on their size.

Concentration is moderate globally and varies by region. We found no sourced market-share table, so we rank by sales: Whirlpool about $16B in 2025, Techtronic $8.3B in the first half, Haier RMB 221.8B in nine months. Pricing power looks stronger in differentiated categories: Techtronic's gross margin was 42.9% and SharkNinja's 50.6%, against 13.1% for Whirlpool. Moats are brands, battery platforms, retailer relationships and, for Whirlpool, a US footprint that makes about 80% of the major appliances it sells there. Consolidation continues: Electrolux has formed three joint ventures with Midea in North America, and Picea bought iRobot.

Trade policy dominates. The 50% Section 232 duty on the steel content of listed appliances took effect 23 Jun 2025; Whirlpool's Q3 saw a 225 basis point sequential tariff drag from incremental Section 232 duties, and it assumes only announced tariffs in its 2026 outlook. We could not confirm the current rate schedule from a primary notice. Refunds of earlier emergency-power duties are now flowing: Stanley Black & Decker saw about 430 basis points of gross margin benefit and $0.67 of EPS, SharkNinja recognized $109.6M and Electrolux cited refunds in cash flow. Whirlpool's 10-K says environmental and energy rules did not have a material effect on its capex or competitiveness.

Technology and social factors matter at the margin. Euromonitor says AI features are standard in premium appliances, Whirlpool launched an in-door nugget ice maker, and Techtronic is pushing cordless conversion of petrol tools, including lithium riding mowers. Data governance is a new theme for connected products: iRobot created iRobot Safe, with an independent board, to handle US and EU consumer data after the Picea deal. Geopolitics is an emerging risk: Electrolux cites higher raw-material and logistics costs from the Middle East conflict.

Economics differ sharply by model. Damodaran's January 2026 data shows pre-tax operating margins of 7.2% for Furn/Home Furnishings and 16.8% for Machinery against 14.4% for the market, with gross margins of 30.3%, 37.5% and 37.8%. Damodaran has no separate appliance group, so we use these as proxies. Company figures are more informative: Whirlpool's trailing operating margin was 1.8% and ROIC 2.6%, Stanley Black & Decker's 7.7% and 5.8%, SharkNinja's 14.8% and 25.2%. Techtronic's first-half EBIT margin was 9.9% and Electrolux's Q3 adjusted margin 2.7%.

Operating leverage is high because plants and warehouses are fixed costs. Whirlpool says volume deleverage and fuel costs left net cost take-out below $150M of about $250M gross savings. Capital intensity is moderate: Damodaran's net capex is 5.9% of sales for Furn/Home Furnishings, while Techtronic's first-half capex was 1.1% of sales. Free cash flow is strongest where margins are: Stanley Black & Decker produced $585M in Q3 while Whirlpool's nine-month free cash flow was -$1,081M. Damodaran's ROIC of 11.9% for Furn/Home Furnishings compares with 9.6% for the market.

Guidance is split. Whirlpool cut 2026 to net sales of about $14.5B, ongoing EBIT margin of 2.0% to 2.2%, ongoing EPS of about -$1.30 and free cash flow of about $300M, with Q4 ongoing EPS about -$0.35. It says most structural cost benefits land in 2027 and it is cautiously optimistic. Stanley Black & Decker raised adjusted EPS to $5.95 to $6.25 from $5.20 to $5.80, but Q3 included about $0.67 of refunds. SharkNinja raised 2026 sales growth to 18% to 19% and adjusted EPS to $6.65 to $6.75, with refunds excluded from adjusted figures.

Others show slower trends. Electrolux's organic sales growth was 3.5% in Q3 and it now sees volume, price and mix contributing neutrally to operating income for 2026. Haier's nine-month net profit fell 13.67%, though it says Q3 profit grew excluding FX and about RMB 500 million of one-offs. Techtronic targets a 10.0% EBIT margin by 2027 against 9.9% now.

We did not find consensus estimate tables or revision data we could open, so we do not state where we differ from consensus. Our read is that earnings quality is the main issue: refunds inflate Stanley Black & Decker's 2026 base, and Whirlpool's 2027 recovery depends on price holding and housing stabilising.

Valuation is split by quality. On 20 Nov 2026, Stanley Black & Decker traded on 17.3x forward earnings with a 10.8% free-cash-flow yield, a $15.85B market value and EV/EBITDA of 12.4. SharkNinja traded on 29.2x forward earnings, 24.7x EV/EBITDA and a 1.7% free-cash-flow yield with a $29.96B market value. Whirlpool's forward P/E was not available because of losses; its market value was $1.63B, EV/EBITDA 12.8, and free-cash-flow yield -15.3%.

Against datasets, Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E was 20.3 for Furn/Home Furnishings, 24.1 for Machinery, 16.9 for Household Products and 27.7 for the market. The SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF had a forward P/E of 18.1 on 19 Nov 2026. SharkNinja's 1.7% yield partly reflects weak cash conversion, with nine-month operating cash flow of $107.4M on $5.15B of sales. Whirlpool's 3.6% dividend yield sits against negative free cash flow, which looks hard to sustain without the guided recovery. We did not find ten-year average multiples for this group that we could open, so we do not compare with its own history.

Momentum is sharply divided. Over the 52 weeks to 20 Nov 2026, SharkNinja was up 143.3%, Stanley Black & Decker up 71.6% and Whirlpool down 64.7%. In the SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF, SharkNinja was the largest holding at 4.18% on 19 Nov 2026; Whirlpool and Stanley Black & Decker were not in the top ten, and the fund held $1.46B with a -1.01% return year to date to 31 Oct.

Short interest was 5.1% of float for Stanley Black & Decker and 9.2% for SharkNinja. The page's figure for Whirlpool was 0.06%, but it showed a previous-month figure of about 17.5 million shares, so we treat it as unreliable. Stanley Black & Decker repurchased about $250M of stock in Q3 and approved a new $1B authorization. We did not find ETF flow or institutional ownership data we could open. Our read is that positioning favors growth brands and cash generators, while Whirlpool is priced for stress, and its Q4 and 2027 price-and-cost delivery will test that.

Leisure products is splitting in two. Toys and collectibles are booming: US toy dollar sales rose 20% in January to September 2026, Hasbro's Q3 revenue rose 15%, while Mattel grew 4% but cut its full-year outlook after softer point-of-sale. Big-ticket recreation is growing more modestly: Polaris sales rose 11% and Brunswick's 7%, yet new powerboat retail units fell 7.1% in the 12 months to April. Golf and outdoor names are flat to down: Acushnet sales fell 1.3% and YETI trimmed its outlook. Tariff refunds flatter margins at most of them.

Leisure products companies design, make and sell goods people buy for fun and recreation: toys and games, sporting goods, golf equipment, fitness gear, outdoor coolers and drinkware, boats, engines and off-road vehicles. Customers are mostly households, reached through mass retailers, specialty dealers, e-commerce and the companies' own sites. Revenue comes from product sales, plus licensing, subscriptions and digital games at some names. GICS places Hasbro, Mattel, Polaris, Brunswick and Peloton here. Apparel and footwear sit in Apparel, Accessories and Luxury Goods and Footwear, bicycle retailers and sporting goods stores sit in specialty retail, and video game publishers sit in Entertainment.

Toys, games and collectibles: Dolls, vehicles, action figures, building sets, plush, board games and trading cards sold mainly through mass retailers and online, with strong seasonality into the holidays. e.g. Mattel Barbie and Hot Wheels, Hasbro Transformers and Magic: The Gathering

Powersports and off-road vehicles: Motorized recreational vehicles such as off-road vehicles, side-by-sides, snowmobiles and motorcycles, sold through franchised dealers at high price points and often financed. e.g. Polaris RZR and Ranger, Harley-Davidson, BRP

Recreational boats, engines and marine parts: Boats and outboard engines for fishing and leisure, plus the parts, electronics and accessories that sell into the large installed base. e.g. Brunswick Mercury Marine, Sea Ray and Boston Whaler, Malibu Boats

Golf equipment: Clubs, balls, gloves and bags sold through golf shops and retailers; balls are bought repeatedly, clubs are replaced on product cycles. e.g. Acushnet Titleist balls and clubs, Callaway Golf

Outdoor and premium lifestyle products: Branded coolers, drinkware, packs and camping gear sold at a premium on brand strength, direct to consumers and through wholesale partners. e.g. YETI coolers and Rambler drinkware
Connected fitness: Exercise equipment tied to a paid content subscription, so the hardware sale starts a recurring revenue stream. e.g. Peloton bikes, treadmills and app subscriptions

Consumer confidence and discretionary income: Leisure goods are postponable. When household budgets tighten, boats, vehicles and exercise equipment are cut first and sales fall faster than overall spending.
Interest rates and consumer credit: Boats and vehicles are usually financed, and dealers finance their stock. Higher rates lift monthly payments and dealer costs, which cuts orders.

Tariffs and sourcing: Most toys, golf gear and drinkware are made in Asia, so duties raise landed cost. Companies pass some on in price, absorb some and re-source, which moves gross margin within a few quarters.
Franchise strength and licensing: A hit film, game or collectible line lifts a toy maker's volume and price. A fading brand does the reverse, so revenue can swing by double digits.
Retail and dealer inventory: Retailers and dealers hold the stock. When they over-order, the maker's shipments run ahead of sales and later drop; lean stock means orders follow real demand.
Operating leverage: Plants, design teams and marketing are largely fixed costs, so extra volume raises profit faster than revenue and a volume fall cuts it faster.
Point of sale (POS): What consumers actually buy at the register. It leads a manufacturer's own shipments, because retailers stock up or run down inventory.
Gross billings: Mattel's measure of sales before discounts and allowances. Net sales are billings less those deductions.
Sell-in versus sell-through: Sell-in is what the maker ships to retailers or dealers; sell-through is what shoppers buy from them. A gap builds inventory that is later worked down.
Licensing and royalties: Toy and outdoor makers pay film and brand owners for the right to use a character or logo, or earn royalties from others using theirs. It adds demand but costs margin.
Floorplan financing: Credit that dealers use to stock boats and vehicles. Higher rates raise dealer carrying costs and make them order less.

Wholesale versus direct-to-consumer (DTC): Wholesale sells to retailers at a lower price per item but with less selling cost; DTC sells to shoppers at full price with higher marketing and fulfilment cost.
Collectibles and kidults: Toys and cards bought by adult fans. They tend to carry higher prices and strong demand for franchises such as Pokemon or Magic.
Seasonality: Toys earn most of their profit in the second half of the year before holidays, while boats, golf and outdoor gear peak in spring and summer.
IEEPA tariffs: Import duties imposed under an emergency-powers law that were later struck down. Importers can claim refunds, which show up as one-off profit.
Adjusted EBITDA: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, adjusted for items management calls unusual. Several companies here guide to it.
Installed base: Boats, vehicles or bikes already in owners' hands. They generate repeat sales of engines, parts, accessories or subscriptions.
Product cycle: Golf clubs and similar durables are redesigned every year or two. The launch timing can pull sales between quarters.
Holiday point-of-sale: Mattel cut its 2026 sales growth guide to 1% to 4% on softer point-of-sale late in Q3, even as Circana shows toy dollar sales up 20% through September.
Quality of earnings: Mattel booked $88M and Hasbro about $55M of tariff refunds in Q3, Polaris $10M and Acushnet expects about $30M in 2026, so reported margins overstate the run rate.
Big-ticket demand: powerboat retail units were down 7.1% on a rolling 12-month basis to April 2026, while Brunswick says dealer pipelines are lean.
Consumer-brand momentum is uneven: Peloton subscriptions fell 9%, YETI cut its sales outlook and Callaway guided a fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA loss of $45M to $53M.
Retail concentration: Walmart, Target and Amazon together took about 44% of Mattel's 2024 sales, so one buyer's inventory decisions can move a quarter.
Hasbro, Mattel, Polaris, Brunswick, Acushnet, YETI, Peloton, Callaway Golf

Revenue comes mainly from selling physical products, with licensing, digital games and subscriptions on top. Hasbro's Q3 revenue of $1.595B included $747.2M from Wizards of the Coast and digital gaming and $827.9M from Consumer Products. Peloton's Q1 FY2027 revenue was $559.2M, up 2%, while paid subscriptions fell 9%.

Customers are households, reached through retailers or dealers. Mattel's three largest customers, Walmart, Target and Amazon, accounted for about 44% of its 2024 sales. YETI's Q3 sales split between wholesale at $237.3M and direct-to-consumer at $272.2M. Polaris and Brunswick sell through franchised dealers.

Main costs are materials, manufacturing, freight, tariffs, royalties, marketing and, for dealers' customers, financing support. Mattel paid $244.1M of royalty expense in 2024 and runs principal plants in China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand. Mattel guides to an adjusted gross margin of roughly 48% for 2026, excluding refunds.

Pricing power rests on brand, franchise and category. YETI earned a 57.7% gross margin in Q3, Peloton 61.3% and Mattel 55.0% adjusted, against a Damodaran gross margin of 39.8% for the broader recreation group in January 2026. Boats and vehicles carry thinner margins: Polaris's gross margin was 21.2%.

Main assets are brands and intellectual property, plants, inventory and receivables. Polaris held $1,544.9M of inventory at 30 Sep 2026; Brunswick's finished goods were reported at about $834M, per a summary of its 10-Q. Liabilities vary: Mattel had $2,335.0M of long-term debt, while YETI had about $69.9M.

Mixed. Toy makers that outsource or own light plants are asset-light, while boat, engine and vehicle makers run factories and carry dealer-support obligations. Damodaran puts net capex at 1.34% of sales for the broader recreation group against 4.23% for the whole market in January 2026. YETI guides capex of $60M to $70M.

We did not find a single reliable, citable global market size for leisure products. Useful guides are Circana's data showing US toy dollar sales up 20% in January to September 2026, and NMMA's count of 214,292 new powerboat retail units in the 12 months to April 2026.

Main segments are toys and games (Mattel, Hasbro), powersports and boats (Polaris, Brunswick), golf (Acushnet, Callaway), outdoor lifestyle (YETI) and fitness (Peloton). Mattel's Q3 gross billings split into dolls $703.2M, vehicles $679.8M, action figures, building sets and games $450.8M and infant and preschool $220.8M.

Makers sit between component suppliers and retailers or dealers. Mattel makes most core products in its own plants and uses third parties mainly for non-core items. Brunswick's Propulsion segment sells engines to boat builders, and its parts and accessories segment earned a 24.6% adjusted margin selling into the installed base.

The industry has shifted toward franchises, adult buyers and online. Circana says consumers aged 12 and over drove most 2026 toy growth, with collectibles up 56% and TikTok Shop toy sales near $1.6B. Big-ticket categories have moved the other way: powerboat retail units fell 7.1% in the year to April 2026.

Sales concentrate in North America: 89% of Polaris's Q3 sales were there. We did not find a sourced regional split for the rest of the group. Production concentrates in Asia and Mexico for toys, which Mattel's plants in China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand show.

There are dozens of significant public competitors plus many private ones. Mattel's 10-K names Hasbro, Jazwares, LEGO, The Pokemon Company and Spin Master among toy rivals. On 20 Nov 2026 market caps were $15.72B for Hasbro, $4.63B Brunswick, $4.58B Acushnet, $3.91B Mattel, $3.63B Polaris, $2.63B YETI and $2.22B Peloton.

Leaders by sub-segment: Hasbro and Mattel in toys, Brunswick in marine engines, Polaris in off-road vehicles, Acushnet in golf balls. We did not find a published market-share table we could open, so we do not give shares. Polaris itself said its North American off-road vehicle retail sales rose low single digits while the industry was flat.

Fragmented across the industry, concentrated within niches. Large toy franchises, marine engines and golf balls each have a few strong players, while sporting goods, fitness and outdoor products have many brands. Acushnet's golf ball sales were $209.1M in Q3, up 3.3%.

Barriers are moderate. A brand and distribution take years to build: Mattel depends on three retail customers for about 44% of sales, and Brunswick and Polaris rely on dealer networks. Digital channels such as TikTok Shop, now nearly 5% of US toy sales, lower barriers for new entrants.

Scale helps in sourcing, licensing and retailer negotiations. Hasbro's 27.5% operating margin and Mattel's 8.7% operating margin, on trailing data from StockAnalysis, show how much a hit franchise can matter beyond scale. Brunswick's engine business sells across competing boat builders, which spreads its fixed costs.

Mixed. Many toys and basic sporting goods are close to commodities, while franchises, premium drinkware and brand-name golf balls are differentiated. YETI's 57.7% gross margin against Polaris's 21.2% reflects branded consumer goods versus vehicles.

Retailers and dealers hold the bargaining power. Mattel's top three customers bought about 44% of sales in 2024 and licensors such as Disney and NBCUniversal gain leverage through royalties. Suppliers are numerous, so trade policy rather than suppliers sets cost shocks.

Revenue growth comes from franchise strength, pricing, new products, adult buyers and share gains. Hasbro's Wizards of the Coast and digital gaming revenue rose 31% in Q3. Circana shows toy dollar sales up 20% on units up 18% and average selling price up 2%.

Operating margins reflect gross margin, tariffs, royalties, marketing and operating leverage. Hasbro's adjusted operating margin rose to 33.9% from 25.6%, and Brunswick's rose to 10.1% from 7.8%. Damodaran's pre-tax operating margin for the broader recreation group was 9.69% against 12.82% for all US firms in January 2026.

Key cost variables are materials, freight, tariffs and wages. Mattel received $88M of tariff refunds in Q3 and its adjusted gross margin rose to 55.0% from 50.2%. YETI said lower net tariff costs added 200 bps to gross margin. Polaris guides about $1.09 of 2026 adjusted EPS from tariff refunds.

Rates matter most for financed big-ticket goods. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 with two members preferring a hike. NMMA said inflation, high interest rates and slowing housing starts were weighing on discretionary spending, with consumer confidence at 92.8 in April. Damodaran's debt to EBITDA for the broader group is 4.78.

Sensitive to household spending and prices. The Fed called activity strong and inflation elevated. In October 2026 BLS toy prices rose 1.8% and recreation commodities 0.7% from September; year-on-year figures were not published for those series because of missing October 2025 data. Oil and commodity inputs feed into freight and material costs.

Mixed. Big-ticket goods are cyclical: Brunswick's wholesale growth has run beside weak retail unit sales. Toys are seasonal and franchise-driven, with a long-term low-growth base that hits get lifted by cycles. Subscription lines such as Peloton's add recurring revenue but have seen subscriber declines.

Growth is uneven. Damodaran's expected five-year EPS growth for the broader recreation group is 9.95% against 13.95% for all US firms. Recent quarterly revenue ranges from Hasbro's +15% and Polaris's +11% to Acushnet's -1.3% and Callaway's -5.6%.

Margins vary widely. Damodaran puts the broader recreation group at a 39.79% gross margin and 9.69% unadjusted pre-tax operating margin, against 37.76% and 12.82% for the market (January 2026). StockAnalysis operating margins range from 27.52% at Hasbro to 3.06% at Polaris on trailing data.

Returns are decent at the leaders. Damodaran shows after-tax ROIC of 14.26% for the broader recreation group against 10.08% for the market, though its page carries conflicting dates. StockAnalysis ROIC was 34.58% at Hasbro, 18.69% at YETI, 14.35% at Acushnet, 9.62% at Polaris, 9.51% at Mattel and 8.08% at Brunswick.

Leverage is moderate to high. Damodaran's market debt to capital is 38.98% for the broader group against 25.93% for the market, with interest coverage of 2.26 versus 6.90.
