Valuation on 23 Nov 2026: Mohawk forward P/E 15.9x and EV/EBITDA 6.5x, La-Z-Boy 12.8x and 8.1x, Somnigroup 18.2x and 15.3x. Source figures are StockAnalysis.com aggregates, not company data.

Regulation: Section 232 duties of 25% on upholstered furniture, kitchen cabinets and vanities carry a deferred increase, and Section 301 tariffs of 10% to 12.5% replaced Section 122 tariffs on 24 Jul 2026, per Ethan Allen. Further changes are possible.

Technology and AI: the effect is mostly indirect, through online marketing, personalization, robotics in plants and ERP systems. Somnigroup's Dreams unit fell 34.7% after an ERP rollout disrupted operations, which shows execution risk in digital change.

Demographics: household formation and the age of first-time buyers drive demand. We did not find a sourced figure, so this is judgment: delayed first purchases and aging owners mean fewer new-home furnishing cycles, while replacement demand continues.

Consumer behavior has moved toward online and showroom-light buying, and toward value. Purple's wholesale revenue fell from $51.5M to $35.6M while its showrooms rose to 57. La-Z-Boy's Joybird online brand fell 29%. October shopping was significantly softer at La-Z-Boy.

New competitors and models include online brands and private-label imports. Sleep Number's assets went to a Canadian retailer for $529.5M of cash after Chapter 11, showing how weaker brands get absorbed. Purple is exploring strategic alternatives.

Supply chain and geopolitics: furniture imports shifted from China (down 35.8% in 2025) to Vietnam and others, and the Somnigroup CEO cited the Ukraine and Middle East wars as risks. Any new tariff, freight or country-rule change reroutes sourcing.

Substitutes include used and rental furniture and lower-priced imports, but we did not find sourced data on them. Within the group, the biggest risk is leverage: Purple has $135.1M of current related-party debt and negative adjusted EBITDA for nine months.
Pent-up demand if mortgage rates fall: NAR's chief economist sees sizable pent-up demand with distressed sales at only 2% of transactions.
Consolidation synergies: Somnigroup targets $75M a year of run-rate synergies from Leggett & Platt and leverage was already down to 2.69x.
Cash-rich survivors can buy stores and gain share: La-Z-Boy has $247M of cash, no debt and retail written sales up 11%.
Product refresh cycles, such as Purple's planned 2027 mattress collections, and tariff refunds can help margins.

A prolonged housing freeze: October existing-home sales were the lowest since August 2010, and NAR's chief economist said buying is hard at the highest mortgage rates since 2000 bar one month in 2023.
Higher tariffs: the delayed Section 232 increase on furniture and cabinets could still come into force.
Weak balance sheets and failures: Sleep Number was sold in Chapter 11 and Purple faces a debt maturity.
Margin pressure from volume deleverage, as seen at Ethan Allen where adjusted operating margin fell to 2.2% from 7.2%.

Our read is that the next three to five years are set by housing turnover and by who survives consolidation. If mortgage rates ease from the current 7.28% and sales recover from a 16-year low, volume leverage should return quickly to firms with fixed costs already in place, such as Mohawk and the furniture makers. Bedding looks set to be led by one very large integrated player, while smaller brands face distress or sale. The tariff path adds uncertainty: the scheduled increase was only deferred. Strong balance sheets, as at La-Z-Boy and Ethan Allen, are an advantage in a long trough, but Ethan Allen's margin shows even debt-free firms suffer when volume falls.

The cycle is at the housing trough. Existing-home sales were 3.75 million annualized in October 2026, down 5.5% on the month, 8.8% on the year and the lowest since August 2010, according to NAR. Its chief economist tied this to mortgage rates at their highest since 2000 apart from one month in 2023, and the median price was $416,700, up 0.4%. Freddie Mac's 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.28% on 19 Nov 2026, up from 7.11% the week before and 6.26% a year earlier.

For home furnishings this matters more than almost any other macro variable. People buy beds, sofas and floors when they move or remodel. Mohawk described a weak demand environment with adjusted volume down about 4% in Q3 and guided to softer market conditions in Q4. La-Z-Boy saw significantly softer consumer shopping in October after strong early-quarter trends. Ethan Allen cited a soft housing market and lower design center traffic.

On trade policy, Section 301 tariffs of 10% to 12.5% took effect on 24 Jul 2026 in place of the earlier 10% Section 122 tariffs, per Ethan Allen's release, and the scheduled Section 232 rise on upholstered furniture was deferred by a year. We did not open a source on the dollar or inflation, so we make no claim there.

We did not find a reliable single estimate of the global addressable market for these companies. The best sized facts we opened are on trade: US household furniture and bedding imports were $29.6B in 2025, down 12.7% from $33.9B in 2024 and 28.5% below $41.4B in 2022. That tells us the market has been shrinking or shifting to domestic and other channels since the pandemic peak, though it is import data only.

Structural demand rests on household formation, home turnover and replacement. Most spending replaces worn items, which gives a base, and the housing freeze delays the discretionary layer on top. NAR's chief economist argues that, with steady job growth, a fall in rates could release sizable pent-up demand. Our read is that the delay compounds: each quarter of low turnover postpones purchases that will return together, which can make the recovery sharp but its timing unknowable.

Elasticity is high. Mohawk's price and mix added about 4% to Q3 sales while volume fell about 4%, so pricing is protecting revenue but not units. La-Z-Boy's retail written sales rose 11%, helped by acquired and new stores, while same-store written sales declined slightly. Growth in this group is currently coming from acquisitions and store openings rather than from underlying demand.

Rivalry is intense and fragmented outside bedding. Somnigroup is the clear consolidator after closing its all-stock Leggett & Platt deal on 26 Aug 2026 at about $2.3B including debt, giving former Leggett holders about 9% of the company. Its Q3 sales were $2,350.8M, with $372.6M from Leggett for the stub period.

Buyer power is high where large retailers or online platforms control access to shoppers; Purple's wholesale sales fell to $35.6M from $51.5M in Q3. Supplier power is moderate and being internalised, as Somnigroup's purchase of a key component supplier shows. The threat of new entrants is low at scale but high for niche or online brands, though failures are common: Sleep Number sold substantially all its assets for $529.5M of cash in Chapter 11, closing on 31 Jul 2026. Substitutes are weak for beds and floors but include used goods and cheaper imports.

Moats come from brands, owned retail and vertical integration. Tempur Sealy North America earned a 64.7% gross margin and 33.2% operating margin in Q3. Ethan Allen's 59.6% gross margin reflects its brand and in-house production, about 75% of custom furniture being made in North America. Market shares by company were not found in the sources we opened.

Politics and trade policy are the main outside forces. Section 232 duties on upholstered furniture, kitchen cabinets and vanities were set at 25%, with a proclamation signed 31 Dec 2025 delaying the scheduled increase by a year; the fact sheet gives 25% as the current rate and does not state the new effective date of the increase. Ethan Allen says Section 301 tariffs of 10% to 12.5% took effect on 24 Jul 2026.

Tariff policy has also produced one-off gains. La-Z-Boy's wholesale margin benefited from refunds and pricing actions net of tariff costs, and Somnigroup said tariff refunds helped North America's Q3 gross margin. That inflates the run rate, and we think investors should treat it as non-recurring.

Technology is mostly an execution risk here. Somnigroup's Dreams business fell 34.7% in Q3 after a new ERP system disrupted operations. Online sales are also a swing factor: Mattress Firm's sales fell 5.8% on softer online sales, and La-Z-Boy's Joybird online brand saw delivered sales fall 29% to $25M. Geopolitical wars were cited by Somnigroup's CEO as macro risks. Environmental and chemical rules affect foam and flooring but we did not open a source on them.

Margins differ widely by model. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 27 US furniture and home furnishings firms show a 30.3% gross margin, 9.75% EBITDA margin, 6.59% operating margin and 1.10% net margin. The after-tax ROIC for the group is 13.13% unadjusted, 10.59% after lease and R&D adjustment, and 17.82% normalized over ten years.

Company data bracket that. Mohawk's Q3 gross margin was 25.5% and adjusted operating margin 7.2% on net sales of $2,786.0M. La-Z-Boy's gross margin was about 44.6% and adjusted operating margin 5.0% versus 7.1% a year earlier. Ethan Allen's gross margin was 59.6% and adjusted operating margin 2.2%. Somnigroup's adjusted operating margin was 15.5% (16.2% a year earlier), and the Leggett business had a gross margin of 17.7% and an adjusted operating margin of 11.0%. Purple's gross margin was 43.4%, down 410 basis points, and adjusted EBITDA was a $0.5M loss.

Operating leverage is high: Ethan Allen's sales fell 11.8% and its operating margin from 6.8% to 1.3%. Cash conversion is strong at the large firms: Mohawk's nine-month free cash flow was $626.3M, up 78%, and Somnigroup's nine-month operating cash flow was $831.9M. Capex needs differ: Mohawk guides to about $445M for 2026 and La-Z-Boy spent $31M in the quarter.

Company outlooks are cautious. Mohawk guided Q4 adjusted EPS to $1.35 to $1.45 on low single-digit sales growth, softer market conditions than in Q3 and four fewer shipping days; its nine-month adjusted EPS was $8.27. La-Z-Boy guided Q3 FY2027 sales of $505M to $525M and an adjusted operating margin of 4.0% to 5.5%, against a Q2 margin of 5.0%.

Somnigroup revised its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $2.85 to $2.95, about 7% growth at the midpoint. Q3 adjusted EPS was $1.04, up 9.5%. Ethan Allen's adjusted operating margin fell to 2.2% from 7.2% in its first quarter. Purple kept 2026 revenue guidance at $420M to $440M but cut adjusted EBITDA guidance to $15M to $20M.

We found no sector consensus figures for this group, so we do not quote any. Our read is that earnings quality is lower than headlines suggest. Tariff refunds, acquisition revenue and a one-off warranty effect all moved margins in the latest quarters. If housing stays flat, the likelier revisions are downward for retailers and furniture makers, while Mohawk and Somnigroup have cost and synergy levers that smaller firms lack.

Valuation is mixed. On 23 Nov 2026, per StockAnalysis.com, Mohawk traded on a forward P/E of 15.9x, an EV/EBITDA of 6.5x and a free cash flow yield of 10.6%, with a market value of $8.42B. La-Z-Boy was on 12.8x forward earnings and 8.1x EV/EBITDA with a 7.2% FCF yield and a 3.6% dividend yield, at a $1.17B market value. Somnigroup was on 18.2x forward earnings and 15.3x EV/EBITDA with a 5.0% FCF yield and $13.95B market value.

Against Damodaran's January 2026 group margins, the multiples imply a trough-earnings discount for the flooring and furniture names and a premium for Somnigroup, which has the highest margins and the integration story. We did not find long-run historical multiples for these stocks in the sources we opened, so we cannot say how the current levels sit against their own history.

Mohawk's FCF yield of 10.6% suggests the market is pricing a prolonged trough, and 17.1x trailing earnings against 15.9x forward implies modest recovery. La-Z-Boy's lower multiple partly reflects its fall in margin and a softer outlook. Somnigroup's multiple depends on delivering the $75M synergies and de-leveraging from 2.69x. The stock-page figures are third-party aggregates and should be checked against filings.

Prices show a split market. Over 52 weeks to 23 Nov 2026, Mohawk was up 31.70%, La-Z-Boy down 20.23% and Somnigroup down 30.66%. Mohawk's gain with weak volume suggests investors are looking through the trough at free cash flow and buybacks: it held $816.8M of cash against $1,782.7M of debt at quarter end. La-Z-Boy returned $32M to shareholders in the quarter and raised its dividend 12% to $0.27.

Short interest in Somnigroup was 9.21% of float on the latest StockAnalysis.com data, a notable level for a company of its size, and its price rose 5.08% on 23 Nov 2026 to $60.58. Short interest for the others was not found in the pages we opened.

We did not find ETF flow or institutional ownership data for this sub-industry, so we make no claim there. Ethan Allen's governance is also in motion, with stockholders electing five directors at the 4 Nov 2026 annual meeting after $1.3M of proxy contest fees in the quarter. Sleep Number's stock is expected to be cancelled with no value to holders, and Purple is in a strategic review. Breadth is thus poor, with winners and failures in the same group.

Leisure facilities is splitting into winners and weather- or traffic-exposed operators. Gyms are strong: Americans' fitness membership hit a record 81 million, Life Time's revenue rose 14.2% and Planet Fitness raised guidance. Parks and ski are weaker: Vail's skier visits fell 13.4% and pass units are down about 12%, Six Flags took a $687.7M impairment, and United Parks' attendance fell 4.7%. Studio franchisor Xponential is shrinking. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% with two votes to hike. Damodaran's US recreation group trades at 10.4x EBITDA against 19.7x for the market.

These companies sell access to places where people exercise, play or ride: gyms and fitness studios, theme and water parks, ski resorts and golf venues. Customers are households and, for some parks and clubs, corporate and group buyers. Revenue comes from memberships and passes, single-day tickets, in-venue spending on food, lessons, rentals and merchandise, and, for franchisors, royalties. GICS also places franchised studio brands here. Equipment makers such as golf clubs sit in Leisure Products, hotels and casinos in other Hotels, Resorts & Cruise Lines and Casinos & Gaming, and live-event promoters in Entertainment.

Fitness clubs: Large gyms charging monthly dues. Operators own the clubs or franchise them. Low-priced models want many members; premium models sell more services per member. e.g. Planet Fitness (franchised, low price), Life Time (owned, premium athletic country clubs)

Boutique fitness studios: Small, class-based studios for one discipline such as Pilates or stretching, usually franchised, that sell memberships and class packs. e.g. Xponential Fitness brands including Club Pilates, StretchLab and Pure Barre

Ski resorts: Mountain resorts selling season passes and lift tickets, plus lodging, ski school, rentals and food. Snow and weather decide how many people come. e.g. Vail Resorts Epic Pass, other regional operators

Theme and amusement parks: Parks selling day tickets and season passes, with extra spending on food, games and merchandise. Rides and shows are large fixed investments. e.g. Six Flags (including the former Cedar Fair parks), United Parks (SeaWorld, Busch Gardens)

Water parks and resort-style attractions: Seasonal water-based parks and attractions, sometimes with hotels, that depend on summer weather and school calendars. e.g. Six Flags water parks, United Parks' Aquatica and Discovery Cove

Golf and entertainment venues: Courses, driving ranges and venues combining sport with food and drink, earning green fees, memberships and hospitality revenue. e.g. Topgolf (now majority owned by Leonard Green funds), municipal and private golf clubs
Weather and snowfall: Parks and ski resorts earn most of their profit in a few months. A poor snow year or a wet summer cuts visits against mostly fixed costs, so profit moves by more than revenue.

Consumer spending and confidence: Discretionary leisure falls when households feel squeezed. Low-priced gyms and annual passes are more resilient than day tickets, travel-linked visits and premium add-ons.
Pricing and pass mix: Raising prices lifts revenue per visit but can lose casual visitors. A larger share of passes brings cash early and steadies revenue at the cost of a lower yield per visit.
Membership growth and churn: Gym revenue builds from members joining minus members leaving. Promotions, new locations and a strong January lift joins, while cancellations offset them.
Capital spending and new locations: New rides, lifts, clubs and studios attract visitors or members but cost cash up front. Returns depend on how quickly new capacity fills.

Leverage and interest rates: Many operators carry debt against steady fees and passes. Higher rates raise interest cost, and a profit drop pushes leverage up and limits buybacks, dividends and growth spending.

Season pass: A prepaid ticket for unlimited or many visits in a season. It brings cash in early, smooths revenue and lowers the average price per visit, but it makes demand less sensitive to weather once bought.
Deferred revenue: Cash collected for passes and memberships before the service is delivered. It sits on the balance sheet as a liability and turns into revenue over the season.

Attendance and per capita spending: Park revenue is visitors multiplied by what each one spends in the gate and inside the park. Splitting growth into the two shows whether volume or pricing is carrying results.
Skier visit: One person on a mountain for any part of a day. Resorts also report effective ticket price, the lift revenue earned per visit.
Same club sales: Revenue growth from clubs open for at least a year, which strips out the effect of new openings. Planet Fitness and other franchisors use it as their main health measure.

System-wide sales: Sales of all franchised and company-owned locations. A franchisor books only royalties and fees on franchised ones, so system-wide sales show the size of the brand, not its revenue.
Franchise royalty: A percentage of franchisee sales paid to the brand owner, typically with no matching operating cost, which makes franchisor margins high and stable.
Average unit volume (AUV): Average annual sales per location. It shows whether new and existing units are earning enough to justify opening more.
Attrition (churn): The share of members who cancel in a period. Membership models need joins to exceed cancellations, so small shifts in churn change growth.

Adjusted EBITDA: Operating profit before depreciation, amortization and items management excludes. It is the main profit measure and the base for debt ratios, but it ignores heavy ride and club capital spending.
Net debt leverage: Debt less cash divided by adjusted EBITDA. Fixed-cost operators with seasonal swings are judged on this ratio because falling EBITDA raises it quickly.
Maintenance versus growth capex: Maintenance spending keeps rides, lifts and clubs safe and fresh; growth spending adds new attractions or locations. The split shows how much cash flow is truly free.
Refranchising: Selling company-owned locations to franchisees. It brings cash and cuts capital needs but swaps full club profit for a royalty.
Vail's 2026/27 pass book: units were down about 12% and dollars down about 6% through 18 Sep 2026, and management says the weakness is concentrated in lower-frequency destination passes.

Six Flags' turnaround: October attendance was softer than planned after weather and the Six Flags Over Georgia incident, and Q4 same-park adjusted EBITDA is guided to $140M to $150M against $167M a year earlier.
Planet Fitness' review of its domestic corporate-owned clubs, which could move some clubs to franchisees and change its mix of royalty and club revenue.
Xponential's strategic review, with net new studios cut to 124 to 130, same store sales down 7.5% and about $521M of long-term debt.
Rates and consumer cost pressure: the Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% with two dissents in favour of a hike, and the 12-month CPI rate was 3.7% in September.
Vail Resorts, Planet Fitness, Life Time, Six Flags Entertainment, United Parks & Resorts, Xponential Fitness

Revenue streams differ by model. Planet Fitness earns franchise royalties of about 6.7% on average plus equipment sales and corporate-club dues. Life Time earns dues and in-center spending. Parks sell tickets, passes and in-park spending, and Vail sells passes, lift tickets and lodging, ski school and retail.

Customers are mainly households. Gym members pay monthly dues, which at Planet Fitness start at $15 for the Classic card and $24.99 for Black Card. Pass holders were about 61% of Six Flags' same-park Q3 attendance, and season passes were 49% of US skier visits.

Costs are mostly fixed: labor, rent or land, utilities, maintenance, insurance and marketing. Because they barely move with volume, a visit shortfall hits profit hard. Vail, for example, cut visits 13.4% and reported EBITDA fell 11.7%.

Pricing power rests on brand, location and scarcity. Vail's effective ticket price rose 11.5% in FY2026 even as visits fell, and Life Time's average revenue per membership rose 12.0%. Low-price gyms rely on value and convenience, and Planet Fitness' $15 entry price is itself the product.

Major assets are land, buildings, rides, lifts and equipment. Liabilities include debt and, for pass sellers, deferred revenue; Six Flags had $331.3M of deferred revenue and $4.91B of total debt at 27 Sep 2026. United Parks carried $2,276.5M of debt against $26.3M of cash at 30 Sep 2026.

Owners are capital-intensive and franchisors asset-light. Life Time plans $885M to $910M of growth capital in 2026 against guided revenue of $3.38B to $3.39B. Planet Fitness franchisees fund most clubs, with 2,604 of 2,896 clubs franchised at the end of 2025.

No single sub-industry market-size figure was available from sources we opened. Demand indicators are sizeable: 81 million Americans were fitness facility members in 2025, up 5.2%, and the US ski industry recorded 52.6 million visits in 2025-26.

Main segments are fitness clubs and studios, theme and water parks, ski resorts and golf. In 2025 fitness had about 7 billion visits, US golf rounds topped 500 million, and parks and ski are concentrated around destination and regional markets.

In the value chain, suppliers are ride and fitness-equipment makers, construction firms, utilities and land owners; customers are households. Franchisors such as Planet Fitness require franchisees to buy equipment from it or approved vendors and replace it every five to nine years.

The industry has moved toward recurring revenue and consolidation. Passes and memberships now drive demand, with 49% of ski visits from pass holders, and Six Flags was formed by a 2024 combination with Cedar Fair and has since sold seven parks to EPR Properties and closed one.

Geography is concentrated in North America for the main bellwethers. Vail runs 37 North American ski areas plus Australian resorts, Six Flags operates in the US, Canada and Mexico, and 20.1M of the US's 52.6M ski visits were in the Rocky Mountain region.

There are many competitors across segments, but each local market has few. Public bellwethers include Vail, Planet Fitness, Life Time, Six Flags, United Parks and Xponential, with a long tail of private, municipal and independent operators.

Leaders by segment: Vail in ski by pass reach, Planet Fitness by members (21.5M), Life Time in premium clubs (196 centers), Six Flags in regional parks with 20 amusement parks and 14 water parks, and United Parks in marine parks (13 parks). We did not find audited market-share figures.

Structure is fragmented overall and concentrated locally. A resort or park often has no close substitute within driving distance, while gyms face many nearby alternatives from low-cost chains, boutiques, home equipment and digital apps.

Barriers to entry are high for parks and resorts: land, permits, ride capacity and brand are costly to replicate. They are lower for gyms and studios, where a lease and equipment are enough, which is why the filings of Planet Fitness flag intense competition.

Economies of scale matter in purchasing, marketing and pass networks. Vail's multi-resort Epic Pass and its efficiency program, which saved $45M in FY2026, rely on scale. Planet Fitness uses its 86 franchisee groups and 2,962 clubs to spread brand and technology costs.

Products are differentiated by location, brand and experience, but entry-level gyms and day tickets are close to commodity and compete on price. Vail said it is leaning into being more competitive on price for lift products.

Customers hold bargaining power in gyms and day tickets, because cancelling is easy and substitutes exist, and weaker in destinations with limited supply. Suppliers have moderate power: Planet Fitness flags dependence on a limited number of equipment suppliers.

Revenue growth comes from visits or members, price and in-venue spending, plus new locations. Planet Fitness grew revenue 9.0% on a 1.5% same club sales gain plus openings, while Life Time's came from higher dues and new centers.

Operating margins depend on fixed-cost coverage, so volume swings move them. Vail's Resort Reported EBITDA margin was 26.3% in FY2026, and Six Flags' same-park adjusted EBITDA rose 1.1% on 1.4% same-park revenue growth.

Key cost variables are labor, utilities, maintenance and insurance, property taxes and marketing. Vail expected about 4% cost inflation in FY2027, a $20M rebound in incentive pay and $10M more marketing.

Interest rates matter through debt and discretionary budgets. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 with two votes for a hike, and Six Flags and Vail carry leverage of about 6.0x (our calculation) and 3.9x.

Inflation, jobs and GDP shape discretionary leisure. The 12-month CPI rate was 3.7% in September 2026. Consumers trade down or delay trips when squeezed, while low-priced gyms tend to hold up better; Planet Fitness' same club sales rose 1.5%.
The group is cyclical with secular growth pockets. Weather and consumer spending make parks and ski cyclical, while fitness has structural growth, with members up 5.2% and visits above the 2019 peak.
Growth is uneven. Life Time revenue rose 14.2% in Q3 and Planet Fitness 9.0%, while United Parks fell 1.1% and Vail's FY2026 revenue fell about 4.3%. Xponential revenue fell 21%.

Margins: Damodaran's January 2026 US Recreation group (49 firms) had an after-tax operating margin of 7.14% against 11.88% for the total market. Company margins vary: Vail's Resort EBITDA margin was 26.3% and Life Time's Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $256.3M on $893.5M of revenue.

Returns on capital are modest. Damodaran's Recreation after-tax return on capital was 8.87% against 9.76% for the market in January 2026, and the group's cost of capital was 6.76% with beta 1.02. Recreation is a broader group than GICS leisure facilities.

Leverage varies sharply. Life Time's net debt was 1.3x adjusted EBITDA, Vail's 3.9x, United Parks' about 3.9x on our calculation, Six Flags' about 6.0x on our calculation, and Xponential had $521.1M of debt against $27.2M of cash.

Free cash flow is positive but strained at the weaker names. United Parks' nine-month free cash flow was $122.1M, down 9.2%; Six Flags' nine-month operating cash flow rose 36.5% to $498.5M while capex fell; Vail said free cash flow covers its capital plan and dividend even at the low guidance end.

Capital needs are large for owners. Vail plans about $215M to $220M of core calendar 2026 capital, Six Flags guided $350M to $375M of 2026 capex, and Life Time $885M to $910M of growth capital. Franchisors need little.

Valuation: Damodaran's Recreation group traded at 10.39x EV/EBITDA for positive-EBITDA firms against 19.73x for the market in January 2026. FactSet's S&P 500 forward P/E was 18.3 and Consumer Discretionary's, the highest sector, was 25.1 on 13 Nov 2026; we did not find a sub-industry forward P/E.

Regulation is a modest risk but real: safety oversight of rides after incidents, franchise rules, pricing and auto-renewal rules for memberships, and data privacy. Planet Fitness lists brand damage, litigation and privacy compliance as risks, and Six Flags' October softness was linked to an incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.

Technology and AI affect mostly marketing, pricing and guest apps rather than the core experience. Vail is pushing a digital guest journey through the My Epic app, and Planet Fitness flags digital fitness and home equipment as competition. Substitution of the physical visit is limited.

Demographics help fitness: members aged 65 and over grew 8.6% and Gen Z has 35.5% penetration. An older and wealthier base also supports premium clubs and ski, while fewer young skiers would be a long-term risk; we found no sourced figure for that.

Consumer behavior is shifting toward passes and experiences. Daily and multi-day ticket users fell from 51% of ski visits in 2015-16 to 32% in 2024-25, and Vail is seeing buyers delay pass purchases after a poor season.
New competitors and models matter in fitness: low-cost chains, boutique studios and digital apps pressure incumbents. Xponential's same store sales decline of 7.5% suggests boutique saturation.

Geopolitical and supply risks are secondary: lower international visitation to the US, which Vail expects to persist, and equipment and ride supply. Climate is the larger structural risk, with 2025-26 snowfall 33% below the 10-year average.

Substitutes include home gyms, streaming workouts, other travel and entertainment, and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which Planet Fitness lists as a possible effect on gym demand. Parks and ski compete with cruises, streaming and short trips for the same leisure budget.
Fitness penetration keeps rising, with 81 million US members, record visits and 65-plus members up 8.6%.
Recurring pass and membership models can be expanded: United Parks' 2027 pass sales were up more than 15% and Six Flags' active pass base grew 7.1%.
Refranchising and asset sales can fund growth and buybacks: Planet Fitness announced a $500M repurchase authorization and a review of corporate clubs.
Premium operators can keep adding centers: Life Time plans 14 new centers in 2026.
A repeat of a weak snow year would again cut skier visits, which fell to 52.6M from 61.6M in 2025-26.
Higher rates and sticky inflation could squeeze households and keep borrowing costs high for levered operators.
Leveraged park and studio operators have little room for error, with Six Flags' leverage near 6.0x on our calculation and Xponential in a strategic review.
Weight-loss drugs and digital fitness could slow gym demand.

Our read is that the next three to five years favor recurring-revenue, asset-light and premium fitness models over weather-exposed, heavily indebted parks. Fitness has structural support from record membership and visits, and Life Time's growth and low leverage show strong execution. Parks and ski have more repair work: Six Flags is restructuring, United Parks is leaning on 2027 passes, and Vail has to rebuild a pass base that fell about 12%. Weather is the swing factor, and rates plus the consumer decide how fast recovery comes. Franchisors can grow with little capital but depend on franchisee returns, as Xponential's cuts show.

Leisure facilities sit at the discretionary end of consumer spending, so the cycle reaches them through household budgets, borrowing costs and weather. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 in a 10-2 vote, with Governor Cook and President Hammack preferring a quarter-point increase, and it described inflation as elevated. The all-items CPI rose 3.7% in the 12 months to September 2026, and rose 0.4% in October with core up 0.3%.

For the sub-industry the pattern is a squeezed consumer rather than a recession. Gyms are holding up: Planet Fitness raised its 2026 same club sales outlook to about 1.5% to 2% and Life Time lifted guidance. Trip-based businesses are weaker, and Vail sees a possible slowdown in high-end travel and lower international visitation. Levered operators are exposed to rates: Vail's net debt is 3.9x EBITDA and Six Flags' is about 6.0x by our calculation. We did not find a sourced figure for currency effects.

Demand has a clear structural base in fitness. The Health & Fitness Association counted 81 million US members in 2025, up 5.2%, equal to 26.1% of Americans aged six and over, with about 7 billion visits, above the 2019 peak. Gen Z had the highest penetration at 35.5%, and members aged 65 and over grew 8.6%. Planet Fitness ended Q3 with about 21.5 million members, up roughly 4%, while Life Time's memberships rose 2.2% and revenue per membership rose 12.0%.

Outdoor and park demand is more cyclical. US skier visits fell to 52.6M in 2025-26 from 61.6M as snowfall averaged 112 inches against 169 for the 10-year average. Golf is steadier: rounds rose just over 1% in 2025 to more than 500 million, though facility count fell about 3% over 2020 to 2025. Parks are mixed, with Six Flags' same-park attendance down 0.2% in Q3 and United Parks' down 4.7%. We did not find a sourced total addressable market for the sub-industry.

Using Porter's five forces, rivalry is high in gyms, where Planet Fitness, Life Time, boutique brands, local clubs and home fitness compete on price and experience. Threat of new entrants is high for gyms and studios but low for parks and resorts, where land, permits and capacity are hard to replicate. Threat of substitutes is moderate and includes home workouts, GLP-1 drugs and other leisure spending. Buyer power is high in day tickets and memberships; supplier power is moderate, with Planet Fitness flagging dependence on a limited number of equipment suppliers.

Concentration is local. Vail operates 37 North American ski areas, Six Flags 20 amusement parks and 14 water parks, United Parks 13 parks and Life Time 196 centers. Planet Fitness had 2,962 clubs at 30 Sep 2026, with 2,604 of 2,896 franchised at the end of 2025. Moats come from destination scarcity, brand and pass networks; Vail says it outperforms the industry on comparable unlimited passes. Pricing power is stronger at premium sites than in low-price gyms.

Regulation is a background factor. Safety rules apply to rides and lifts, and incidents have commercial effects: Six Flags said its October attendance was softer than planned after weather and the Six Flags Over Georgia incident and ride closures. Franchise relationships, consumer-protection rules on memberships and data privacy are listed risks for Planet Fitness. We did not find sourced figures on new legislation.

Technology is changing the guest relationship more than the product. Vail is pushing a digital journey through the My Epic app, in-app commerce and gear rental; Planet Fitness cites digital fitness and home equipment as competition. Climate and weather are the sharper environmental risk, with 2025-26 US snowfall 33% below the 10-year average and Rocky Mountain visits down to 20.1M from 26.5M. Political factors include trade and visitor flows: Vail expects international visits to the US to stay low. Corporate actions also reshape the field: Topgolf was majority sold to Leonard Green funds at a valuation of about $1.1B.

Economics are driven by fixed costs and capital intensity. Damodaran's January 2026 US Recreation group (49 firms) earned an after-tax operating margin of 7.14% and an after-tax return on capital of 8.87%, against 11.88% and 9.76% for the whole market. The same group's cost of capital was 6.76%. Recreation is a broader group than GICS leisure facilities, so we use it only as a guide.

Operating leverage is visible in the bellwethers. Vail's visits fell 13.4% and Resort Reported EBITDA fell 11.7% to $745.7M, a 26.3% margin. Life Time's Q3 revenue rose 14.2% and adjusted EBITDA rose 16.5% to $256.3M. Six Flags' Q3 same-park revenue rose 1.4% and adjusted EBITDA 1.1%, while United Parks' revenue fell 1.1% and adjusted EBITDA fell 5.1%. Franchisors earn high margins on royalties: Planet Fitness corporate clubs had a 37.8% segment margin and the royalty is about 7%. Free cash flow is positive but heavily committed to capex and debt service.

Reported results diverge. Life Time raised 2026 revenue guidance to $3.38B to $3.39B and adjusted EBITDA to $958M to $962M. Planet Fitness raised revenue growth to about 8% and adjusted EBITDA growth to about 6.5%. Vail guided FY2027 Resort Reported EBITDA to $805M to $865M against $745.7M in FY2026. Six Flags guided Q4 same-park adjusted EBITDA of $140M to $150M against $167M a year earlier.

United Parks gave no formal guidance but said it sees a clear path to significantly higher attendance, revenue, adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow in 2027. Xponential kept revenue guidance at $250M to $260M and narrowed adjusted EBITDA to $91M to $94M. FactSet's S&P 500 forecasts, 28.3% earnings growth for Q4 2026 and 16.2% for CY2027, are index-wide; we did not find sub-industry consensus estimates. Our view is that the FY2027 Vail range is a recovery call that depends on snow and pass conversion, with the pass book still down.

No sub-industry multiple was available from sources we opened, so we use Damodaran's January 2026 US Recreation group (49 firms): 10.39x EV/EBITDA for firms with positive EBITDA, against 19.73x for the total market, and 23.96x EV/EBIT against 29.12x. The low EBITDA multiple reflects capital intensity and debt; the EV/EBIT gap is narrow, which shows how much depreciation these businesses carry.

At the market level, FactSet showed an S&P 500 forward P/E of 18.3 on 13 Nov 2026 against 19.8 for five years and 19.1 for ten, with Consumer Discretionary the highest sector at 25.1. That sector includes large non-leisure names, so it is not a read on the group. Company-level anchors are scarce: we did not open a market-data source for current company multiples. Our read is that fitness franchisors and premium clubs carry growth premiums, while parks and ski are priced for recovery that 2027 pass sales must support.

We did not find sourced ETF flow, short interest or relative-strength data for this sub-industry, so we do not quote any. What the filings show is where management is putting capital. Planet Fitness bought back about 1.0M shares for $50.0M in Q3, announced a new authorization of up to $500M and bought Be-Fit in Portugal for about $114.8M. Vail pays a $2.22 quarterly dividend and expects leverage to fall to about 3.5x by the end of FY2027.

Portfolio actions signal stress at the weaker names. Topgolf Callaway sold 60% of Topgolf to Leonard Green funds and used proceeds to repay $1B of debt, leaving Callaway Golf as a separate company. Xponential's board is exploring alternatives including a sale or merger. Six Flags cut 2026 capex guidance to $350M to $375M and recorded a $687.7M impairment. Market breadth is therefore split between gyms with rising guidance and parks and ski still working through a weak season.

Education Services is a small, idiosyncratic group whose results depend on enrollment, regulation and, for online learners, product engagement rather than the economic cycle. Operating margins in Damodaran's education industry sit slightly above the market and forward P/E is far below it. Third-quarter reports were mixed: Grand Canyon Education grew service revenue 2.4% and Duolingo grew bookings 12%, while Strategic Education booked a $134.1M impairment on Australia. Federal aid and accountability rules are the main swing factor for U.S. schools.

Education Services companies sell learning for a fee: for-profit universities and career schools, online degree providers, tutoring and test-prep, and consumer learning apps. Customers are students, employers and, indirectly, governments that pay through grants and loans. Revenue is mostly tuition or subscriptions, so enrollment and retention matter most. Not-for-profit universities and public schools sit outside the investable universe, and child care or corporate training providers can sit in neighbouring consumer services groups instead.

Online and hybrid degrees: Bachelor's and graduate programs delivered mostly online, sometimes run under contract for another university. e.g. Grand Canyon Education and Grand Canyon University, Strategic Education's Capella and Strayer, Adtalem's nursing and medical schools
Career and vocational schools: Short programs that train for a specific trade or license, such as healthcare, cosmetology or technology. e.g. Universal Technical Institute, Lincoln Tech, Adtalem

University services (OPM): Marketing, enrollment, technology and support services sold to a university in return for a share of tuition. e.g. Grand Canyon Education's service agreement with Grand Canyon University
Consumer learning apps: Subscription or ad-supported apps that teach languages and other skills to individuals on their phones. e.g. Duolingo, Coursera consumer plans
Tutoring and test prep: Paid instruction for school-age students and exam candidates, in person or online. e.g. Stride's K-12 programs, Chegg, regional tutoring chains

Employer and workforce learning: Courses and credentials bought or subsidised by employers to upskill staff. e.g. Strategic Education's employer-affiliated enrollments and Sophia Learning, Coursera for Business

Enrollment and starts: New student starts and continuing students set tuition revenue. Employer partnerships, healthcare demand and marketing spend move these numbers a quarter or more before revenue follows.
Federal aid and accountability rules: Eligibility for loans and grants, loan caps and earnings tests decide which programs students can afford and which schools can stay open.
Contract terms with partner universities: A service provider's revenue depends on a negotiated share and the list of billable services. A change in either resets margins overnight.
Marketing efficiency: Online schools and apps spend heavily to attract students or users. If the cost of a lead rises faster than lifetime value, margin falls even when revenue grows.
Labour-market outcomes: Weak hiring can send workers back to school, but graduates' earnings feed the accountability tests that govern funding, so a soft job market helps and then hurts.
Technology and AI: Cheaper content creation and tutoring tools can raise engagement and cut costs, but they also lower barriers for rivals and may substitute for paid courses.
Enrollment: The number of students enrolled at a point in time. It is the base on which tuition revenue is built, so changes in enrollment drive revenue more than price does.
Title IV: The U.S. federal student aid programs, including Pell Grants and federal loans. Schools that lose Title IV eligibility lose most of their paying students.
Earnings premium test: A federal measure comparing graduates' earnings with those of a baseline group. Programs that fail repeatedly can lose access to federal aid.
OPM: Online program manager: a company that runs a university's online programs and takes a share of tuition.
Revenue share: The percentage of a student's tuition a service provider keeps under contract. Changes to it move margin directly.
Persistence / retention: The share of students who keep studying from one term to the next. High retention lowers the cost of replacing students.
Bookings: Cash value of subscriptions sold in a period. Revenue is recognised over the subscription life, so bookings lead revenue.
DAU / MAU: Daily and monthly active users of an app. A rising DAU-to-MAU ratio signals habit and tends to precede higher conversion to paid plans.
Paid conversion: The share of free users who become paying subscribers. Small shifts matter because most users pay nothing.
Cost to acquire a student: Marketing and admissions spending divided by new starts. It is a main driver of margin in online education.
Impairment: A non-cash write-down when an acquired business is worth less than its book value. It signals the buyer's growth expectations have fallen.
International student visas: Government approvals that let overseas students study abroad. Caps or tighter rules cut enrollment at schools that depend on them.
The Education Department's earnings-premium accountability rule starts on 1 July 2027 and can cut off aid, including Pell Grants, to programs that fail two of three years.

Grand Canyon Education's first full quarter under the amended services agreement narrowed billable revenue to tuition and academic fees, so margins and ground enrollment (-4.1%) are the numbers to track.
Strategic Education said persistent immigration constraints forced a reassessment of Australia/New Zealand growth, so further impairments or restructuring there are a risk.
Duolingo's paid-subscriber growth (+14%) is lagging user growth (+29%), and the company says a bottom in subscriber growth is still a couple of quarters away.
The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% with two members preferring a rise, which matters for student-loan costs and for how the market discounts long-dated education earnings.
Grand Canyon Education, Duolingo, Strategic Education, Adtalem Global Education, Coursera, Stride, Laureate Education

Revenue comes mainly from tuition and fees paid by students, often funded by federal loans and grants, plus service fees from universities (Grand Canyon Education earned $840.2M of service revenue in the first nine months of 2026) and consumer subscriptions (Duolingo's Q3 bookings were $316.1M).

Customers are students and families, employers who sponsor employees (34.7% of Strategic Education's U.S. higher-education enrollment is employer-affiliated), universities that outsource services, and individual app users.

Principal costs are instruction and academic support, student recruitment and advertising, and for service providers, technology and counselling staff. Duolingo reports a 72.9% gross margin, and Grand Canyon Education an adjusted operating margin of 20.5% in Q3, so recruitment and general costs are the large items below gross profit.

Pricing power rests on accreditation, brand and outcomes. Online degrees compete against low-priced public universities, so providers lean on convenience, employer relationships and healthcare programs. Federal loan limits cap what many students can pay, which limits price rises in practice.

The main assets are students under contract (deferred tuition), real estate for campus-based schools, goodwill from acquisitions and, for apps, content and user bases. Strategic Education's $134.1M Australia impairment shows acquired goodwill is the asset most exposed to bad news.

Most of the group is asset-light. Grand Canyon Education spent $29.6M on capex in nine months against $840.2M of revenue, and Damodaran puts the industry's net capex at 0.65% of sales. Campus-based schools and universities with their own buildings are more capital-intensive.

No single authoritative market-size figure for the investable education-services group was available to us. We can say it is small relative to the sector: the listed bellwethers have revenues from roughly $1.2B (Duolingo's 2026 guidance) to a few billion dollars. Growth varies widely: Duolingo guides to 12% bookings growth, Strategic Education expects flat 2027 revenue.

Main segments are online and hybrid degrees, career and vocational schools, university services, employer-linked credentials and consumer apps. Strategic Education alone spans U.S. higher education, Australia/New Zealand and an education-technology unit that grew 11.9% in Q3 2026.

In the value chain, suppliers are faculty, content and technology vendors; customers are students and employers; and governments sit in the middle as payers, regulators and visa gatekeepers. Student aid decisions therefore feed straight into demand for the whole group.

The industry has shifted from physical campuses to online delivery, from stand-alone schools to outsourced service contracts, and recently towards short, skills-based and employer-paid credentials and app-based learning. Duolingo's daily users grew 29% year on year in Q3 2026.

Sales are concentrated in the United States, where federal aid underpins most spending, with significant exposure to Australia and New Zealand for Strategic Education (17,101 students) and an international student market sensitive to visa policy.

There are many competitors, but few at scale. The listed group is only a handful of companies, while thousands of public, private non-profit and other for-profit institutions compete for the same students, so the listed names are small players in a very large market.

Market leaders by their own reporting include Grand Canyon University (139,170 enrollments) through its service partner, Strategic Education (about 84,725 U.S. students) and, for apps, Duolingo (13.1M paying subscribers). We found no sourced market-share data across the whole group.

The industry is fragmented overall, with concentration in niches: Grand Canyon is a large online player and Duolingo dominates consumer language apps, but nothing like an oligopoly exists in degrees or tutoring.

Barriers to entry are mostly regulatory and reputational: accreditation, access to federal aid and, increasingly, passing earnings tests. These barriers protect incumbents from small start-ups but also allow regulators to remove incumbents.

Economies of scale appear in marketing, technology and shared administrative services. Grand Canyon Education reports a 24.4% year-to-date operating margin on service revenue, which suggests scale in outsourced services; Duolingo's adjusted EBITDA margin was 25.5% in Q3.

Programs are partly commoditised (many online degrees look alike) and partly differentiated through brand, employer ties and programs such as nursing, which grew 9% in total enrollment at Strategic Education. Duolingo is differentiated by its product experience.

Students have the stronger bargaining position in a market with many alternatives, and employers and governments increasingly set terms. Suppliers such as faculty or technology vendors have little leverage. A partner university can reset terms, as the amended Grand Canyon agreement did.

Revenue growth comes from enrollment growth, price increases and retention for schools, and from users and conversion to paid for apps. Grand Canyon Education's partner enrollments grew 5.2% to 145,270, while Duolingo's paid subscribers grew 14%.

Operating margins depend on marketing efficiency, instructional cost per student and contract terms. In Damodaran's data, education has a pre-tax operating margin of 13.54%, a little above the total market's 12.75%.

Key costs are staff pay, student acquisition and technology. Wage inflation and advertising prices are the most important cost variables; regulatory compliance and legal costs can also be significant.

Interest-rate sensitivity is moderate: low debt (Damodaran's industry debt to EBITDA is 2.57x) limits direct impact, but rates affect student borrowing costs and valuation of long-dated growth. The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% in October 2026.

Weak labour markets and recessions can lift adult enrollment while tight markets and inflation can push people into jobs rather than school. Federal budget and loan policy matter more than GDP; we found no sourced estimate of GDP sensitivity.

The group is a blend: school enrollment has a countercyclical streak and is largely secular, while consumer apps depend on discretionary spending and engagement. Overall, regulation and execution decide results more than the business cycle.

Revenue growth is uneven: Grand Canyon Education's service revenue rose 5.3% in the first nine months, Duolingo guides to 18% revenue growth for 2026 and Strategic Education's consolidated revenue rose 1.6% in Q3.
Margins in Damodaran's January 2026 data: gross margin of 45.82%, net margin 8.79% and pre-tax lease-adjusted operating margin 13.54%, versus 37.76%, 9.74% and 12.75% for the total market.

ROE for the education industry is 15.90% in Damodaran's data, against 17.21% for the total market. Companies such as Grand Canyon Education earn far higher returns on a small capital base, so the industry average understates the best operators.

Debt is modest. Damodaran shows book debt to capital of 38.29% and debt to EBITDA of 2.57x versus 6.52x for the market. Grand Canyon Education reports no debt and Strategic Education had no revolver borrowings at 30 Sep 2026.
Free cash flow is generally strong relative to earnings. Duolingo's Q3 free cash flow was $75.3M, a 24.4% margin, and Strategic Education's nine-month free cash flow was $136.7M.
Capital expenditure needs are low: Damodaran's net capex is 0.65% of sales for education against 4.23% for the market, and Grand Canyon Education spent $29.6M on capex in nine months.
Valuation is lower than the market: forward P/E of 18.11x versus 27.66x, and EV/EBITDA of 9.26x for positive-EBITDA education firms versus 19.73x for the total market (Damodaran, January 2026).

Regulation is the largest risk. The Department of Education has finalised an earnings-premium test effective 1 July 2027 that can remove federal aid from failing programs, and a school whose aid mostly flows to low-earning programs could lose all Title IV eligibility.

Technology and AI may help (lower content and tutoring costs, better engagement) or hurt (free AI tutors substituting for paid courses and degrees). We found no sourced quantification, and treat this as a real but unmeasured risk.

Demographics matter: shrinking cohorts of 18-year-olds in some countries reduce the pool of traditional students, while adult learners and employer-sponsored students offer partial offsets. Ground enrollment at Grand Canyon University fell 4.1% while online grew 7.1%.

Consumer behaviour is shifting towards flexible, shorter, cheaper credentials and employer-funded learning. Strategic Education reports employer-affiliated enrollment at 34.7% of its U.S. higher-education base.

New competitors include public universities with low-cost online programs, technology platforms and AI-native tutoring apps. Duolingo's paid subscriber growth lags its user growth, a sign of monetisation pressure.
Geopolitical and policy risk is concentrated in international students: Strategic Education impaired its Australian business by $134.1M after persistent immigration constraints.
Substitutes include free online content, on-the-job training, apprenticeships and employer in-house academies. We did not find sourced estimates of how much spending these have taken.
Workforce Pell and employer-sponsored credentials may widen the market for short, job-linked programs, which suits healthcare and trades training.
Healthcare enrolment is growing: Strategic Education's healthcare programs grew 9% in Q3 2026, and Grand Canyon's off-campus sites grew 12.6%.
Consumer learning apps can still grow users and conversion: Duolingo guides to $1.30B of 2026 bookings and holds $1.4B of cash and short-term investments.
Low capital intensity and strong cash flow allow large buybacks, such as Grand Canyon Education's $278.3M repurchased year to date.
Accountability rules effective July 2027 may shut off aid to weaker programs, and ACE disputes the legality of cutting all Title IV aid.
Contract and partner risk: Grand Canyon Education's revenue now depends on a narrower amended agreement with Grand Canyon University.
Immigration policy can reduce international enrolment overnight, as in Australia.
AI-driven substitution and rising user acquisition costs could compress margins for apps and online schools.

Over the next three to five years we expect results to depend on policy and execution more than on the economy. The July 2027 accountability rule is the clearest event: programs with strong graduate earnings, such as healthcare, should be favoured, while weaker programs face closure or exit from federal loans. Low debt and capital needs leave room for buybacks and for operators to adapt. Consumer apps carry higher growth but need paid conversion to catch up with user growth. Our read is that the group will stay dispersed: a few well-run operators compound while others face impairments, as Strategic Education's Australia write-down shows.

Education Services is less tied to the business cycle than most consumer groups, but the macro backdrop still matters. At its 28 October 2026 meeting the Federal Reserve held the target range at 3.75%-4.00% by a 10-2 vote, with two members preferring a quarter-point increase, and described activity as expanding at a strong pace and inflation as elevated.

Price pressure is visible: the BLS reported all-items CPI up 0.4% in October after 0.6% in September, and core up 0.3%, though 12-month changes were not published for October because of a data gap in October 2025. Higher rates raise the cost of borrowing for students and parents, and our read is that sustained inflation adds pressure on household budgets and on schools' wage bills. Education companies themselves carry little debt, so direct interest cost is small: Damodaran shows the industry at 2.57x debt to EBITDA against 6.52x for the market.
Currency matters mainly for Strategic Education, whose Australian and New Zealand revenue produced favourable foreign-currency effects in Q3.

We found no authoritative single estimate of the addressable market for investable education services, so we describe demand through company data. Online degree enrollment is growing at the leaders: Grand Canyon Education's partner enrollments rose 5.2% to 145,270, led by online students (+7.1%) while on-campus students fell 4.1%. Healthcare is the strongest category, with healthcare 54% of Strategic Education's U.S. enrollment and up 9%.

Consumer learning is the fastest-growing area. Duolingo's daily active users reached 64.9M, up 29%, and paid subscribers 13.1M, up 14%, with 2026 bookings guided to about $1.30B. The gap between user and subscriber growth shows demand is strong but monetisation is slowing.

Demographics are a mixed picture. Employer-affiliated students now make up 34.7% of Strategic Education's U.S. enrollment, which supports adult demand. Demand is moderately cyclical: downturns raise adult enrollment, but government funding, rather than the economy, sets the ceiling. International demand has weakened in Australia, where enrollment fell 9.1%. Our judgement is that long-term prospects are decent for healthcare and skills programs and uncertain for generic degrees.

Using Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense in degrees and tutoring but concentrated in a few niches; the threat of new entrants is moderated by accreditation and aid eligibility but not by capital, as Grand Canyon Education spent only $29.6M on capex in nine months. Buyer power is high because students can choose among many providers and increasingly employers and governments set price through aid and sponsorship. Supplier power is low, though a partner university can reset the contract: Grand Canyon's amended agreement narrowed billable services to tuition and academic fees.

The threat of substitutes is rising: free content, employer academies and AI tutors. Concentration is low overall; leaders include Grand Canyon (139,170 enrollments), Strategic Education (84,725 U.S. students) and Duolingo (13.1M paying subscribers). We found no sourced market shares for the group as a whole.

Moats come from accreditation, brand, employer relationships and, for apps, habit and network effects. Pricing power is limited by federal loan caps and low-cost alternatives, so margins reflect efficiency more than price.

Regulation is the dominant factor. Under the Department of Education's final accountability rule, programs must pass an earnings-premium test; failing two of three years can end access to federal aid, and the main rule takes effect on 1 July 2027, a year later than first proposed. Institutions where half or more of aid flows to failing programs could lose all Title IV eligibility including Pell Grants, which ACE disputes. A voluntary 'parachute' option lets institutions exit federal loans to keep Pell eligibility.

Politically, the setting also covers immigration: Strategic Education attributed its $134.1M non-cash impairment to persistent international student immigration constraints. Legal and contractual risk is real too: Grand Canyon Education's amended services agreement shows how a restructured relationship can change revenue and margin.

Technology is both opportunity and threat. Duolingo is discontinuing its top Max subscription tier and shifting users to Family plans, a reminder that AI-era product tiers are still in flux. Environmental factors are minor. Social factors include the move to skills-based and employer-paid learning.

Education looks profitable but not exceptional on industry averages. Damodaran's January 2026 data show a 45.82% gross margin, 8.79% net margin and 13.54% pre-tax operating margin, compared with 12.75% for the total market, with ROE of 15.90% against 17.21%. Net capex is only 0.65% of sales.

Company data show a wide spread. Grand Canyon Education's operating margin was 24.4% year to date, or 25.3% adjusted, on service revenue of $840.2M, and the company carries no debt. Strategic Education's adjusted operating margin was 15.7% in Q3, with U.S. higher education at 10.3% and its ed-tech unit at 42.5%. Duolingo's gross margin was 72.9% and adjusted EBITDA margin 25.5%.

Operating leverage is high for apps and service providers: costs are largely fixed, so extra enrollments or subscribers flow through. Free cash flow is solid: Duolingo generated $75.3M in Q3 and Strategic Education $136.7M in nine months. The weak point is returns on acquisitions, as the Australian impairment shows.

Third-quarter 2026 results show slowing growth at some names and acceleration at others. Grand Canyon Education guided full-year 2026 service revenue of $1,160.7M to $1,161.7M and adjusted EPS of $10.09 to $10.13, with Q4 adjusted EPS of $3.63 to $3.67. Q3 adjusted EBITDA fell 3.2% to $73.5M, hit by the narrower amended agreement.

Duolingo guided Q4 bookings of $382M (+13%) and revenue of $322M (+14%), with full-year adjusted EBITDA of $323M, a 26.5% margin. Strategic Education did not publish a 2026 outlook in its release, though management said the most likely outcome for consolidated revenue next year is flat.

We could not find a published consensus earnings-growth figure or revision trend for the group, so we do not compare guidance with consensus here. Our read is that the market is looking through slow top-line growth at the school operators because of heavy buybacks (Grand Canyon repurchased $278.3M year to date), and that the real debate is the 2027 accountability rule and enrolment quality rather than near-term EPS.

On Damodaran's January 2026 data, education has a forward P/E of 18.11x against 27.66x for the total market, a PEG of 0.79, and an EV/EBITDA of 9.26x for positive-EBITDA firms against 19.73x for the market. Business and consumer services, a neighbouring industry, trade at a forward P/E of 18.70x.

That gap reflects investors' regulatory worries: the group is cheap on earnings but exposed to policy that could change which programs get funded. Free cash flow yield is hard to compute without current prices, which we did not source, so we do not state one. Growth implied by price looks modest for the school operators, which suggests the market expects flat-to-low-growth earnings; Duolingo, with 12% bookings growth, is a growth-style exception.

We could not source a longer-run history of the group's multiple, so we cannot say how today's discount compares with its own past. Normalised earnings are also hard to judge for Strategic Education after a $134.1M non-cash impairment.

We did not find reliable, current data on relative price performance, ETF flows, short interest or institutional positioning for Education Services, so we make no quantitative claims on those points. The group is small and has few dedicated funds, which in our experience means individual stocks trade on company news, such as quarterly enrolment data and regulatory announcements, more than on sector flows.

The capital-return picture is available from company filings and is a form of positioning. Grand Canyon Education has repurchased $278.3M year to date, its board added $355.0M to the authorisation, and $394.5M remained available at 2 November 2026. Strategic Education repurchased $101.3M in nine months and pays a $0.60 quarterly dividend. Duolingo repurchased $82.0M under a $400M program through 30 October.

Our read is that buybacks provide support but do not substitute for enrolment growth, and the next test is the 2027 accountability rule and how the Fed's higher-for-longer stance feeds into student borrowing.

Specialized Consumer Services is a mixed bag of recurring, need-based services: funeral and cemetery care, tax preparation, child care and back-up care. Third-quarter results show steady but unspectacular growth: Service Corporation International lifted revenue 5% but trimmed its 2026 EPS guidance on lower funeral volumes, and Bright Horizons took a $290.0M goodwill impairment, mostly Australia. H&R Block reaffirmed fiscal 2027 guidance. Damodaran's business and consumer services industry trades at 18.7x forward earnings against 27.7x for the market.

Specialized Consumer Services holds consumer-facing businesses that do not fit elsewhere in the Consumer Services group. In practice that means funeral homes and cemeteries, tax preparation, child care and employer back-up care, home warranties, car washes and weight-management programs. Customers are households (and sometimes employers who pay for a benefit). Revenue is typically fees per service or per subscription, and demand tends to be steadier than for restaurants or hotels because many of these services are needed, not optional. Education providers sit in the neighbouring Education Services industry.

Funeral services: Arranging and conducting funerals and cremations, usually through a local funeral home with a long family reputation. e.g. Service Corporation International's Dignity Memorial homes, Carriage Services
Cemetery and preneed: Burial plots, mausoleum space and memorials, often sold years ahead of need and paid for in installments or by trust. e.g. SCI cemetery and property sales
Tax preparation: Assisted tax filing in offices and online, plus do-it-yourself software and related financial products. e.g. H&R Block, Intuit's competing products (outside this group)

Child care and back-up care: Employer-sponsored child care centers and short-notice care for children and adults that employees can use when normal arrangements fail. e.g. Bright Horizons full service centers and back-up care
Home warranties and car washes: Plans that pay for home system repairs, and subscription-style car wash memberships. e.g. Frontdoor, Mister Car Wash
Personal development and wellness: Subscription-based weight-management, coaching and similar programs. e.g. WW International
Volume of services: Funeral calls track deaths and, for child care, enrollment. Flat volumes mean growth must come from price and mix.
Pricing and mix: Higher prices lift revenue per service, while a shift toward cremation or lower-priced packages offsets it.
Cost inflation and wages: Staff pay, health insurance and selling compensation are the biggest cost lines, so labour inflation squeezes margins when prices lag.
Seasonality and the calendar: Tax preparation earns most of its profit in a few months, so one season decides the year.
Regulation and legal exposure: Rules on funeral pricing, tax-preparer conduct, child safety and licensing can raise costs or limit practices.
Capital allocation and leverage: Consolidators borrow to acquire and repurchase shares, so interest rates and credit availability affect returns.
Preneed: Funeral or cemetery goods and services bought in advance. Cash is held in trust or insurance until needed, producing deferred revenue and a backlog of future business.
Cremation rate: The share of dispositions that are cremations. Cremations generally bring in less revenue per case than burials, so a higher rate lowers average revenue per service.
Average revenue per service: Total funeral revenue divided by the number of services performed. It shows how pricing and mix move without volume changes.
Comparable (same-store) results: Results from locations open in both periods. They show underlying growth, excluding acquisitions and closures.
Seasonality: A pattern where most earnings land in one part of the year, as with tax preparation, which earns its profit in the winter and spring and loses money in other quarters.
Back-up care: Employer-paid care for children or adults used on short notice. It is sold as a benefit per employer and used per day, so revenue scales with usage.
Full-service center: A child care center operated for an employer or community. It is fixed-cost heavy, so enrollment (utilisation) drives margin.
Maintenance capex: Spending needed to keep existing sites in working order, as opposed to growth spending on new locations or acquisitions.
Roll-up: Strategy of buying many small local businesses and running them under one brand to gain purchasing, marketing and back-office scale.
Goodwill impairment: A non-cash write-down when an acquisition is worth less than carried on the books. It signals lower expected profits.
Membership / subscription: Recurring fees for access, as at car washes or warranty plans. They give predictable revenue but make churn the key risk.
SCI cut 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $3.94-$4.04 on lower funeral volumes and higher healthcare costs, so the next quarter's funeral call volumes and cost trends matter.
Bright Horizons impaired $290.0M of goodwill, primarily Australia, and cut full-year guidance, so watch whether Australia is restructured.
H&R Block's fiscal 2027 outlook (revenue $4.11B-$4.16B, adjusted EPS $6.04-$6.24) depends on the January-April tax season, where results are decided.
The cremation rate keeps rising (63.4% projected for 2025), which pressures revenue per funeral even as it supports volumes and cemetery and memorial sales.
The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% with two members wanting a hike, which matters for the heavily indebted names: SCI carries about $5.2B of debt.
Service Corporation International, H&R Block, Bright Horizons, Frontdoor, Mister Car Wash, Carriage Services, WW International

Revenue is fee based and recurring in nature: SCI earned $602.6M of funeral and $504.6M of cemetery revenue in Q3 2026, H&R Block earns fees from tax preparation and related services, and Bright Horizons earns fees from center care ($522.0M), back-up care ($286.4M) and advisory services ($33.1M).

Customers are households (funeral, tax, car wash) and employers who buy care as a benefit (Bright Horizons). Demand is often tied to life events such as a death, a tax deadline or a child's care need rather than to discretionary choice.

Principal costs are staff, facilities and, for sellers, selling compensation and advertising. SCI blamed higher selling compensation, advertising and health insurance costs for lower cemetery gross margin (33.2% against 34.3%), and H&R Block's quarterly operating expenses rose 11.1% on field compensation and occupancy.

Pricing power comes from trust, local reputation, regulation and scarcity of locations. Funeral and cemetery operators raise prices steadily: SCI's average revenue per funeral service rose 2.8% to $6,022. Tax preparation and child care face more price-sensitive customers.

Major assets are real estate (funeral homes, cemetery land, child care centers), trust funds for preneed sales, and goodwill from acquisitions. Major liabilities are debt and deferred revenue: SCI had $5.17B of debt and $1.82B of deferred revenue at 30 Sep 2026.

The mix varies: funeral and cemetery operators and child care providers are asset-heavy by our judgment (SCI plans $335M of maintenance capex in 2026), while tax preparation and subscription services are largely asset-light.

We found no single sourced estimate for the size of the whole Specialized Consumer Services group. Company data help: SCI Q3 revenue was $1,107.3M, H&R Block guides fiscal 2027 revenue of $4.11B-$4.16B and Bright Horizons guides about $3.07B for 2026.

Main segments are death care (funeral and cemetery), tax and financial services, child and dependent care, home services and subscription programs. Death care is steady and aging-related; tax and care are tied to institutions such as the tax code and employer benefits.

In the value chain, suppliers include caskets, land, insurance and trust managers (death care), software and labor (tax) and teachers and facilities (child care); customers are households and employers. Employer benefits and tax law are the key upstream institutions.

The industry has consolidated into larger chains, shifted from burial to cremation (a projected 63.4% of U.S. dispositions in 2025 against 31.6% for burial) and moved services online, as H&R Block's assisted and DIY mix shows.

Activity is concentrated in the United States: SCI and H&R Block are mostly U.S.; H&R Block's international services grew to $74.8M in Q1 and Bright Horizons' impairment related primarily to Australia.

Competitors are numerous in each niche but few are large. The group's leaders are individual niche champions: SCI in death care, H&R Block in assisted tax preparation and Bright Horizons in employer-sponsored child care. We found no sourced figure for number of significant competitors overall.

We found no sourced market-share figures for SCI, H&R Block or Bright Horizons, though each is a well-known brand in its niche. We believe independent funeral homes and cemeteries still make up most of the market by number.

Fragmented in most niches, with consolidation by roll-up. Local independents compete with national chains, and the chains grow by buying them, which is why acquisition and divestiture gains and losses appear in SCI's results.

Barriers to entry are modest in tax preparation and child care (licenses and trust build slowly) and high in cemeteries, where land and perpetual-care obligations limit new entrants. Brand and employer contracts are major barriers for Bright Horizons.
Economies of scale arise in purchasing, marketing, technology and shared back-office functions. Scale is most valuable in tax and subscription businesses; funeral homes remain local.

Services are partly commoditised (basic tax filing, car washes) and partly differentiated by trust, location and care quality (funerals, child care). Cremation shift adds pressure on revenue per case.

Customers hold the bargaining power in tax and subscriptions because of free or cheap alternatives, while sellers hold more in death care because customers rarely shop around in a time of loss. Employers hold the power in back-up care and can renegotiate contracts. Suppliers have limited leverage.
Revenue growth comes from price, volume and acquisitions. SCI's comparable funeral revenue rose 3.3% and cemetery revenue 4.0% in Q3 2026, with preneed sales production up 6% and 5%.
Operating margins depend on volume, labor cost and selling expenses. SCI's funeral gross margin was 17.4% and cemetery 33.2% in Q3, and Damodaran puts the group's pre-tax operating margin at 12.32%.
Key cost variables are wages and benefits, healthcare costs, advertising and real estate. SCI named higher health insurance and selling compensation as drags on 2026 earnings.

Interest-rate sensitivity is high for the leveraged names: SCI's $5.17B of debt and Bright Horizons' revolver borrowings mean higher rates raise interest expense and lower valuations. The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% on 28 October 2026.

Inflation lifts costs and, with a lag, prices. Unemployment affects tax and child care demand mildly; GDP matters little to funerals; commodity prices matter little except fuel and land. October 2026 CPI rose 0.4% month on month.

The group is largely defensive: death care is non-cyclical, tax preparation is mandated annually, and child care is need-based. Cyclicality enters through employer headcount (Bright Horizons) and discretionary memberships (car washes, wellness).
Growth is single-digit: SCI's Q3 revenue grew 5% and adjusted EPS grew 11% to $0.97, H&R Block's Q1 revenue grew 10.2% and Bright Horizons' Q3 revenue grew 5%.

Margins in Damodaran's January 2026 data for business and consumer services: gross margin of 33.38%, net margin 7.03% and pre-tax lease-adjusted operating margin 12.32%, versus 37.76%, 9.74% and 12.75% for the total market.
ROE for business and consumer services is 18.20%, against 17.21% for the total market in Damodaran's data. We did not source an industry ROIC figure for this group.

Leverage is moderate overall but high at consolidators: Damodaran shows book debt to capital of 51.40% and debt to EBITDA of 2.77x, with market debt to capital of 16.64%. SCI's debt was $5.17B and H&R Block's long-term debt $1.49B.

Free cash flow is solid at the best companies: SCI expects about $750M of adjusted free cash flow in 2026 on operating cash flow of $1,055M-$1,115M, and Bright Horizons generated $208.1M of operating cash flow in nine months.

Capital needs range from light to moderate. Damodaran's net capex is 3.36% of sales for the industry; SCI's 2026 maintenance capex is $335M and Bright Horizons spent $69.4M net on fixed assets in nine months.
Valuation: forward P/E of 18.70x and EV/EBITDA of 14.26x for positive-EBITDA firms in Damodaran's January 2026 data, against 27.66x and 19.73x for the total market.

Regulatory risk is niche specific: funeral pricing rules and cemetery trust rules, tax-preparer regulation and tax law changes, and child safety rules. Bright Horizons booked $23.4M of expense for certain safeguarding matters.

Technology and AI could automate tax preparation, bringing pressure on H&R Block's assisted business, and can also help operators cut costs. We found no sourced quantification of AI's effect on this group.

Demographics are favourable for death care (aging) and unfavourable for child care in places where birth rates are falling. NFDA projects cremation at 63.4% of U.S. dispositions in 2025 against 31.6% for burial, and we expect the trend to continue, reducing revenue per case.

Consumer behaviour is shifting toward cremation, online tax filing and flexible work, which cuts demand for office-based care and tax offices. H&R Block's Q1 assisted consumer revenue was small and seasonal, so behaviour in the main season matters.
New competitors include free tax filing options, online memorial and direct-cremation providers and, in child care, government-funded alternatives. We did not find sourced estimates of their share.
Geopolitical and supply-chain risk is low for most services; international operations such as Bright Horizons' Australian centers carry local policy and oversupply risk, which led to its impairment.
Substitutes include DIY tax software, direct cremation and informal care by relatives; these tend to take share in downturns.
Aging populations should support steady death-care volumes and preneed sales, which grew 6% (funeral) and 5% (cemetery) in Q3 2026 at SCI.
Employer demand for dependent-care benefits supports back-up care, which grew from $253.4M to $286.4M in a year at Bright Horizons.
Scale players can keep buying small independents and repurchasing shares: SCI returned $464M to shareholders in nine months.
