International tax services are growing, with H&R Block's international revenue at $74.8M against $66.5M a year earlier.
Rising cremation lowers revenue per death-care case, and funeral volumes disappointed SCI in 2026.
Labor and health-care cost inflation squeeze margins when prices lag.
Weaker child care economics, primarily in Australia, led to Bright Horizons' $290.0M goodwill impairment.
Higher-for-longer rates raise the cost of the debt used to fund roll-ups.

Over the next three to five years we expect the group to deliver low-to-mid single-digit organic growth, helped by pricing and aging but held back by labour costs, cremation mix and uneven care enrollment. Death care looks the most predictable, with deferred revenue of $1.82B at SCI offering visibility. Tax preparation depends on defending its assisted franchise against software, with a $4.11B-$4.16B revenue outlook for fiscal 2027. Child care has execution risk outside the United States. Leverage is the main amplifier, so we think capital allocation will separate winners from the rest in a higher-rate world.

Specialized Consumer Services is mostly defensive, so its link to the cycle is indirect. At its 28 October 2026 meeting the Federal Reserve held the target range at 3.75%-4.00% by a 10-2 vote, with two members wanting a quarter-point rise, citing a strong pace of activity and elevated inflation. The BLS reported October CPI up 0.4% for the month and core up 0.3%, with 12-month figures unavailable for October because of a data gap in 2025.

Higher rates matter most for leveraged names. SCI had about $5.17B of debt at 30 September 2026, and Bright Horizons had roughly $1.36B including revolver borrowings (our sum of balance sheet lines). Inflation shows up in costs: SCI cited higher health insurance, selling compensation and advertising, and H&R Block's expenses rose 11.1% in its seasonally weak first quarter.

On the demand side, the cycle matters less. Funerals follow deaths, taxes are due every year, and employers buy care as a benefit. Employment trends matter to child care and back-up care, but we found no sourced evidence of weakness there; Bright Horizons' back-up care grew 13%.

We found no authoritative estimate of the group's total addressable market, so we describe demand through the leaders and industry bodies. In death care, NFDA projects the U.S. cremation rate at 63.4% for 2025 against 31.6% for burial. Volumes depend on the number of deaths, which tends to grow slowly with an aging population; SCI nonetheless reported core funeral services down 0.5% in Q3 2026.

Growth therefore comes from price and mix. SCI's average revenue per service rose 2.8% to $6,022 and comparable cemetery revenue rose 4.0%, helped by preneed sales production up 6% (funeral) and 5% (cemetery). Deferred revenue of $1.82B provides a backlog.

In care, Bright Horizons' revenue rose 5%, with back-up care revenue of $286.4M against $253.4M a year earlier. In tax, H&R Block's Q1 revenue rose 10.2% on international, tax protection and small business services. Demand elasticity is low in death care and tax and higher in memberships. Our view is that long-term prospects are steady, with growth near inflation plus a little.

Porter's five forces vary by niche. Rivalry is local in death care and national in tax; the threat of new entrants is low in cemeteries because of land and trust obligations, moderate in tax and child care. Buyer power is low in funerals, where families rarely shop around in a time of loss, and higher in tax, where free and cheap software is available. Supplier power is limited. The threat of substitutes is highest in tax (DIY software) and death care (direct cremation).

Concentration is low by number of outlets, though the large chains hold scale: SCI's quarterly revenue of $1,107.3M dwarfs most independents, and it grows partly through acquisition and divestiture. We found no sourced market-share data.

Moats are reputation, location, preneed relationships and employer contracts. Pricing power is highest in death care: SCI raised average revenue per service 2.8% in a quarter when volumes slipped. In child care, the Australian impairment suggests moats are thinner in some markets.

Regulation shapes each niche. Funeral and cemetery operators are governed by state licensing, trust rules for preneed funds and consumer protection rules. Tax preparation is shaped by tax law and preparer regulation, and H&R Block's results hinge on the tax code and filing season. Child care is regulated for safety and licensing, and Bright Horizons reported $23.4M of expense for certain safeguarding matters while the release did not say where they arose.

Political and economic factors include employer benefit policy, which supports back-up care, and government funding of child care. Social factors are strong: cremation preference is shifting the funeral business model, with NFDA projecting 63.4% cremation in 2025 against 31.6% burial.

Technology is a threat to tax preparation and an efficiency tool for everyone. H&R Block reports growth in small business and international services while its assisted consumer business remains the core. Emerging risks are cost inflation in health insurance and labour, litigation over safeguarding in care, and policy change in the UK and Australia, where Bright Horizons impaired goodwill.

Economics are decent but not exceptional. Damodaran's January 2026 data show gross margin of 33.38%, net margin of 7.03% and pre-tax operating margin of 12.32% for business and consumer services, with ROE of 18.20% and net capex of 3.36% of sales.

Death care margins are lower at the gross level but cash generative: SCI's funeral gross margin was 17.4% and cemetery 33.2% in Q3 2026, and it expects 2026 adjusted free cash flow of about $750M on operating cash flow of $1,055M-$1,115M. Operating leverage is meaningful because buildings and staff are largely fixed, so volume shortfalls hit margin quickly, as they did in 2026.

Bright Horizons earned adjusted EBITDA of $163.3M on $841.5M of revenue, a 19.4% margin by our calculation, while taking a $290.0M impairment. H&R Block loses money in its first quarter (adjusted EBITDA of negative $185.2M) because earnings are concentrated in the tax season, and it guides fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA of $1.11B-$1.14B. Returns depend on seasonality, leverage and the quality of acquisitions.

Management guidance is mixed. SCI lowered 2026 adjusted EPS to $3.94-$4.04 and expects Q4 adjusted EPS of $1.10-$1.20, citing lower funeral volumes than anticipated and higher healthcare, selling compensation and advertising costs. Q3 adjusted EPS was $0.97 versus $0.87 a year ago.

H&R Block reaffirmed fiscal 2027 guidance for revenue of $4.11B-$4.16B, adjusted EBITDA of $1.11B-$1.14B and adjusted EPS of $6.04-$6.24, with Q1 revenue up 10.2%. Bright Horizons lowered 2026 revenue guidance to about $3.07B and adjusted EPS to $4.98-$5.03.

We could not find a sourced consensus earnings growth figure or revision trend for the group, so we cannot say where our view differs from consensus in numerical terms. Our read is that 2026 is a year of modest growth with cost pressure, that SCI's cut was small relative to its earnings and that the larger risk lies in care businesses outside the United States, where the impairment suggests earlier expectations were too high.

On Damodaran's January 2026 data, business and consumer services trade at a forward P/E of 18.70x against 27.66x for the total market, and at an EV/EBITDA of 14.26x for positive-EBITDA firms against 19.73x. The PEG ratio is 1.89 against 1.90 for the market, so the discount on P/E is largely matched by lower growth.

Company-level multiples need current share prices, which we did not source, so we cannot cite a company P/E or free cash flow yield. We can say SCI's guided adjusted EPS of $3.94-$4.04 and about $750M of free cash flow set the earnings base against which investors price it. H&R Block's guided adjusted EPS of $6.04-$6.24 and a repurchase price of $45.68 per share in the first quarter imply a P/E of roughly 7x to 8x on our arithmetic, which looks undemanding.

We could not source a long-run history of the group's multiple. Our judgment is that a discount to the market is typical for slow-growth, leveraged service businesses, and that the discount is deserved where volumes are flat and impairments have appeared, as at Bright Horizons.

We did not find reliable current data on relative price performance, ETF flows, short interest or institutional positioning for this group. There is no large dedicated ETF, so the names trade as part of consumer-services baskets and on individual results; we make no quantitative claims on those points.

Capital returns are the clearest sign of insider confidence. SCI returned $464M in the first nine months of 2026 ($318.9M of buybacks and $145.4M of dividends) and cut its share count to 136.05M from 139.68M. H&R Block bought back 2.2 million shares for $100.3M in its first quarter and has about $500M left on its $1.5B program. Bright Horizons repurchased about 7.7 million shares for $557.7M in nine months, even as it took the impairment.

Our read is that buybacks are supporting earnings per share more than the underlying revenue trend in all three cases, and that the market will look next at SCI's funeral volumes, H&R Block's tax season and Bright Horizons' decision on Australia.

Tire makers are in a thin-margin, cost-pressured stretch. Goodyear's Q3 2026 segment operating income fell to $174M from $287M and it posted a $238M net loss, while Michelin held nine-month revenue at EUR 19.2B and kept its profit and cash guidance and Bridgestone expects roughly $367M of U.S. tariff costs this year. Natural rubber is near a two-year high, tire price rises of 2% to 5% have been announced and replacement demand is soft in North America. Damodaran's rubber and tires industry earns a 2.57% pre-tax operating margin.

Tires & Rubber companies make and sell tires for cars, light trucks, commercial trucks, farm and mining equipment, aircraft and motorcycles. They sell to automakers (original equipment, or OE) and, more profitably, to drivers and fleets who replace worn tires through dealers and retailers. Main raw materials are natural and synthetic rubber, carbon black, steel cord and chemicals. Wheels and other auto parts sit in the neighbouring Automotive Parts & Equipment industry instead.
Passenger and light-truck tires: The largest product line, sold to automakers and, mostly, as replacements to consumers through dealers. e.g. Michelin Pilot, Goodyear Assurance, Bridgestone Turanza
Commercial truck and bus tires: Tires for fleets, where cost per mile and retreading matter and customers buy on total cost of ownership. e.g. Michelin X Line, Goodyear Endurance, Bridgestone Ecopia
Specialty tires: Tires for mining, agriculture, construction and aircraft, made in lower volumes with higher prices. e.g. Michelin mining and aircraft tires, Bridgestone off-the-road tires
Two-wheel tires: Motorcycle and bicycle tires, including premium leisure motorcycle tires. e.g. Michelin, Pirelli motorcycle lines
Services, retreading and fleet solutions: Tire maintenance, retreads and data services that help fleets manage tire costs. e.g. Goodyear fleet services, Bridgestone Bandag
Non-tire polymer products: Rubber and composite products sold outside tires, such as belts, seals and conveyor materials. e.g. Michelin Polymer Composite Solutions
Raw material prices: Rubber, carbon black, steel cord and chemicals are the largest variable costs. Cost increases feed through to margin with a lag of months, until price increases catch up.
Replacement demand: Miles driven and the age of the vehicle fleet set how fast tires wear out. Soft replacement demand cuts volumes and mix at the same time.
Vehicle production: OE tire volumes move with automakers' output, which depends on consumer demand, credit and supply chains.
Trade policy: Tariffs and anti-dumping duties change which tires are imported and who bears the cost. They help local producers and hurt importers.
Plant utilisation and fixed costs: A tire plant costs much to run whatever it produces, so volume drops hurt margins quickly.
Premium mix and pricing: Selling more large-rim and higher-spec tires raises revenue per tire, which is how leaders hold profit when volumes slip.
Original equipment (OE): Tires sold to automakers for new vehicles. Volumes follow vehicle production, and prices are negotiated tightly.
Replacement market: Tires sold to replace worn ones. It is larger and steadier than OE because tires wear out regardless of new car sales, and margins are higher.
Price-mix: The effect on revenue of selling at different prices and of selling more premium, larger-size tires. It is how tire makers grow revenue when unit volumes are flat.
Natural rubber: Rubber harvested from trees in Southeast Asia. Its price swings with weather, supply and demand and feeds tire costs with a lag.
Synthetic rubber: Oil-based rubber made from feedstocks such as butadiene. It tracks oil and petrochemical prices.
Rim size / premium mix: Larger-rim tires (18 inches and up) sell for more and earn higher margin, so a shift to larger rims lifts revenue per tire.
Tariffs and anti-dumping duties: Import taxes that raise the cost of imported tires. Makers with local factories gain relative to importers.
Capacity utilization: How much of a plant's capacity is used. Fixed costs are large, so low utilisation hurts margin sharply.
Segment operating income: Operating profit before certain one-off items such as restructuring. It is the figure companies like Goodyear use to compare divisions.
Retread: A worn truck tire given a new tread. It extends tire life and is sold at a lower price than a new tire.
Rationalization charges: Costs of closing plants and cutting jobs. They are excluded from adjusted earnings but are real cash costs.
Goodyear's cash position: nine-month operating cash flow was negative $764M, with $990M of debt due within a year against $812M of cash at 30 Sep 2026.
Whether announced 2% to 5% price increases stick as natural rubber trades near a two-year high and ANRPC sees a supply deficit of about 280,000 tonnes in 2026.
North American replacement demand: Bridgestone cited a 5% market decline in passenger and light-truck replacement and 13% in truck and bus in the first half of 2026.
U.S. tariff costs: Bridgestone expects about $367M of tariff impact in 2026, and Goodyear cited $48M of higher tariffs and other costs in Q3.
EU anti-dumping duties on Chinese car and light-truck tires took effect on 8 July 2026, at up to 45.3%, which could reroute Chinese supply.
Michelin, Bridgestone, Goodyear, Continental, Pirelli, Sumitomo Rubber, Hankook, Yokohama Rubber

Revenue comes mainly from selling tires to automakers (OE) and to drivers and fleets through replacement channels, plus smaller services and non-tire businesses. Michelin's nine-month revenue of EUR 19.2B split into Consumer EUR 10.4B, Transportation EUR 4.3B, Specialties EUR 3.3B and Polymer Composite Solutions EUR 1.15B.

Customers are automakers (OE), tire dealers and distributors, retailers and commercial fleets. Michelin noted weaker OE demand across segments but higher replacement volumes for its brand, which shows how differently the two channels behave.

The largest costs are raw materials (natural and synthetic rubber, carbon black, steel), labour, energy and freight. Goodyear's Q3 segment operating income was reduced by $48M of higher tariffs and other costs, partly offset by $90M of savings from its Goodyear Forward program.

Pricing power is limited in OE, where automakers negotiate hard, and better in replacement, where brand, quality and dealer relationships matter. Michelin's price-mix was +1.1% over nine months and turned positive in Q3 after input cost increases.
Major assets are factories, inventory and brands. Liabilities are heavy: Goodyear had $6,030M of long-term debt and finance leases and $990M due within a year at 30 Sep 2026, against $812M of cash.

The industry is capital-intensive. Goodyear spent $481M on capex in nine months, though Damodaran's net capex for the industry is roughly zero (-0.03% of sales), showing that investment is only about maintaining the asset base.

Published global tire market estimates vary widely with definition, from roughly $143B to $282B for 2025 in the research reports we saw, and we could not open an authoritative source to resolve that, so we do not give a single figure. Company data show scale: Michelin's nine-month revenue was EUR 19.2B and Bridgestone guides about $30B for 2026.
The main segments are passenger and light-truck tires (Michelin's Consumer segment, EUR 10.4B), commercial truck and bus tires (Transportation, EUR 4.3B), specialty tires (EUR 3.3B) and two-wheel.

In the value chain, suppliers are rubber growers and processors, petrochemical firms, carbon black and steel cord makers; customers are automakers and the replacement channel. Natural rubber is supplied from Southeast Asia, where ANRPC forecasts 2026 output of about 15.32 million tonnes against consumption of 15.60 million.

The industry has moved to larger, higher-spec tires, to Asia as a production base and to local-for-local plants, and recently to defensive trade measures: the EU imposed duties of up to 45.3% on Chinese car and light-truck tires from 8 July 2026.

Production and sales are spread across North America, Europe and Asia, with China the largest single growth and supply source. Bridgestone reported North American replacement markets down in the first half of 2026 and a flat European market over nine months, so trends differ by region.

A small number of global leaders plus many regional and Chinese makers. The significant competitors named in company filings and results include Michelin, Bridgestone, Goodyear, Continental, Pirelli and Asian groups such as Sumitomo, Hankook, Yokohama and Sailun.

We could not open a source with current global market shares. Michelin, Bridgestone and Goodyear are widely regarded as the three largest by revenue, and Bridgestone's global H1 2026 revenue of about $14.69B gives a sense of scale.

The industry is moderately concentrated at the top and fragmented below. Lower-cost Asian brands are taking share in many markets, which is why the EU imposed anti-dumping duties of 4.3% to 45.3% on Chinese car and light-truck tires.
Barriers to entry are high for premium tires: plant costs, brand, dealer networks and OE approvals. They are lower for budget tires, where Chinese manufacturers have scaled quickly.
Economies of scale are large in purchasing, plants and distribution. Fixed costs are high, so under-used capacity hurts. Goodyear's Q3 result shows how lower volume (-3.3%) cut profit sharply.

The product is partly commoditised at the budget end and differentiated at the premium end, through safety, wear, noise, EV-specific designs and brand. Michelin's +1.6% mix effect over nine months shows premium mix helps.
Customers have power in OE (a few large automakers) and in fleets; suppliers of natural rubber have power when supply is short, as in 2026 when prices reached a two-year high.

Revenue growth comes from replacement volumes, OE volumes, price-mix and acquisitions. Michelin's nine-month revenue rose 1.0% at constant exchange rates with volumes down 0.8% and price-mix up 1.1%; Goodyear's organic sales rose 1.6% in Q3.

Operating margins depend on volume, mix, raw material costs and plant use. Damodaran puts rubber and tires at a 2.57% pre-tax operating margin and 17.99% gross margin, against 5.80% operating margin for auto parts.

Key cost variables are natural rubber, synthetic rubber and oil-linked inputs, labour, energy and tariffs. Spot natural rubber in China rose about 14% in 2026 to about RMB 17,900 per tonne by early September.
Interest-rate sensitivity is high because of leverage and car financing: Damodaran shows debt to EBITDA of 5.67x, and rates affect vehicle sales. The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% in October 2026.

Inflation raises costs (the BLS reported tires up 0.3% in October 2026 month on month), while GDP and employment affect driving miles and fleet freight. Oil price links through synthetic rubber and driving costs.

Cyclical for OE and mildly cyclical for replacement, which is steadier since worn tires must be replaced. Commercial truck tires follow freight activity. Overall it is a low-growth, cyclical-defensive hybrid.

Revenue and earnings growth are low and volatile. Goodyear's Q3 net sales fell 2.3% and it reported a $238M net loss; Michelin's nine-month revenue rose 1.0% at constant exchange rates; Bridgestone's H1 revenue rose 9.7% and adjusted operating profit 19.7% in dollar terms.

In Damodaran's January 2026 data, rubber and tires has a 17.99% gross margin, -9.49% net margin and 2.57% pre-tax operating margin, below auto parts (15.84%, 0.72%, 5.80%) and the total market (37.76%, 9.74%, 12.75%). The group is small, so averages swing with a few companies.

ROE is -36.41% for rubber and tires against 2.17% for auto parts and 17.21% for the total market, in Damodaran's data. We did not source an industry ROIC; the operating margin of 2.57% implies low returns on capital.
Debt is high. Damodaran shows book debt to capital of 74.12% and debt to EBITDA of 5.67x. Goodyear reported $6,030M of long-term debt and finance leases at 30 Sep 2026.

Free cash flow is weak at Goodyear: nine-month operating cash flow was negative $764M and capex $481M, which gives roughly negative $1.2B by our arithmetic, though the figure relates to a release that appears on EDGAR as a draft. Michelin guides free cash flow before M&A above EUR 1.6B for 2026.
Capital expenditure needs are substantial in absolute terms (Goodyear $481M in nine months), but Damodaran's net capex ratio of -0.03% of sales suggests spending broadly matches depreciation.

Valuation multiples are low: EV/EBITDA of 6.74x for rubber and tires with positive EBITDA against 19.73x for the market, and a forward P/E of 15.13x for auto parts, which we use as a neighbour because the P/E table we opened did not list rubber and tires.

Regulatory and trade policy are major: U.S. tariffs (Bridgestone's estimate of about $367M for 2026) and the EU's anti-dumping duties on Chinese tires from July 2026 change costs and competition. Safety, tire wear and environmental rules are other risks.

Technology risk includes EV-specific tire demands (heavier cars wear tires faster) and software-defined vehicles; AI is more of an efficiency tool than a threat. We found no sourced quantification of either effect.
Demographics matter through miles driven and vehicle ownership. Older drivers drive less, but a bigger car fleet in emerging markets adds demand. We found no sourced estimate.

Consumer behaviour: drivers trade down to lower-priced brands when budgets tighten, and replacement markets can fall; Bridgestone reported a 5% decline in North American passenger and light-truck replacement in the first half of 2026.
New competitors are mainly Asian low-cost makers expanding abroad, which prompted EU duties of up to 45.3% on non-cooperating Chinese firms.

Geopolitical and supply-chain risk is high: natural rubber is concentrated in Southeast Asia, where leaf-fall disease, aging trees and El Nino weather cut supply, and butadiene prices hit records on geopolitical tension.
Substitutes are limited in the near term: vehicles need tires. Longer term, shared mobility, fewer miles driven and airless tires are possible but unsourced risks to volume.
Premium mix and larger rims lift revenue per tire even when volumes are flat, as in Michelin's +1.6% mix effect.
Self-help programs can lower costs: Goodyear delivered $90M of benefits from Goodyear Forward in Q3 2026.
Trade measures against low-cost imports, such as EU duties of up to 45.3%, can help local producers keep volume and price.
A recovery in truck OE demand is under way in North America, with Michelin noting Class 8 orders and production improving in Q3.
Natural rubber near a two-year high and a projected supply deficit could keep raw material costs rising faster than prices.
Tariffs are a large cost for importers: Bridgestone expects about $367M in 2026.
Weak replacement demand in North America lowers volumes and mix at once.
High leverage and negative cash flow leave Goodyear exposed if conditions worsen.

We expect the next three to five years to reward scale, premium mix and cost discipline, while punishing leverage. Michelin and Bridgestone, with positive cash flow guidance and an Americas operating margin of 9.1% at Bridgestone, look better placed than Goodyear, which is still reshaping its portfolio and burning cash. Raw materials and trade measures will move margins more than volume, and replacement markets should stabilise as the vehicle fleet ages. The risks are a longer period of weak replacement demand in North America and rubber inflation outrunning price increases. Valuation multiples are low, but the industry's returns have been poor.

Tire demand follows vehicle production and miles driven, so the cycle matters but less than for most autos. At its 28 October 2026 meeting the Federal Reserve held the target range at 3.75%-4.00% by a 10-2 vote, with two members preferring a rise, describing activity as expanding at a strong pace and inflation as elevated. For a leveraged industry (Damodaran puts debt to EBITDA at 5.67x) that matters, since higher rates raise interest costs and make vehicle financing dearer.

Inflation is evident in the BLS data: October CPI rose 0.4% in the month, tires rose 0.3% and motor vehicle parts and equipment 0.2%, while 12-month changes were not published because of a gap in October 2025 data. Energy was a large contributor to price pressure earlier in the autumn, with the energy index up 5.2% in September.

Currency also matters: Michelin reported a 1.6% currency drag on nine-month revenue, so its constant-currency growth of 1.0% exceeds what it reported in euros. Our read is that a strong-growth, higher-rate, higher-energy-cost backdrop is a mixed one for tire makers: it supports vehicle use but raises input costs and the cost of capital.

Estimates of the global tire market in research reports ranged widely, from roughly $143B to $282B for 2025 depending on definition, and we could not open an authoritative source, so we do not rely on one. What company data show is a market with flat-to-slightly-lower volumes and growth from price and mix: Michelin's nine-month volumes fell 0.8% while price-mix added 1.1%.

Replacement demand is the stable core but is regionally uneven. Bridgestone reported that the North American passenger and light-truck replacement market fell 5% and truck and bus 13% in the first half of 2026, while in Europe it saw a flat market over nine months and a 1% fall in Q3. Michelin said its own brand's replacement volumes rose 4%. OE demand is weak in Europe and North America for cars, but recovering for North American heavy trucks.

Secular drivers are the growth of the global fleet, larger rim sizes and EV-related tire requirements; headwinds are fewer miles per vehicle and trade-down. Demand is moderately cyclical for OE and much less so for replacement. Our view is that long-term volume growth is low single digit at best, with value growth coming from mix.

Porter's five forces: rivalry among the global leaders is intense, and pricing is closely watched. The threat of new entrants is moderate: building scale and brand is expensive, but Chinese makers have done so quickly, which prompted EU duties of 4.3% to 45.3%. Buyer power is strong in OE, where automakers and fleets negotiate, and weaker in consumer replacement. Supplier power rises when natural rubber is short, as in 2026. The threat of substitutes is low in the near term.

Concentration is moderate at the top. Michelin (EUR 19.2B of nine-month revenue), Bridgestone (about $14.69B in H1) and Goodyear ($4.5B in Q3) are the leaders by size among those we opened, though we have no sourced market-share data.

Moats are brand, dealer networks, OE approvals and scale in production. Pricing power is real but limited: Bridgestone's North American replacement sales fell 3% against a 5% market decline in passenger and light-truck, showing relative strength, while Goodyear's volumes fell 3.3%. The 2026 price rises of 2% to 5% announced by Michelin, Bridgestone and others are described as below their cost increases by one Chinese maker.

Policy is the most active factor. Bridgestone estimated U.S. tariff impact of about $158M in the first half of 2026 and about $367M for the year, in line with its plan. Goodyear reported $48M of higher tariffs and other costs in Q3. Europe went the other way: the EU announced final anti-dumping duties on Chinese car and light-truck tires effective 8 July 2026: 4.3% for Hankook, 24.4% for other cooperating companies such as Sailun and Linglong and 45.3% for non-cooperating firms.

Economic and political factors include geopolitical tension that pushed butadiene, a synthetic rubber feedstock, to record highs and lifted demand for natural rubber. Environmental factors include tire-wear regulation and recycling; we did not source specific rules, so we only flag them as emerging risks.

Technology matters through EV-specific tires and fleet data services. Michelin and Bridgestone both highlight premium and specialty segments where technology differentiates. Social factors include trade-down in weaker economies. In our judgement the policy mix, tariffs in the U.S. and anti-dumping in Europe, favours producers with local plants.

Industry economics are poor on average and better for leaders. Damodaran's January 2026 data show rubber and tires with a 17.99% gross margin, a -9.49% net margin and a 2.57% pre-tax operating margin, ROE of -36.41% and debt to EBITDA of 5.67x. The group is small, so one or two loss-makers drive the average.

Company results differ. Bridgestone's Americas adjusted operating margin was 9.1% in the first half of 2026, and its global adjusted operating profit rose 19.7% to about $1.78B on revenue of about $14.69B. Goodyear's Q3 segment operating income was $174M on $4.5B of sales, about 3.9% by our arithmetic, and it lost $238M.

Operating leverage is high because plants have large fixed costs: Goodyear's volume decline of 3.3% pushed segment operating income down from $287M to $174M despite $90M of savings. Capital intensity is substantial, with Goodyear's nine-month capex at $481M, and free cash flow is the weak point: Goodyear's nine-month operating cash flow was negative $764M, while Michelin guides above EUR 1.6B of free cash flow before M&A.

Earnings expectations are muted. Michelin confirmed 2026 guidance of segment operating income growth at constant exchange rates and scope, and free cash flow before M&A above EUR 1.6B, though it no longer expects tire volumes to return to growth in Q4. Bridgestone left its 2026 forecast unchanged at about $30B of revenue and $3.43B of adjusted operating profit.

Goodyear's third quarter was a miss on profitability: adjusted loss per share of $0.11 against adjusted earnings of $0.28 a year earlier, with segment operating income of $174M. We did not find guidance in the release we opened and could not source consensus estimates or revision trends for this industry, so we do not claim to differ from consensus on numbers.

Our read: the earnings drivers into 2027 are price against raw materials, tariff pass-through and volume recovery. Natural rubber at a two-year high and an expected supply deficit argue for cost pressure that price increases of 2% to 5% may not fully cover. The cost savings programs (Goodyear Forward's $90M in Q3) are the main internal lever.

Multiples are low because returns are low. In Damodaran's January 2026 data, rubber and tires trade at an EV/EBITDA of 6.74x for firms with positive EBITDA against 19.73x for the total market, though EV/EBIT is 22.84x, reflecting thin operating profit. The auto parts neighbour trades at a forward P/E of 15.13x against 27.66x for the market.

Earnings are too depressed and volatile to give a meaningful price-to-earnings ratio for the group; the industry net margin is -9.49%. EV/EBITDA is the better lens, and the gap between 6.74x EV/EBITDA and 22.84x EV/EBIT shows how much depreciation absorbs.

We did not obtain current share prices, so we cannot give free cash flow yields or compare with the group's own history. Our judgment is that the discount to the market is deserved while returns on capital stay near the cost of capital and leverage is high, and the shares of the leaders are priced for modest recovery rather than a sharp rebound. Growth implied by price is therefore low; the main upside case rests on margin repair, not volume.

We did not find reliable, current data on relative price performance, ETF flows, short interest or institutional positioning for tire makers. The group has no large dedicated ETF, and the U.S.-listed pure play is Goodyear, so we make no quantitative claims about flows or breadth.

What the filings show is balance-sheet pressure and defensive action. Goodyear ended September with $812M of cash against $990M of debt and finance leases due within a year, and it is selling assets: it completed the sale of its Dunlop brand in May 2025 and its Chemical business in October 2025, which reduced Q3 2026 net sales by $177M. Michelin, in contrast, is guiding to free cash flow above EUR 1.6B.

Bridgestone's reported share performance in North America shows the competitive picture: its passenger and light-truck replacement sales fell 3% against a 5% market decline, and its OE sales rose 8%. Our read is that investor attention is on cost pass-through, tariff exposure and balance sheets, and that the leaders with stronger cash flow will be favoured over leveraged names until replacement demand recovers.

Motorcycle makers are having a two-speed year: strong in Asia and Europe, weak at Harley-Davidson. Honda's motorcycle unit earned about 439 billion yen of operating profit in April-September 2026 on revenue of 2,272.5 billion yen, and Yamaha's Land Mobility profit rose 91.5% in nine months. Bajaj Auto's export two-wheeler billings rose 43.2% while domestic sales rose only 1.8%. Harley's motorcycle operating margin was 4.6% as it cut shipments 8% to clear dealer stock. European registrations rose 16.8% in the first half; US sales were flat. We found no sourced sub-industry forward multiple; the sector trades at 24.3x.

Motorcycle manufacturers design, build and sell motorcycles, scooters, mopeds and three-wheelers, mostly through dealers. Most of the world's volume is low-priced commuter transport in Asia, while the profitable niches are premium and leisure bikes in developed markets. Revenue comes from vehicles, plus parts, accessories, apparel and, at some makers, retail finance. GICS places pure motorcycle makers here, while automakers sit in Automobiles, and components suppliers elsewhere. Several large groups, such as Honda and Yamaha, also make cars, boats or engines, so motorcycles are only part of their results.

Commuter motorcycles: Small, fuel-efficient bikes (typically under 200cc) used for daily transport, sold in huge volumes at low prices in India, Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa. e.g. Hero Splendor, Honda Shine, Bajaj Pulsar
Scooters and mopeds: Step-through vehicles with automatic gearing, popular with urban riders and women in Asia and with city commuters in Europe. e.g. Honda Activa, TVS Jupiter, Vespa

Premium and mid-size motorcycles: Bikes above roughly 250-350cc bought for leisure and status. They carry higher prices and much higher margins than commuters. e.g. Royal Enfield Classic, KTM Duke, Triumph Speed 400
Heavyweight and cruiser motorcycles: Large touring and cruiser bikes, the core of the US premium market, sold on brand and lifestyle. e.g. Harley-Davidson Street Glide, Honda Gold Wing
Off-road and adventure bikes: Competition, trail and dual-sport bikes for dirt and mixed riding, a large category in the US and Europe. e.g. KTM, Husqvarna, Yamaha WR
Electric two-wheelers: Battery scooters and motorcycles. Volumes are rising fast in India but are still small for developed-market premium electric bikes. e.g. TVS iQube, Bajaj Chetak, LiveWire

Parts, accessories, apparel and finance: Higher-margin add-ons sold with and after the bike, including retail loans at brands that run a finance arm. e.g. Harley-Davidson Financial Services, genuine parts
Volume and exports: Units sold drive revenue and spread fixed costs. Fast-growing export markets can offset slow home markets, as at Indian makers.
Mix and pricing: Selling more large, high-priced models and holding list prices lifts revenue per bike and gross margin faster than volume alone.
Input costs: Steel, aluminium, rubber and electronics make up most costs. When they rise faster than prices, EBITDA margin shrinks until prices catch up.
Credit availability: Most bikes are financed, so loan rates and approvals move demand, especially for first-time and lower-income buyers.
Tariffs and currencies: Import duties raise costs for bikes crossing borders, and a weak home currency inflates translated overseas profits for exporters such as Japanese makers.
Regulation and electrification: Emission rules and EV subsidies change which models are viable, and force development spending that is hard to recover in small premium niches.
Displacement (cc): Engine size in cubic centimetres. Under about 150cc usually means a commuter; above 350cc usually means a premium bike. It maps closely to price and margin.
Wholesale vs retail: Wholesale (shipments) is what the maker sells to dealers; retail is what dealers sell to riders. When they diverge, dealer inventory is being built or run down.
Dealer inventory: Bikes sitting unsold at dealers. Excess stock forces discounts, so makers sometimes ship fewer bikes than they retail to restore health.
Mix: The share of higher-priced models in sales. A small shift toward premium bikes can lift margins more than a price rise.
EBITDA margin: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization as a percent of revenue. Indian makers quote it as their main profit measure.
Captive finance: A finance subsidiary that lends to buyers and dealers. It supports sales and earns interest, but adds credit risk and debt.
Exports: Bikes built in one country and sold in another. For Indian makers they diversify away from a domestic market that is growing slowly.
Pass-through: Raising prices to recover higher input costs or tariffs. How quickly a maker can do this decides whether margins hold.
Platform: A shared engine and frame used across several models, which spreads development cost and lets partners build and sell each other's bikes.
Premiumization: Customers trading up to larger, pricier bikes as incomes rise. It is the main route to higher margins for commuter-heavy makers.
Localization: Building bikes and sourcing parts inside the market where they are sold, to avoid import tariffs and cut freight.
Harley-Davidson now expects 2026 gross tariff costs of about $105M-$120M, up from $75M-$90M, and says 2027 gross costs should not exceed 2026.
LiveWire has withdrawn guidance and disclosed substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern, and Harley says it does not intend to fund its losses.
Indian margins are squeezed by input costs: Hero's standalone EBITDA margin was 13.39% against a 14-16% target, and Eicher's fell to 23.7% from 24.5%.
Europe's first-half rebound, up 16.8%, has to hold through autumn, as ACEM itself cautioned.
The US market is flat: motorcycles excluding scooters rose 0.3% in the first nine months of 2026 and scooters fell 13%.
Honda, Hero MotoCorp, Bajaj Auto, TVS Motor, Yamaha Motor, Eicher Motors (Royal Enfield), Harley-Davidson, Piaggio

Revenue comes mainly from selling vehicles to dealers or distributors, plus parts, accessories, apparel and, at a few brands, retail finance. Harley-Davidson's motorcycle unit booked $964.0M of revenue in Q3 2026 and its finance arm $110.8M; Honda's motorcycle unit booked ¥2,272.5bn in April-September.

Customers are individual riders served through independent dealers, with fleets and ride-hailing a smaller part. In India, SIAM's director general linked demand to easier credit and replacement purchases in rural and urban areas. At Harley, dealers have been asking for more bikes after a 26% inventory cut.

Materials and components are by far the largest cost. At Bajaj Auto's standalone business, raw materials and components were Rs 13,227.93 crore of Rs 15,965.28 crore total expenses, about 83% on our calculation. Harley's motorcycle gross margin was 28.1% in Q3 2026.

Pricing power comes from brand and segment, not volume. Eicher's Royal Enfield earned a 23.7% EBITDA margin and Harley said its realization of list price was at a two-year high, while commuter-focused Hero earned 13.39%. Commuter buyers compare on price and fuel economy.

Main assets are factories, tooling and brands; liabilities are mostly working capital and, for finance arms, borrowings. Harley held $2.08B of cash against combined debt of about $2.34B, including its finance business. Bajaj Auto reported surplus cash of Rs 15,500 crore and Piaggio net debt of EUR 469.7M.

Moderately capital-intensive. Assembly and engine plants and model development need steady investment, but less than car making. Harley guides 2026 capital investment of $140M-$165M on over $3B of nine-month motorcycle revenue, and Piaggio invested EUR 76.8M in nine months.

A third-party estimate puts the global motorcycle and scooter market at USD 154.5 billion in 2025, growing at 7.6% a year to 2035. This is a market-research marketing estimate and definitions differ widely, so we treat it as low-confidence. Honda alone sold 11.9M motorcycles in April-September 2026.

The segments are commuters, scooters, premium and mid-size bikes, heavyweight cruisers and tourers, and off-road. In India's October 2026 dispatches, motorcycles were 1,423,118 units, scooters 1,096,756 and mopeds 57,936. In the US, on-highway bikes were 61% of motorcycle sales, led by cruisers, up 8%.

Makers sit between metal, component and electronics suppliers and a dealer network, with finance providers beside them. Raw materials were a roughly one-point drag on Harley's Q3 gross margin, and Bajaj Auto's component costs are most of its expenses. Dealers are the customer interface and carry inventory.

The industry has moved from regional champions toward global platforms and partnerships. KTM's parent is now Bajaj Mobility AG, and its first-half 2026 sales of 147,572 motorcycles included 58,568 sold in India by Bajaj Auto. Electric models are scaling in India, with TVS electric sales of 186,186 in Jul-Sep while Harley's LiveWire faces going-concern doubt.

Sales are concentrated in Asia, which the estimate puts at about 74% of market value. India alone shipped 2,577,810 two-wheelers in October 2026. Europe's five largest markets registered 636,490 motorcycles in the first half, and Harley sold 25,603 bikes in North America in Q3.

Dozens of makers compete, but few have scale. One estimate says the top five, Honda, Hero MotoCorp, Yamaha, TVS and Bajaj Auto, hold 52.5% of global revenue. Below them sit Eicher, KTM, Triumph, Harley-Davidson and Piaggio.

Honda leads: the same estimate gives it over 28.7% of 2025 revenue, and it sold 11.9M motorcycles in six months. By quarterly volume, Hero shipped 18.68 lakh units, TVS 19.19 lakh two- and three-wheelers and Bajaj Auto 1.28M two-wheelers.

Concentrated at the top globally but local in practice: Indian volume is dominated by Indian makers and Honda, while US premium rests on a few brands and Europe is split among Japanese, Italian, Austrian and British names. KTM, Husqvarna and GasGas sold 89,004 bikes outside India in H1 2026; Piaggio sold 273,600 two-wheelers in nine months.

Barriers are brand, dealer reach, service networks and scale in engines and sourcing. In our view they are high in commuter bikes and lower in niches; yet even a funded electric entrant, LiveWire, has not reached viability and now carries going-concern doubt, which shows how hard it is to break in.

Scale matters. Honda's motorcycle unit earned about 19% on our calculation from reported figures, while Harley's motorcycle unit earned 4.6% on 33,616 shipped bikes in the quarter, and KTM's owner posted a 5.4% EBITDA margin in H1 while recovering volume.

Both. Commuter bikes are close to commodities that compete on price and fuel economy, with Hero at 13.39% EBITDA margin. Premium and heritage brands are differentiated: Eicher at 23.7% and Piaggio at 16.9%.

Buyers are many and small, so individual customers have little leverage, but dealers do: Harley has been correcting a dealer overstock. Suppliers gain leverage when commodities spike; Hero avoided precise guidance because of daily commodity volatility and Yamaha cited Middle East-related procurement costs.

Revenue growth depends on volume, mix, price and exports. Bajaj Auto's export two-wheeler billings rose 43.2% while domestic sales rose 1.8%, and Royal Enfield volume rose 15.2%. In the US, Harley's shipments fell 8% even as retail rose.

Margins depend on mix, scale and input costs. TVS lifted EBITDA margin 30 basis points to 13%; Hero's fell to 13.39% against a 14-16% medium-term target as commodities rose. Harley is targeting $150M of fixed-cost savings.

Key costs are raw materials and components, labour, freight and tariffs. Raw materials cost Harley about one point of gross margin in Q3; Eicher's product-related costs rose to 58.0% of revenue from 56.3% in a grouping calculated by the source.

Rates matter because most bikes are financed. India's industry body linked recent demand to easier credit. Harley carries finance receivables of about $2.2B held for investment, so credit conditions affect it twice, on demand and on its own lending book. This is our read; we found no sourced rate sensitivity.

Premium and leisure bikes respond to consumer confidence and employment, while commuter bikes track rural income and fuel prices. The US market was flat in 2026, with motorcycles up 0.3% and scooters down 13%. Currency also matters: Yamaha's results were translated at 159 yen to the dollar.

A mix. Asian commuter demand is closer to secular growth, with Indian two-wheeler dispatches up 16.1% in October. Developed-market leisure riding is cyclical but has recovered: European registrations are about 27% above 2019.

Growth is uneven. In Jul-Sep 2026 revenue rose 34% at Bajaj Auto standalone, 44% at TVS, 21% at Hero and 20.3% at Eicher, while Harley's motorcycle revenue fell 10% and Piaggio's nine-month revenue rose 2.7%.

No motorcycle-only dataset was available. Damodaran's US Auto & Truck group (33 firms) shows a 10.41% gross and 2.32% pre-tax operating margin and the Recreation group (49 firms) 39.79% and 9.69%, as of January 2026. Company margins run higher at the best makers: Honda about 19%, Piaggio 16.9% EBITDA.

Damodaran's January 2026 data show return on equity of 3.16% for Auto & Truck and -12.76% for Recreation; we did not find a motorcycle-specific ROIC. Leading Indian makers look far better: Bajaj Auto's standalone pre-tax profit was Rs 4,457.49 crore on Rs 20,003.43 crore of revenue, about 22% on our calculation.

Leverage differs by maker. Damodaran's book debt-to-capital is 60.31% for Auto & Truck and 72.01% for Recreation, but 16.44% and 38.99% at market value. Bajaj Auto held Rs 15,500 crore of surplus cash, while Piaggio's net debt was EUR 469.7M.

Free cash flow is solid at disciplined makers. Harley generated $275.9M of operating cash flow and spent $64.4M on capital in nine months, so about $211.5M by our calculation. Bajaj Mobility's free cash flow was EUR -22.1M in H1 while recovering.

Capital spending is moderate. Harley guides $140M-$165M for 2026 and Piaggio spent EUR 76.8M in nine months, down 25%. Spending climbs with electric development and capacity additions, which is where weaker makers have struggled.

Multiples are hard to read. Damodaran's January 2026 forward P/E is 49.04x for Auto & Truck and 38.02x for Recreation, inflated by depressed earnings. FactSet's Consumer Discretionary sector was 24.3x on 5 Nov 2026 against 17.7x for the S&P 500. No motorcycle-specific multiple was publicly available.

Tariffs are the clearest rule risk: Harley now expects gross 2026 tariff costs of $105M-$120M and expects recoveries of a similar amount, and Yamaha says US tariffs weighed on profit. We did not source details of emissions or safety rules, which also shape product plans.

Electrification is the main technology risk. Indian electric scooter volumes are scaling, with TVS at 186,186 units and Bajaj Auto's electric two- and three-wheelers near 200,000, while LiveWire has doubts about its going concern. We found no sourced evidence that AI changes the economics soon; connected features are a cost, not yet a revenue line.

Demographics cut both ways. US cruisers rose 8% in 2026, ending a decline that began in 2021, but a younger rider base is what many leisure brands need. We did not find sourced rider-age data, so this remains our judgment.

Buying habits are shifting at the low end. US scooter sales fell 13%, with e-bikes possibly taking some of that market, while Indian scooters grew 31.6% in October. Premium buyers are moving toward adventure and mid-size models.
Competition is arriving from Asia. Bajaj Auto's exports rose 43.2%, and a Bajaj-owned KTM sold 147,572 motorcycles globally in H1 2026, up 81%.

Supply chains and geopolitics matter through costs: Yamaha cited Middle East-related procurement costs, Hero cited daily commodity volatility and Piaggio gave no full-year forecast, saying it depends on geopolitical and economic stability.

Substitutes include cars, public transport, e-bikes and ride-hailing. The MIC notes e-bikes may be taking part of the scooter market. In emerging markets, rising incomes can lead buyers to move up to small cars, though we found no sourced figure for that.
Premium demand in India is returning: Royal Enfield's above-350cc models returned to growth in October after falling 9% in H1.
Indian makers are scaling exports, with Bajaj Auto's up 43.2% in Jul-Sep and TVS exporting about five lakh vehicles.
European registrations are about 27% above 2019 and rose 16.8% in H1 2026.
Harley is aiming for $350M of motorcycle EBITDA in 2027 and $150M of fixed-cost savings.
Tariffs raised Harley's gross cost estimate for 2026 and Yamaha cited them as a drag.
Input-cost inflation is already compressing margins at Hero and Eicher.
The US market is flat and its scooters are falling.
LiveWire's going-concern doubt shows the risk in electric premium bikes.

Our read is that the next three to five years favour makers with scale and exposure to Asian premiumization, such as Honda, Bajaj, TVS and Royal Enfield, whose profits are growing in a market still widening. Developed-market leisure riding looks recovered rather than booming, and its earnings depend on tariff recovery and cost discipline, as Harley's reset shows. Electrification is the largest uncertainty: it is gaining share in India but unproven at the premium end. Margins will probably stay narrower than in 2024-25 if input costs persist. This is judgment, not a forecast.

The cycle is two-speed. In Asia and Europe, demand is expanding: India's October two-wheeler dispatches rose 16.1% year on year, and SIAM's director general pointed to easier credit and replacement buying. European registrations in the five largest markets rose 16.8% in the first half of 2026, although ACEM itself said the trend must hold through autumn.

The US is flat. Industry motorcycle sales excluding scooters rose 0.3% in the first nine months, while Harley's North American retail rose 9% in Q3 from a low base and a deliberately trimmed dealer inventory.

Currency and trade policy matter as much as the cycle. Honda's raised forecast reflected favourable exchange rates and efforts to reduce the US tariff impact, including moving production to the US; Yamaha translated results at 159 yen to the dollar and said US tariffs weighed on profit. We did not open central-bank rate material, so we do not give a sourced policy-rate path; our judgment is that lower borrowing costs help financed purchases, particularly in India.

Demand is structurally Asian and growing. One market-research estimate puts the 2025 global motorcycle and scooter market at USD 154.5 billion, with Asia Pacific at about 74% of value and a 7.6% annual growth forecast to 2035. We treat that as a rough guide because research houses define the market differently.

Growth is shifting toward scooters and premium bikes. In India's October 2026 data, scooters rose 31.6% while motorcycles rose 6.6% and exports rose 26.5%. Royal Enfield's smaller models and EVs grew 24% in April-September, while above-350cc sales fell 9% before returning to growth in October.

In developed markets demand is recovering from a post-pandemic lull. European registrations are about 27% above 2019. In the US, on-highway bikes rose 2% in the first nine months and cruisers 8%, reversing a decline since 2021, while off-highway bikes fell 4% and scooters 13%. Our view is that commuter demand is steady and income-driven, whereas leisure demand is cyclical and discretionary.

Rivalry is intense at the commuter end, where five makers hold an estimated 52.5% of global revenue and Honda leads with over 28.7%. Hero's 13.39% EBITDA margin shows how competitive commuter pricing is.

Barriers to entry are high in scale segments: dealer networks, service reach, engine engineering and brand take years to build. The threat of new entrants is therefore low outside electric niches, and LiveWire's going-concern doubt shows even a famous brand struggles. Supplier power is moderate and rises when commodity prices spike, as Hero and Yamaha noted.

Buyer power is low per customer, but dealers have leverage: Harley's inventory cut of 26% followed a period of overstock. The threat of substitutes comes from cars, e-bikes and scooters, with US scooters down 13% as e-bikes gain.

Moats are strongest at heritage and premium brands. Eicher's 23.7% EBITDA margin and Honda's roughly 19% operating margin in motorcycles on our calculation compare with Harley's 4.6%, suggesting that scale and mix matter more than nameplate alone.

Politics and trade are the dominant outside forces. Harley now expects 2026 gross tariff costs of about $105M-$120M, up from $75M-$90M, with recoveries offsetting most of it. Yamaha said US tariffs weighed on its profit, and Honda's forecast raise included work to reduce US tariff impact.

Economic and social factors are favourable in India, where credit access and replacement demand support volumes. Technological change is led by electrification: TVS sold 186,186 electric two-wheelers in the quarter, up 133%, and Bajaj Auto's electric scooters and three-wheelers were close to 200,000 units.

In the premium electric niche the picture is different: LiveWire's 2026 nine-month revenue was $22.1M against a $53.4M operating loss. Environmental and legal factors, such as emission standards and battery rules in Europe and India, shape product plans, but we did not open the regulations themselves, so we leave them out of the numbers. Our view is that electrification will arrive first in Indian urban commuting, not in Western leisure riding.

Margins sort the industry. Honda's motorcycle unit earned ¥439.1bn on ¥2,272.5bn of revenue, about 19% on our calculation. Yamaha's Land Mobility segment earned ¥170.0bn on ¥1,472.1bn, about 11.5% on our calculation. Piaggio's nine-month EBITDA margin was 16.9%.

In India, Eicher's EBITDA margin was 23.7%, TVS's 13% and Hero's 13.39%. At Harley, motorcycle operating margin was 4.6% and year-to-date operating income was $135.6M on $3,123.8M of revenue. Damodaran's US Auto & Truck group has a pre-tax operating margin of 2.32% and Recreation 9.69%, as of January 2026, and neither is motorcycle-specific.

Operating leverage is high: fixed plant and development costs mean volume swings move profit sharply, as Harley's 10% revenue fall cut operating income 18%. Return on equity for Auto & Truck was 3.16% and for Recreation -12.76%; free cash flow at Harley was about $211.5M in nine months by our calculation. We did not find motorcycle-specific ROIC.

Guidance is mixed. Harley raised 2026 motorcycle operating income guidance to $25M-$55M, with 135,500-139,000 units, and withdrew LiveWire guidance. Yamaha kept its full-year forecast unchanged at ¥260bn operating profit after earning ¥235.2bn in nine months, and Honda raised its group operating profit forecast to ¥780bn from ¥650bn.

Hero expects its EBITDA margin to recover to 14-16% as commodities stabilize and plans three to four premium launches by March. Piaggio gave no full-year forecast. Harley restated a $350M motorcycle EBITDA goal for 2027 and $150M of cost savings.

We found no public consensus estimates or revision data for the sub-industry, so we cannot say how guidance compares with the Street. Our view is that Asian earnings have the stronger momentum, since volumes and exports are growing, but margin risk from input costs is real. Harley's recovery depends on cost cuts and tariff recovery rather than volume, so it carries more execution risk. Harley's Q3 EPS of $0.40 compares with $3.10 a year earlier, a gap its release ties largely to a finance-arm sale in 2025.

We found no publicly available forward multiple for the motorcycle sub-industry itself. The nearest benchmarks are broad. FactSet put the Consumer Discretionary sector at 24.3x forward earnings on 5 November 2026, the highest of any sector, against 17.7x for the S&P 500 and a 10-year average of 19.1x. That sector is dominated by other businesses, so it says little about motorcycles.

Damodaran's January 2026 US data give Auto & Truck a forward P/E of 49.04x and Recreation 38.02x, with a PEG ratio of 11.71 and 1.83. Those multiples are inflated by depressed earnings in small samples, so we would not read them as a price signal.

Our view is that the market likely prices Asian leaders for sustained growth and premium Western brands for recovery, but we can not support this with sourced multiples. Harley's nine-month diluted EPS of $1.38 against $5.03 a year earlier shows how far earnings have to rebuild; its 2027 targets of $350M of motorcycle EBITDA imply a recovery, and whether it is priced in depends on a price we did not source.

We did not find sourced ETF flow, short-interest or price-momentum data for the sub-industry, and there is no dedicated motorcycle ETF that we could verify, so we do not report positioning figures rather than estimate them.

What we can say from company actions: Harley returned $110M to shareholders in Q3, $91M of it buybacks, and raised its quarterly dividend to $0.1875 from $0.18. Yamaha raised its year-end dividend by 10 yen to 35 yen, and the Indian leaders hold large cash balances, with Bajaj Auto at Rs 15,500 crore.

At sector level, FactSet reported that Consumer Discretionary companies had the lowest share beating revenue estimates, at 54%, and that the sector's Q3 net profit margin was 10.0% against 10.2% a year earlier. Our read is that the leaders are in Asia, where volumes are growing, while US and European riding demand looks steady rather than accelerating.

Textiles is a slow-growing, price-taking corner of consumer discretionary, and the results are splitting by region and fibre. World textile and garment exports reached $914B in 2025, still 4.2% below the 2022 peak, and synthetics now supply 71.7% of fibre demand. US apparel import value fell about 8% in the first half of 2026 after effective duty rates peaked near 34%. Toray's fibres segment lifted core operating income 18.3% in the June quarter, while US mill Culp lost $10.2M in fiscal 2026 and Unifi's quarterly adjusted EBITDA swung to $8.2M from -$4.1M. We found no sourced consensus or multiple for the sub-industry; the Consumer Discretionary sector trades at 24.2x forward earnings.

Textile companies turn fibres into yarn, fabric and finished materials. They sell mainly to other manufacturers, not to shoppers: garment makers, furniture and mattress makers, car makers and industrial buyers. They earn money on volume and a thin spread over raw material costs, so cost, scale and customer relationships matter more than brands. GICS puts fabric and yarn producers here, while branded apparel, footwear and luxury goods sit in separate sub-industries. Toray in Japan, Indorama in Thailand and the US mills Unifi and Culp show the range.

Synthetic yarn and fibre: Polyester and nylon filament and staple made from petrochemicals, used in clothing, carpets, car interiors and industrial goods. It is the largest fibre family and is sold largely on price. e.g. Unifi REPREVE recycled polyester, Toray nylon and polyester, Indorama Ventures fibres
Woven and knit fabric: Yarn made into cloth for apparel, home textiles and industrial use. Mills sell to garment makers who cut and sew it. e.g. Toray apparel fabrics, Asian and Turkish fabric mills
Upholstery fabric: Decorative and performance fabric sold to furniture makers. Demand follows housing turnover and furniture orders. e.g. Culp upholstery fabrics
Mattress fabrics: Knit and woven covers and ticking sold to mattress makers. Orders follow bedding unit demand. e.g. Culp bedding fabrics

Industrial and automotive textiles: Airbag fabric, tyre cord, filters and nonwovens sold to industrial customers on specification, which gives somewhat steadier pricing than apparel. e.g. Toray industrial textiles, Indorama tyre cord
Recycled and sustainable fibres: Yarn made from recycled bottles or other waste, sold at a premium to brands with sustainability goals. e.g. Unifi REPREVE
Raw material spread: Polyester and nylon follow oil and chemical prices; cotton follows crop size. Producers earn a margin only when they can pass cost changes through to customers.
Utilisation and overcapacity: Heavy Chinese capacity pushes prices toward cost. When plants run below capacity, fixed costs spread over fewer units and margins compress.
Retail and inventory cycle: Brands and retailers order ahead, then pause to clear stock. Mill revenue swings more than shoppers' spending.
Trade policy: Tariffs change where garments are sewn and so where fabric is bought, shifting volume between regions and fibres.
Housing and durables demand: Upholstery and mattress fabric orders follow furniture and bedding sales, which follow housing turnover and credit costs.
Energy and labour cost: Spinning, dyeing and finishing use heat and power and, in many places, much labour, so cost position decides who survives a downturn.
Vertical integration: One company controls several steps, such as fibre, yarn and fabric. It can lower cost and control quality but ties up more capital.
Spread: The gap between the price of a product, such as polyester yarn, and the cost of its raw material. It is the main driver of profit for fibre makers.
Filament versus staple: Filament is a continuous strand; staple is short fibres spun together like cotton. They go to different fabrics and have separate price cycles.
MMF: Man-made fibre, the trade term for synthetics and cellulosics such as polyester, nylon and viscose, as opposed to natural fibres such as cotton.
Capacity utilisation: The share of a plant's capacity that is running. Costs are largely fixed, so small changes in utilisation swing margins a lot.
Cut-make-trim: The sewing stage where cut fabric becomes garments, mostly done in Asia. It sits downstream of the textile mill and sets where fabric demand comes from.
Rules of origin: Trade rules about where inputs must come from for a garment to enter duty-free. They explain why some US mills sell to Central American sewers.
Tariff and de minimis: Import duties raise the landed cost of goods; de minimis is the exemption for low-value parcels, which the US ended worldwide on 29 Aug 2025.
Inventory destocking: Customers work down stock instead of ordering, so mills see sales fall faster than end demand and then rebound.
Adjusted EBITDA: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and one-off items. Mills quote it, but it ignores the heavy capital spending needed to keep plants running.
US tariff policy keeps moving: the Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs on 20 Feb 2026 and a temporary 10% Section 122 surcharge replaced part of them.
Cotton is cheap against its recent past but not collapsing: the ICE December future settled at 78.67 cents per pound on 12 Nov 2026 and US mill demand was described as light.
Polyester overcapacity is the main profit threat for fibre makers: Indorama's Fibers EBITDA was flat at THB 924M in the third quarter of 2026.
Rates are not helping: the Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 with two members preferring a hike.
Small US mills are fragile: Culp had $8.3M cash and $19.1M of debt at 3 May 2026 and expects a roughly $7.0M IEEPA tariff refund.
Toray Industries, Indorama Ventures, Unifi, Culp

Revenue is mainly sales of yarn, fibre and fabric by weight or length to manufacturers. Toray's Fibers & Textiles segment earned ¥259.9B in the April to June 2026 quarter; Culp sells bedding and upholstery fabric, with bedding $116.6M of its $203.5M fiscal 2026 sales. Brands and services are small next to physical product.

Customers are other manufacturers: garment sewers, furniture and mattress makers, car makers and industrial buyers. A concentrated customer base gives them leverage. Unifi sells recycled yarn under its REPREVE name; in our understanding garment orders flow from retailers to sewers, who choose the mills.

The big costs are raw materials (petrochemicals for polyester and nylon, cotton for natural yarn), energy, labour and depreciation on plant. Toray said rising raw material prices tied to the Middle East hit both apparel and industrial uses in the June 2026 quarter. Culp's gross margin of 12.4% shows how little is left after materials and plant cost.

Pricing power is weak for commodity yarn and fabric because buyers compare price and many mills can supply. It is stronger where the product is specified, such as automotive and industrial textiles, or tied to a certified recycled content. Toray said it used price pass-through and cost cuts to offset higher raw materials, which is the usual defence.

Major assets are spinning, weaving, knitting and finishing plants, inventory and receivables. Major liabilities are bank debt and supplier credit. Culp held inventory of $47.5M against $8.3M of cash and $19.1M of debt at 3 May 2026; Unifi had debt principal of $92.4M.

The business is capital-intensive, especially fibre and spinning, where plants are costly and must run near full. Asset-light models exist for converters and sourcing agents. Damodaran's apparel sample shows capex at 133% of depreciation, but that group is mainly branded apparel; mills carry heavier fixed assets than that proxy.

The textile and garment trade was $914B of exports in 2025, up from about $560B in 2006, a 2.61% compound annual rate. Growth averaged only about 1% a year between 2011 and 2019. Total fibre demand was 119.8M tonnes in 2025.

Main segments are fibre (synthetic and natural), yarn, fabric, home and industrial textiles and, in trade data, garments. Knit garments were $289.1B or 31.6% of world textile exports and knit and woven garments nearly 60%. Synthetics took 71.7% of fibre demand and cotton 21.1%.

Mills sit in the middle of the chain: they buy fibre and chemicals from producers and sell fabric to sewers and brands. Cotton fibre is bought on futures-linked prices, while polyester follows oil chemicals. The ICE December cotton future settled at 78.67 cents per pound on 12 Nov 2026.

The industry has moved from developed economies to Asia. Between 2006 and 2025 the share of China, Bangladesh and Vietnam in world textile exports rose from 27.6% to 44.3%. Korea's exports fell from $40.8B to $7.9B and the US share fell from 4.05% to 2.59%.

Production and sales are concentrated in Asia. China exported $292.0B of textiles in 2025, Bangladesh $58.0B and Vietnam $55.0B, and the top 15 exporters held 77.6% of the total. The US remains the largest importer at $113.4B, though its share fell to 13.70%.

In our judgment there are thousands of significant competitors worldwide, from state-backed Chinese groups to family mills in India, Pakistan, Turkey and Bangladesh. Listed names are few: Toray, Indorama, Unifi and Culp are the ones we could source.

No sourced global market-share table for textile producers was available to us. By country, China held $292.0B of 2025 textile exports and the top three exporters held 44.3%. Toray and Indorama are large fibre makers, but we do not have a reliable share for either.

The industry is fragmented and, outside integrated majors, commoditised. The top 15 exporting economies hold 77.6% of trade, but within each country mills are numerous. Indorama said overcapacity hit hardest in its CPET and Fibers segments, which shows how supply drives results.

Barriers to entry are moderate: plants are costly, but know-how is widespread and Asian governments subsidise capacity. Bangladesh's rise from $9.9B to $58.0B of exports and Vietnam's from $6.5B to $55.0B show that new entrants can scale in two decades.

Economies of scale matter in fibre and spinning, where large integrated plants have lower unit cost, and in dyeing, where large mills run at higher utilisation. Indorama is large and integrated; small US mills such as Culp, at $203.5M of sales, have limited scale.

Most output is commoditised, with differentiation in technical, recycled and performance fabrics. Unifi's REPREVE recycled yarn is sold as a branded ingredient, and Toray cites specified industrial uses. Even so, price remains the main selection criterion for apparel fabrics.

Customers hold more bargaining power: brands and sewers can shift orders across countries within a season. Suppliers of oil, chemicals and cotton hold power in short supply. ICAC's data on US imports show buyers moved away from China, with its share down 11.2 points in man-made-fibre apparel in 2025 against the 2020-2024 average.

Revenue growth is driven by global apparel and home demand, fibre prices passed through to customers, share shifts between countries and, in specialty textiles, volumes of cars and industrial goods. Toray's June 2026 quarter revenue rose 8.3%, helped by price pass-through and a gradual automotive recovery.

Operating margins depend on the spread over raw materials, plant utilisation, energy and labour cost, and mix. Unifi's gross margin moved from -0.8% to 9.9% in a year as cost actions and volume recovered. Culp's bedding margin improved to 9.2% from 7.0%.

Key cost variables are oil-based chemicals, cotton, energy and labour. US cotton spot averaged 75.07 cents per pound in the week to 12 Nov 2026, up from 59.88 cents a year earlier, which is a headwind unless mills can pass it on.

Rate sensitivity is high through financing and demand: mills carry debt, and furniture and bedding orders depend on housing and credit. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026 with two dissenters preferring a hike. Unifi cut debt principal by $15.6M in fiscal 2026.

Textiles respond to inflation by squeezing buyers, to unemployment by lowering apparel and furniture spending, and to GDP through trade volumes. The WTO projects world merchandise trade volume growth of 1.9% in 2026 after 4.6% in 2025. Commodity prices matter most through oil and cotton.

The industry is cyclical and has weak secular growth; the growth is in synthetics and in Asian production rather than in the sector as a whole. Between 2006 and 2025, about 92% of the rise in fibre demand came from synthetics while cotton demand was broadly flat. We think of it as a low-growth cyclical industry.

Revenue growth is slow and uneven. World textile exports grew at 2.61% a year over 2006-2025 and fell 7.7% in 2023. Culp's sales fell 4.6% to $203.5M in fiscal 2026; Toray's fibres revenue grew 8.3% in the June 2026 quarter. Earnings are volatile and often negative for small mills.

Margins are thin for mills against brands. Culp's fiscal 2026 gross margin was 12.4% with an operating loss of $7.2M; Unifi's quarterly gross margin was 9.9%. Damodaran's apparel group shows a 56.88% gross margin and 3.85% net margin, but that sample is mainly brands and not mills.

Returns are low except for brands. Damodaran's January 2026 table gives apparel a 15.78% return on capital and 8.92% after-tax operating margin. Culp lost money and Unifi had a net loss of $1.2M in its latest quarter, so mills sit well below that proxy. We found no sourced ROE for the sub-industry.

Leverage is moderate on average but heavy for weak mills. Damodaran's apparel group has book debt to capital of 56.25% and debt to EBITDA of 3.47. Unifi's net debt was about $67.4M, and Culp's net debt was about $10.9M with $24.2M of liquidity.

Free cash flow is lumpy and tied to inventory. Unifi's operating cash flow was $26.5M in fiscal 2026 versus -$21.3M a year earlier. Culp's operating cash flow was -$9.4M and free cash flow about -$10.0M before adjustments. Cash generation depends on working capital released in downturns.

Capex needs are high relative to earnings for fibre and spinning but low in maintenance mode. Unifi cut capex to $5M from $10.5M, and Culp spent just $596K. Damodaran's apparel sample has capex at 133.48% of depreciation, and the weak mills are investing below that.

Valuation multiples are moderate. Damodaran's apparel group trades at 10.30x EV/EBITDA for positive-EBITDA firms and a 24.89x forward P/E in January 2026. Multiples for mills alone were not available; the Consumer Discretionary sector forward P/E is 24.2x.

Regulation and trade policy are the largest risk. US effective duties on apparel rose from 16% in January 2025 to about 34% at the peak, and the Supreme Court ended the IEEPA basis on 20 Feb 2026. Culp expects a $7.0M refund, which shows how much policy moves results.

Technology disruption is incremental: automation, digital printing and recycling technology change costs. AI has little direct effect. Recycled fibre is a growth niche, but we found no sourced estimate of its market size, so we treat it as an opportunity for specialists such as Unifi.

Demographic change is modest. Population growth supports volume, but cotton per capita use fell from 3.46 kg to 3.09 kg while non-cotton fibre use rose from 1.60 kg to 11.53 kg. Ageing markets such as the US, Japan and Europe have lost share of imports.

Changing consumer behaviour hurts demand: US apparel imports fell 8.5% in cotton-dominant and 8.2% in man-made-fibre-dominant categories in January to June 2026. Shoppers trading down, buying second-hand and buying online push brands to cut costs and fabric orders.

New competitors keep arriving: Bangladesh and Vietnam took exports to $58.0B and $55.0B and Poland went from $3.9B to $21.4B. Chinese fibre overcapacity is a persistent threat; Indorama blamed Chinese tyre-cord overcapacity for margin pressure.

Geopolitics and supply chain risks include tariffs, Middle East conflict that raised raw material prices for Toray, and shipping disruption. WTO's baseline for 2026 world merchandise trade growth is only 1.9% and could fall to 1.4% if energy prices stay high.

Substitutes are other fibres: synthetics have taken most of the growth from cotton, and cotton share of fibre demand fell from 68.3% in 1960 to 21.1% in 2025. Within synthetics, recycled and bio-based fibres substitute for virgin polyester.
Recycled and traceable fibres could earn premiums as brands meet sustainability targets, as with Unifi's REPREVE.
Sourcing diversification away from China is creating demand in Vietnam, Bangladesh, India and nearshore regions, with China's share of US man-made-fibre apparel imports down 13.1 points by mid-2026.
Automotive and industrial textile demand is recovering gradually, which supports specified, higher-margin fabrics.
Tariff refunds and lower debt can repair small US mills' balance sheets, as Culp's roughly $7.0M refund and Unifi's planned $60M property sale show.
Chinese and Asian polyester overcapacity can hold spreads near zero for years.
Tariffs and trade rules can change again, as the 2026 court ruling and temporary replacement surcharge show.
Weak consumer demand for apparel and furniture could extend the 2026 import decline.
Higher oil and energy prices raise raw material costs faster than mills can pass them on.

Over the next three to five years we expect textiles to stay a low-growth, cyclical business in which scale and cost position decide results. Trade data show the industry's centre of gravity moving to Asia and fibre demand shifting to synthetics, so Western mills must differentiate on recycled, technical or nearshore products or shrink. Tariff policy has become a larger swing factor than demand. Our read is that integrated groups with industrial exposure, such as Toray, are better placed than small single-market mills, whose recent results show recovery from a low base. A rate path that eases would help housing-linked fabrics, but the Fed has not yet turned that way.

Textiles sits late in a slow cycle. The WTO estimates world merchandise trade volume grew 4.6% in 2025 and forecasts only 1.9% in 2026, or 1.4% if oil and gas prices stay high. ICAC describes the garment industry as slower-growing, more uncertain and more geographically differentiated, with demand shaped by tariffs and industrial policy as much as by growth.

Monetary policy is not a tailwind. The Fed held the federal funds range at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 Oct 2026, called inflation elevated, and had two members who wanted a quarter-point increase. For textile makers that means expensive working capital and housing-linked demand for upholstery and bedding that is not improving quickly.

Currency and input costs matter. Toray said Middle East developments raised raw material prices in the June 2026 quarter, though it passed some of this through. The US seven-market cotton spot average was 75.07 cents per pound in the week to 6 Nov 2026, against 59.88 cents a year earlier. Our read is that mills have a cost problem and a demand problem at once.

The addressable market is large but growing slowly. World textile and garment exports were $914B in 2025, a 2.61% compound annual rise since 2006, with growth near 1% a year between 2011 and 2019. Total fibre demand reached 119.8M tonnes in 2025, and about 92% of the increase since 2006 came from synthetics.

Demand is cyclical. Exports fell 14.2% in the financial crisis, jumped to a record $954B in 2022 and fell 7.7% in 2023. The US, the largest importer at $113.4B, has slipped to 13.70% of world textile imports. In 2026 US apparel imports were $32.7B in the first half, with both cotton and man-made-fibre categories down by more than 8%.

Structural drivers are population growth, rising incomes in Asia and Africa, and the substitution of synthetics for cotton. Per capita cotton use fell from 3.46 kg to 3.09 kg while non-cotton fibre use rose from 1.60 kg to 11.53 kg. Demographics help volumes modestly, but our view is that demand for fabric will grow no faster than world output and that most of the gain will go to Asian producers.
